title: Auditing Emergent LLM-Agent Collaboration through Cooperation-Obligation Coupling
summary: LLM-agent systems can solve complex tasks through dynamic self-organization and emergent cooperation. Auditing this process is essential because plausible intermediate or final outputs can conceal incomplete or unsupported work and poorly allocated responsibility, ultimately compromising response quality. While existing approaches may record messages, tool calls, provenance, or task dependencies, an auditability gap exists as they do not jointly represent what work remains, who is responsible for it, and what evidence justifies each work-state transition. We address this auditability gap by proposing \emph{Integrated Cooperation-Obligation REpresentation} (iCORE). It creates a unified encoding $X=(G,Q,Π)$ integrating observable interactions as a cooperation graph $G$, evolving work and assignments as an obligation graph $Q$, and the audit map $Π$ linking them with verifiable properties and evidence. This iCORE representation enables the auditor to certify two complementary properties: {Work soundness}, where every active decision-relevant work assertion must have a finite justification through $G$ and $Π$; and {Agent-assignment stability}, which requires that no feasible alternative agent improve the declared contribution value for an evaluated obligation by more than $ε$. We establish local-to-global soundness and assignment-regret guarantees and a performance bound under stated conditions. iCORE is an instrumentation layer over workflows. Numerical results show that the full coupled state exactly reconstructs soundness and assignment defects in two execution modes and that, relative to passive full-state observation, iCORE-Audit yields absolute trajectory-quality improvements of $11.5\%$ and $26.4\%$ in controlled and real-LLM execution, respectively, with corresponding absolute terminal-performance improvements of $15.1\%$ and $31.0\%$.

AI.tldr: iCORE is a unified representation framework for auditing LLM-agent collaboration that tracks what work remains, who's responsible, and what evidence justifies each work-state transition, enabling verification of work soundness and agent-assignment stability.
AI.motivation: LLM-agent systems can produce plausible outputs while hiding incomplete work, poor allocation of responsibility, and unsupported reasoning, compromising response quality. Existing approaches don't jointly represent what work remains, who is responsible, and what evidence justifies work-state transitions, creating an auditability gap.
AI.method: Proposed Integrated Cooperation-Obligation REpresentation (iCORE) creates a unified encoding X=(G,Q,Π) with three components: cooperation graph G (observable interactions), obligation graph Q (evolving work and assignments), and audit map Π (linking them with verifiable properties and evidence). This enables certification of work soundness and agent-assignment stability.
AI.result: iCORE exactly reconstructs soundness and assignment defects in two execution modes. Compared to passive full-state observation, iCORE-Audit yields absolute trajectory-quality improvements of 11.5% (controlled) and 26.4% (real-LLM), with terminal-performance improvements of 15.1% and 31.0% respectively.
AI.conclusion: iCORE effectively addresses the auditability gap in LLM-agent systems by providing a unified framework that enables verification of work soundness and assignment stability, significantly improving system performance and auditability without requiring full state observation.

title: Stop Shipping AI Agents on Faith: Capability Is Not Production Readiness
summary: AI agents are moving into production workflows where they retrieve information, call tools, maintain state, and act on behalf of users or organizations, but many release decisions still rely on capability signals, demos, or behavioral tests that do not show whether an agent is ready to operate under production constraints. Capability is therefore not production readiness. This paper introduces the ProofAgent Index (PAI), a governance readiness index for AI agents. PAI combines four dimensions of deployment evidence: Evaluation, Context, Compliance, and Governance. Evaluation measures observed behavior, Context measures the operating environment that shapes that behavior, Compliance measures alignment with applicable rules and controls, and Governance measures whether the organization can authorize, monitor, audit, and control the agent during operation. PAI is implemented inside ProofAgent Harness, an open source infrastructure for auditable AI agent evaluation and governance. Validation across two heavily regulated domains, healthcare and finance, shows that PAI carries held out readiness signal and separates higher risk from lower risk configurations. The results show that context engineering strongly changes reliability, capability improves behavior but does not determine readiness, and governance evidence must remain visible rather than averaged away. PAI reframes agent release from a faith based deployment decision into an auditable readiness decision.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ProofAgent Index (PAI), a governance readiness index for AI agents that combines evaluation, context, compliance, and governance dimensions to determine production readiness, shifting agent release decisions from faith-based to auditable evidence-based decisions.
AI.motivation: Current AI agent deployment decisions rely on inadequate signals like capability demonstrations or behavioral tests that don't reflect real production constraints, creating a gap between capability and actual production readiness in critical domains like healthcare and finance.
AI.method: Developed the ProofAgent Index (PAI) framework with four dimensions: Evaluation (observed behavior), Context (operating environment), Compliance (alignment with rules/controls), and Governance (organizational authorization/monitoring/control capabilities). Implemented PAI within the open-source ProofAgent Harness infrastructure for auditable evaluation and governance, then validated it across heavily regulated healthcare and finance domains.
AI.result: PAI successfully carries held-out readiness signal and separates higher-risk from lower-risk configurations. Key findings: context engineering significantly impacts reliability, capability improves behavior but doesn't determine readiness, and governance evidence must remain visible rather than being averaged away in assessments.
AI.conclusion: The ProofAgent Index reframes AI agent release from faith-based deployment decisions into auditable readiness decisions by providing a comprehensive governance readiness framework that addresses the critical gap between agent capability and production readiness under real-world constraints.

title: Scaling LLM-Driven Multi-Agent Systems: Design Principles and Architectural Scalability Analysis
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems have the potential to enable collective intelligence and scale toward solving highly complex tasks through coordinated ensembles of specialized agents. However, despite their theoretical potential, the architectural design space remains largely non-systematized and lacks broadly established design principles. Furthermore, the scalability characteristics of such systems are only partially understood so far. This paper makes two contributions. We first distill four design principles for scalable MAS architectures from a structured analysis of prior work: simplicity, elastic feedback, sequential workflows with optional loops, and summary-based communication. We operationalize these principles in a reference architecture whose topology is formalized as a constrained directed workflow graph, and we evaluate four configurations of increasing complexity on a standardized benchmark of terminal-based system engineering tasks using two LLMs of differing capability. Our findings show that scaling yields measurable accuracy improvements with approximately linear cost growth, but only when the underlying LLM exceeds a minimum capability threshold. Performance peaks at intermediate complexity, then degrades due to timeouts and evaluation limitations. In addition, persistent consistency issues emerge as a central challenge across all scaling levels. These results provide concrete design guidance for practitioners and highlight consistency and evaluation standardization as key targets for future research.

AI.tldr: LLM-based multi-agent systems need systematic design principles; paper proposes 4 scalable architecture principles and shows scaling yields benefits only with capable LLMs, but faces consistency issues.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems have potential for collective intelligence but lack systematic architectural design principles and understanding of scalability characteristics.
AI.method: 1. Distilled 4 design principles from prior work analysis: simplicity, elastic feedback, sequential workflows with optional loops, summary-based communication. 2. Operationalized principles in a reference architecture formalized as constrained directed workflow graph. 3. Evaluated 4 configurations of increasing complexity on terminal-based system engineering benchmark using two LLMs of different capabilities.
AI.result: Scaling yields measurable accuracy improvements with approximately linear cost growth, but only when LLM exceeds minimum capability threshold. Performance peaks at intermediate complexity then degrades due to timeouts and evaluation limitations. Persistent consistency issues emerged as central challenge across all scaling levels.
AI.conclusion: Provides concrete design guidance for practitioners, highlighting consistency and evaluation standardization as key targets for future research in LLM-based multi-agent systems.

title: Argonaut: Interactive Visual Exploration for Distributed Optimization
comment: 6 pages, 8 figures. Accepted in ACSOS 2026 [artifacts track]
summary: Distributed discrete-choice optimization in decentralized settings is often hard to explore and navigate: disentangling what other agents choose, how their choices are interdependent, and how they collectively reach a global objective quickly becomes intractable as the system scales. The major limitation is observability of the search process. Existing methods are largely centralized and offer limited support, visualizing only the final solution or providing algorithm backends over a fixed dataset, so how a solution is reached stays a black box. We present Argonaut, a lightweight, containerized optimization dashboard that enables interactive, visual exploration of the entire search process for multi-agent discrete-choice optimization in decentralized settings. Users upload datasets, construct agents and options, modify the decision space and its parameters on the fly, and run multiple algorithm backends to inspect how each configuration shapes local agent decisions and the resulting global objective. By uniting system construction, optimization, and analysis in one interactive loop, the first of its kind, Argonaut makes distributed discrete-choice optimization a human-in-the-loop process rather than a one-shot, black-box computation. We evaluate Argonaut on real-world household-electricity, shared-mobility, and sensor-data-exchange datasets scaling to 5600 agents and up to 1M solutions under brute force. Built on a Node.js interface with extensible Java and Python optimization backends, it maintains a typical runtime of 200 agents over 100 decision attributes in under 30 seconds.

AI.tldr: Argonaut is an interactive visualization dashboard for distributed discrete-choice optimization that makes the search process transparent and human-in-the-loop, scaling to thousands of agents while maintaining reasonable runtime performance.
AI.motivation: Distributed discrete-choice optimization in decentralized settings becomes intractable as systems scale, with limited observability of the search process. Existing methods are centralized, showing only final solutions or providing algorithm backends over fixed datasets, making the solution process a black box that's hard to explore and navigate.
AI.method: Argonaut is a lightweight, containerized optimization dashboard that enables interactive visual exploration of the entire search process. Users upload datasets, construct agents and options, modify decision spaces and parameters on the fly, and run multiple algorithm backends to inspect how configurations shape local agent decisions and global objectives.
AI.result: The system was evaluated on real-world datasets (household-electricity, shared-mobility, sensor-data-exchange) scaling to 5600 agents and up to 1M solutions under brute force. Built on Node.js with extensible Java/Python backends, it maintains runtime of 200 agents over 100 decision attributes in under 30 seconds.
AI.conclusion: Argonaut makes distributed discrete-choice optimization a human-in-the-loop process rather than a one-shot black-box computation, unifying system construction, optimization, and analysis in an interactive loop - the first system of its kind to provide such transparency and flexibility.

title: Recursive transformers for semiconductor thermo-mechanical reliability
summary: Transformer-based surrogate models are increasingly used to replace expensive first-principles simulation in engineering design. But conventional transformer architectures are often over parameterized for the small, low-dimensional datasets typical of engineering design spaces, where large simulation data is expensive to generate. Under these conditions, excess parameter capacity leads to overfitting rather than improved accuracy, while also incurring unnecessary memory and compute overhead. This motivates a shift towards architectures that focus on additional compute rather than additional learnable parameters. This paper presents a hardware-aware evaluation of three recursive transformer paradigms for surrogate thermo-mechanical analysis of advanced packages: a)Tiny Recursive Model, b) our proposed Depth Recursive transformer, c) and a simple recursive transformer. We systematically compare their predictive performance (Recall, Mean Reciprocal Rank), parameter count, computational complexity (FLOPs), providing practical design guidelines for selecting recursive transformer architectures under resource-constrained scenarios. We validate this principle on two low-dimensional engineering prediction tasks: 1) thermo-mechanical reliability analysis of advanced semiconductor packages, where stress and warpage from thermal cycling must be evaluated repeatedly across a design-of-experiments sweep under costly finite element analysis (FEA). 2) Laplace PDE iterative numerical solver for capacitance field. Overall, recursive weight-sharing transformers provide an effective and generalizable trade-off between prediction accuracy, parameter efficiency, and computational cost for small data engineering surrogate modeling.

AI.tldr: Recursive weight-sharing transformers provide parameter-efficient, computationally effective surrogate models for small engineering datasets, outperforming conventional over-parameterized transformers in resource-constrained scenarios.
AI.motivation: Conventional transformer architectures are over-parameterized for small, low-dimensional engineering datasets typical of design spaces, leading to overfitting, unnecessary memory/compute overhead, and poor performance when simulation data is expensive to generate.
AI.method: Proposes hardware-aware evaluation of three recursive transformer paradigms: 1) Tiny Recursive Model, 2) Depth Recursive transformer (proposed), 3) Simple recursive transformer. Compares predictive performance (Recall, Mean Reciprocal Rank), parameter count, and computational complexity (FLOPs) for resource-constrained scenarios.
AI.result: Recursive weight-sharing transformers provide effective trade-off between prediction accuracy, parameter efficiency, and computational cost for small-data engineering surrogate modeling, validated on thermo-mechanical reliability analysis of semiconductor packages and Laplace PDE iterative numerical solver tasks.
AI.conclusion: For small-data engineering surrogate modeling, architectures focusing on additional compute rather than additional learnable parameters (via recursive weight-sharing) offer better performance and efficiency than conventional over-parameterized transformers in resource-constrained scenarios.

title: Multi-Head Attention Residuals
summary: Transformers propagate information across depth through a single additive residual stream: every sublayer reads only the most recent state. Attention residuals relax this by letting each sublayer attend, through a learned softmax. However, that read uses a single query shared across the entire width, so every feature subspace must read the depth history through one distribution. The cost of this forced compromise grows with how much the subspaces disagree about which layers to read, and disagreement grows with model width. We introduce Multi-Head Attention Residuals (MHAR): the routing query is reshaped into H per-subspace heads, each with its own softmax over the depth history. The read becomes block-diagonal, the reshape adds zero parameters and negligible compute, and H = 1 recovers attention residuals exactly. Trained from scratch on a deduplicated Nemotron-based anneal corpus that is quality-filtered and STEM- and code-heavy, MHAR improves validation loss over a standard Transformer at 100M, 350M, and 1B (-0.061, -0.149, and -0.140). It achieves the best result among four methods in every setting, with the gain increasing from 100M to the larger scales. The head count is a real design axis rather than a free knob: validation loss is U-shaped with respect to H, with a flat optimum at H = 4 or H = 8 across scales. We adopt H = 8 for large-scale models; over-splitting beyond this point (H = 16) consistently gives back part of the gain. A direct probe of the trained queries confirms that learned subspace disagreement is the underlying driver. Fused Triton routing kernels increase attention-residual training throughput from 0.2-0.5x to 0.55-0.88x of the baseline while maintaining near-baseline peak memory. An identity-preserving conversion using delta attention residuals supports 8B mid-training, yielding improvements of +3.2 on GSM8K and +3.1 on GPQA.

AI.tldr: MHAR introduces multi-head attention residuals that allow different feature subspaces to have separate routing distributions over depth history, improving Transformer performance with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: Standard attention residuals force all feature subspaces to read depth history through a single shared distribution, causing performance compromises that worsen with model width as subspaces disagree about which layers to read.
AI.method: MHAR reshapes the routing query into H per-subspace heads, each with its own softmax over depth history, creating a block-diagonal read structure with zero parameter and negligible compute overhead.
AI.result: MHAR improves validation loss over standard Transformers across scales (100M, 350M, 1B), achieves best results among four methods, with optimal head count H=4 or 8. Trained 8B model shows improvements on GSM8K (+3.2) and GPQA (+3.1).
AI.conclusion: MHAR successfully addresses the subspace disagreement problem in attention residuals through multi-head routing, demonstrating scalable improvements with minimal computational cost, validated across multiple model sizes and benchmarks.

title: $Σ$-Mem: An Online Reliability Memory for LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Memory is central to long-horizon LLM agents, yet existing memory systems primarily preserve interaction content rather than modeling which agents can be trusted and under what conditions. This limitation is particularly important in multi-agent systems, where a central model may be unable to directly verify plausible or correlated peer responses. We introduce $Σ$-Mem, an online reliability memory that records historical competence evidence for individual peers and peer relationship evidence across the peer set. Both forms of evidence are maintained as real symmetric states and updated from post-decision correctness feedback. By Weyl's inequality, the spectral change caused by each event-level update is bounded, enabling stable online adaptation without retraining the underlying models. $Σ$-Mem provides a general write-and-read interface: the same memory can be used for residual steering of a central model, response-free peer routing, or reliability-weighted voting. Across five Qwen-family models, $Σ$-Mem adapts to counterfactual reliability shifts and generalizes to unseen peers and task domains. Direct memory readouts also outperform majority voting and the best fixed peer over the full OOD evaluation set. Moreover, performance improves consistently as more correctness feedback becomes available, indicating that $Σ$-Mem progressively accumulates actionable reliability information. These results establish reliability memory as a reusable foundation for adaptive coordination in LLM-based multi-agent systems.

AI.tldr: Σ-Mem is an online reliability memory system for multi-agent LLM coordination that tracks peer competence and relationships through symmetric matrix states, enabling stable adaptation without retraining and improving performance over time through correctness feedback.
AI.motivation: Existing memory systems for LLM agents primarily preserve interaction content but fail to model which agents can be trusted under what conditions. This limitation is critical in multi-agent systems where a central model cannot directly verify plausible peer responses, creating a need for reliability tracking mechanisms.
AI.method: Introduces Σ-Mem, an online reliability memory that records two forms of evidence: 1) historical competence evidence for individual peers, and 2) peer relationship evidence across the peer set. Both are maintained as real symmetric states updated from post-decision correctness feedback. Uses Weyl's inequality to bound spectral changes from updates, enabling stable online adaptation without retraining underlying models. Provides write-and-read interface supporting residual steering, peer routing, and reliability-weighted voting.
AI.result: Across five Qwen-family models, Σ-Mem adapts to counterfactual reliability shifts and generalizes to unseen peers and task domains. Direct memory readouts outperform majority voting and the best fixed peer over full OOD evaluation. Performance improves consistently as more correctness feedback becomes available, demonstrating progressive accumulation of actionable reliability information.
AI.conclusion: Σ-Mem establishes reliability memory as a reusable foundation for adaptive coordination in LLM-based multi-agent systems, providing stable online adaptation without retraining and improving decision-making through accumulating competence and relationship evidence.

title: Regularizing modality contribution drift in multimodal continual learning
summary: Multimodal continual learning (MMCL) aims to learn emerging knowledge from multimodal data while preserving knowledge. To mitigate forgetting, current MMCL methods usually focus on cross-modal representation alignment or semantic similarity, but they overlook whether the relative contributions of individual modalities and their interactions remain stable across incremental tasks. We term this decision-level shift Modality Contribution Drift (MCD) and quantify it with the MCD score, which combines contribution-strength and relative-reliance changes under controlled interventions on modality subsets. Theoretical and empirical analyses further explain why current MMCL methods cannot reliably mitigate this drift. To this end, we propose Continual Modality Contribution Drift Regularization (CMCDR), which preserves the modality contribution structure of previously learned tasks. Since MMCL settings differ in whether old exemplars are available, CMCDR includes both replay-based and replay-free versions. The replay-based version uses modality-subset interventions as diagnostic probes on stored old samples, compares their contribution profiles between the current model and a frozen previous model, and constrains changes in old-sample modality-specific and interaction contributions. The replay-free version uses current-task samples as probes and distills the frozen model's old-task contribution responses, thereby regularizing the observed contribution profile without exemplars. Experiments on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual visual question answering validate the generality and effectiveness of CMCDR.

AI.tldr: CMCDR addresses modality contribution drift in multimodal continual learning by regularizing how modalities contribute across tasks, with replay-based and replay-free versions to handle different data availability settings.
AI.motivation: Current MMCL methods focus on cross-modal representation alignment or semantic similarity but overlook whether relative modality contributions and interactions remain stable across incremental tasks. This "Modality Contribution Drift" (MCD) problem causes forgetting, as models may shift their reliance on different modalities over time.
AI.method: Proposes Continual Modality Contribution Drift Regularization (CMCDR) with two versions: 1) Replay-based: Uses stored old samples and modality-subset interventions as diagnostic probes, comparing contribution profiles between current and frozen previous models to constrain changes. 2) Replay-free: Uses current-task samples as probes to distill the frozen model's old-task contribution responses, regularizing contribution profiles without exemplars.
AI.result: Experiments on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual visual question answering validate CMCDR's generality and effectiveness in mitigating modality contribution drift and reducing forgetting compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: CMCDR effectively addresses the overlooked problem of modality contribution drift in multimodal continual learning by preserving modality contribution structures, with both replay-based and replay-free strategies making it applicable to different MMCL settings.

title: KernelGenBench: A Multi-Source and Multi-Chip Benchmark for LLM-based Kernel Generation
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/flagos-ai/KernelGenBench
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have significantly increased the demand for efficient accelerator kernels, but kernel development remains a highly specialized and labor-intensive task. The recent rise of LLMs and agentic frameworks offers a promising pathway toward automatic kernel generation. However, despite rapid progress, there is still no comprehensive benchmark to rigorously evaluate LLM-generated kernels across diverse operator sources or heterogeneous hardware platforms. We present KernelGenBench, a unified benchmark for systematically evaluating LLM- and agent-generated Triton kernels across diverse operator sources and heterogeneous hardware platforms. It comprises two complementary sub-benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (Multi-Source), evaluating 210 operators from three sources beyond standard PyTorch-centric tasks, and KernelGenBench-MC (Multi-Chip), measuring performance portability across six heterogeneous hardware platforms using a 110-operator subset. Our large-scale evaluation, consuming over 15 billion tokens, shows: (1) agent-based methods consistently outperform pure LLM sampling methods, while cuBLAS operators are the most challenging across all methods; (2) generation performance varies significantly across hardware platforms, with even recent kernel-specialized agents experiencing severe cross-platform degradation (e.g., AutoKernel drops from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E); (3) autonomous kernel generation remains highly cost-intensive, with specialized agent methods averaging 5.11 million tokens per successful operator (AKO4all reaches 5.19 million), orders of magnitude higher than simple LLM sampling approaches.

AI.tldr: KernelGenBench is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LLM-generated GPU kernels across diverse operator sources and hardware platforms, revealing that agent-based methods outperform LLM sampling but suffer from poor cross-platform portability and high computational costs.
AI.motivation: There is increasing demand for efficient accelerator kernels for LLMs, but kernel development is specialized and labor-intensive. While LLMs and agentic frameworks offer potential for automatic kernel generation, there's no comprehensive benchmark to rigorously evaluate these LLM-generated kernels across diverse operator sources or heterogeneous hardware platforms.
AI.method: The authors present KernelGenBench, a unified benchmark with two sub-benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (Multi-Source) evaluates 210 operators from three sources beyond standard PyTorch tasks, and KernelGenBench-MC (Multi-Chip) measures performance portability across six heterogeneous hardware platforms using a 110-operator subset. The evaluation consumed over 15 billion tokens.
AI.result: Large-scale evaluation shows: (1) agent-based methods consistently outperform pure LLM sampling, with cuBLAS operators being most challenging; (2) generation performance varies significantly across hardware platforms, with severe cross-platform degradation (e.g., AutoKernel dropping from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E); (3) autonomous kernel generation remains highly cost-intensive, with specialized agents averaging 5.11 million tokens per successful operator.
AI.conclusion: KernelGenBench provides the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LLM-generated kernels, revealing significant challenges in cross-platform performance portability and high computational costs of current automated kernel generation methods, highlighting areas for future improvement in this emerging field.

title: VISA: A Structured Description Protocol for Agent-Based Simulation Models Towards Machine Reproducibility
summary: Agent-based models (ABMs) are difficult to reproduce: their behavior is spread across prose narratives, platform-specific code, and implicit assumptions, so that two readers routinely reconstruct different models from the same documentation. We present VISA, a structured, symbol-based description protocol that specifies a model in eight interconnected tables---four at the agent level (Agent, Variable, Sensing, Internal Function) and four at the model level (Associated Data, Input/Output, Schedule, Validation)---under the principle of minimality with completeness. VISA makes a model machine-parseable and unambiguous via two artifacts: nineteen executable consistency rules that turn model validity into a checkable property, and three reusable LLM-executable skills (authoring, checking, and code generation) that operationalize the full author--check--code--reproduce loop. We validate the protocol on three external, independently authored ABMs spanning three platforms: we reproduce two cross-language (NetLogo to Python) directly from their VISA specifications, and we capture a third, an industrial AnyLogic model, in eight tables (passing all nineteen rules) while honestly demarcating where reproduction is blocked by a proprietary movement library and unavailable data---itself a transparency contribution. VISA moves the reproduction barrier from the model, where it is invisible, to a named, localized dependency, where it is actionable.

AI.tldr: VISA is a structured, symbol-based description protocol for agent-based models that makes them machine-parseable and unambiguous through eight interconnected tables and executable consistency rules, enabling easier reproduction and identifying reproduction barriers.
AI.motivation: Agent-based models are difficult to reproduce because their behavior is spread across prose narratives, platform-specific code, and implicit assumptions, leading to different readers reconstructing different models from the same documentation.
AI.method: VISA uses eight interconnected tables (four at agent level: Agent, Variable, Sensing, Internal Function; four at model level: Associated Data, Input/Output, Schedule, Validation) under the principle of minimality with completeness. It includes 19 executable consistency rules and three reusable LLM-executable skills (authoring, checking, and code generation).
AI.result: The protocol was validated on three external ABMs: two were reproduced cross-language (NetLogo to Python) directly from VISA specifications, and a third industrial AnyLogic model was captured in eight tables passing all 19 rules while honestly demarcating where reproduction was blocked by proprietary libraries and unavailable data.
AI.conclusion: VISA moves the reproduction barrier from being invisible within the model to localized, named dependencies where it becomes actionable, contributing to transparency and reproducibility in agent-based modeling.

title: DoTime: A Synthetic Benchmark Generator for Interventional and Counterfactual Time Series
summary: Most benchmarks for causal inference over time series are observational, small, or domain-specific, leaving interventional and counterfactual estimation under-served exactly where it matters most, such as in healthcare, policy evaluation, and climate science. We introduce \textbf{DoTime}, an open, scalable, and theoretically grounded generator of multivariate temporal structural causal models (TSCMs) with interventions, released as the \code{dotime} PyPI package together with four frozen evaluation suites. Beyond existing work, it adds capabilities absent from prior generators: continuous-time intervention \emph{windows}, counterfactual sampling modes with a positivity guard, regime-switching SCMs as a strict generalization of interrupted time series, non-stationary dynamics by construction with switching SCM parameters, and deterministic ramp and sinusoidal intervention profiles that place trends and structural breaks \emph{inside} the evaluation window. Moreover, it demonstrates the suitability of the generator as a prior for a causal foundation model reference implementation. The released suites span a training-scale snapshot of $100{,}000$ trajectories and eight named identification structures, each with exact ground truth: paired interventional trajectories from the same SCM throughout, and shared-noise counterfactuals in the continuous-time suite. We ship reference baseline implementations with an evaluation harness, and pose a falsifiable claim: interventional training buys a measurable direction-accuracy advantage over an observational model of identical capacity. It is tested across three training seeds per arm. Under structure-matched evaluation on held-out episodes, the interventional prior-fitted network's (PFN) gap is positive in every structure, trajectory length, and seed tested.

AI.tldr: DoTime is a scalable temporal SCM generator for causal inference evaluation, featuring interventions, counterfactuals, and non-stationary dynamics, with released evaluation suites and baseline models.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks for causal inference over time series are limited: they're mostly observational, small, or domain-specific, leaving interventional and counterfactual estimation underserved in critical areas like healthcare, policy evaluation, and climate science.
AI.method: The authors introduce DoTime, an open-source Python package (dotime) that generates multivariate temporal structural causal models (TSCMs) with interventions. It includes novel features: continuous-time intervention windows, counterfactual sampling with positivity guard, regime-switching SCMs, non-stationary dynamics, deterministic ramp/sinusoidal intervention profiles, and serves as a prior for causal foundation models.
AI.result: The released evaluation suites include 100,000 trajectories with exact ground truth, paired interventional trajectories, and shared-noise counterfactuals. Experimental results show that interventional training provides measurable direction-accuracy advantages over observational models of identical capacity, with positive performance gaps across all tested structures, trajectory lengths, and seeds.
AI.conclusion: DoTime successfully addresses the gap in interventional/counterfactual temporal causal inference benchmarks. The generator is theoretically grounded, scalable, and demonstrates that interventional prior-fitted networks outperform observational models, providing a valuable resource for evaluating causal methods in time series domains.

title: RadHarmony: Radiological Data Handling in the Era of Agentic AI
summary: Training deep learning models on radiological images requires integrating heterogeneous datasets across different sources, file formats, directory layouts, label schemas, and annotation types. We present RadHarmony, an open-source Python library that provides a unified API for loading, harmonizing, and augmenting radiological datasets, with a primary focus on chest radiographs and early support for computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). RadHarmony standardizes metadata from 24 public datasets into a single tabular format, wraps MONAI's map-style datasets for deep-learning-ready sample delivery with optional on-disk caching, and supports classification labels, segmentation masks, bounding boxes, and radiology report text through a single interface, with an interactive visualization tool for dataset exploration and verification. To lower the barrier for integrating new datasets, RadHarmony introduces an AI-agent skill that guides the full integration workflow from raw data inspection through code generation and testing. We demonstrate the library's utility by pretraining RadHarmony-ViT, a reference vision transformer baseline that combines three heterogeneous chest radiograph datasets with no dataset-specific code. The code and pretrained model weights are available at https://github.com/f10409/RadHarmony.

AI.tldr: RadHarmony is an open-source Python library that provides a unified interface for loading, harmonizing, and augmenting heterogeneous radiological datasets, with AI-assisted integration tools and pretrained models.
AI.motivation: Training deep learning models on radiological images is challenging due to heterogeneous datasets with different sources, file formats, directory layouts, label schemas, and annotation types across medical imaging.
AI.method: Developed RadHarmony, a Python library that standardizes metadata from 24 public datasets into a single tabular format, wraps MONAI's datasets for deep learning sample delivery, supports various annotation types through a unified interface, includes visualization tools, and provides AI-agent skills for automating dataset integration workflow.
AI.result: Successfully demonstrated the library's utility by pretraining RadHarmony-ViT, a vision transformer baseline that combines three heterogeneous chest radiograph datasets without dataset-specific code, showing practical integration capabilities.
AI.conclusion: RadHarmony addresses the critical problem of dataset heterogeneity in medical imaging research by providing a comprehensive tool for unified dataset access, harmonization, and augmentation, with AI-assisted integration to lower adoption barriers for new datasets.

title: AgentRadio: Passive Awareness for Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Collaboration
summary: Understanding large codebases is a long-horizon task for Large Language Model (LLM) agents: answering a single question can require building and running the software, tracing execution across files, and synthesizing evidence over tens of minutes. On SWE-Atlas QnA, a benchmark of long-horizon questions over production repositories, a single Claude Code agent (Opus 4.6) resolves only 32.3% of tasks. Dividing the work among agents with clean contexts mitigates this limitation. However, the subtasks of code comprehension are interdependent. One agent's findings can rewrite another's task, so agents must coordinate during execution, not only at phase boundaries. Existing multi-agent systems support such exchange only between phases, through staged handoffs or synchronized rounds. Communication and work remain mutually exclusive. A discovery made mid-execution cannot be shared until the next boundary. We present AgentRadio, an asynchronous message-passing layer that equips coding-agent harnesses with three primitives: threads, messages, and waiting for mentions. The last runs as a background task, surfacing teammates' messages without interrupting foreground work, so each agent remains passively aware of its peers and folds new findings into its ongoing task. Under a five-phase protocol of division of labor and negotiation, four agents organized by AgentRadio resolve 62.1% of tasks, 29.8 points above a single agent and above Claude Code with the newer Opus 4.8 (57.2%). Rubric-level analysis shows the gain growing with task difficulty, consistent with mid-course correction as the underlying mechanism. Our code is available at https://github.com/Coral-Protocol/AgentRadio.

AI.tldr: AgentRadio enables asynchronous message-passing between coding agents, allowing mid-execution coordination that improves long-horizon code comprehension tasks by 29.8 percentage points over single agents.
AI.motivation: Understanding large codebases requires long-horizon tasks where findings are interdependent across files and agents. Existing multi-agent systems only allow communication between phases, not during execution, causing delays in sharing important discoveries.
AI.method: AgentRadio provides three primitives: threads, messages, and "waiting for mentions" (a background task that surfaces teammate messages without interrupting foreground work). Combined with a five-phase protocol of division of labor and negotiation, it enables asynchronous coordination.
AI.result: On SWE-Atlas QnA benchmark, four agents organized by AgentRadio resolve 62.1% of tasks, compared to 32.3% for a single Claude Code agent (Opus 4.6) and 57.2% for Claude Code with Opus 4.8. This represents a 29.8-point improvement over single agents.
AI.conclusion: Asynchronous coordination through AgentRadio significantly improves performance on long-horizon code comprehension tasks, with gains increasing with task difficulty, demonstrating the value of mid-course correction during agent collaboration.

title: PlatformBid: An Auto-Bidding Benchmark from a Unified Advertising Platform's Perspective
summary: Real-time bidding is central to computational advertising, comprising three elements: Supply Side Platform (SSP) selling ad impressions, Demand Side Platform (DSP) bidding for advertisers, and Ad Exchange conducting auctions between them. Traditional auto-bidding algorithms focus solely on the DSP side, maximizing advertiser conversions by adjusting bids against competitors. However, current big ad platforms, such as social media and e-commerce companies, now integrate SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange functions internally. From such ad platforms' perspective, the goal of the auto-bidding algorithms is not only to maximize the advertisers' conversions, but also the total revenue of the platform. Given the lack of platform-centric evaluation frameworks and the pressing need to advance auto-bidding research, we propose PlatformBid - the first comprehensive benchmark designed from a unified ad platform's perspective. To accurately reflect the real-world auto-bidding scenarios, we define three representative settings: (1) homogeneous competition with identical algorithms across advertisers, (2) heterogeneous competition with diverse algorithmic strategies, and (3) promotional competition where some advertisers surge budgets for boosting sales during promotional events like Black Friday. We systematically evaluate a broad spectrum of existing auto-bidding methods across these settings, encompassing classical control methods, RL-based methods, and recent generative methods. Besides these methods, we further propose a novel auto-bidding method based on flow-matching, termed BidFlow, which leverages the flow-matching method's expressive policy representation to effectively handle dynamic competitive environments. Online experiments on Kuaishou further show a +0.68\% improvement in target cost, providing deployment evidence for the offline-online consistency of PlatformBid.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces PlatformBid, a benchmark for auto-bidding algorithms from a unified ad platform perspective, evaluating existing methods across three competition settings and proposing BidFlow, a flow-matching-based method that improves target cost in online experiments.
AI.motivation: Traditional auto-bidding algorithms focus only on the DSP side, maximizing advertiser conversions, but modern integrated ad platforms (combining SSP, DSP, Ad Exchange) aim to maximize both advertiser conversions and total platform revenue. There is a lack of platform-centric evaluation frameworks, creating a need for a benchmark that reflects real-world auto-bidding scenarios from a unified platform perspective.
AI.method: The authors propose PlatformBid, a comprehensive benchmark with three representative competition settings (homogeneous, heterogeneous, promotional). They systematically evaluate existing auto-bidding methods (classical control, RL-based, generative) and introduce BidFlow, a novel auto-bidding method based on flow-matching to leverage expressive policy representation for dynamic competitive environments.
AI.result: PlatformBid is established as the first comprehensive benchmark from a unified ad platform perspective. Evaluation across three competition settings shows the performance of various auto-bidding methods. The proposed BidFlow method demonstrates effectiveness in dynamic competitive environments. Online experiments on Kuaishou show a +0.68% improvement in target cost, indicating offline-online consistency.
AI.conclusion: The paper introduces PlatformBid as a novel benchmark for evaluating auto-bidding algorithms from a unified ad platform perspective, addressing the gap in platform-centric evaluation frameworks. It also proposes BidFlow, a new flow-matching-based auto-bidding method, which shows promise in handling dynamic competition and achieves a slight improvement in target cost in online experiments, demonstrating offline-online consistency.

title: Asymmetric Collapse in Model Merging: When Refusal Over- writes Recognition
comment: Accepted into COLM AIW, waiting decision for AdvML-Frontiers x CoTMA and HAIPS
summary: Model merging is often used to combine capabilities from separately fine-tuned models without additional training, but it is unclear whether standard merging methods preserve multiple safety-relevant behaviors simultaneously. We study this question through a controlled case study using two Gemma-3-1B-IT finetunes on two complementary safety objectives: CARES harm-level classification and WildJailbreak adversarial refusal. We merge the two fine-tunes using Linear, SLERP, TIES, and DARE-TIES, and evaluate the merged models on classification accuracy, attack resistance, and benign compliance. Across all four methods, attack resistance transfers significantly more than classification accuracy: merged models retain 81-85% jailbreak refusal rates while CARES accuracy falls to at most 12.9%. Weight-space measurements suggest that this asymmetry is not caused by strongly opposing task-vector directions: the two task vectors are nearly orthogonal (cosine similarity 0.011). Instead, the refusal fine-tune induces consistently larger per-layer task-vector magnitudes, causing magnitude-sensitive methods to favor refusal updates. These results show that standard model merging can collapse safety recognition into broad refusal when safety-relevant task vectors differ substantially in scale.

AI.tldr: Model merging methods preserve attack resistance significantly better than safety classification accuracy when combining safety-oriented fine-tuned models, with merged models retaining 81-85% jailbreak refusal rates but only up to 12.9% CARES classification accuracy due to magnitude differences in task vectors.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether standard model merging methods preserve multiple safety-relevant behaviors simultaneously when combining separately fine-tuned models, specifically examining if merging techniques can maintain both safety classification accuracy and adversarial attack resistance.
AI.method: Used two Gemma-3-1B-IT models fine-tuned on complementary safety objectives: CARES harm-level classification and WildJailbreak adversarial refusal. Merged models using four methods (Linear, SLERP, TIES, and DARE-TIES) and evaluated on classification accuracy, attack resistance, and benign compliance. Conducted weight-space analysis measuring task-vector directions and magnitudes.
AI.result: Attack resistance transferred significantly more than classification accuracy across all four merging methods. Merged models retained 81-85% jailbreak refusal rates while CARES accuracy fell to at most 12.9%. Weight analysis showed task vectors were nearly orthogonal (cosine similarity 0.011) but refusal fine-tune had consistently larger per-layer task-vector magnitudes, causing magnitude-sensitive methods to favor refusal updates.
AI.conclusion: Standard model merging methods can collapse safety recognition into broad refusal when safety-relevant task vectors differ substantially in scale, rather than maintaining balanced capabilities. The asymmetry in preservation is driven by magnitude differences in task vectors, not by opposing directions.

title: Using Theory of Mind to Arbitrate between Social and Non-social Learning
summary: Social learning is a powerful mechanism through which agents learn about the world from others. However, humans sometimes choose direct experience over social learning, which can carry time and cognitive resource costs. How do people balance social and non-social learning? We propose a Rational Mentalizing model of the decision to engage in social learning. This model estimates the utility of social learning by reasoning about another agent's goal and the informativeness of their future actions. It then weighs the utility of social learning against the utility of non-social learning. Using a novel game where players choose between observing other agents or exploring the environment, we show that the Rational Mentalizing model can quantitatively capture human trade-offs between these strategies. These findings suggest that selective social learning is guided by 'Theory of Mind' in the service of utility maximization.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a Rational Mentalizing model that explains how people balance social vs. non-social learning through mentalizing about others' goals and actions to maximize utility.
AI.motivation: While social learning is effective, humans sometimes prefer direct experience despite its costs. The paper aims to understand how people decide between social and non-social learning strategies.
AI.method: Proposed a Rational Mentalizing model that estimates utility of social learning by reasoning about another agent's goal and action informativeness, then compares it with non-social learning utility. Tested using a novel game where participants choose between observing agents or exploring the environment.
AI.result: The Rational Mentalizing model quantitatively captures human trade-offs between social and non-social learning strategies, showing it can explain human decision-making patterns.
AI.conclusion: Selective social learning is guided by Theory of Mind processes that serve utility maximization, suggesting people rationally balance learning strategies based on mentalizing about others.

title: Beyond KV Reconstruction: Functional Reconstruction for MLA Draft Models in Speculative Decoding
summary: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) is increasingly important for long-context LLM inference because compact latent states replace the growing key-value (KV) cache and reduce decoding memory traffic. Yet most capable open checkpoints use multi-head or grouped-query attention (MHA/GQA), so conversion is needed to obtain MLA's cache efficiency without retraining from scratch. Speculative decoding offers complementary acceleration, but its speedup depends on agreement between draft proposals and target verification. We find that direct MHA/GQA-to-MLA conversion can sharply reduce this agreement: low-rank factorization and RoPE handling introduce attention-function errors that may be tolerable for standalone generation but substantially lower draft-token acceptance. We therefore formulate MLA draft construction as functional reconstruction rather than cache compression. Our end-to-end (E2E) method optimizes each converted MLA attention module to reproduce the post-output-projection response of its original MHA/GQA counterpart on calibration hidden states. This converter-agnostic post-conversion procedure preserves the converted cache and inference graph and requires neither verifier logits nor verifier supervision. We evaluate 192 model-converter-backend-method-task configurations spanning four Llama/Qwen draft-target pairs, TransMLA and MHA2MLA, HF and vLLM, and four 200-prompt tasks. With a 0.5-percentage-point reporting tolerance, Functional Reconstruction materially improves acceptance in 37 of 64 matched task cells, leaves 26 practically unchanged, and materially decreases one. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://github.com/swyhahaha/FunctionalMLA.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a functional reconstruction method to improve draft-token acceptance when converting MHA/GQA LLMs to MLA for speculative decoding, addressing the agreement reduction problem that occurs with direct conversion methods.
AI.motivation: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) reduces memory traffic in long-context LLM inference by using compact latent states instead of growing KV caches. However, most capable open checkpoints use MHA/GQA, requiring conversion. Direct conversion methods reduce draft-token agreement in speculative decoding, limiting acceleration benefits.
AI.method: Proposes an end-to-end functional reconstruction method that optimizes each converted MLA attention module to reproduce the post-output-projection response of its original MHA/GQA counterpart on calibration hidden states. This converter-agnostic approach preserves the converted cache and inference graph without requiring verifier logits or supervision.
AI.result: Evaluated across 192 configurations (4 Llama/Qwen draft-target pairs, TransMLA and MHA2MLA converters, HF and vLLM backends, 4 tasks). With 0.5% tolerance, functional reconstruction improved acceptance in 37 of 64 matched task cells, left 26 practically unchanged, and decreased only one.
AI.conclusion: Functional reconstruction effectively addresses the draft-token acceptance degradation problem when converting MHA/GQA models to MLA for speculative decoding, providing a practical post-conversion optimization that maintains cache efficiency while improving speculative decoding performance.

title: Divergence Decoding: Training-Free Capability Fusion
summary: While large language models excel in reasoning, these generalists often lack knowledge for specialized scientific domains. Conversely, domain models~(specialists), while knowledgeable, suffer from specialization side-effects including diminished logic and reduced robustness.To address this dilemma, we introduce Divergence Decoding, a training-free framework for capability fusion. It reconstructs the "draft-and-verify" skeleton of speculative decoding into an adaptive routing mechanism. The core is using Jensen-Shannon divergence to monitor the distributional disagreement between the two models at each token. When the specialist exhibits significant divergence, our method identifies it as a potential reasoning risk and instantaneously routes control to the generalist. This allows the dynamic injection of general reasoning while preserving domain expertise, achieving inference-time policy composition of the generalist and the specialist.We evaluate Divergence Decoding across diverse model families (Qwen and Llama series) on challenging scientific benchmarks (GPQA, ChemBench, and ChemCoTBench). Experimental results demonstrate that Divergence Decoding outperforms both the domain-specialized and general-purpose models, effectively surpassing the performance of most single-model baseline. This suggests that Divergence Decoding provides a general, training-free paradigm for fusing diverse LLM capabilities through adaptive inference-time collaboration.

AI.tldr: A training-free framework called Divergence Decoding that fuses general reasoning from large language models with domain expertise from specialized models through adaptive routing at inference time, outperforming both individual model types.
AI.motivation: Large language models (generalists) excel at reasoning but lack specialized scientific domain knowledge, while domain models (specialists) have deep expertise but suffer from reduced logical reasoning and robustness due to over-specialization. This creates a dilemma where neither type alone provides optimal performance for scientific tasks requiring both broad reasoning and deep domain knowledge.
AI.method: Divergence Decoding adapts the "draft-and-verify" skeleton of speculative decoding into an adaptive routing mechanism. It uses Jensen-Shannon divergence to monitor distributional disagreement between generalist and specialist models at each token generation step. When significant divergence is detected (indicating potential reasoning risk from the specialist), control is instantly routed to the generalist, enabling dynamic injection of general reasoning while preserving domain expertise.
AI.result: Evaluated across diverse model families (Qwen and Llama series) on challenging scientific benchmarks (GPQA, ChemBench, and ChemCoTBench), Divergence Decoding outperforms both domain-specialized and general-purpose models, effectively surpassing most single-model baselines.
AI.conclusion: Divergence Decoding provides a general, training-free paradigm for fusing diverse LLM capabilities through adaptive inference-time collaboration, enabling effective combination of general reasoning skills with specialized domain knowledge without requiring model retraining.

title: Autonomous Event-Driven Multi-Agent Orchestration for Enterprise AI at Scale
summary: Enterprise AI aims to move toward continuous event monitoring, detection, and action across specialist agents, yet existing multi-agent systems largely assume discrete request-response workflows and remain underexplored at enterprise scale. We evaluate DAG Plan and Execute and ReAct across 208 production-derived enterprise scenarios spanning Persona (<10 agents), Department (20-80), and Enterprise (200) scales, and introduce a Task Manager for continuous operation via priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption. Results show that scale, not task complexity, dominates orchestration performance: both architectures perform well at small scale but degrade at enterprise scale as agent discovery noise becomes the primary bottleneck, with simple tasks degrading more sharply than complex ones. DAG Plan and Execute offers higher precision and structured parallelization at smaller scales, but its higher overhead worsens at enterprise scale; ReAct is more robust by handling failures incrementally. The Task Manager reduces high-priority queue latency by 14-75% and improves related-event correctness by over 20 percentage points at enterprise scale.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent AI systems struggle at enterprise scale due to agent discovery bottlenecks; a Task Manager with priority inference improves performance significantly at scale.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent systems assume discrete request-response workflows and are underexplored at enterprise scale, while Enterprise AI needs continuous event monitoring, detection, and action across specialist agents.
AI.method: Evaluated DAG Plan and Execute vs ReAct across 208 production-derived enterprise scenarios at three scales (Persona, Department, Enterprise). Introduced Task Manager with priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption for continuous operation.
AI.result: Scale, not task complexity, dominates performance degradation. DAG offers better precision at small scale but suffers higher overhead at enterprise scale; ReAct handles failures better. Task Manager reduces high-priority latency by 14-75% and improves related-event correctness by 20+ percentage points at enterprise scale.
AI.conclusion: Agent discovery noise is the primary bottleneck at enterprise scale. Continuous operation requires specialized orchestration like the Task Manager to manage priority, event merging, and preemption for effective enterprise-scale AI systems.

title: RLPF: Reinforcement Learning from Performance Feedback for Code Generation
summary: Code models are increasingly trained with execution feedback, but most training signals still stop at correctness. This leaves an important gap for systems code: two programs can pass the same tests while differing greatly in runtime. We study how to train code agents to prefer faster correct implementations, rather than treating efficiency only as an evaluation metric. The key difficulty is that runtime is a fragile reward. It is meaningful only after a program is correct, varies across tasks, and gives little guidance when most sampled programs fail to compile or run. We propose \textbf{RLPF}, reinforcement learning from performance feedback, which turns execution outcomes into a staged reward. Failed programs are ordered by execution progress, while correct programs are ranked by their relative improvement from the baseline toward the expert reference. This gives useful feedback before correctness and performance-sensitive feedback after correctness. Fine-tuning Qwen3-32B with RLPF on PerfCodeBench raises correct-and-runnable solutions from $11.1\%$ to $54.6\%$ and improves relative efficiency from $8.1\%$ to $38.6\%$. The trained model becomes competitive with stronger open-weight systems, and its optimization behavior transfers modestly to EffiBench-X. Additional studies show that model-generated references provide useful but weaker supervision, and that the full composite reward is more reliable than correctness-only or runtime-only baselines. These results suggest that code agents can be trained not only to pass tests, but also to optimize the programs they write.

AI.tldr: Code agents can be trained to optimize program efficiency through reinforcement learning from performance feedback (RLPF), which ranks programs by execution progress and relative efficiency improvements.
AI.motivation: Current code models focus on correctness but ignore runtime efficiency, creating a gap where two correct programs can have vastly different performance. Traditional training treats efficiency only as an evaluation metric rather than a learning objective.
AI.method: Proposes RLPF (Reinforcement Learning from Performance Feedback), a staged reward system that: 1) ranks failed programs by execution progress, and 2) ranks correct programs by their relative efficiency improvement from a baseline toward an expert reference.
AI.result: Fine-tuning Qwen3-32B with RLPF on PerfCodeBench increased correct-and-runnable solutions from 11.1% to 54.6% and improved relative efficiency from 8.1% to 38.6%. The model becomes competitive with stronger systems and shows modest transfer to EffiBench-X.
AI.conclusion: Code agents can be trained not only for correctness but also for optimization through performance-sensitive feedback. The composite reward system (RLPF) is more effective than correctness-only or runtime-only approaches, though expert references remain important for supervision.

title: PIE-APT: A Unified Framework for Temporal Planning and Contradiction Hunting via Incremental Direct-Derivation Abduction
summary: Reasoning and planning over Dynamic Knowledge Graphs (DKGs) present significant challenges, especially in open-world environments with incomplete information. Existing action formalisms often face decidability issues and the Ramification Problem, while managing incomplete knowledge via structural abduction requires expansive combinatorial search. This paper introduces a unified framework with two integrated modules---\textbf{PIE-Abducer} (incremental direct-derivation abduction) and \textbf{PIE-APT} (Abductive Planning for Temporal KGs)---operating natively on the highly expressive Description Logic. We model state transitions along a linear timeline as non-monotonic updates to deductively closed DL theories. Treating the incremental reasoner as a black-box and representing actions natively in OWL without external modal operators preserves logical decidability. To address incomplete knowledge, \textbf{PIE-Abducer} circumvents traditional Minimal Hitting Set (MHS) enumeration. Instead of combinatorial syntactic search, it injects the logical negation of a target goal into a consistent branch and extracts missing premises via direct refutation consequences. \textbf{PIE-APT} then employs a recursive \textit{Generate-and-Test} architecture, interleaving backward-chaining A* search with \textbf{PIE-Abducer} up to a bounded causal depth, followed by strict validation via forward-chaining Temporal Projection. We evaluate four OWL benchmarks stressing semantic abilities absent in classical planning: parameterized goals with witness search, mid-search DL entailment, open-world assumption injection, and adversarial contradiction hunting. Results demonstrate qualitative superiority over classical planners and prove our direct-derivation approach quantitatively outperforms an MHS-faithful baseline during abductive enrichment.

AI.tldr: A unified framework with two modules (PIE-Abducer and PIE-APT) for reasoning and planning on Dynamic Knowledge Graphs using Description Logic, addressing decidability and the Ramification Problem while handling incomplete knowledge through novel abductive methods.
AI.motivation: Reasoning and planning over Dynamic Knowledge Graphs face significant challenges in open-world environments with incomplete information. Existing approaches have decidability issues, suffer from the Ramification Problem, and require expensive combinatorial search for structural abduction.
AI.method: Two integrated modules: PIE-Abducer uses incremental direct-derivation abduction that injects logical negation of goals to extract missing premises via refutation consequences instead of combinatorial Minimal Hitting Set enumeration. PIE-APT employs recursive Generate-and-Test architecture with backward-chaining A* search interleaved with PIE-Abducer up to bounded causal depth, followed by forward-chaining Temporal Projection validation.
AI.result: Evaluated on four OWL benchmarks testing semantic abilities absent in classical planning. Results show qualitative superiority over classical planners and quantitative outperformance over Minimal Hitting Set-faithful baseline during abductive enrichment.
AI.conclusion: The unified framework successfully addresses challenges in Dynamic Knowledge Graph reasoning by preserving logical decidability, avoiding combinatorial search issues, and providing both qualitative and quantitative improvements over existing approaches.

title: Skill Use or Skill Theater? Evaluating the Reasoning Backroom in Skill-Augmented Language Agents
summary: Reusable skills are becoming a standard interface for extending language agents with task procedures. Yet evaluators usually infer skill use from visible reasoning or the agent's own attribution. These signals show what the agent appears to use, not whether the skill changed its decision. We ask whether skill-augmented agents exhibit a \textbf{Reasoning Backroom}, a systematic gap between stated skill use and intervention-measured influence. We introduce BACKTRACE, an evaluation framework that pairs each skill-conditioned answer with a matched no-skill counterfactual, intervenes on skill meaning, wording, identity, content, and assignment, and elicits attribution only after the answer is committed. We instantiate the framework as BACKROOMBench, a verified testbed spanning controlled logic and competition mathematics, multiple skill conditions, single-agent and multi-agent settings, and diverse model families. Our evaluation reveals a pervasive provenance failure. Across models and domains, stated skill use often remains stable while causal reliance and signed utility vary, producing both silent uptake and performative use. Behavioral effects follow procedural content more reliably than displayed skill identity, whereas stated attributions respond strongly to artifact availability. Observational detectors based on direct skill-use claims, text mentions, trace similarity, and an LLM judge do not identify which decisions actually depend on the skill. In multi-agent systems, skill influence can survive communication even after its source is lost, while no-skill teams still name skills and sources that were never supplied. These findings establish the Reasoning Backroom as a general AI provenance problem whose audit requires intervention.

AI.tldr: Paper introduces BACKTRACE framework to detect Reasoning Backroom - systematic gap between stated skill use and actual causal influence in skill-augmented language agents, revealing pervasive provenance failures.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of skill-augmented language agents only measure visible reasoning or agent attribution, which shows what agents appear to use but not whether skills actually changed decisions. There's a need to detect systematic gaps between stated skill use and actual causal influence.
AI.method: Introduces BACKTRACE evaluation framework that pairs skill-conditioned answers with matched no-skill counterfactuals, intervenes on skill meaning, wording, identity, content, and assignment, and elicits attribution only after answer commitment. Instantiates as BACKROOMBench testbed spanning logic, mathematics, multiple skill conditions, single/multi-agent settings, and diverse models.
AI.result: Reveals pervasive provenance failure: stated skill use often stays stable while causal reliance and signed utility vary (silent uptake and performative use). Behavioral effects follow procedural content more than displayed skill identity. Observational detectors fail to identify skill-dependent decisions. In multi-agent systems, skill influence survives communication after source loss, and no-skill teams still name never-supplied skills.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning Backroom is a general AI provenance problem requiring intervention-based audit, not just observational evaluation. Skill influence doesn't reliably correlate with stated use, necessitating causal measurement frameworks like BACKTRACE.

title: SDO: Structure-Aware Data Organization for Efficient LLM Post-Training
summary: Post-training of large language models is expensive, and existing efficiency improvements mainly focus on selecting informative samples or designing training schedules. However, data organization itself is usually treated as a static preprocessing step: embedding-based grouping methods construct fixed partitions before training and cannot adapt to the evolving sample exposure during optimization. As a result, all samples receive similar exposure despite their different optimization needs, leading to redundant updates for some samples while leaving others under-optimized. To address this problem, we propose SDO (Structure-Aware Data Organization), a plug-and-play data organization framework with an exposure-driven feedback mechanism that organizes mini-batch composition and sample exposure according to representation-space structure. SDO operates epoch by epoch on frozen external embeddings, avoiding model warm-up training overhead: within each epoch, locality-aware batching forms coherent mini-batches via KNN neighborhood traversal; across epochs, exposure-balanced scheduling records per-sample participation and reduces the sampling probability of over-exposed samples to preserve long-term coverage. Across SFT, DPO, and GRPO, SDO accelerates convergence, with the largest gains observed in the early-to-mid phase, producing more coherent gradients and more balanced accuracy across question types without permanently excluding training samples.

AI.tldr: SDO is a data organization framework that dynamically organizes mini-batches using representation-space structure and exposure tracking to optimize training efficiency without permanently excluding samples.
AI.motivation: Current post-training methods treat data organization as static, using fixed partitions that can't adapt to evolving sample exposure during optimization. This leads to inefficient training where some samples get redundant updates while others remain under-optimized.
AI.method: SDO uses frozen external embeddings and operates epoch by epoch with two key mechanisms: (1) locality-aware batching via KNN neighborhood traversal for coherent mini-batches, and (2) exposure-balanced scheduling that tracks per-sample participation and reduces sampling probability for over-exposed samples.
AI.result: SDO accelerates convergence across SFT, DPO, and GRPO training methods, with largest gains in early-to-mid training phases. It produces more coherent gradients and more balanced accuracy across question types without permanently excluding training samples.
AI.conclusion: SDO provides an effective plug-and-play framework for dynamic data organization that improves training efficiency by adapting mini-batch composition and sample exposure to representation-space structure and optimization needs.

title: PAUSE: A User-Centric Benchmark for Personal AI Assistants in Unified Service Environments
summary: Personal AI assistants are increasingly deployed as task-oriented, tool-augmented agents that operate within unified service environments to support everyday user activities. In realistic settings, such assistants must reason over persistent user state, respect user-specific configurations and permissions, and sustain long-horizon, constraint-aware interactions across multiple services. Existing benchmarks, however, often fragment service contexts or abstract away user state, limiting their ability to evaluate user-centric personal assistant behavior in realistic service settings. We introduce PAUSE, a user-centric benchmark for evaluating personal AI assistants in stateful, service-integrated environments. PAUSE captures core challenges of real-world assistant deployment by requiring agents to coordinate actions across heterogeneous user-owned resources while maintaining consistency with environment state, authorization constraints over multi-turn interactions. The benchmark incorporates explicit user-agent interaction via realistic user simulation, enabling evaluation beyond static tool execution. To support principled and reproducible evaluation, PAUSE adopts a multi-regime evaluation framework aligned with task characteristics. Open-ended service management tasks are assessed using semantic and trajectory-level behavioral metrics, while constraint-intensive tasks admit deterministic, state-based verification. Benchmark results show that even state-of-the-art proprietary models fail to reach 70% task completion on scenarios requiring stateful reasoning and configuration awareness, revealing consistent and interpretable failure patterns. Finally, we present a user-centric synthesis pipeline that enables scalable generation of coherent service environments, user configurations, and reliably annotated tasks, supporting benchmark extensibility and future research.

AI.tldr: PAUSE is a benchmark for evaluating personal AI assistants in stateful, service-integrated environments with realistic user interactions, highlighting that even state-of-the-art models struggle with stateful reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks fragment service contexts and abstract away user state, limiting their ability to evaluate user-centric personal assistant behavior in realistic service settings where assistants must handle persistent user state, user-specific configurations, and long-horizon interactions across multiple services.
AI.method: Introduces PAUSE benchmark featuring: 1) heterogeneous user-owned resources requiring coordination, 2) environment state consistency maintenance, 3) authorization constraints over multi-turn interactions, 4) explicit user-agent interaction via realistic user simulation, and 5) multi-regime evaluation framework with semantic/behavioral metrics for open-ended tasks and deterministic state-based verification for constraint-intensive tasks.
AI.result: Benchmark results show state-of-the-art proprietary models fail to reach 70% task completion on scenarios requiring stateful reasoning and configuration awareness, revealing consistent and interpretable failure patterns.
AI.conclusion: PAUSE addresses limitations of existing benchmarks by capturing core challenges of real-world assistant deployment and provides a scalable synthesis pipeline for generating coherent service environments and annotated tasks to support future research in user-centric AI assistant evaluation.

title: Evaluating Agentic Bioinformatics through Function, Evidence, and Validation
summary: Large language model agents increasingly plan, execute, and interpret biological analyses, yet fluent responses, successful tool calls, and benchmark performance alone do not establish scientific credibility. Existing reviews primarily organize biological agents by application, architecture, and agentic capability, but do not jointly operationalize the accountability of agent-generated workflows. We address this gap by treating the inspectable workflow trajectory, rather than architecture or final output alone, as the primary unit of analysis. We introduce the Function--Evidence--Validation (FEV) framework, which separates demonstrated workflow operations, traceable support for actions and claims, and use-case-specific validation. Using FEV, we map 109 agentic or agent-adjacent systems and 28 benchmark or evaluation resources, representing 128 unique publications across genomics, single-cell and spatial omics, protein science, drug discovery, computational pathology, and general bioinformatics automation. Across domains, planning and tool-mediated execution have advanced more rapidly than replayability, provenance, robust scientific assessment, external validation, and prospective empirical testing. We therefore argue that agentic bioinformatics should be assessed through workflow correctness rather than final-answer correctness alone. FEV provides a practical basis for comparing systems and designing transparent, auditable, and scientifically accountable bioinformatics workflows.

AI.tldr: Introduces the Function–Evidence–Validation (FEV) framework to evaluate LLM agents in bioinformatics by analyzing workflow trajectories rather than just final outputs, revealing gaps in reproducibility and scientific validation.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of LLM agents in bioinformatics focus on fluent responses and benchmark performance but fail to establish scientific credibility. Existing reviews don't properly operationalize accountability for agent-generated workflows.
