AI.method: Proposes treating workflow trajectories as the primary unit of analysis. Introduces the FEV framework that separates workflow operations (Function), traceable support (Evidence), and use-case-specific validation (Validation). Applied to 109 agentic systems and 28 evaluation resources across multiple biological domains.
AI.result: Analysis of 128 publications shows planning and tool execution have advanced faster than reproducibility, provenance, scientific assessment, and external validation. Identifies need for workflow correctness assessment rather than just final-answer correctness.
AI.conclusion: The FEV framework provides a practical basis for comparing systems and designing transparent, auditable, and scientifically accountable bioinformatics workflows. Agentic bioinformatics should prioritize workflow correctness over final outputs alone.

title: Rethinking EEG-Based Disease Diagnosis: Decoupling Instance Representation Learning from Subject-Level Supervision
summary: EEG-based disease diagnosis requires one prediction per subject, yet common pipelines segment recordings into short instances, inherit the subject label for every instance, and train instance-level classifiers. This assumes that all instances provide equally reliable diagnostic evidence. Multiple instance learning (MIL) avoids inherited labels by treating each subject as a bag. However, EEG datasets contain far fewer subjects than instances, which can limit the quality of the representations learned by end-to-end MIL. We propose BridgeMIL, a two-stage framework that decouples instance representation learning from subject-level supervision. Stage 1 pretrains the encoder without inherited instance labels by aligning temporally nearby windows and independently sampled within-subject sub-bags. Variance and covariance regularization prevent collapse and reduce redundancy without negative pairs. Stage 2 transfers the encoder to an attention-based MIL aggregator, applies supervision only to subject predictions, and limits representation drift through feature retention. Across three EEG disease datasets and five representative backbones, BridgeMIL attains the highest mean accuracy in 14 of 15 dataset-backbone settings and an overall mean accuracy of 76.57%, 4.28 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline. Further analyses reveal substantial variation in inherited-label reliability across instances, greater performance sensitivity to subject scarcity than to instance scarcity, and a more structured representation space with distinct subject-wise clusters and improved separation between diagnostic classes. Together, these findings underscore the importance of aligning supervision with the subject-level prediction objective while learning from abundant EEG instances without assigning disease labels to individual instances.

AI.tldr: BridgeMIL is a two-stage EEG disease diagnosis framework that decouples instance representation learning from subject-level supervision to avoid the unreliable practice of inheriting disease labels for individual EEG windows.
AI.motivation: Current EEG diagnosis pipelines segment recordings into short instances and inherit subject labels for every instance, which assumes all instances provide equally reliable diagnostic evidence. Multiple instance learning (MIL) treats subjects as bags but suffers from limited subject numbers in EEG datasets, constraining end-to-end learning quality.
AI.method: Two-stage framework: Stage 1 pretrains encoder without inherited labels using temporal alignment of nearby windows and within-subject sub-bag sampling, with variance and covariance regularization to prevent collapse. Stage 2 transfers encoder to attention-based MIL aggregator with subject-level supervision only, using feature retention to limit representation drift.
AI.result: BridgeMIL achieved highest mean accuracy in 14 of 15 dataset-backbone settings across three EEG disease datasets, with overall mean accuracy of 76.57% (4.28 percentage points higher than strongest baseline). Analyses showed substantial variation in inherited-label reliability, greater sensitivity to subject scarcity than instance scarcity, and more structured representation space with clear subject clusters and better class separation.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully demonstrates the importance of aligning supervision with subject-level prediction objectives while learning from abundant EEG instances without assigning disease labels to individual windows. This approach addresses fundamental limitations in EEG disease diagnosis pipelines.

title: SkillMentor: LLM Agent Self-Evolution via Learning Blind-Spot Diagnosis
summary: Agent self-evolution has primarily focused on learning how to act, while overlooking an equally important capability: learning to discover what an agent does not know. Existing approaches typically assume that failure discovery is given, focusing on how to repair failures once they are identified. We ask whether blind-spot diagnosis itself can be learned. We thus study diagnosis as an agent capability separate from execution, and exclude two alternative sources of progress: executor adaptation and human supervision. Under these constraints, performance cannot improve through executor updates or annotated examples, forcing all improvements to originate from the learned diagnostic capability. We propose SkillMentor, which trains a Mentor policy via reinforcement learning to generate diagnostic tasks, identify recurrent failure modes, and curate them into reusable corrective skills. Across AppWorld and BFCLv3, SkillMentor improves executor performance by an average of 44.2%. These results suggest that blind-spot diagnosis is a learnable capability, enabling self-evolution without updating executor weights or relying on human-curated data.

AI.tldr: SkillMentor learns to diagnose AI agent blind spots without human supervision or executor updates, improving performance by 44.2% through automated failure mode identification and skill curation.
AI.motivation: Current agent self-evolution focuses only on learning to act while assuming failure discovery is given. The paper questions whether blind-spot diagnosis itself can be learned as a separate capability, moving beyond just repairing identified failures.
AI.method: SkillMentor trains a Mentor policy via reinforcement learning to generate diagnostic tasks, identify recurrent failure modes, and curate them into reusable corrective skills. The approach excludes executor adaptation and human supervision, forcing all improvements to come from learned diagnostic capability.
AI.result: Across AppWorld and BFCLv3 environments, SkillMentor improves executor performance by an average of 44.2%, demonstrating that blind-spot diagnosis is learnable without updating executor weights or using human-curated data.
AI.conclusion: Blind-spot diagnosis is a learnable capability that enables autonomous agent self-evolution, allowing agents to discover what they don't know without human supervision or executor weight updates.

title: Policy Gradient Steering: Interventions from Behavioral Objectives
summary: Activation steering has emerged in large language models as a lightweight alternative for dynamically changing a model's behavior at inference time. However, we show that existing steering methods fail to steer even a simple policy in a two-route gridworld environment. To address this limitation, we propose Policy Gradient Steering (PGS), which formulates steering as a reinforcement learning problem. PGS accumulates gradients of a temporary behavioral objective over a small set of rollouts or demonstrations to construct a removable task vector. We first demonstrate the calibration and reversibility of PGS in a two-route gridworld environment. Using chess puzzles, we then evaluate independently fitted PGS vectors both in isolation and in combination, finding that compatible tactical objectives accumulate constructively. Finally, in competitive football, we show that PGS can alter specific team behaviors and that its effects transfer across opponents. Together, these results show that policy gradients provide a natural interface for constructing temporary and composable behavioral adaptations across diverse decision-making domains.

AI.tldr: Policy Gradient Steering (PGS) uses reinforcement learning to create removable task vectors for dynamically changing LLM behaviors, enabling temporary and composable behavioral adaptations across various decision-making domains.
AI.motivation: Existing activation steering methods fail to effectively steer even simple policies in gridworld environments, highlighting the need for more robust steering techniques that can dynamically modify model behavior at inference time.
AI.method: PGS formulates steering as a reinforcement learning problem, accumulating gradients of temporary behavioral objectives over small sets of rollouts or demonstrations to construct removable task vectors that can be added or removed from the model.
AI.result: PGS demonstrated calibration and reversibility in gridworld, constructive accumulation of compatible tactical objectives in chess puzzles, and ability to alter specific team behaviors in competitive football that transfer across opponents.
AI.conclusion: Policy gradients provide a natural interface for constructing temporary and composable behavioral adaptations across diverse decision-making domains, addressing limitations of existing steering methods.

title: Flat Score, Amplified Failures: How the Error Budget Masks Damage in Quantized LLM Agents
summary: Post-training quantization to 4-bit weights is widely reported to be nearly lossless. We test this claim for multi-turn, tool-calling agents, where it now matters most. On $τ^2$-bench, across two open-weight model families in dense and MoE variants and two domains (eight cells, 456 episodes each, at 16-, 8-, and 4-bit weights), quantization indeed looks free on the standard metric. No cell shows a score change that survives multiple-comparison correction, and in the cell that carries the largest process damage, equivalence testing bounds the change within $\pm$7.5 points. The process tells a different story. Quantization amplifies the failure the model already exhibits at full precision (tool-name hallucination in telecom, with the same directional trend in retail entity errors) by up to 2.5$\times$ in volume (+17.6 points per task), while creating essentially no new failures. The failure set is the same at every precision (rank correlation $\geq$ 0.94, 0.18% novel events). The score stays flat because the benchmark's ten-error budget absorbs the extra failures. Shrinking the budget to two errors re-exposes a score gap of 17 points, and it does so only in the one cell where quantization added error volume, exactly as the masking account predicts. A targeted error-repair prompt, run for five telecom models at every precision, removes the damage exactly and only where it lives. Both diagnostics, the per-channel error rate and success under a shrinking budget, come from logs benchmarks already collect; we suggest reporting them alongside task reward.

AI.tldr: While 4-bit weight quantization appears lossless on standard metrics for multi-turn tool-calling agents, it actually amplifies existing model failures by up to 2.5x, though benchmark error budgets mask this damage until the budget is reduced.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the widely-held belief that 4-bit weight quantization is nearly lossless, particularly for multi-turn, tool-calling agents where precision matters most. Despite reports of minimal impact on standard metrics, the authors suspect quantization might have hidden negative effects that aren't captured by current evaluation approaches.
AI.method: The researchers systematically tested quantization effects using the τ²-bench across two open-weight model families (in dense and MoE variants) and two domains. They conducted 456 episodes per configuration at 16-, 8-, and 4-bit weight precisions. They used multiple-comparison correction and equivalence testing, then analyzed error logs and developed targeted diagnostics including per-channel error rates and success under shrinking error budgets.
AI.result: Quantization doesn't create new failure modes but amplifies existing ones by up to 2.5x (e.g., tool-name hallucination in telecom domain). Standard metrics show no significant score changes due to the benchmark's generous error budget (10 errors), but shrinking the budget to 2 errors reveals a 17-point performance gap. Targeted error-repair prompts successfully mitigate quantization damage where it occurs. Failure sets remain consistent across precisions (rank correlation ≥ 0.94).
AI.conclusion: 4-bit quantization isn't truly lossless for complex tool-calling agents; it amplifies pre-existing model weaknesses. Standard evaluation metrics can mask this damage due to generous error budgets. The paper recommends reporting additional diagnostics (per-channel error rates and performance under shrinking error budgets) alongside task reward to better reveal quantization effects.

title: Beyond the Bidirectional Promise: Re-evaluating the Robustness of Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) offer a compelling alternative to autoregressive (AR) generation by enabling bidirectional context and iterative refinement. However, their reliability under natural input noise and adversarial attacks remains under-explored. To address this, we systematically evaluate DLM robustness and calibration against AR baselines, using two parameter-matched pairs (LLaDA-8B vs. LLaMA-3-8B and Dream-7B vs. Qwen2.5-7B) across 32 natural perturbation conditions, adversarial gradient probes, and mechanistic hidden-state analyses. This paired design effectively isolates architecture-intrinsic properties from weight-dependent behaviors. We find a nuanced robustness profile: while highly stochastic DLM loss landscapes naturally resist gradient-based adversarial suffixes, they provide no guaranteed defense against natural noise, proving that everyday robustness is weight-dependent rather than inherently architectural. Furthermore, DLMs exhibit systematic overconfidence, presenting a practical deployment hazard. Most crucially, mechanistic probing reveals that all models perfectly encode input corruption, isolating behavioral fragility entirely to a decoder routing failure. Consistent with this diagnosis, we show that surface-level prompt patching fails to improve over noisy baselines. Ultimately, DLM robustness cannot be patched on; it must be fundamentally integrated into the iterative decoding loop.

AI.tldr: DLMs show architecture-intrinsic resistance to gradient attacks but have weight-dependent natural noise robustness, systematic overconfidence issues, and mechanistic fragility in decoder routing.
AI.motivation: To systematically evaluate Diffusion Language Models' reliability under natural input noise and adversarial attacks compared to autoregressive baselines, as their robustness properties remain under-explored despite advantages like bidirectional context.
AI.method: Used parameter-matched pairs (LLaDA-8B vs. LLaMA-3-8B, Dream-7B vs. Qwen2.5-7B) with 32 natural perturbation conditions, adversarial gradient probes, and mechanistic hidden-state analyses to isolate architecture-intrinsic properties from weight-dependent behaviors.
AI.result: DLMs show nuanced robustness: resist gradient-based adversarial attacks due to stochastic loss landscapes but lack guaranteed defense against natural noise (weight-dependent). They exhibit systematic overconfidence and mechanistic probing reveals perfect input corruption encoding with decoder routing failures causing behavioral fragility.
AI.conclusion: DLM robustness cannot be superficially patched; it must be fundamentally integrated into the iterative decoding loop, as surface-level prompt modifications fail to improve over noisy baselines.

title: APO: Unsupervised Atomic Policy Optimization for 3D Structure Prediction of Atomic Systems
summary: Predicting the 3D structures of atomic systems is fundamental to advancing material science and drug discovery. While flow-matching models (, FlowDPO) have recently shown promise in this domain, their performance relies heavily on alignment with ground-truth coordinates via supervised preference learning. However, obtaining experimental labels for novel crystal phases or de novo proteins is prohibitively expensive, creating a bottleneck for structural modeling in data-scarce regimes. In this work, we propose (Atomic Policy Optimization), a fully unsupervised alignment framework that eliminates the need for ground-truth reference structures. APO adapts group-relative policy optimization to 3D atomic environments, utilizing a novel dual-reward mechanism: (i) a that reinforces the policy's dominant latent structural modes through eigen-decomposition of sample similarities, and (ii) a that enforces thermodynamic stability. Our framework enables the model to ``self-correct'' by identifying physically plausible configurations within sampled groups. Extensive benchmarks on crystal and antibody structure prediction demonstrate that APO consistently outperforms fully supervised baselines, achieving a new state-of-the-art in match rates and structural fidelity. Furthermore, we show that APO effectively straightens probability paths, significantly improving inference efficiency. Our results suggest that intrinsic physical consistency can serve as a superior guide for alignment compared to noisy, supervised coordinate matching.

AI.tldr: APO is an unsupervised framework for 3D atomic structure prediction that eliminates need for ground-truth labels by using group-relative policy optimization with dual rewards for structural consistency and thermodynamic stability.
AI.motivation: Current flow-matching models rely on expensive experimental labels for novel crystal phases or de novo proteins, creating bottlenecks in data-scarce regimes where obtaining ground-truth structures is prohibitively expensive.
AI.method: Atomic Policy Optimization (APO) adapts group-relative policy optimization to 3D atomic environments with dual-reward mechanism: 1) Mode consistency reward using eigen-decomposition of sample similarities to reinforce dominant latent structural modes, and 2) Thermodynamic consistency reward to enforce physical stability.
AI.result: APO consistently outperforms fully supervised baselines on crystal and antibody structure prediction benchmarks, achieving new state-of-the-art in match rates and structural fidelity. It also effectively straightens probability paths, improving inference efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Intrinsic physical consistency serves as superior guide for alignment compared to noisy supervised coordinate matching, enabling effective "self-correction" through identification of physically plausible configurations within sampled groups without ground-truth references.

title: The Kinetics of Training: A Driven-Nucleation Rate Law for Emergence, Plasticity Loss, and Circuit Control in Language Models
summary:
A capability appears in a language model when the last parts of its circuit align in one stochastic attempt, and getting all but one right is worth nothing. We show this no-partial-credit joint alignment is the rate-limiting step of capability formation. Two fingerprints: in a shortcut-free apparatus a five-part circuit missing three waits as long as a three-part circuit missing three (1.19-1.37), so the wait counts missing parts, not size; and on Pythia across seven capabilities and three scales, ablating one part leaves a median 17% of the capability in 32 of 32 discriminating cells, where partial credit predicts 50-83% (p = 2e-10), while a random non-part head leaves 100%.
  One rare event whose barrier grows with missing parts yields a rate equation -- sites x attempts x drive x exp(-beta*K), minus destruction -- read three ways, each preregistered with frozen constants. Forward: a capability flat at baseline ignites at a step of our choosing once the mix passes a concentration floor (10/10 above, 0/12 below), and while still flat its arrival is datable from its precursor to 5% median error on six held-out models. Backward: the delay to learn a withheld capability grows with waiting until, past a critical step, it never ignites -- yet validation loss falls smoothly throughout, so standard monitors are blind to it. We locate the damage (heads commit to the base data) and isolate the cure: re-initializing only the query-key slices restores learnability (6/6) while the value slices do nothing (0/6). We prove the mechanism in a controlled gated-attention model: occupation forces a deadline whose consequences need no mixing assumption. Completed: SGD's noise fails the fluctuation-dissipation test, so we install one and anneal, melt and pin circuits on schedule. Scope: conjunction circuits in transformers to 1.4B.

AI.tldr: Capability formation in transformers requires full circuit alignment with no partial credit; rate-limiting step follows exponential decay law based on missing circuit parts, not model size.
AI.motivation: To understand why capability formation in language models appears abruptly and why partial circuit alignment provides little benefit, revealing the fundamental mechanics of capability emergence.
AI.method: Empirical analysis using Pythia models across scales, capability ablation experiments, controlled circuit timing tests, and mathematical modeling with rate equations. Includes intervention via query-key slice reinitialization and controlled gated-attention model experiments.
AI.result: Capability formation follows exponential decay law: wait time ~ exp(-β*K) where K is missing parts. Ablating one part leaves only 17% capability vs 50-83% predicted by partial credit models. Capabilities ignite only after reaching concentration threshold, and validation loss fails to signal unlearnable capabilities. Query-key slice reinitialization restores learnability (6/6).
AI.conclusion: Transformer capabilities emerge via rare, no-partial-credit events where all circuit parts must align simultaneously. This explains sudden capability emergence, provides predictive power for timing capability arrival, and reveals specific architectural vulnerabilities (query-key slices) that determine learnability.

title: Bridging Inference-Time Scaling and Episodic Memory with Action-Centric Graphs
summary: Recent advancements in inference-time scaling have significantly unlocked the complex reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models~(LLMs). However, for agents, these approaches suffer from a critical inefficiency, operating in a stateless manner and engaging in redundant search processes. Existing memory mechanisms largely rely on the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, leading to prohibitive computational costs. In this paper, we propose a novel framework, \textit{GAMER}~(Graph-based Action-centric Memory with Episodic Reasoning), that bridges the gap between inference scaling and episodic memory. Our approach models historical reasoning as a dynamic \textit{Action-Centric Graph}. By decoupling the memory mechanism from LLMs, our method can save token/money usage by providing less memory context than memory mechanism baselines. To extract knowledge from the graph effectively, we use a dual-stream Temporal Difference learning mechanism to estimate the positive~(suggestion) and negative~(avoidance) value of action nodes based on past successes and failures. During the inference phase, this learned value function optimizes decision-making bi-directionally, so that positive values provide action suggestions, while negative values indicate high-risk actions. By performing efficient searches on the graph, our method significantly improves the efficiency of inference scaling. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that \textit{GAMER} achieves superior performance by \textbf{20.81\%/6.17\%} for success/progress rate compared to vanilla baselines.

AI.tldr: GAMER introduces a graph-based memory framework that decouples memory from LLMs to improve inference-time scaling for AI agents, reducing redundant search and computational costs while achieving significant performance gains.
AI.motivation: Current inference-time scaling approaches for LLM agents are inefficient because they operate statelessly with redundant search processes. Existing memory mechanisms rely too heavily on LLM reasoning, leading to prohibitive computational costs and token usage.
AI.method: The proposed GAMER framework models historical reasoning as a dynamic Action-Centric Graph, decoupling memory from LLMs. It uses dual-stream Temporal Difference learning to estimate positive (suggestion) and negative (avoidance) values of action nodes based on past successes and failures. During inference, this learned value function optimizes decision-making bidirectionally through efficient graph searches.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple benchmarks show GAMER achieves 20.81% improvement in success rate and 6.17% improvement in progress rate compared to vanilla baselines, while reducing token/money usage by providing less memory context than memory mechanism baselines.
AI.conclusion: GAMER successfully bridges the gap between inference scaling and episodic memory by creating an efficient, decoupled memory system that improves agent reasoning efficiency and performance while reducing computational costs.

title: Benchmarking the Residual: What Long-Horizon Evaluations Add Beyond Matched Short-Task Performance
summary: Long-horizon benchmarks often show that agents fail more as tasks become longer. This observation is useful for deployment, but it does not by itself explain why failure occurs. More stages create more opportunities for ordinary errors to compound; longer tasks may also contain harder individual decisions or become harder as conversation history, tool outputs, and environment changes accumulate. We use trajectory-induced degradation to mean this last possibility: earlier execution makes later work harder. When the harmful accumulation is specifically the text visible to the model, it is often called context rot. In this position paper, we argue that to claim a "long-horizon failure", benchmarks must compare actual full-task success against a baseline prediction built from short, individual stages. We call the log-ratio between this prediction and actual success the horizon residual. The comparison must use the same agent configuration and specify in advance how stages, checkpoints, information, and budgets will be chosen. The residual shows that the full rollout differs from the chosen baseline; targeted experiments are still needed to explain why.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework for analyzing long-horizon failures in AI agents, introducing "horizon residual" - the log-ratio between predicted success (based on short stages) and actual full-task success - to distinguish between compounding errors and trajectory-induced degradation.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks show agents fail more on longer tasks, but don't explain why failures occur. There's a need to distinguish between different causes: ordinary errors compounding, harder individual decisions, or trajectory-induced degradation (where earlier execution makes later work harder).
AI.method: Proposes comparing actual full-task success against a baseline prediction built from short, individual stages using the same agent configuration. Introduces "horizon residual" (log-ratio between predicted and actual success) to measure the gap between full rollout and baseline prediction. Requires specifying stages, checkpoints, information, and budgets in advance.
AI.result: The horizon residual reveals whether full rollout performance differs significantly from what would be expected from individual stage performance. This framework enables distinguishing between different types of long-horizon failures, though targeted experiments are still needed to explain specific causes.
AI.conclusion: To properly claim "long-horizon failure," benchmarks must compare actual performance against stage-based predictions using the horizon residual framework. This provides a more rigorous way to analyze why agents fail on longer tasks, separating trajectory-induced degradation from other failure modes.

title: Dimensionality and Measurement Precision in HLE's Multiple-Choice Subset
summary: Humanity's Last Exam (HLE) is widely used to evaluate frontier language models. HLE organizes its questions into eight subject-domain categories, whose subscores are often interpreted as evidence of distinct capabilities. However, no study has assessed whether these labels correspond to empirically separable latent constructs, nor whether the benchmark effectively differentiates between models of similar ability. We evaluate 29 LLMs on the text-only multiple-choice subset of HLE ($J = 428$ items) and apply psychometric methods to assess both the dimensionality of the benchmark and the distribution of its measurement precision. Fitting a two-parameter logistic IRT model, we find convergent evidence that HLE measures a single general reasoning factor: McDonald's $ω_h = 0.998$, domain labels explain only 3.5\% of item response variance, within- and between-domain residual correlations are nearly identical (Cohen's $d = 0.016$), and domain-specific ability estimates are near-redundant with the total score ($r \geq 0.81$). A separate analysis of the test information function reveals that measurement precision concentrates at moderate ability levels and drops sharply above $θ= 0$, where frontier models sit. These findings suggest that HLE's domain subscores do not warrant distinct capability interpretations and that the benchmark's ability to discriminate among the strongest models is limited.

AI.tldr: HLE benchmark primarily measures a single general reasoning factor rather than distinct domain-specific capabilities, and has limited precision for discriminating top-performing models.
AI.motivation: The Human Last Exam (HLE) benchmark's domain subscores are often interpreted as evidence of distinct capabilities, but no study has validated whether these labels correspond to empirically separable latent constructs or whether the benchmark effectively differentiates between models of similar ability.
AI.method: Evaluated 29 LLMs on the text-only multiple-choice subset of HLE (428 items) using psychometric methods. Applied two-parameter logistic IRT modeling to assess dimensionality and measurement precision. Used McDonald's ω_h for factor analysis, examined variance explained by domain labels, compared residual correlations, and analyzed test information function.
AI.result: 1) HLE measures a single general reasoning factor (ω_h = 0.998). 2) Domain labels explain only 3.5% of item response variance. 3) Within- and between-domain residual correlations are nearly identical (Cohen's d = 0.016). 4) Domain-specific ability estimates are highly redundant with total score (r ≥ 0.81). 5) Measurement precision concentrates at moderate ability levels and drops sharply above θ=0 where frontier models sit.
AI.conclusion: HLE's domain subscores should not be interpreted as distinct capabilities, and the benchmark has limited ability to discriminate among the strongest models due to low measurement precision at higher ability levels.

title: TIER-MoE: Trust-Informed Expert Routing via Conditional Modality Risk for Multimodal Fusion in Biomedical Classification
summary: The promise of multimodal fusion lies in combining complementary sources of evidence, yet more evidence does not always yield a better prediction. Recent multimodal models have advanced fusion through richer cross-modal interaction and sample-adaptive fusion. However, the influence assigned to a modality during fusion does not reveal whether that source is unreliable, redundant, or poorly matched to a specialized expert. To address this limitation, we introduce TIER-MoE, a risk-guided subspace mixture-of-experts model that defines sample-specific modality reliability as the prediction loss its unimodal predictor is expected to incur. This risk is learned from out-of-fold predictions generated by models that were not trained on the corresponding sample. TIER-MoE combines the estimated risk with expert-specific subspace compatibility for sparse modality-expert routing, while an always-active shared path preserves multimodal complementarity. We evaluate TIER-MoE on four public multimodal biomedical datasets spanning Alzheimer's disease status, skin-lesion malignancy, and retinal classification. Results demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art methods in predictive performance and probability calibration, with consistent improvements in Macro-F1 and Brier score and strong zero-shot generalization to an external cohort.

AI.tldr: TIER-MoE is a risk-guided subspace mixture-of-experts model that uses out-of-fold prediction loss to estimate modality reliability and enables sparse modality-expert routing while preserving multimodal complementarity through a shared path.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal fusion models assign influence to modalities without revealing whether the source is unreliable, redundant, or poorly matched to specialized experts. The limitation is that more evidence doesn't always yield better predictions, necessitating a way to assess modality reliability at the sample level.
AI.method: TIER-MoE defines sample-specific modality reliability as the prediction loss its unimodal predictor is expected to incur, learned from out-of-fold predictions. It combines estimated risk with expert-specific subspace compatibility for sparse modality-expert routing, while maintaining an always-active shared path to preserve multimodal complementarity.
AI.result: Evaluation on four public multimodal biomedical datasets (Alzheimer's disease, skin-lesion malignancy, and retinal classification) shows superiority over state-of-the-art methods in predictive performance and probability calibration, with consistent improvements in Macro-F1 and Brier score, plus strong zero-shot generalization to an external cohort.
AI.conclusion: TIER-MoE effectively addresses the limitation of not knowing whether a modality is unreliable, redundant, or mismatched to experts by using risk-guided subspace routing, resulting in better multimodal fusion performance and calibration while maintaining complementary information through a shared path.

title: Leveraging Trajectory Graphs for Pre-Execution Error Diagnosis in Agentic LLM Systems
summary: Large Language Model~(LLM)-based agents have demonstrated exceptional performance across a wide range of complex interactive tasks. However, they often struggle with long-horizon interactive tasks common in domains, such as embodied AI. The complexity and vast action spaces in these settings lead to compounding errors, where a single suboptimal action can derail an entire trajectory, causing the agent to exhaust its limited step budget on inefficient or unrecoverable paths. To overcome this without costly fine-tuning, we draw inspiration from software debugging, where execution logs are analyzed to preemptively catch errors. We propose \textit{Trajectory Graph Copilot}, a novel framework that acts as a ``copilot'' for LLM agents by diagnosing potential action errors before they are executed. At its core,\textit{Graph Debugger} models historical trajectories as a probabilistic graph and uses a Graph Neural Network to identify sequential action patterns that frequently lead to failure. Functioning as a proactive diagnostic sandbox, our method provides early warnings on potentially flawed actions, prompting the agent to self-correct. This pre-action error diagnosis prevents costly mistakes, significantly enhancing the agent's ability to complete long-horizon tasks successfully. The extensive experiments on four benchmarks with three LLM agents demonstrate a $14.69\%$ pass ratio improvement on average.

AI.tldr: Trajectory Graph Copilot is a framework that uses graph neural networks to proactively identify and prevent action errors in LLM agents during long-horizon interactive tasks, achieving significant performance improvements without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents struggle with long-horizon interactive tasks in domains like embodied AI, where complex action spaces lead to compounding errors - a single suboptimal action can derail entire trajectories, causing agents to exhaust their limited step budgets on inefficient paths.
AI.method: The proposed Trajectory Graph Copilot framework includes a Graph Debugger that models historical trajectories as a probabilistic graph and uses a Graph Neural Network to identify sequential action patterns that frequently lead to failure. It acts as a proactive diagnostic sandbox providing early warnings on potentially flawed actions before execution, prompting agents to self-correct.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four benchmarks with three LLM agents demonstrate a 14.69% pass ratio improvement on average, showing the framework effectively prevents costly mistakes and enhances agents' ability to complete long-horizon tasks successfully.
AI.conclusion: The Trajectory Graph Copilot framework successfully addresses the challenge of compounding errors in long-horizon interactive tasks by providing pre-action error diagnosis, significantly improving LLM agent performance without requiring costly fine-tuning.

title: EvoCause: LLM-Guided Evolution of Causal Graphs for Root Cause Analysis
summary: Modern telecommunication, cloud, and microservice systems emit correlated alarm cascades when components fail. Root cause analysis (RCA) aims to identify the small set of alarms that initiate each cascade. A common approach learns a causal graph from observational logs and predicts all zero-in-degree alarms in each incident-induced subgraph. However, the learned graph remains fixed and cannot benefit from expert diagnoses of historical incidents. We close this loop with EvoCause. Expert labels constrain which alarms should be source nodes but do not specify the edge edits needed to satisfy those constraints. EvoCause uses a large language model (LLM) to propose semantically plausible graph edits, while deterministic code validates node identities and acyclicity and retains the best graph on a labeled alignment set. At test time, the refined graph alone produces transparent predictions without an LLM call. We also release TeleRCA, an expert-annotated benchmark from a production telecommunication network containing $485{,}681$ alarm events spanning $194$ alarm types over $5{,}621$ resources. On synthetic data, EvoCause initialized with the PC causal discovery algorithm outperforms the unrefined PC baseline, raising Node F1, Case EM, and Graph F1 by $11.59$, $9.40$, and $4.59$ percentage points, respectively, while reducing nSHD by $0.2379$. On TeleRCA, replacing human-readable alarm titles with anonymous identifiers lowers Node F1 and Case EM by $6.12$ and $8.04$ percentage points, respectively, indicating that alarm-name information contributes to graph refinement.

AI.tldr: EvoCause improves RCA in telecom systems by using LLMs to refine causal graphs with expert feedback, outperforming baselines on synthetic and real benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional root cause analysis learns fixed causal graphs from alarm logs but cannot incorporate expert diagnoses of historical incidents, creating a missed opportunity for improvement.
AI.method: EvoCause uses LLMs to propose semantically plausible graph edits constrained by expert labels, with deterministic code validating node identities and acyclicity, then retains the best graph on labeled alignment set for transparent predictions.
AI.result: On synthetic data, EvoCause outperforms PC baseline with 11.59pp Node F1, 9.40pp Case EM, 4.59pp Graph F1 gains; real TeleRCA benchmark shows alarm-name information contributes significantly to refinement (6.12-8.04pp drops without it).
AI.conclusion: EvoCause successfully closes the loop between expert knowledge and automated RCA by refining causal graphs through LLM-proposed semantic edits, demonstrating significant performance improvements while maintaining transparent predictions.

title: VAmoS Bench: Voice Agent Simulation Bench
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Agent implementations: https://github.com/veris-ai/riley-agent
summary: Production voice agents span cascaded, speech-to-speech, and hybrid architectures. Voice-agent benchmarks typically measure component quality and conversational properties such as word error rate, latency, naturalness, and turn-taking. Fewer measure whether the agent handled a phone call correctly on its own. Contact centers refer to this as ``containment'': the share of phone calls the automated system resolves without handing off to a human. On some phone calls the right outcome is refusal or a redirect. To address this gap, we introduce VAmoS Bench, the Voice Agent Simulation Bench. It measures complete voice-agent systems end to end in a stateful customer-support task. The agent is Riley, a credit-card support representative for a fictional bank who can freeze, cancel, replace, or activate a card. Each of 100 scenarios supplies a simulated caller with a private goal and a seeded PostgreSQL backend. The platform uses each scenario to populate and activate an isolated simulation in which the caller reaches Riley over audio; roughly one-third apply adversarial pressure. The agent can use five tools that execute real SQL against the backend. Each scenario also defines binary assertions. A grader evaluates them against the complete trace of what the caller and agent said and what the agent did, including tool invocations, arguments, and returned rows. This catches an agent that claims to have changed a card without updating the database, as well as one that makes the right database change while disclosing protected information. This first benchmark version focuses on financial services. Its evaluation protocol supports an evolving leaderboard: additional voice agents can be evaluated on the same version, while later versions can expand the tasks and scenarios.

AI.tldr: VAmoS Bench is a new benchmark for evaluating complete voice-agent systems in customer-support tasks, focusing on whether agents can handle phone calls correctly on their own (containment) rather than just measuring component quality.
AI.motivation: Current voice-agent benchmarks mainly measure component quality (word error rate, latency, naturalness, turn-taking) but don't adequately measure whether the agent can correctly handle phone calls independently without human handoff. There's a need to evaluate "containment" - the ability to resolve calls autonomously.
AI.method: VAmoS Bench is a stateful customer-support simulation platform with 100 scenarios featuring simulated callers with private goals and a seeded PostgreSQL backend. The agent (Riley, a credit-card support rep) interacts with callers over audio and can use five SQL tools. Each scenario defines binary assertions evaluated by a grader against complete traces of interactions, speech, and tool usage.
AI.result: The benchmark provides an end-to-end evaluation framework that can catch agents that claim actions without database changes or make correct database changes while disclosing protected information. Roughly one-third of scenarios apply adversarial pressure to test robustness.
AI.conclusion: VAmoS Bench addresses the gap in complete voice-agent system evaluation, focusing on practical "containment" measurement in financial services customer support. It supports an evolving leaderboard and can be expanded to more tasks and scenarios in future versions.

title: THGFM: Dual-Branch Temporal Heterogeneous Graph Fusion Model
summary: Temporal heterogeneous graphs offer a natural abstraction for dynamic relational systems in which diverse node and relation types co-exist and evolve over time. Learning on such graphs requires jointly modeling cross-type structural heterogeneity and the temporal dynamics of interactions, yet existing methods still struggle to reconcile parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with relation-aware specialization, and typically inject time only as additive features outside the attention kernel. We propose \textbf{THGFM}, a web-scale temporal heterogeneous graph fusion model that addresses both limitations within a unified dual-path architecture. THGFM couples a \textit{Shared-Space Temporal Attention} branch for parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with a \textit{Relational Type-Partitioned Temporal Attention} branch for relation-aware specialization, and integrates them through \textit{Dual-Path Relational--Shared Fusion}, instantiated with \textit{Type-Conditioned Non-Competitive Gated Sum Fusion}: a adaptive mechanism that assigns independent, type-conditioned feature-wise gates to the shared and specialized branches, allowing both to be amplified or suppressed without zero-sum competition. To directly incorporate relative time into the attention score, THGFM further introduces \textit{Rotary Temporal Attention}, which rotates queries and keys by half-phases of relative time before matching. THGFM consistently outperforms baseline graph transformer models on academic graphs benchmarks, delivering a $+3.25\%$ six-task mean gain, with peak relative gains of $+12.37\%$ on OAG-CS PV, $+4.87\%$ on PF-$L_2$, and $+1.18\%$ on PF-$L_1$, and $+4.24\%$, $+3.73\%$, and $+4.61\%$ on OGBN-MAG, HTAG-ArXiv, and HTAG-DBLP, respectively.

AI.tldr: THGFM is a temporal heterogeneous graph model with dual-path architecture combining shared-space attention for cross-type transfer and relational partitioned attention for specialization, using rotary temporal encoding and adaptive fusion mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Existing methods struggle to reconcile parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with relation-aware specialization, and typically only add time as external features rather than integrating it into attention mechanisms.
AI.method: Proposes dual-path architecture with Shared-Space Temporal Attention for cross-type transfer and Relational Type-Partitioned Temporal Attention for specialization, fused via Type-Conditioned Non-Competitive Gated Sum Fusion. Uses Rotary Temporal Attention to directly incorporate relative time into attention scores.
AI.result: Outperforms baseline graph transformer models with +3.25% six-task mean gain, achieving peak gains up to +12.37% on OAG-CS PV, +4.87% on PF-L₂, and improvements on multiple academic graph benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: THGFM effectively addresses limitations of existing methods by unifying efficient cross-type transfer with relation-aware specialization and properly integrating temporal dynamics into attention mechanisms.

title: Position, Not Provenance: Separating Reasoning Mediation from Sycophancy in Medical Vision-Language Models
summary: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) generate chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning before answering clinical questions, but whether this reasoning causally influences predictions remains unclear. We present CoT-Mediate, a behavioral framework that perturbs a single clinically meaningful attribute within a model's own generated reasoning and measures whether the resulting prediction follows the edited reasoning. Our framework combines a dual-arm protocol comparing re-prompted evidence with prefix-forced continuation, together with a provenance-controlled intervention that varies only the attributed source of identical reasoning to disentangle reasoning mediation from sycophancy. We evaluate LLaVA-Med and MedGemma on 1,000 VQA-RAD samples each. Prefix-forced continuation consistently yields higher mediation faithfulness than re-prompting, while the provenance analysis reveals distinct model-specific deference behaviors. Across both models, removing visual evidence increases reliance on injected reasoning, whereas laterality is the least faithfully tracked clinical attribute. These results show that the mechanism used to inject reasoning substantially affects measured faithfulness and that contextual position, rather than stated provenance, is the primary determinant of whether medical VLMs use their generated reasoning.

AI.tldr: A framework called CoT-Mediate reveals that medical vision-language models often don't causally use their generated chain-of-thought reasoning, and the method of reasoning injection significantly affects measured faithfulness.
AI.motivation: Medical VLMs generate chain-of-thought reasoning before answering clinical questions, but it's unclear whether this reasoning actually causally influences the model's predictions or is just performative.
AI.method: Developed CoT-Mediate framework that perturbs single clinically meaningful attributes in the model's own generated reasoning, then measures if predictions follow the edited reasoning. Uses dual-arm protocol comparing re-prompted evidence vs prefix-forced continuation, plus provenance-controlled intervention to disentangle reasoning mediation from sycophancy.
AI.result: Prefix-forced continuation yields higher mediation faithfulness than re-prompting. Provenance analysis reveals distinct model-specific deference behaviors. Removing visual evidence increases reliance on injected reasoning, while laterality is the least faithfully tracked clinical attribute. Contextual position is primary determinant of whether medical VLMs use generated reasoning.
AI.conclusion: The mechanism used to inject reasoning substantially affects measured faithfulness, and contextual position (not stated provenance) is the main factor determining whether medical VLMs use their generated reasoning, raising questions about the reliability of chain-of-thought in clinical applications.

title: INCLAIR: Inception-Based Longitudinal Clinical Anomaly Detection with Informed Reasoning
summary: Detecting anomalies in longitudinal clinical profiles is clinically important but difficult: abnormal evidence is often sparse, patient histories have unequal length, and expert explanations are costly. We propose INCLAIR, a framework that scores each observation against multiple historical contexts, aggregates evidence at the profile level, and generates grounded natural-language explanations under limited expert supervision. Under stated within-profile exchangeability assumptions, the complete mean subsequence score takes an order-$l$ U-statistic form, yielding a variance decomposition and an incomplete-subset approximation that controls combinatorial inference cost independently of profile length. The same analysis shows that mean aggregation attenuates localized anomalies by a factor set by the anomaly support and profile length, motivating validation-selected top-$k$ pooling. Across three clinical datasets, INCLAIR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. We further validate practical relevance through a case study on longitudinal steroid profiles, comparing INCLAIR's predictions and explanations against domain-expert assessments supported by DNA analysis. The results show that INCLAIR enables clinically actionable anomaly detection under limited expert supervision.

AI.tldr: INCLAIR is a framework for detecting anomalies in longitudinal clinical data that scores observations against multiple historical contexts, aggregates evidence, and generates natural language explanations with limited expert supervision.
AI.motivation: Anomaly detection in longitudinal clinical profiles is challenging due to sparse abnormal evidence, variable patient history lengths, and high costs of obtaining expert explanations.
AI.method: INCLAIR scores observations against multiple historical contexts, aggregates evidence at profile level using mean subsequence scores (order-l U-statistics), and generates grounded natural-language explanations with limited expert supervision.
AI.result: INCLAIR outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across three clinical datasets, and a case study on longitudinal steroid profiles shows its predictions align well with domain expert assessments supported by DNA analysis.
AI.conclusion: INCLAIR enables clinically actionable anomaly detection under limited expert supervision by providing robust detection and meaningful explanations for sparse anomalies in longitudinal clinical data.

title: ZUNA1.1: A more flexible EEG foundation model for Denoising and Super-resolution
summary: We introduce ZUNA1.1, a 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder for flexible EEG signal reconstruction. ZUNA1.1 is capable of reconstructing variable length sequences of up to 30s, with an arbitrary number of EEG channels at arbitrary scalp locations, and can reconstruct arbitrary temporal intervals within channels in addition to reconstructing entire channels. We demonstrate that ZUNA1.1 performs at least on par with our earlier ZUNA1 model, while being far more flexible and capable of handling a wide range of reconstruction tasks. ZUNA1.1 continues to substantially outperform standard EEG denoising and reconstruction methods such as spherical spline interpolation, which is ubiquitously deployed in the MNE package. The ZUNA1.1 model is released open source under the permissive Apache 2.0 license.

AI.tldr: ZUNA1.1 is a 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder that enables highly flexible reconstruction of EEG signals with variable sequence lengths, arbitrary channel configurations, and selective temporal intervals.
AI.motivation: Current EEG signal reconstruction methods lack flexibility in handling variable sequence lengths, arbitrary numbers of channels at different scalp locations, and selective temporal intervals within channels. Standard methods like spherical spline interpolation (used in MNE) have limitations in performance and flexibility.
AI.method: The authors developed ZUNA1.1, a diffusion autoencoder architecture with 380 million parameters that can reconstruct EEG signals with: 1) variable length sequences up to 30s, 2) arbitrary numbers of EEG channels at arbitrary scalp locations, and 3) selective reconstruction of arbitrary temporal intervals within channels in addition to full channel reconstruction.
AI.result: ZUNA1.1 performs at least as well as the earlier ZUNA1 model while offering significantly greater flexibility for diverse reconstruction tasks. It substantially outperforms standard EEG denoising and reconstruction methods like spherical spline interpolation, which is widely used in the MNE neuroscience analysis package.
AI.conclusion: ZUNA1.1 represents a significant advancement in EEG signal reconstruction by providing a highly flexible, high-performance model that handles various real-world EEG analysis scenarios. The model is released as open source under the Apache 2.0 license, facilitating broader adoption in the neuroscience community.

title: MedLLM: An Open Medical Language Model at the Sub-Billion Scale
summary: Open medical language models have converged on a single scale: every widely used system runs at 7B parameters or more, leaving the sub-billion regime uncharacterized. We present MedLLM, an open 0.1B-parameter medical language model trained through a fully open three-phase pipeline: general pretraining with curriculum sequence-length scheduling, domain fine-tuning on MedFineWeb, a reference-guided medical corpus we release that is selected from general web data by embedding similarity to medical question-answering (QA) data, and preference-aligned fine-tuning combining SFT with direct preference optimization (DPO). Across medical benchmarks, MedLLM shows a pattern visible only at sub-billion scale: medical competence does not degrade uniformly under compression but splits by task type. On context-grounded QA it comes within $2.9$pp of a medically adapted 7B model and surpasses the instruction-tuned and general-purpose 7B baselines; on knowledge-recall QA it stays near the task floor on clinical-vignette MedQA yet significantly exceeds every 7B and sub-7B baseline on MedMCQA, indicating that where recall fails the constraint is model capacity rather than adaptation. This dissociation is masked at 7B, where both capabilities are present, and surfaces only when capacity is scarce.

AI.tldr: MedLLM is a 0.1B-parameter open medical language model that shows a surprising pattern: medical task performance doesn't degrade uniformly with smaller size but splits by task type, with near 7B performance on context-grounded QA while struggling more with knowledge recall tasks.
AI.motivation: Current open medical language models all operate at 7B parameters or more, leaving the sub-billion parameter regime unexplored. The authors want to understand how medical competence scales down to smaller model sizes and what patterns emerge when model capacity is scarce.
AI.method: Three-phase open training pipeline: 1) General pretraining with curriculum sequence-length scheduling, 2) Domain fine-tuning on MedFineWeb (a medical corpus selected from web data using embedding similarity to medical QA data), 3) Preference-aligned fine-tuning combining supervised fine-tuning with direct preference optimization (DPO).
AI.result: MedLLM shows that medical competence doesn't degrade uniformly under compression - it splits by task type. On context-grounded QA, it comes within 2.9 percentage points of medically-adapted 7B models and beats general 7B baselines. On knowledge-recall QA, it struggles on clinical vignette MedQA but significantly exceeds all 7B and sub-7B baselines on MedMCQA.
AI.conclusion: At sub-billion scale, medical capabilities dissociate by task type - context-grounded QA remains strong while knowledge recall suffers due to capacity constraints. This dissociation is masked at 7B where both capabilities are present, revealing that different medical tasks have different capacity requirements.

title: Modeling Decisions in Blockchain Analytics: A Leakage-Aware Evaluation of Tree-Based vs. Sequential Models
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 23rd International Conference on Modeling Decisions for Artificial Intelligence (MDAI 2026)
summary: Sybil bots are Ethereum actors that imitate legitimate users to extract airdrop rewards or influence governance. Recent Sybil detection methods increasingly use deep learning and treat blockchain activity as a quasi-linguistic sequence. However, complex sequence models are computationally expensive for real-time monitoring, and their reported performance may be inflated by label leakage from high-signal smart contracts. We ask whether and how organic users, Sybil bots, and MEV bots differ in the structural complexity of their transaction histories; whether sequential models outperform tree-based tabular models once leakage is reduced; whether transaction order or timing provides the stronger behavioral signal; and whether the resulting models are practical for low-latency deployment. Our approach to leakage-aware Sybil bot detection consists of a Blind-Spot protocol and a Transaction Grammar representation of wallet behavior. The former eliminates shortcuts associated with high-signal contracts, whereas the latter models wallets using rhythm, EVM execution structure, and intent. We evaluate this approach on Ethereum actor classification by comparing Transformer and BiLSTM sequence models against XGBoost and SVM baselines. We contribute a framework for leakage-aware Ethereum actor classification and a Transaction Grammar representation of wallet behavior. Our results demonstrate that, under leakage-aware evaluation, XGBoost outperforms Transformer-based sequence models while providing lower latency and estimated energy use.

AI.tldr: XGBoost outperforms Transformer models for Sybil bot detection when accounting for label leakage, offering lower latency and energy use while using transaction structure complexity features instead of sequential modeling.
AI.motivation: Recent Sybil detection methods use deep learning on blockchain sequences but face issues: 1) computationally expensive for real-time monitoring, 2) potentially inflated performance from label leakage through high-signal smart contracts, 3) need to understand whether organic users, Sybil bots, and MEV bots differ in transaction structural complexity.
AI.method: Proposes a leakage-aware Sybil detection approach with: 1) Blind-Spot protocol to eliminate shortcuts from high-signal contracts, 2) Transaction Grammar representation capturing wallet behavior through rhythm, EVM execution structure, and intent. Compares Transformer and BiLSTM sequence models against XGBoost and SVM baselines for Ethereum actor classification.
AI.result: Under leakage-aware evaluation, XGBoost outperforms Transformer-based sequence models. XGBoost also provides lower latency and estimated energy use compared to complex sequential models.
AI.conclusion: Tree-based tabular models (XGBoost) are more practical than sequential deep learning models for real-time Sybil detection when properly accounting for label leakage, with better performance, lower latency, and reduced energy consumption using Transaction Grammar features.

title: A dataset of rated conceptual arguments
summary: Large language models have improved rapidly on tasks with verifiable answers, such as mathematics and programming. Much less is known about their ability to reason about what we call conceptual questions: questions for which no ground truth is realistically accessible and no widely accepted resolution methodology exists, but on which progress can still be made by debating arguments. Most philosophical questions are of this kind, as are central components of questions in AI safety, decision theory, and social choice. Our approach is based on the view that while bottom-line conclusions on such questions are hard to evaluate, individual contextualized arguments can be evaluated far more reliably. We therefore introduce a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques of 442 position texts, spanning topics from AI safety and decision theory to ethics and politics, with 1,458 ratings by six expert raters along dimensions including centrality, strength, correctness, and clarity. We propose two scoring functions and benchmark a range of models. Performance tracks general capability rankings.

AI.tldr: LLMs are tested on evaluating conceptual arguments (AI safety, ethics, etc.) where ground truth is inaccessible, using a dataset of 951 critiques rated by experts across multiple dimensions.
AI.motivation: While LLMs perform well on tasks with verifiable answers (math, programming), their ability to reason about conceptual questions - where no ground truth exists but progress can be made through argument evaluation - is largely unknown. This gap is important because many philosophical, AI safety, decision theory, and social choice questions fall into this category.
AI.method: Created a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques of 442 position texts across AI safety, decision theory, ethics, and politics. Six expert raters provided 1,458 ratings along dimensions including centrality, strength, correctness, and clarity. Two scoring functions were proposed to evaluate models' performance on argument evaluation.
AI.result: Tested a range of models and found that performance tracks general capability rankings - more capable models generally perform better at evaluating conceptual arguments, suggesting this ability emerges alongside other reasoning capabilities.
AI.conclusion: While evaluating bottom-line conclusions on conceptual questions is difficult, individual contextualized arguments can be evaluated more reliably. The work establishes a benchmark for assessing LLMs' ability to reason about questions without clear ground truth, which is crucial for domains like AI safety and ethics.

title: Compression-Based Behavioral Similarity for Open-World Sybil Discovery on Ethereum
comment: Accepted as a full paper and scheduled for presentation at the European Conference on Advances in Databases and Information Systems (ADBIS 2026)
summary: Sybil attackers are Blockchain actors that adopt the characteristics of regular users to exploit airdrops or influence governance. Current methods of Sybil actor detection include constructing graphs, which requires token transfers between examined wallets. Machine learning algorithms have been employed as well, but they treat the task as a closed-set classification problem, making them vulnerable to frequent changes in attack strategies or evasion tactics. We address the following questions: can compression-based similarity differentiate Sybil bots, organic users, and arbitrage bot wallets without direct financial links? What is the effect of high-signal contracts on the discovery of Sybils, and how robust are behavioral graphs under temporal drift and adversarial perturbations? Our approach synthesizes a symbolic Transaction Grammar from EVM (Ethereum Virtual Machine) traces, capturing separately transaction rhythm, execution structure, and functional intent. The high-signal contracts are filtered with our own protocol, called the Blind-Spot Protocol. Gzip-based NCD is used to construct a behavioral graph for Sybil discovery. We validate this framework against supervised machine learning baselines, a temporal split, and synthetic camouflage stress tests. Ultimately, we contribute a leakage-aware behavioral framework for Sybil candidate discovery. Its core NCD primitive requires no supervised training and can expand suspicious seed wallets without explicit funding links. We position the method as a training-free local discovery primitive for open-world blockchain audits, rather than as a formal open-set recognition system.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a compression-based behavioral framework for detecting Sybil actors in blockchain networks without requiring direct financial links between wallets, using symbolic transaction grammar and Gzip-based NCD for similarity measurement.
AI.motivation: Current Sybil detection methods have limitations: graph-based approaches require token transfers between wallets, and machine learning methods treat the problem as closed-set classification, making them vulnerable to evolving attack strategies and evasion tactics. The authors aim to address whether compression-based similarity can differentiate Sybil bots from legitimate users without direct financial links.
AI.method: The approach synthesizes a symbolic Transaction Grammar from EVM traces, capturing transaction rhythm, execution structure, and functional intent. High-signal contracts are filtered using a Blind-Spot Protocol. Gzip-based Normalized Compression Distance (NCD) constructs behavioral graphs for Sybil discovery without requiring supervised training.
AI.result: The framework is validated against supervised machine learning baselines, temporal splits, and synthetic camouflage stress tests. The method proves effective at discovering Sybil candidates without explicit funding links, demonstrating robustness under temporal drift and adversarial perturbations.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes a leakage-aware behavioral framework for Sybil candidate discovery that doesn't require supervised training and can expand suspicious seed wallets without explicit funding links. It positions the method as a training-free local discovery primitive for open-world blockchain audits rather than a formal open-set recognition system.

title: Automated Transcript Analysis for Detecting Flaws in Agentic Benchmarks
summary: Capabilities of frontier models are often assessed using agentic benchmarks. To trust these results, benchmarks must accurately measure what they claim to and be free from invalidating flaws. Previous manual audits of benchmarks such as SWE-Bench-Verified have uncovered several validity issues in transcripts. However, manual review is difficult to scale, and it is unclear whether automated methods can reliably surface flaws that compromise benchmark validity. In this paper, we developed AI scanners to detect four types of validity issues: ground truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, and answer format ambiguity. We produced grading rubrics for each to instruct human labeling, and evaluated the scanners against human labels on a held-out test set of Inspect Evals benchmarks. Our scanners identified several verified quality issues in five widely used benchmarks, including cases unlikely to be caught by random manual inspection. Not all cases were identified, and scanner performance varied substantially across benchmarks, criteria and models. We highlight several open challenges to be addressed to improve scanners for stronger quality assurance claims, including broader standardization gaps in the evaluation field that degrade scanner performance. Together, these results serve as a proof of concept for using automated transcript analysis to audit benchmark quality more broadly.

AI.tldr: AI scanners can detect validity flaws in agentic benchmarks, but performance varies across benchmarks and criteria, highlighting challenges for automated benchmark quality assurance.
AI.motivation: Agentic benchmarks are used to assess frontier models, but their validity is crucial for trusting results. Manual audits (like SWE-Bench-Verified) find validity issues but don't scale well, and it's unclear if automated methods can reliably detect benchmark-compromising flaws.
AI.method: Developed AI scanners to detect four validity issues: ground truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, and answer format ambiguity. Created grading rubrics for human labeling and evaluated scanners against human labels on held-out test sets from Inspect Evals benchmarks.
AI.result: Scanners identified verified quality issues in five widely used benchmarks, including cases unlikely to be caught by random manual inspection. Scanner performance varied substantially across benchmarks, criteria, and models, with not all cases identified.
AI.conclusion: Automated transcript analysis shows promise for broader benchmark quality auditing, but open challenges remain including standardization gaps that degrade scanner performance. Results serve as proof of concept for automated benchmark quality assurance.

title: Explorative Modeling: Unlocking a Third Pretraining Axis and End-to-End Generation
summary: The deep learning revolution, kicked off by AlexNet, taught us that end-to-end training beats decomposing a problem into hand-designed stages. Generative modeling, however, has remained the exception-despite generative models being remarkably capable, they are still not trained end-to-end. This is because, at its core, generative modeling is about handling distributions with many modes, and existing scalable approaches handle this the same way, by factoring the generation procedure, which prevents end-to-end generation. In this work, we introduce Explorative Modeling, a new paradigm that instead factors the training loop, exploring K candidate matches between model generations and data, and training on the best, so predictions commit to modes rather than blurring them. We find Explorative Models (XMs) useful in two settings. First, increasing exploration adds a third pretraining axis beyond parameters and data for existing generative models-where scaling exploration monotonically improves performance across both continuous and discrete domains (images, video, and language). Notably, gains from exploration increase with scale, climbing from 7% to 36% as data scales and from 13% to 23% as models grow, with efficiency gains more than doubling at 3x the compute. Concretely, exploration improves FLOP efficiency by 4.1x, sample efficiency by 6.2x, parameter efficiency by 47%, lifts the strongest of image-generation recipes to a near-state-of-the-art 1.43 FID on ImageNet without guidance, enables scaling how end-to-end existing models are, and unlocks scaling generalization. Second, XMs enable end-to-end reconstructive generative modeling, matching diffusion on control tasks with 16-256x fewer inference steps. Together, these results establish XMs as both a new pretraining axis for existing generative models and a standalone end-to-end generative modeling paradigm.

AI.tldr: Explorative Modeling introduces a new paradigm that factors training instead of generation, using K candidate matches to train on the best, enabling end-to-end generative modeling and improving performance across images, video, and language.
AI.motivation: While deep learning has embraced end-to-end training for most tasks, generative modeling remains an exception because existing approaches factor the generation procedure to handle multi-modal distributions, preventing true end-to-end generation.
AI.method: Explorative Modeling factors the training loop instead of the generation procedure. It explores K candidate matches between model generations and data, then trains on the best match, allowing predictions to commit to modes rather than blurring them across distributions.
AI.result: XMs add a third pretraining axis (beyond parameters and data) that monotonically improves performance across continuous and discrete domains. Gains increase with scale: from 7% to 36% with data scaling, 13% to 23% with model growth. Efficiency gains: 4.1x FLOP efficiency, 6.2x sample efficiency, 47% parameter efficiency. Achieves 1.43 FID on ImageNet without guidance. Enables end-to-end reconstructive modeling matching diffusion performance with 16-256x fewer inference steps.
AI.conclusion: Explorative Models establish both a new pretraining axis for existing generative models and a standalone end-to-end generative modeling paradigm, solving the core problem of multi-modal distribution handling that has prevented true end-to-end generative training.

title: AI Literacy: An Exercise in Power-Knowledge
summary: As generative artificial intelligence becomes one of the most significant systems of knowledge production in our society today, questions relating to who can access and shape that production grow increasingly important in our discourse. This paper argues that the existing frameworks for AI literacy, which are dominated by technical competency and responsible-use principles, are insufficient because they enforce a "consumer" orientation toward AI rather than fostering genuine epistemic agency. Based upon Foucault's concept of power-knowledge, Freire's pedagogy of critical consciousness, and scholarship of digital literacy, this paper proposes a reconceptualization of AI literacy as a critical practice that equips individuals not just to use AI systems, but to critically evaluate them, resist their structuring assumptions, and participate in their governance. The paper further argues that unequal access to AI tools in society recapitulates longstanding epistemic injustices, and that a literacy framework oriented toward empowerment must account for these structural inequities. A three-part framework of AI literacy based on the notions of contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance frames this literacy as a cultivation of epistemic "agents" rather than the training of competent consumers of AI-generated information.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a critical AI literacy framework that goes beyond technical competency to foster genuine epistemic agency and address structural inequities in AI access and governance.
AI.motivation: Existing AI literacy frameworks focus too much on technical competency and responsible use, creating a "consumer" orientation rather than fostering genuine epistemic agency. This consumer approach fails to address power imbalances in AI knowledge production and recapitulates epistemic injustices through unequal access to AI tools.
AI.method: The paper develops a theoretical framework drawing on Foucault's concept of power-knowledge, Freire's pedagogy of critical consciousness, and scholarship of digital literacy. It proposes a three-part framework of AI literacy based on contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance.
AI.result: The paper introduces a reconceptualized AI literacy framework that positions individuals as epistemic agents rather than consumers. This framework emphasizes: 1) contextual use (understanding how AI operates in specific contexts), 2) critical interrogation (questioning AI's structuring assumptions and power dynamics), and 3) participatory governance (engaging in AI system development and oversight).
AI.conclusion: A critical AI literacy framework is necessary to address power-knowledge relations in AI systems and combat epistemic injustices. By shifting from training competent consumers to cultivating epistemic agents, this approach enables individuals to critically evaluate AI systems, resist their biases, and participate meaningfully in AI governance while accounting for structural inequities in access.

title: The Convergence Behavior of Adam under Heavy-Tailed Noise
summary: We establish the first convergence guarantees for the plain vector-form \emph{Adam} optimizer under heavy-tailed stochastic noise. While several Adam variants are known to achieve optimal iteration complexity in bounded-variance nonconvex optimization, little is understood about their behavior when stochastic gradients admit only a bounded $p$-th central moment for some $p \in (1,2]$, a setting increasingly observed in modern deep learning. To address this gap, we generalize the recent online-to-nonconvex conversion framework to accommodate heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise. Building on this generalized framework, we develop a discounted regret analysis for Adam, without restrictive parameter coupling. Our results show that Adam converges to $(ρ,ε)$-stationary points under heavy-tailed noise. However, it exhibits a suboptimal iteration complexity and $p$-dependent convergence, a suboptimality that persists even in the bounded-variance case ($p=2$). When the domain radius is known and used to control the online-learner output, a standard setup in related literature, the convergence rate improves to match the optimal complexity. These findings provide new theoretical insight into the robustness and limitations of Adam in heavy-tailed regimes.

AI.tldr: Adam optimizer achieves convergence under heavy-tailed noise but shows suboptimal iteration complexity; convergence improves to optimal when domain radius is known.
AI.motivation: While Adam variants achieve optimal iteration complexity with bounded-variance noise, little is understood about their behavior under heavy-tailed stochastic noise where gradients only have bounded p-th central moments (p ∈ (1,2]), a setting increasingly observed in modern deep learning.
AI.method: Generalize the recent online-to-nonconvex conversion framework to accommodate heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise, then develop discounted regret analysis for Adam without restrictive parameter coupling.
AI.result: Adam converges to (ρ,ε)-stationary points under heavy-tailed noise, but exhibits suboptimal iteration complexity and p-dependent convergence (persisting even with p=2). Convergence rate improves to match optimal complexity when domain radius is known and used to control online-learner output.
AI.conclusion: The study provides new theoretical insight into Adam's robustness and limitations in heavy-tailed regimes, showing it converges but with suboptimal complexity unless domain information is available.

title: Using Large Language Models for Idea Generation in Innovation
summary: This research evaluates the efficacy of large language models (LLMs) in generating new product ideas.
