To do so, we compare three pools of ideas for new products targeted toward college students and priced at 50 dollars or less. The first pool of ideas was created by university students in a product design course before the availability of LLMs. The second and third pools of ideas were generated by GPT-4 from OpenAI using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, respectively. We evaluated idea quality using standard market research techniques to predict average purchase intent probability. We used text mining to assess idea similarity and human raters to evaluate idea novelty. We find that AI-generated ideas outperform human-generated ideas in terms of average purchase intent, with few-shot prompting yielding slightly higher intent than zero-shot prompting. However, AI-generated ideas are perceived as less novel and exhibit higher pairwise similarity, particularly with few-shot prompting, indicating a less diverse solution landscape. When focusing on the quality of the best ideas rather than the average ideas, we find that AI-generated ideas are seven times more likely to rank among the top 10 percent of ideas, demonstrating a significant advantage over human-generated ideas. We propose that this seven-to-one advantage is a conservative estimate because it does not account for the greater productivity of AI. Our findings suggest that despite some drawbacks, AI creativity presents a substantial benefit in generating high-quality ideas for new product development.

AI.tldr: AI-generated product ideas outperform human-generated ones in purchase intent, but are less novel and diverse. Few-shot prompting works best, and AI ideas are 7x more likely to be top-tier.
AI.motivation: To evaluate and compare the efficacy of large language models (LLMs) versus humans in generating new product ideas, specifically examining idea quality, novelty, and diversity.
AI.method: Compared three idea pools: (1) human-generated by university students pre-LLMs, (2) GPT-4 zero-shot prompted, (3) GPT-4 few-shot prompted. Evaluated using market research techniques for purchase intent probability, text mining for similarity, and human raters for novelty.
AI.result: AI-generated ideas outperformed human-generated in average purchase intent, with few-shot slightly better than zero-shot. However, AI ideas were less novel and had higher similarity (less diverse). Most significantly, AI ideas were 7 times more likely to rank in the top 10% of ideas.
AI.conclusion: Despite drawbacks in novelty and diversity, AI creativity provides substantial benefits for generating high-quality product ideas, with a conservative 7:1 advantage over humans that would be even greater considering AI's productivity.

title: FunL2O: LLM-Guided Feature Function Design for Learning to Optimize
summary: Learning-to-optimize (L2O) methods accelerate repeated optimization by training models to predict solutions, warm starts, branching decisions, or other forms of solver guidance. A critical yet largely overlooked component of these pipelines is the feature function that maps problem instances to inputs for machine learning models. Existing L2O methods typically rely on hand-crafted features, making representation design manual and largely fixed across domains. We introduce FunL2O, the first unified framework for automating feature design through LLM-driven program evolution for L2O. In a FunSearch-style loop, an LLM proposes executable feature functions, while a fixed evaluation process retrains the original L2O model and measures downstream optimization performance. We evaluate FunL2O on linear and quadratic programming tasks involving solution prediction and warm-starting, as well as on mixed-integer optimization tasks using GNN-guided backdoor branching and Predict-and-Search. Across continuous and discrete optimization tasks and four LLMs, the evolved features consistently outperform hand-crafted representations. These results establish LLM-driven feature evolution as a general and effective approach to automating representation design in L2O.

AI.tldr: FunL2O introduces the first LLM-driven framework for automated feature design in Learning-to-Optimize (L2O) methods, replacing hand-crafted features with evolved representations that consistently outperform manual designs across various optimization tasks.
AI.motivation: Current L2O methods rely on manually designed feature functions that are domain-specific, fixed, and don't adapt across different optimization problems. This manual representation design is a critical but overlooked bottleneck in L2O pipelines.
AI.method: FunL2O uses a FunSearch-style loop where an LLM proposes executable feature functions. These features are evaluated by retraining the original L2O model and measuring downstream optimization performance. The framework is applied to linear/quadratic programming tasks (solution prediction, warm-starting) and mixed-integer optimization tasks (GNN-guided backdoor branching, Predict-and-Search).
AI.result: Across continuous and discrete optimization tasks tested with four different LLMs, the evolved features consistently outperform hand-crafted representations. This demonstrates improved optimization performance through automated feature design.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven feature evolution is a general and effective approach for automating representation design in L2O methods, establishing a new paradigm for enhancing optimization performance through learned feature representations.

title: ECG-InterpBench: Benchmarking the Interpretability of ECG Foundation Models with Matched-Scale Sparse Autoencoders
comment: Research paper. Includes supplementary material and publicly available source code
summary: Existing benchmarks for electrocardiogram foundation models primarily evaluate downstream predictive performance, providing limited insight into whether their internal representations can be faithfully decomposed, clinically interpreted, or reproduced across independent analyses. We introduce ECG-InterpBench, a benchmark designed to systematically evaluate the interpretability of ECG foundation-model representations. ECG-InterpBench uses sparse autoencoders as standardized measurement instruments and matches their capacity across models to enable controlled comparisons. We evaluate six frozen ECG foundation models across five standardized encoder depths, five matched dictionary widths, and three random seeds, producing a 450-cell interpretability atlas comprising 75 exactly matched six-model comparison blocks. The benchmark evaluates complementary dimensions of representation interpretability, including sparse reconstruction fidelity, single-feature accessibility and coverage of 49 clinically meaningful ECG measurements, and cross-seed feature reproducibility. The evaluation further quantifies patient-sampling uncertainty, depth- and seed-dependent variation, and sensitivity to the sparsity parameterization. The benchmark reveals that ECG foundation models exhibit distinct interpretability profiles. A matched replication on MIMIC-IV-ECG confirms that reconstruction fidelity and clinical accessibility identify different leading models. The benchmark is accompanied by executable evaluation code, standardized manifests, cell-level metrics, and reproducibility audits. ECG-InterpBench complements performance-centered ECG benchmarks by providing a capacity-controlled and reproducible framework for comparing ECG foundation models across distinct dimensions of representation interpretability.

AI.tldr: ECG-InterpBench is a new benchmark for evaluating interpretability of ECG foundation models using standardized sparse autoencoders, enabling controlled comparisons across models on dimensions like reconstruction fidelity, clinical feature accessibility, and reproducibility.
AI.motivation: Existing ECG foundation model benchmarks focus mainly on downstream predictive performance but provide limited insight into whether internal representations can be faithfully decomposed, clinically interpreted, or reproduced across independent analyses.
AI.method: Uses sparse autoencoders as standardized measurement instruments with matched capacity across models. Evaluates six frozen ECG foundation models across five encoder depths, five dictionary widths, and three random seeds (450-cell atlas). Measures sparse reconstruction fidelity, accessibility of 49 clinically meaningful ECG measurements, and cross-seed feature reproducibility.
AI.result: Reveals distinct interpretability profiles across ECG foundation models. Matched replication on MIMIC-IV-ECG shows reconstruction fidelity and clinical accessibility identify different leading models. Provides comprehensive evaluation of patient-sampling uncertainty, depth/seed variation, and sparsity parameterization sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: ECG-InterpBench provides a capacity-controlled, reproducible framework for comparing ECG foundation models across distinct dimensions of representation interpretability, complementing existing performance-centered benchmarks.

title: DeepResearch Agent System
summary: The DeepResearch Agent System is a large language model system engineered for deep information retrieval, multi-step reasoning, and autonomous research tasks. Built upon a sparse activation architecture with 30 billion total parameters of which only 3 billion are activated per token, the system achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple agent search benchmarks while delivering 3.2 times faster inference compared to dense counterparts of equivalent scale. The system supports a 128K-token context window with hierarchical attention mechanisms that yield 18.7% accuracy and 23.4% recall improvements over standard long-context approaches. A dual-mode reasoning engine provides both a ReAct paradigm for basic multi-step problem solving and an IterResearch mode for high-performance iterative research with up to 20 reasoning steps, collectively delivering a 31.2% accuracy improvement over single-pass baselines. Multi-tool coordination integrates retrieval, computation, web search, and file parsing modules to achieve 92.1% tool-use accuracy. A reinforcement learning optimization framework based on the GRPO algorithm provides token-level policy gradients that improve training stability by 35% and accelerate convergence by 42%. An automated data synthesis pipeline with seed-based expansion achieves a 92.5% usability rate. Benchmark results include 87.3% on Humanity's Last Exam, 85.3% on BrowserComp Chinese, and 91.2% on WebWalkerQA. The system is fully open-sourced, including data synthesis, training, and inference code, and supports applications in academic research, business analysis, R&D support, and education.

AI.tldr: DeepResearch Agent System: A 30B sparse activation LLM system for autonomous research with 3.2x faster inference than dense models, featuring multi-step reasoning, 128K context, multi-tool coordination, and RL optimization, achieving SOTA on agent benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To create an efficient autonomous research agent system that can perform deep information retrieval and multi-step reasoning while overcoming the computational inefficiencies of dense large language models, particularly for long-context research tasks.
AI.method: Built on sparse activation architecture (30B total parameters, 3B activated per token) with hierarchical attention for 128K context, dual-mode reasoning (ReAct & IterResearch up to 20 steps), multi-tool coordination (retrieval, computation, web search, file parsing), RL optimization using GRPO algorithm, and automated data synthesis pipeline.
AI.result: Achieves 3.2x faster inference than dense counterparts, 18.7% accuracy and 23.4% recall improvements for long-context, 31.2% accuracy improvement over single-pass baselines, 92.1% tool-use accuracy, 35% training stability and 42% faster convergence improvement, with benchmark scores of 87.3% on Humanity's Last Exam, 85.3% on BrowserComp Chinese, and 91.2% on WebWalkerQA.
AI.conclusion: The DeepResearch Agent System demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on autonomous research benchmarks while being significantly more efficient than dense models, with its open-source release enabling applications in academic research, business analysis, R&D, and education.

title: Context-Informed Ship Trajectory Prediction via Conditional Attention
comment: Accepted for publication at the 2026 29th International Conference on Information Fusion (IEEE FUSION)
summary:
Long-term ship trajectory prediction is a fundamental capability for maritime safety and autonomous navigation. While recent Transformer-based architectures have improved forecasting horizons, they predominantly rely on historical kinematic states, treating vessel motion as an isolated system. In reality, maritime navigation is profoundly modulated by extrinsic factors like weather and constrained by static vessel characteristics. Existing multimodal approaches fundamentally model the joint distribution over states and contexts, treating environmental variables as peer features rather than encoding the directional physical dependence of vessel dynamics on environmental conditions.
  In this work, we propose the Conditional Informer, a novel encoder-decoder architecture that formulates trajectory prediction as a conditional generation task. We employ a dedicated Conditional Attention mechanism where the vessel state explicitly queries environmental contexts through cross-attention, encoding the physical prior that weather modulates - but is not generated by - vessel dynamics. Furthermore, to address the intermittency of real-world data, we introduce a Modality Masking training strategy to prevent catastrophic degradation during sensor fallback. Extensive experiments on AIS and ERA5 data demonstrate that our approach outperforms kinematic and concatenation-based baselines by 15.4% in prediction accuracy when context is available. Crucially, Modality Masking prevents shortcut learning, reducing fallback error by nearly an order of magnitude compared to unconstrained models.

AI.tldr: Conditional Informer architecture improves long-term ship trajectory prediction by modeling weather as a directional modulator of vessel dynamics rather than a peer feature, with modality masking to handle sensor fallback.
AI.motivation: Existing Transformer-based approaches treat vessel motion as isolated from environmental factors, modeling weather and vessel characteristics as joint features rather than encoding the physical dependence of vessel dynamics on environmental conditions. Real maritime navigation is profoundly affected by weather and constrained by static vessel characteristics.
AI.method: Proposed Conditional Informer with dedicated Conditional Attention mechanism where vessel state explicitly queries environmental contexts through cross-attention, encoding the physical prior that weather modulates but is not generated by vessel dynamics. Also introduced Modality Masking training strategy to prevent catastrophic degradation during sensor fallback.
AI.result: Outperforms kinematic and concatenation-based baselines by 15.4% in prediction accuracy when context is available. Modality Masking prevents shortcut learning, reducing fallback error by nearly an order of magnitude compared to unconstrained models.
AI.conclusion: Conditional formulation and modality masking enable more physically grounded and robust long-term ship trajectory prediction that properly handles the directional relationship between vessel dynamics and environmental factors.

title: What makes prompts a graph: necessary and sufficient conditions for prompt graph engineering
summary: Prompts stopped being isolated strings some time ago. In real systems, one model call feeds another, retrieval interleaves with generation, routers branch, and aggregators merge parallel results. Practice converged on a single structure to hold this together: the graph. Frameworks such as LangGraph, DSPy, and Prompt Flow expose it openly, and research systems already optimize it automatically. The vocabulary, however, lags behind. Graph names, variously, a reasoning topology inside one sampling strategy, a multi-agent conversation, or an orchestration artifact, while prompt engineering still evokes writing one good string. What is missing is a reference definition treating prompts as nodes of an explicit, executable, improvable graph. We build that definition through conceptual analysis over sources with persistent identifiers, complemented by primary grey literature. We reconstruct the genealogy of the idea, from dataflow graphs and build systems, through prompt chaining and the thought topologies (chain, tree, graph), to graphs compiled and optimized as artifacts. We then propose a constitutive definition of prompt graph engineering, state its four conditions (explicit structure, separation between structure and prompt content, executable semantics, and the graph as a first-class engineering artifact), and operationalize them as an inclusion and exclusion test. We draw the boundary against six neighboring concepts and apply the test to six real systems (LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow, AutoGen, CrewAI, and Claude Code subagents); it includes and excludes consistently. We close with a research agenda organized along four design tension axes. The contribution is an operational definition and a shared vocabulary for a practice that industry already exercises daily without naming precisely.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a formal definition of "prompt graph engineering" as a shared vocabulary for modern AI systems where prompts form executable graphs rather than isolated strings.
AI.motivation: Current AI systems use complex prompt structures (chains, trees, graphs) with models feeding into each other, retrieval integrated with generation, branching routers, and merging aggregators. However, the vocabulary hasn't kept up - terms like "reasoning topology," "multi-agent conversation," or "orchestration artifact" vary inconsistently, while "prompt engineering" still implies writing single strings rather than building structured graphs.
AI.method: The authors conduct conceptual analysis over sources with persistent identifiers and primary grey literature. They reconstruct the genealogy of prompt graph concepts, analyze real-world systems, propose a constitutive definition with four conditions (explicit structure, separation between structure/content, executable semantics, and graph as first-class artifact), operationalize these as inclusion/exclusion tests, and apply them to six real systems.
AI.result: The paper successfully defines prompt graph engineering and establishes four necessary conditions. The inclusion/exclusion test consistently categorizes real systems (includes LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow; excludes or partially includes AutoGen, CrewAI, Claude Code subagents). The analysis draws boundaries against six neighboring concepts and organizes a research agenda along four design tension axes.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is an operational definition and shared vocabulary for prompt graph engineering, providing conceptual clarity for a practice that industry already exercises daily without precise naming. This enables better research, development, and optimization of modern AI systems built around executable prompt graphs.

title: Good Rankers, Bad Objectives: Bilinear Contrastive Critics under Expressive Policy Search
summary: Good action rankings do not make a contrastive critic safe to maximize. These critics increasingly act as value-like objectives for best-of-$K$ selection, planning, and critic-guided generation. Unbounded bilinear scores can let large embedding norms inflate off-support values, but cosine bounding does not remove the failure. A controlled support decomposition attributes most raw bilinear regret to norm drift. Cosine and hybrid critics nevertheless select off-support actions from most pools and incur comparable regret. Contrastive scores are weakly calibrated or inverted in the top score decile across four OGBench navigation tasks, and they fail to order fixed-query actions by value. Bellman-trained TD-Q succeeds, including in a parameter-matched function-class control. Realized costs depend on the task: simulator rollouts reveal single-step selection costs on PointMaze and the exact-$Q^*$ toy but well-powered nulls on AntMaze and HumanoidMaze, where the controller can self-correct. A training/readout decomposition traces the lost ordering to the cosine training objective; raw-trained embeddings retain weak ordering after inference-time normalization. Candidate maximization can therefore exploit false positives caused by norm drift, score saturation, or in-support misranking. Contrastive critics remain useful compatibility rankers on navigation and manipulation tasks, but action selection requires a value-calibrated scalar.

AI.tldr: Contrastive critics with cosine similarity fail as value objectives for action selection despite ranking well, while TD-Q works; contrastive critics remain useful for compatibility ranking but not for value-based action selection.
AI.motivation: Contrastive critics are increasingly used as value-like objectives for action selection tasks (best-of-K, planning, critic-guided generation), but there's concern about their safety and calibration when maximizing them for action selection.
AI.method: Analyzed contrastive critics with bilinear scores, tested cosine bounding and hybrid critics, evaluated on OGBench navigation tasks, compared to Bellman-trained TD-Q, conducted parameter-matched function-class control, and performed training/readout decomposition analysis.
AI.result: Contrastive critics are weakly calibrated or inverted in top score decile, fail to order fixed-query actions by value, and select off-support actions despite cosine bounding. TD-Q succeeds where contrastive critics fail. Norm drift is identified as main cause of raw bilinear regret, while contrastive critics remain useful as compatibility rankers.
AI.conclusion: Good action rankings do not guarantee safe contrastive critics for maximization; they require value-calibrated scalars for action selection but remain useful as compatibility rankers. Candidate maximization can exploit false positives from norm drift, score saturation, or in-support misranking.

title: From Minds to Models: The Intersection of Psychology and LLM Behaviours
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are often compared with the human mind because their decision-making is complex, non-linear and difficult to interpret. Psychological methods developed to investigate unobservable mental processes may therefore help examine LLM behaviour, particularly in government and healthcare. Building on prompt-based adaptations of the Implicit Association Test, this study tested whether ChatGPT produced sentiment differences across racial conditions in open-ended text. Fourteen base questions were crossed with eight racial categories and a race-agnostic control, producing 126 prompts. Each was submitted once to GPT-3.5T, GPT-4 and GPT-4T, yielding 378 responses. Sentiment scores were derived from categorical labels and source scores: positive labels retained the source score, negative labels were assigned its negative, and neutral responses were coded zero. A two-way ANOVA found a small main effect of racial condition, F(8, 351) = 2.04, p = .042, partial-eta squared = .044, but no effect of model, F(2, 351) = 0.07, p = .933, and no interaction, F(16, 351) = 0.23, p = .999. However, the effect was not retained in a rank-transformed sensitivity analysis, F(8, 351) = 1.53, p = .145, and Tukey-corrected comparisons found no significant pairwise differences. An uncorrected European-Indigenous Australian comparison was significant, but was selected post hoc and is reported only as hypothesis-generating. Evidence for sentiment differences was therefore weak and analysis-dependent. Sentiment scoring also cannot distinguish evaluative bias from the valence of historical content elicited by a prompt. We outline design changes needed to address these limitations and argue for interdisciplinary development of behavioural measures of model bias.
  Keywords: Implicit Bias, Psychological Research Methods, Artificial Intelligence, ChatGPT, Large Language Models, Sentiment Analysis

AI.tldr: Researchers used psychological methods adapted from the Implicit Association Test to examine whether ChatGPT shows racial bias in sentiment across different LLM models, finding only weak evidence of bias that was not robust to statistical corrections.
AI.motivation: LLMs exhibit complex decision-making similar to human cognition, making psychological methods useful for examining their behavior. The study aims to investigate whether LLMs show racial bias in sentiment generation, particularly relevant for applications in government and healthcare where fairness is crucial.
AI.method: The study adapted the Implicit Association Test methodology to test racial sentiment bias in LLMs. Researchers crossed 14 base questions with 8 racial categories plus a race-agnostic control (126 total prompts), submitted once to GPT-3.5T, GPT-4, and GPT-4T (378 responses). Sentiment scores were calculated using categorical labels and source scores (positive=source score, negative=negative of source, neutral=0). Statistical analysis used two-way ANOVA and sensitivity analysis with rank transformation.
AI.result: The ANOVA found a small main effect of racial condition but no effect of model version and no interaction. However, the effect disappeared in sensitivity analysis using rank transformation, and Tukey-corrected comparisons found no significant pairwise differences. One uncorrected European-Indigenous Australian comparison was significant but was post hoc. Overall evidence for racial sentiment differences was weak and dependent on analytical choices.
AI.conclusion: The study found minimal evidence of racial bias in ChatGPT sentiment generation, but methodological limitations exist. Sentiment scoring cannot distinguish between evaluative bias and historical content valence. The authors call for interdisciplinary development of better behavioral measures of model bias with improved design.

title: SE(3)-MeanFlow: Few-Step Protein Backbone Generation on Lie Groups
summary: Generative modeling of protein backbones promises the de novo design of proteins with prescribed structural and functional properties. Existing diffusion and flow-matching models produce high-quality backbones on SE(3)^N, but inference requires numerically integrating an ODE over hundreds of network evaluations, each involving a Lie group exponential map - a bottleneck for high-throughput design campaigns. We introduce SE(3)-MeanFlow, a few-step generative framework that extends MeanFlow from Euclidean space to the Lie group geometry of protein frames. Working natively in the Lie algebra so(3) and in R^3, we derive closed-form average-velocity identities for rotations and translations, giving simulation-free training targets. We further introduce an SE(3) alpha-Flow objective that removes the Jacobian-vector product from the rotation branch and serves as a warm-up stage, after which training switches to a small-t stabilized MeanFlow loss that is used for the remainder of pretraining and for rectification-based post-training. In protein backbone generation, SE(3)-MeanFlow matches or exceeds flow-matching baselines that use several times more sampling steps, and its advantage widens in the few-step regime, where rectification lets it lead at every matched budget - at a modest cost in diversity.

AI.tldr: SE(3)-MeanFlow: A few-step protein backbone generation method using Lie algebra closed-form velocities and rectification for faster inference with minimal quality loss.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion and flow-matching models for protein backbone design require computationally expensive ODE integration with hundreds of network evaluations and Lie group exponential maps, creating a bottleneck for high-throughput protein design campaigns.
AI.method: Extends MeanFlow from Euclidean space to SE(3) Lie group geometry of protein frames; works natively in Lie algebra so(3) and R^3; derives closed-form average-velocity identities for rotations/translations (simulation-free training); introduces SE(3) alpha-Flow objective (removes Jacobian-vector product) as warm-up stage; uses small-t stabilized MeanFlow loss for pretraining; employs rectification-based post-training for few-step generation.
AI.result: SE(3)-MeanFlow matches or exceeds flow-matching baselines that use several times more sampling steps; advantage widens in few-step regime where rectification enables leading performance at every matched computational budget with modest diversity cost.
AI.conclusion: The method provides an efficient few-step generative framework for protein backbone design that overcomes computational bottlenecks of existing approaches while maintaining or improving generation quality, particularly beneficial for high-throughput protein design applications.

title: Wiring diagram extraction and gluing: a case study in classifying figure skating jumps using 3D dataset
summary: Hasse clustering is an algorithm that extracts common patterns in sequential data and represents them in graphical forms. As the number of expected clusters grows, however, the algorithm can become infeasible to run due to combinatorial complexity. In this article, we describe a theory of gluing wiring diagrams, allowing iterative applications of Hasse clustering to achieve the same result as a single application. We test our theory in the context of classifying videos of figure skating jumps.

AI.tldr: Hasse clustering algorithm becomes infeasible with many clusters due to combinatorial complexity; new theory of gluing wiring diagrams allows iterative applications to achieve same result as single application, tested on figure skating jump classification.
AI.motivation: The Hasse clustering algorithm becomes computationally infeasible as the number of expected clusters increases due to combinatorial complexity, limiting its practical application on complex sequential data.
AI.method: Developed a theory of gluing wiring diagrams that enables iterative applications of Hasse clustering to achieve equivalent results to a single application, overcoming the combinatorial complexity problem.
AI.result: Successfully tested the proposed theory in the specific application domain of classifying videos of figure skating jumps, demonstrating practical feasibility.
AI.conclusion: The gluing wiring diagrams theory provides a scalable approach to Hasse clustering by enabling iterative computation that maintains equivalence to single-pass results, making the algorithm practical for complex sequential data analysis tasks like video classification.

title: Neural Network-Assisted CLEAN for Channel Modeling in Low-SNR Regimes
summary: Accurate multipath parameter estimation is critical for modern wireless communication systems, particularly in challenging low-SNR environments. Traditional Maximum Likelihood Estimation algorithms, such as CLEAN, provide high-resolution parameter extraction but suffer from prohibitive computational complexity due to exhaustive grid search. Conversely, purely data-driven deep learning approaches lack physical grounding and struggle to generalize across variable multipath densities and off-grid parameters. To address these limitations, this paper proposes Neural Network-Assisted CLEAN (NN-CLEAN), a hybrid framework that embeds a multi-head residual network directly into the iterative CLEAN extraction loop. By replacing the exhaustive grid search with rapid, parallelizable forward passes while delegating residual subtraction to exact mathematical models, NN-CLEAN isolates physical multipath parameters without accumulating non- physical errors. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that NN-CLEAN achieves estimation accuracy exceeding 96% at 5 dB SNR, matching the traditional Grid-Search CLEAN (GS- CLEAN) baseline, while providing a massive reduction in computational complexity and substantially outperforming subspace methods and standalone one-shot neural networks. Crucially, NN-CLEAN exhibits a near-flat scaling in execution runtime and memory consumption as batch sizes increase. This highly efficient parallelization establishes NN-CLEAN as a robust, real- time solution for channel estimation in MIMO systems.

AI.tldr: NN-CLEAN is a hybrid framework that combines neural networks with CLEAN algorithm to accelerate multipath parameter estimation while maintaining accuracy comparable to traditional grid-search methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional Maximum Likelihood Estimation methods like CLEAN have prohibitive computational complexity due to exhaustive grid search, while purely data-driven deep learning approaches lack physical grounding and struggle to generalize across variable multipath densities and off-grid parameters.
AI.method: NN-CLEAN embeds a multi-head residual network directly into the iterative CLEAN extraction loop, replacing exhaustive grid search with rapid, parallelizable forward passes while delegating residual subtraction to exact mathematical models to isolate physical multipath parameters without accumulating non-physical errors.
AI.result: NN-CLEAN achieves estimation accuracy exceeding 96% at 5 dB SNR, matching traditional Grid-Search CLEAN baseline, with massive reduction in computational complexity and substantially outperforming subspace methods and standalone one-shot neural networks. It exhibits near-flat scaling in execution runtime and memory consumption as batch sizes increase.
AI.conclusion: NN-CLEAN establishes itself as a robust, real-time solution for channel estimation in MIMO systems through highly efficient parallelization, combining the accuracy of physics-based methods with the efficiency of deep learning approaches.

title: World Action Planner: Generalizable Decision-Making with Action-Conditioned World Models
summary: Building generalizable agents for diverse applications remains a fundamental challenge. While imitation learning-based policies succeed in specific training environments, they often fail to generalize to novel scenes and tasks. In this work, we propose World Action Planner, a robot planning system that leverages the reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and the physical grounding of a multi-task pose-image conditioned world model. Our system enables an agent to propose initial action plans and iteratively refine them via optimization and search, reasoning over imagined world model rollouts. We demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance across compositional tasks, new layouts, and zero-shot generalization scenarios, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art end-to-end policy models such as VLAs and WAMs. Project website at worldactionplanner.github.io

AI.tldr: World Action Planner uses VLMs and world models for robotic planning via iterative refinement, achieving better generalization than end-to-end policies
AI.motivation: Imitation learning policies often fail to generalize to novel scenes and tasks, creating need for more generalizable robotic agents
AI.method: Combines VLM reasoning with multi-task pose-image conditioned world model; proposes initial action plans then iteratively refines via optimization/search over imagined rollouts
AI.result: Superior performance across compositional tasks, new layouts, and zero-shot generalization; outperforms state-of-the-art VLAs and WAMs
AI.conclusion: World Action Planner represents effective approach for building generalizable robotic agents by leveraging combined strengths of VLMs and world models

title: FADEx: Feature Attribution and Distortion-based Explanation of Dimensionality Reduction
comment: 18 pages, 17 figures, to be published in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
summary: Dimensionality Reduction (DR) is a fundamental tool for high-dimensional data exploration, reducing the complexity of latent spaces of machine learning models, and assisting in the explanation of complex opaque models. However, non-linear DR techniques often function as opaque transformations themselves, making it challenging to understand how individual features influence instance positioning in the reduced space. This lack of transparency complicates the analysis and interpretation of structural patterns, hindering the ability to reason about the organization of high-dimensional data based on the projected layout. In order to address this challenge, dimensionality reduction explanation methods have shown promise in improving the understanding of the observed groups and cluster structures. Unfortunately, existing DR explanation approaches tend to suffer from limitations such as multiple attributions per feature and restricted applicability to specific dimensionality reduction methods, which hinder their use. In this work, we propose FADEx, a novel local per-instance feature attribution method that leverages local linear approximation via first-order Taylor expansion and Singular Value Decomposition to provide explanations. FADEx computes the local linear models via weighted least squares, eliminating the need for out-of-sample data mapping, making it agnostic to the DR method, while simultaneously providing local feature attributions and distortion analysis. Through qualitative and quantitative evaluations, comparisons with existing methods, and case studies, we demonstrate FADEx's effectiveness and versatility in providing explanations and analytical resources for analyzing the behavior of DR methods. The results indicate FADEx yields robust and reliable explanations, outperforming existing approaches in several aspects.

AI.tldr: FADEx is a novel local feature attribution method that explains non-linear dimensionality reduction outputs by computing feature importance through local linear approximation and SVD, making it DR-method agnostic without requiring out-of-sample mapping.
AI.motivation: Non-linear dimensionality reduction techniques are often opaque transformations, making it difficult to understand how individual features influence instance positioning in reduced spaces. Existing DR explanation methods have limitations like multiple attributions per feature and restricted applicability to specific DR methods.
AI.method: FADEx uses local linear approximation via first-order Taylor expansion and Singular Value Decomposition to provide explanations. It computes local linear models via weighted least squares, eliminating the need for out-of-sample data mapping. The method is agnostic to the DR method while providing both local feature attributions and distortion analysis.
AI.result: Through qualitative and quantitative evaluations, comparisons with existing methods, and case studies, FADEx demonstrates effectiveness and versatility in providing explanations for DR methods. It yields robust and reliable explanations, outperforming existing approaches in several aspects.
AI.conclusion: FADEx addresses the interpretability gap in non-linear dimensionality reduction by providing a flexible, DR-method-agnostic explanation framework that enables better understanding of how features influence projection layouts while overcoming limitations of existing approaches.

title: CORE: In-Context Reconstruction for Unified Tabular Anomaly Detection
summary: Tabular anomaly detection (TAD), which focuses on identifying abnormal samples that deviate from the majority in tabular data, has received growing attention. Recently, there has been an emerging trend towards unified TAD, which seeks to detect anomalies across different datasets using a single generalizable model. In unified TAD, aligning heterogeneous data remains challenging. While existing methods often rely on distance-based unified feature construction, they may obscure the semantics of the original features. Moreover, existing approaches typically formulate anomaly detection as a binary classification task, which may overlook diverse anomaly patterns from various datasets and be misled by unrepresentative synthetic anomalies. To address these challenges, we propose an in-COntext REconstruction approach for unified TAD (CORE for short). It introduces a decorrelated feature alignment module to directly align heterogeneous features into a unified representation space, which retains their semantic information. Meanwhile, CORE formulates unified TAD as an in-context reconstruction problem, eliminating the need for labeled or synthesized anomalies. Specifically, the in-context reconstruction module reconstructs each sample by leveraging contextual normal samples to capture dataset-specific distributions, such that reconstruction errors reflect its deviation from normality, facilitating unified TAD on arbitrary unseen datasets.

AI.tldr: CORE proposes a unified tabular anomaly detection approach using in-context reconstruction and decorrelated feature alignment, eliminating the need for labeled anomalies and preserving feature semantics.
AI.motivation: Existing unified TAD methods face challenges: (1) distance-based unified feature construction obscures original feature semantics, (2) binary classification formulations overlook diverse anomaly patterns across datasets and can be misled by unrepresentative synthetic anomalies.
AI.method: CORE introduces: (1) a decorrelated feature alignment module that directly aligns heterogeneous features into a unified representation space while retaining semantic information, and (2) formulates unified TAD as an in-context reconstruction problem where each sample is reconstructed using contextual normal samples to capture dataset-specific distributions.
AI.result: Reconstruction errors reflect deviation from normality, enabling unified TAD on arbitrary unseen datasets without requiring labeled or synthesized anomalies during training.
AI.conclusion: CORE addresses key limitations of existing unified TAD methods by preserving feature semantics through direct alignment and eliminating dependency on synthetic anomalies through in-context reconstruction formulation.

title: Schreier-Coset Graph Rewiring
summary: The information flow in the graph neural networks (GNNs) is fundamentally constrained by over-squashing, where structural bottlenecks impede long range information propagation. Graph-rewiring methods, which modify graph topology, have been extensively used to alleviate this. However, existing approaches often introduce prohibitive structural and computational bottlenecks, fail to preserve the critical properties of original graphs, and increase the edge counts massively. We introduce a novel method Schreier-Coset Graph Rewiring , a group-theoretic rewiring method that augments the input graph with a Schreier-Coset graph derived from a special linear group. Our method provides theoretical guarantees, a graph that exhibits spectral gap and a bounded effective resistance, creating a low-resistance bypass for long-range communication. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that SCGR reduces effective resistance by 5-40% across various learning tasks, effectively mitigating connectivity bottlenecks while maintaining competitive accuracy.

AI.tldr: A group-theoretic graph rewiring method (SCGR) that augments graphs with Schreier-Coset graphs to reduce over-squashing in GNNs while maintaining graph properties and computational efficiency.
AI.motivation: Over-squashing in GNNs creates structural bottlenecks that impede long-range information propagation. Existing graph-rewiring methods introduce prohibitive structural/computational bottlenecks, fail to preserve original graph properties, and massively increase edge counts.
AI.method: Schreier-Coset Graph Rewiring (SCGR) augments input graphs with a Schreier-Coset graph derived from a special linear group using group-theoretic principles. This creates a low-resistance bypass for long-range communication.
AI.result: SCGR reduces effective resistance by 5-40% across various learning tasks, effectively mitigates connectivity bottlenecks while maintaining competitive accuracy. Provides theoretical guarantees including spectral gap and bounded effective resistance.
AI.conclusion: SCGR offers an effective solution to over-squashing in GNNs through mathematically principled graph rewiring that preserves original graph properties while improving long-range information flow without prohibitive computational costs.

title: Hidden APIs in Language Models: Discovering Reusable Causal Interfaces from Forked Futures
summary: Identical language-model answers can arise from hidden states that support different future computations, so current-answer probes do not establish a reusable internal interface. We introduce forked futures: future operations are sampled only after a prefix state has formed, and states are compared through the response distributions induced by those operations. This yields an empirical causal quotient over hidden states without requiring researcher-specified latent labels. Shared, Local, Mixture, and Distributed interfaces then compete under prequential causal description length subject to future-signature fidelity and matched capacity constraints. In the two detailed model evaluations, Shared has the lowest held-out description length, with gains of 0.216 nats on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 0.294 nats on Llama-3-8B, while maintaining tightly clustered mean future-signature distortion; a five-backbone sweep preserves the positive direction of Sharedness Gain. The figure-aligned transplantation analysis gives Shared the strongest joint target-correctness, locality, copy-preservation, and composite profile, and API-aligned paths mediate 0.749 of the target effect versus 0.150 for matched null paths. In the blind four-class model-organism test, 14/16 architectures are recovered, with one observed non-Shared to Shared error among 12 non-Shared organisms. These results support an economical reusable causal interface within the tested operation banks, while keeping the claim explicitly conditional on the candidate architectures, interventions, and held-out futures.

AI.tldr: A method called "forked futures" is introduced to identify reusable causal interfaces in language models by comparing hidden states through their induced response distributions to future operations, revealing that Shared interfaces have the lowest description length across multiple model evaluations.
AI.motivation: Current answer probes are insufficient because identical language model answers can emerge from hidden states that support different future computations. This means current methods don't establish reusable internal interfaces that maintain consistent causal properties for future operations.
AI.method: Introduces "forked futures" where future operations are sampled only after a prefix state has formed. States are compared through the response distributions induced by those operations, creating an empirical causal quotient. Four interface types (Shared, Local, Mixture, Distributed) compete under prequential causal description length with future-signature fidelity and matched capacity constraints.
AI.result: Shared interfaces had the lowest held-out description length: 0.216 nats gain on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 0.294 nats on Llama-3-8B, while maintaining tightly clustered mean future-signature distortion. Sharedness showed the strongest joint performance in transplantation analysis (target-correctness, locality, copy-preservation) with API-aligned paths mediating 0.749 of target effect vs 0.150 for null paths. In blind testing, 14/16 architectures were recovered with minimal errors.
AI.conclusion: The results support the existence of an economical reusable causal interface within tested operation banks, though the claim is explicitly conditional on candidate architectures, interventions, and held-out futures. The forked futures approach successfully identifies reusable interfaces without requiring researcher-specified latent labels.

title: Latent States in Neural Networks: Recovering the Temporal Structure of Drifting Data from Model Weights
summary: A temporally drifting data stream may pass through discrete regimes rather than changing continuously. We ask whether such regimes are recoverable from the weights of models trained on the stream, using a hidden Markov model (HMM) fit to the chronologically ordered trajectory of those weights. We study this question in two domains known to drift over time: multimodal misinformation detection, using the Fakeddit dataset; and sentiment analysis, using the Yelp dataset. We train classifiers on consecutive temporal windows and fit an HMM to the trajectory of their aligned weights, recovering latent states that partition each timeline into coherent phases. On both datasets, classifiers generalize better to data from windows sharing the state of their training window than to windows across state boundaries. This within-state transfer advantage survives a control for temporal proximity and modestly exceeds the advantage recovered by a naive partition into contiguous states of equal size. Although the states are estimated solely from model weights, they correlate more strongly with shifts in the data's class distribution than with the weight-space geometry used to estimate them. After class divergence and lag are residualized out, the within-state advantage exceeds its permutation null on both tasks, indicating that the states recover structure relevant to transfer beyond the data distribution. Every effect replicates on both tasks but is attenuated on Yelp, whose label distribution is more temporally stable.

AI.tldr: Researchers use Hidden Markov Models on classifier weight trajectories to detect discrete regimes in drifting data streams, finding that models generalize better within discovered states than across boundaries, beyond just temporal proximity effects.
AI.motivation: Temporal drift in data streams often occurs through discrete regimes rather than continuous change. The paper aims to determine whether such regimes can be recovered from the weights of models trained on sequential data, and whether these discovered states provide meaningful partitions for model generalization.
AI.method: Train classifiers on consecutive temporal windows of drifting data (Fakeddit for misinformation detection and Yelp for sentiment analysis), then fit a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) to the chronologically ordered trajectory of aligned model weights. The HMM recovers latent states that partition each timeline into coherent phases.
AI.result: Classifiers generalize better to data from windows sharing the same HMM state as their training window than to windows across state boundaries. This within-state transfer advantage survives temporal proximity controls and modestly exceeds the advantage from naive contiguous partitioning. States correlate more with data class distribution shifts than with weight-space geometry, and after controlling for class divergence and lag, the within-state advantage exceeds permutation nulls on both tasks.
AI.conclusion: HMMs applied to model weight trajectories can recover meaningful discrete regimes in drifting data streams, providing partitions that enhance model generalization beyond what can be explained by temporal proximity or naive segmentation alone. Effects are stronger on more temporally dynamic datasets (Fakeddit) than stable ones (Yelp).

title: SCOPE: Synthetic Conditional Objectives for Policy Evolution in Black-Box Combinatorial Optimization
comment: 43 pages; Kiet, Duc, and Bang contributed equally
summary: Black-box combinatorial optimization requires systematically identifying high-quality solutions under a limited evaluation budget, yet the unknown objective function provides little guidance for deciding where the search should explore next. We introduce SCOPE, a general framework for Synthetic Conditional Objectives for Policy Evolution in Black-Box Combinatorial Optimization. Rather than directly optimizing the inaccessible objective, SCOPE learns a set of synthetic objectives conditioned on the accumulated search history, where each objective is designed to expose a distinct and potentially useful preference over candidate solutions. These objectives are then used to evolve search policies that generate diverse candidates, whose true quality is subsequently assessed through black-box evaluations. The outer loop adaptively updates and selects synthetic objectives according to how effectively their induced policies discover promising regions. In contrast, the inner loop returns a portfolio of top-performing policies to reduce the risk of relying on a single surrogate preference. This formulation reframes objective design as a mechanism for guiding policy exploration, enabling the search process to exploit observed evidence while maintaining structured diversity across discrete solution spaces. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark problems demonstrate that SCOPE consistently improves black-box search performance under limited evaluation budgets and generalizes well across diverse combinatorial structures.

AI.tldr: SCOPE introduces a framework that learns synthetic objectives conditioned on search history to guide policy evolution in black-box combinatorial optimization, improving performance under limited evaluation budgets.
AI.motivation: Black-box combinatorial optimization faces challenges with limited evaluation budgets and lack of guidance from unknown objective functions, making it difficult to decide where to explore next in the search space.
AI.method: SCOPE learns a set of synthetic objectives conditioned on accumulated search history, each designed to expose distinct preferences over candidate solutions. These objectives evolve search policies that generate diverse candidates, with an outer loop adaptively updating/selecting objectives based on effectiveness, and an inner loop returning a portfolio of top-performing policies.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark problems demonstrate that SCOPE consistently improves black-box search performance under limited evaluation budgets and generalizes well across diverse combinatorial structures.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully reframes objective design as a mechanism for guiding policy exploration, enabling exploitation of observed evidence while maintaining structured diversity across discrete solution spaces.

title: A Lightweight Foundation Model for Collider Physics with Multi-Domain Adaptation
summary: We present a lightweight approach to foundation modeling (\textbf{NEXUS}) that leverages pre-trained learning from collider physics data towards out-of-domain tasks in other scientific datasets, using a fully connected autoencoder model with approximately 3 million parameters. The model pre-trains with no supervision over a large-scale collision dataset from the Large Hadron Collider modeled by charged particle track features. Downstream tasks for collider analyses, such as kinematic regression and event classification, are developed on pre-trained model weights and achieve improved accuracy with only small labeled datasets when compared to equivalent architectures trained from scratch. The benefits of pre-training are additionally investigated through latent space interpretation and application to other domains, including gravitational waves, flood forecasting, and neural activity. Furthermore, the relative computational simplicity of NEXUS is demonstrated compared to transformer approaches at comparable scale, opening the door to power-efficient inference and real-time or edge applications of foundation models in scientific experiments.

AI.tldr: NEXUS is a lightweight foundation model (3M params) that pre-trains on unsupervised LHC collision data, then transfers to diverse scientific tasks with improved accuracy using small labeled datasets.
AI.motivation: To create computationally efficient foundation models for scientific applications that can leverage unsupervised pre-training on large physics datasets and transfer to various downstream tasks across multiple scientific domains, enabling real-time and edge deployment.
AI.method: Uses a fully connected autoencoder model with ~3 million parameters, pre-trained unsupervised on large-scale LHC collision data (charged particle track features). The pre-trained weights are then fine-tuned for downstream tasks like kinematic regression and event classification.
AI.result: Achieves improved accuracy on collider analysis tasks with only small labeled datasets compared to equivalent models trained from scratch. Successfully transfers to other scientific domains (gravitational waves, flood forecasting, neural activity). Demonstrates computational simplicity vs transformers at comparable scale, enabling power-efficient inference.
AI.conclusion: NEXUS provides an effective lightweight foundation modeling approach that enables knowledge transfer from collider physics to diverse scientific tasks while being computationally efficient enough for real-time and edge applications in scientific experiments.

title: ReDiPPO: Reference-Guided Value Calibration and Discrepancy-Aware Token Reweighting for Mathematical Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement learning has emerged as an effective paradigm for enhancing the mathematical reasoning capabilities of large language models. Among existing policy optimization methods, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) remains particularly appealing because its learned critic can, in principle, provide token-level credit assignment. However, in mathematical reasoning tasks characterized by long reasoning horizons and sparse outcome rewards, reliable token-level credit assignment remains challenging. The standard critic often fails to accurately evaluate intermediate reasoning states, resulting in noisy advantage estimates and suboptimal policy updates. In this paper, we propose ReDiPPO, a Reference-guided and Discrepancy-aware PPO framework for mathematical reasoning. ReDiPPO introduces a reference-guided critic that uses reference answers as training-time privileged signals to provide more accurate value estimation. Meanwhile, it retains a standard critic and quantifies the token-level reference-standard discrepancy between the standard value estimate and the reference-guided value estimate. This discrepancy serves as an indicator of difficult reasoning states and is used to reweight the corresponding token-level advantages during PPO optimization. Extensive experiments on diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ReDiPPO improves value-estimation accuracy and consistently outperforms strong policy optimization baselines, including PPO, DAPO, and GSPO, in final reasoning performance. Our code is available on https://github.com/cii030/ReDiPPO.

AI.tldr: ReDiPPO improves mathematical reasoning in LLMs by introducing a reference-guided critic with reference answers as privileged signals for better value estimation, plus a discrepancy measure to identify difficult reasoning states for adaptive advantage weighting.
AI.motivation: Standard PPO's token-level credit assignment fails in mathematical reasoning tasks with long horizons and sparse rewards, leading to inaccurate intermediate state evaluation, noisy advantage estimates, and suboptimal policy updates.
AI.method: ReDiPPO (Reference-guided and Discrepancy-aware PPO) uses dual critics: 1) reference-guided critic leveraging reference answers as privileged signals for accurate value estimation, and 2) standard critic. It computes token-level discrepancy between these critics to identify difficult reasoning states, then reweights advantages accordingly during PPO optimization.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks show ReDiPPO improves value-estimation accuracy and consistently outperforms strong baselines including PPO, DAPO, and GSPO in final reasoning performance.
AI.conclusion: ReDiPPO effectively addresses the credit assignment challenge in mathematical reasoning by leveraging reference answers as privileged guidance and using discrepancy awareness to focus learning on difficult reasoning states, resulting in superior policy optimization for LLM mathematical reasoning.

title: Sparsity Induced Identifiability in Matrix Tri-Factorisation
summary: Matrix factorisation is a fundamental tool for exploiting low-dimensional structure in high-dimensional data, with applications such as data compression, denoising, structure discovery, interpretable representation learning, and dimensionality reduction. Compared to conventional two-factor models, matrix tri-factorisation provides greater modelling flexibility, while sparsity constraints often improve both interpretability and recovery performance. Although the role of sparsity has been extensively studied for two-factor matrix factorisation, rigorous theoretical guarantees for general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation remain largely unexplored. To address this gap, we establish, to the best of our knowledge, the first rigorous theoretical study for sparsity-induced identifiability in general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation. Our analysis is enabled by a novel decomposition strategy that transforms the original problem into two coupled auxiliary factorisation problems, while preserving the structural information necessary to the recovery of the original factor matrices from the observations. Building upon this decomposition, we derive recovery guarantees and structural consistency results that characterise how coefficient sparsity influences the sufficient recovery conditions, convergence behaviour, spectral approximation error, high-probability bounds, and structure preservation. Comprehensive Monte Carlo experiments validate the proposed theory and demonstrate close agreement between the theoretical results and empirical observations.

AI.tldr: The paper provides the first rigorous theoretical study of sparsity-induced identifiability in general real-valued matrix tri-factorization, establishing recovery guarantees and structural consistency results.
AI.motivation: Matrix tri-factorization provides greater modeling flexibility than conventional two-factor models, and sparsity constraints improve interpretability and recovery performance. However, rigorous theoretical guarantees for general real-valued matrix tri-factorization remain largely unexplored despite extensive study of sparsity in two-factor matrix factorization.
AI.method: The authors use a novel decomposition strategy that transforms the original tri-factorization problem into two coupled auxiliary factorization problems while preserving structural information. They then derive recovery guarantees and structural consistency results analyzing how coefficient sparsity influences recovery conditions, convergence behavior, spectral approximation error, high-probability bounds, and structure preservation.
AI.result: The paper establishes the first rigorous theoretical study for sparsity-induced identifiability in general real-valued matrix tri-factorization. It provides characterization of how coefficient sparsity influences sufficient recovery conditions, convergence behavior, spectral approximation error, high-probability bounds, and structure preservation. Comprehensive Monte Carlo experiments validate the theoretical results.
AI.conclusion: The work fills a significant gap in theoretical understanding of matrix tri-factorization, providing foundational theoretical guarantees that demonstrate close agreement between theoretical predictions and empirical observations through Monte Carlo validation.

title: HealthCAT: An Interpretable Encoder-only Transformer Framework for Health Indicator Prediction and Temporal Interpretation of Wearable Sensor Data
summary: Wearable sensors continuously capture fine-grained multivariate time-series data, providing opportunities to model behavioural patterns associated with health outcomes. However, existing deep learning methods prioritise predictive accuracy over interpretability, limiting their application in health research. In this study, we present HealthCAT, a flexible framework that integrates an Encoder-only Transformer with an Attentive Class Activation Token (AttentiveCAT) to generate class-specific, time-step-level interpretations. These interpretations can be mapped back onto behavioural cycles that are relevant to the domain (e.g., time-of-day), supporting individual-level analysis of wearable sensor data. We evaluated HealthCAT using two real-world wearable sensor datasets (306 participants in total). HealthCAT outperformed deep learning baselines by up to 17\% in F1-score and 12\% in accuracy on both datasets ($p<0.05$). In masking experiments, the time steps identified by HealthCAT carried significantly more predictive value than random selection across all masking conditions ($p<0.05$), indicating that the identified time steps are predictively informative. By coupling predictive performance with validated time-step-level interpretability, HealthCAT moves wearable sensor analysis beyond aggregated metrics towards temporal patterns that support health monitoring, behavioural pattern analysis, and intervention design in health research. The significance of this work is that it enables accurate prediction of health indicators from wearable sensor data while providing insights into when and how physical activity patterns occur, rather than relying solely on aggregated summary measures.

AI.tldr: HealthCAT is a flexible framework that combines an Encoder-only Transformer with Attentive Class Activation Token to achieve accurate predictions with interpretable time-step-level explanations for wearable sensor data analysis in health research.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning methods for wearable sensor data analysis prioritize predictive accuracy over interpretability, limiting their application in health research where understanding behavioral patterns and temporal dynamics is crucial.
AI.method: HealthCAT integrates an Encoder-only Transformer with an Attentive Class Activation Token (AttentiveCAT) to generate class-specific, time-step-level interpretations that can be mapped back onto behavioral cycles (like time-of-day), enabling individual-level analysis of wearable sensor data.
AI.result: HealthCAT outperformed deep learning baselines by up to 17% in F1-score and 12% in accuracy on two real-world datasets with 306 participants (p<0.05). In masking experiments, the time steps identified by HealthCAT carried significantly more predictive value than random selection across all masking conditions (p<0.05), demonstrating the predictive informativeness of identified time steps.
AI.conclusion: By coupling strong predictive performance with validated time-step-level interpretability, HealthCAT advances wearable sensor analysis beyond aggregated metrics toward temporal patterns that support health monitoring, behavioral pattern analysis, and intervention design in health research, providing insights into when and how physical activity patterns occur.

title: Expanding Data-Agnostic Pivotal Instances Selection Models with Proximity Trees and Ensemble Learning
summary: As decision-making processes grow more complex, machine learning tools have become essential for tackling business and societal challenges. However, many existing methods rely on decision-making procedures that are difficult to interpret. Since humans naturally make decisions by comparing new cases with a few representative examples, we aim to design an approach that selects such pivots to construct an interpretable predictive model. Inspired by decision trees, we propose a hierarchical, interpretable-by-design pivot selection model based on the similarity between pivots and input instances. Our method functions both as a pivot selection technique and a standalone predictive model. Extending beyond single pivots, we incorporate pairs of pivots that are used by proximity and oblique trees, as well as ensembles, which enhance the versatility and effectiveness of our proposal. Additionally, our approach is data modality-agnostic, leveraging pre-trained networks for data transformation. Experiments across diverse datasets, including tabular data, text, images, and time series, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming alternative instance selection strategies and achieving competitive results against state-of-the-art interpretable models while maintaining a minimal number of pivots.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical pivot selection method that builds interpretable predictive models by comparing new cases with representative examples, working across diverse data modalities.
AI.motivation: Machine learning tools for complex decision-making often lack interpretability. Since humans naturally make decisions by comparing new cases with a few representative examples, the authors aim to design an interpretable approach that selects such pivots for prediction.
AI.method: Proposes a hierarchical, interpretable-by-design pivot selection model inspired by decision trees, based on similarity between pivots and input instances. Extends beyond single pivots to include pairs of pivots (like proximity and oblique trees) and ensembles. Data modality-agnostic using pre-trained networks for transformation.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse datasets (tabular data, text, images, time series) show the approach outperforms alternative instance selection strategies and achieves competitive results against state-of-the-art interpretable models while maintaining minimal pivot numbers.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hierarchical pivot selection method provides an effective interpretable predictive model that mimics human decision-making through representative examples, working across various data modalities with competitive performance.

title: HALO: Heterogeneous Admission through Localized Obligations for Safe Agentic Execution
summary: Recent agentic AI systems may return a heterogeneous response containing notices, requests, handoffs, and actions. Conditions can change before external use, so components from the same response need not remain supported together. Rejecting the whole response discards useful components, whereas checking components independently can leave a dependent without its prerequisite. We present Heterogeneous Admission with Localized Obligations (HALO), a runtime protocol that preserves supported components whose declared prerequisites also remain supported, rechecks each exact action before dispatch, and allows blocked actions to be replaced only by fresh candidates. HALO matched all 96 admission expectations and passed all 20 protocol tests. In structured-response replay, it retained 248/248 supported components, including 128/128 unaffected by unrelated changes, while a whole-response policy retained 0/248. Across ten cold-start PX4/Gazebo sessions, HALO blocked every tested stale route, observed no matching stale setpoint, and completed all fresh recoveries.

AI.tldr: HALO is a runtime protocol for AI agent responses that preserves usable components when conditions change, ensuring actions only execute with valid prerequisites and allowing fresh replacements for blocked actions.
AI.motivation: When AI agent systems return complex heterogeneous responses containing multiple components (notices, requests, handoffs, actions), changing conditions before execution can invalidate some components. Rejecting entire responses wastes usable components, while independent component checking risks executing dependent actions without their prerequisites.
AI.method: Heterogeneous Admission with Localized Obligations (HALO) protocol preserves supported components whose declared prerequisites remain supported, rechecks each action before dispatch, and allows blocked actions to be replaced only by fresh candidates. It uses runtime verification and admission control.
AI.result: HALO matched all 96 admission expectations, passed all 20 protocol tests, retained 248/248 supported components in structured-response replay (including 128/128 unaffected by unrelated changes), while whole-response policy retained 0/248. In ten PX4/Gazebo cold-start sessions, HALO blocked every tested stale route, observed no matching stale setpoint, and completed all fresh recoveries.
AI.conclusion: HALO effectively handles heterogeneous AI agent responses by preserving usable components while ensuring safety through prerequisite verification and allowing graceful recovery, outperforming whole-response policies in retaining supported components.

title: Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps for Few-Step Generation
summary: Discrete diffusion and flow-matching models denoise a sequence over many steps, but to keep each step cheap, they factorize the transition across positions and decide every token independently. This makes few-step generation challenging for text when the target couples two positions, such as a subject and a verb that must agree. An independent update commits to them separately, and many function evaluations are spent repairing the mismatch. Existing few-step methods buy back the lost correlation by distilling or rectifying a slow teacher, and so inherit the teacher's quality ceiling. We ask instead whether a model can express correlated steps natively, and answer with Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps (LKF), a from-scratch flow-map kernel that is a mixture of M factorized components tied by a single shared latent. Conditioned on the latent, each component is cheap, and the mixture is summed over the latent in closed form for small M. We show that a single step places mass on correlated completions with the same sampling time complexity as a factorized model, since one latent is drawn per sequence and reused across the entire denoising trajectory. We also show that the Masked Diffusion Language Model (MDLM) is a special case of our LKF model at M=1. The experiments for unconditional text generation on the One-Billion-Word (LM1B) and WikiText-103 benchmarks show that our LKF model learns strongly heterogeneous components and improves generative perplexity by 2.1x to 3.3x over the likelihood baselines without losing diversity. The gain grows with M, and at M=8, it surpasses distilled and rectified few-step samplers. The source code is available at: https://github.com/mansoor181/lkf.git

AI.tldr: LKF introduces a latent-kernel discrete flow map that enables correlated token generation in few steps, overcoming independent position limitations of standard discrete diffusion models.
AI.motivation: Standard discrete diffusion models factorize transitions across positions, making tokens independent. This causes problems with few-step generation when tokens need correlation (like subject-verb agreement), requiring many steps to fix mismatches. Existing few-step methods rely on teacher models, inheriting their quality limits.
AI.method: Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps (LKF) - a from-scratch flow-map kernel that's a mixture of M factorized components tied by a shared latent. Each component is cheap conditioned on the latent, and the mixture is summed over latent in closed form for small M. Single step generates correlated completions with same time complexity as factorized models.
AI.result: LKF learns heterogeneous components and improves generative perplexity by 2.1x to 3.3x over likelihood baselines on LM1B and WikiText-103 without losing diversity. Gains increase with M, and at M=8, surpasses distilled and rectified few-step samplers. Masked Diffusion Language Model is special case at M=1.
AI.conclusion: Models can express correlated steps natively through LKF's latent-kernel approach, enabling efficient few-step generation with proper token correlations, outperforming existing few-step methods that rely on teacher distillation.

title: Evaluating and Pricing Advertisements in AI-Generated Responses
summary: As search increasingly shifts toward LLM-driven answer engines, advertising is becoming embedded within the generated response itself and should therefore be evaluated for both user utility and commercial value. The key challenge is click-through intent: behavioural logs are unavailable, human annotation resists calibration, and frontier LLM judges conflate intent with linguistic fluency. These gaps compound, as principled pricing presupposes a continuous intent signal, while generating such a signal presupposes supervision that is currently unavailable. We construct the missing supervision through a psychologically grounded agent simulation framework, and distil it into a parameter-efficient evaluator that predicts click-through intent, together with the three companion dimensions of ad quality, as smooth, differentiable estimates. Validated through sign-certain behavioural perturbations, the evaluator surpasses frontier zero-shot judges on relevance sensitivity (79% versus 60-67%), tracks graded content degradation, generalises without error to 103 fictional products, and agrees with human preference in 86% of pairwise judgements across five annotators, with agreement rising in the evaluator's confidence. Upon its estimates we build the pricing layer directly, deriving the unique payment rule under which truthful bidding is optimal, demonstrating it on a best-of-k allocation, and extending the mechanism to non-monotone allocations. The same differentiable signal stands ready as a training objective for ad generation.

AI.tldr: A novel LLM-based advertising evaluation system that predicts click-through intent using psychologically-grounded agent simulation, enables principled pricing, and serves as a training objective for ad generation.
AI.motivation: As search shifts to LLM-driven answer engines with embedded ads, there's a need to evaluate ads for both user utility and commercial value. Current challenges include lack of behavioral logs, calibration issues with human annotation, and frontier LLM judges conflating intent with linguistic fluency, creating gaps in principled pricing and supervision.
AI.method: Construct missing supervision through a psychologically grounded agent simulation framework, distill it into a parameter-efficient evaluator that predicts click-through intent and three companion dimensions of ad quality as smooth, differentiable estimates.
AI.result: The evaluator surpasses frontier zero-shot judges on relevance sensitivity (79% vs 60-67%), tracks graded content degradation, generalizes without error to 103 fictional products, and agrees with human preference in 86% of pairwise judgements with rising agreement in confidence. A pricing layer is built directly upon these estimates.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully addresses the click-through intent evaluation challenge for LLM-driven advertising, providing differentiable signals for pricing and ad generation while establishing truthful bidding mechanisms and demonstrating practical applications in ad allocation.

title: When Does Explicit View Routing Work? A Controlled Study of Multi-View Graph-Text Alignment
summary: Graph-text retrieval typically maps a graph and its description to a single embedding, even when a query concerns only one semantic aspect, such as a class label or molecular property. Multiple heads can separate these aspects, but a change in the query head may alter retrieval even when the wrong text is sent to that head. Such behavior demonstrates architectural channelization, not necessarily semantic routing. We examine the conditions under which this distinction can be resolved.
