Our controlled version of MV-GTA uses deterministic, verifiable text segments; isolated text encoders; view-specific graph heads; and relevance derived from external labels or RDKit descriptors. Correct routing and per-sample derangements form a causal test of whether retrieval depends on content. On BBBP and BACE, correct routing improves label and property nDCG by 0.305 to 0.685 over deranged training. The expected graph head exceeds the best wrong head by 0.303 to 0.453. Topology does not specialize consistently across the two datasets. In a matched three-seed comparison, one joint model obtains mean topology, label, and property nDCG of 0.720/1.000/0.877; three separately trained Single specialists obtain 0.633/0.976/0.859. Property paraphrase augmentation also improves unseen-template nDCG by 0.140 and 0.147 over a matched-exposure canonical control. Consistency and hard-template extensions, however, reduce canonical retrieval in some settings. The evidence is therefore limited to explicit, externally grounded label and property routing and observed multi-interface consolidation. It does not establish free-form routing, consistent three-view specialization, statistical equivalence to specialists, or superior downstream prediction.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether multi-head graph-text retrieval architectures genuinely perform semantic routing (content-based selection) versus architectural channelization (fixed head allocation), using controlled experiments with deterministic text segments and isolated encoders to establish causality.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-text retrieval methods map graph+text to single embeddings, even for queries about specific aspects (class labels, properties). Multi-head approaches might separate aspects, but changing query heads could alter retrieval even with wrong text, suggesting architectural channelization rather than true semantic routing. The paper aims to resolve this distinction.
AI.method: Uses controlled version of MV-GTA with deterministic, verifiable text segments; isolated text encoders; view-specific graph heads; and relevance derived from external labels or RDKit descriptors. Introduces causal test: compare correct routing vs. per-sample derangements (misallocated text) to see if retrieval depends on content. Tests on BBBP and BACE datasets with topology, label, and property queries. Also evaluates property paraphrase augmentation and consistency/hard-template extensions.
AI.result: Correct routing improves label/property nDCG by 0.305–0.685 over deranged training. Expected graph head exceeds best wrong head by 0.303–0.453. One joint model obtains mean topology/label/property nDCG of 0.720/1.000/0.877; three separate Single specialists achieve 0.633/0.976/0.859. Property paraphrase augmentation improves unseen-template nDCG by 0.140–0.147 over canonical control. However, consistency/hard-template extensions sometimes reduce canonical retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Evidence supports explicit, externally grounded label and property routing and multi-interface consolidation, but does not establish free-form routing, consistent three-view specialization, statistical equivalence to specialists, or superior downstream prediction. Study shows limited but clear routing for predefined aspects.

title: Rehearse: Stepping Back from the Confidence Cliff in Self-Improving Autoresearch
summary: Autoresearch improves machine-learning code by proposing changes, running full training jobs, and keeping changes that improve the metric. The efficiency of this loop depends not only on generating ideas, but also on the agent's ability to decide, before spending a training run, whether a proposed modification is likely to work. We study how the reliability of this pre-execution judgment changes over the course of an autoresearch trajectory. In public AutoSOTA logs (Li et al., 2026; Tsinghua FIB Lab, 2026), the fraction of helpful modifications falls from 70% in the first two iterations to 43% by iteration 6+. On 296 same-baseline modification pairs from 39 paper-derived AutoSOTA tasks, each containing one modification that improved the metric and one that did not, with measured outcomes hidden, an LLM judge given candidate rationales but no prior-attempt history reaches 79.5% accuracy on the pairs where strict consensus returns a verdict. On the full 366-pair benchmark, however, this ability weakens substantially late in the loop. As successful changes accumulate, selective accuracy - accuracy conditioned on a strict-consensus verdict - falls from 82.8% to 56.9%, while the judge remains willing to decide. We call this operational pattern the confidence cliff. Rehearse implements the loop change as a lightweight skill for autoresearch loops: propose several ideas, compare them before execution, run the most promising, and judge with a focused memory of similar past attempts and outcomes. This focused outcome memory raises late selective accuracy to 83.5%. Across 4,000 budgeted training runs over three loops, Rehearse improves the endpoint under the same training-run budget on nanochat, image classification, and time-series forecasting.

AI.tldr: Autoresearch agents need to judge code modifications before expensive training runs. As iterations progress, LLM judges become less accurate at predicting helpful changes despite remaining confident - a "confidence cliff". Rehearse improves this by proposing multiple ideas, comparing them before execution, and using focused outcome memory of past attempts.
AI.motivation: The efficiency of autoresearch loops depends on accurately predicting whether code modifications will improve metrics before spending computational resources on full training runs. As modifications accumulate over iterations, LLM judges become less reliable at this prediction task, leading to wasted resources.
AI.method: Analyzed AutoSOTA logs to track helpful modification rates over iterations. Created a benchmark of 296 same-baseline modification pairs from 39 paper-derived tasks. Tested LLM judge accuracy without prior-attempt history. Proposed Rehearse: propose multiple ideas, compare before execution, run most promising, and judge with focused memory of similar past attempts and outcomes.
AI.result: Helpful modification rate falls from 70% in early iterations to 43% by iteration 6+. LLM judge accuracy without history reaches 79.5% on consensus verdict pairs but selective accuracy drops from 82.8% to 56.9% late in loop (confidence cliff). Rehearse raises late selective accuracy to 83.5% and improves endpoint results across 4,000 training runs on nanochat, image classification, and time-series forecasting tasks.
AI.conclusion: The confidence cliff phenomenon shows that as successful changes accumulate, LLM judges become less accurate at predicting helpful modifications while remaining willing to decide. Rehearse successfully mitigates this by incorporating focused outcome memory, significantly improving autoresearch loop efficiency and final results under fixed training-run budgets.

title: Subtract or Replay? Exact Deletion from Language-Model Memory
summary: Exact deletion from persistent language-model memory depends on how that memory represents a record. Addressable influence can be removed by algebraic decrement; influence transformed by later writes inside shared recurrent state requires rebuilding from before the write. We test this distinction in two pretrained models against explicit record-omitted references. First, we replace Gemma 3's global-attention layers with support-vector memory. After low-rank recovery at 1B, decrement and retained-key refit agree at the next-token output to median KL $5.4\times10^{-15}$ over 31 support-token deletions, with $+2.0\%$ perplexity relative to a matched fine-tune. A masked-refit proxy is indistinguishable from the never-ingested floor under elicitation, relearning, sampling, and LiRA attacks. At 4B and 12B, certificate ordering persists but utility cost rises to $11.2\%$ and $44.3\%$. Second, in a 48B Kimi Linear hybrid, additive writes admit a fixed decrement and diagonal decay a corrected one, whereas the delta rule makes $12$--$49\%$ of a record's contribution suffix-dependent. Checkpointed rewind-and-replay deletes real clinical records at contexts up to 18,842 tokens, matching never-ingested logits and all recurrent states bit for bit within a deterministic MLX implementation; replaying a correction provides exact amendment. Exact deletion is therefore a property of memory representation: subtract addressable records and replay entangled writes.

AI.tldr: Exact deletion from language model memory depends on memory representation: addressable records can be removed algebraically, while entangled writes require rebuilding from before the write, with utility costs varying by model size.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of exact deletion from persistent language model memory, motivated by the need for verifiable data removal (like clinical records) and record amendments while maintaining model utility and security.
AI.method: Two approaches tested: 1) Replacing Gemma 3's global-attention with support-vector memory for low-rank recovery and algebraic decrement; 2) Analyzing different write mechanisms in a 48B Kimi Linear hybrid (additive writes, diagonal decay, delta rule) and using checkpointed rewind-and-replay for deletion of entangled records.
AI.result: In Gemma 3, algebraic deletion achieved median KL divergence of 5.4×10^-15 for support-token deletions with +2.0% perplexity at 1B, rising to +44.3% at 12B. For Kimi Linear, checkpointed rewind-and-replay achieved exact deletion matching never-ingested states bit-for-bit up to 18,842 tokens, enabling exact amendments.
AI.conclusion: Exact deletion is fundamentally a property of memory representation: addressable records can be subtracted algebraically, while entangled writes require replay-based reconstruction, providing a principled framework for verifiable data removal in language models.

title: Guiding Large Language Models with Genetic Programming-Evolved Heuristic Knowledge for Dynamic Multi-Mode Project Scheduling
summary: In dynamic multi-mode project scheduling, activities have alternative execution modes and uncertain durations, while precedence relations and limited resources constrain their execution. Heuristic priority rules support fast online decisions, but their design requires substantial domain expertise. Genetic programming (GP) hyper-heuristics can automatically evolve such rules. Large language models (LLMs), meanwhile, provide a flexible interface for interpreting scheduling information and explaining decisions. However, zero-shot LLM decisions may lack domain knowledge, consume many tokens, and vary across repeated queries. GP-evolved rules therefore provide a potential source of scheduling knowledge for guiding LLM decisions. Unlike existing LLM--GP hybrids that use LLMs to support heuristic evolution, we transfer knowledge in the reverse direction, using knowledge extracted from high-quality GP rules to guide an online LLM decision maker. We extract knowledge from high-quality GP rules and inject it through Feature Selection, Feature Hint, Rule Reference, and Rule Follow. These mechanisms are evaluated in terms of scheduling performance, token consumption, decision stability, and the feature focus expressed in generated rationales. GP-derived guidance generally improves the unguided LLM, but its representation matters. Simplifying the decision context or supplying explicit decision logic is more effective than highlighting important features. Feature Selection offers the best token efficiency, whereas Rule Follow achieves strong performance at greater token cost. Guidance also improves decision stability and changes the features expressed in generated rationales.

AI.tldr: GP-evolved scheduling rules can guide LLMs to make better online decisions in dynamic multi-mode project scheduling, with Rule Follow achieving best performance and Feature Selection offering best token efficiency.
AI.motivation: In dynamic multi-mode project scheduling, heuristic priority rules are needed for fast online decisions but require domain expertise to design. LLMs can interpret scheduling info but lack domain knowledge and vary across queries. GP-evolved rules provide scheduling knowledge that could guide LLMs, unlike existing hybrids that use LLMs to support GP evolution.
AI.method: Transfer knowledge from high-quality GP-evolved rules to guide online LLM decision makers through four mechanisms: Feature Selection (simplifying context), Feature Hint (highlighting important features), Rule Reference (supplying explicit decision logic), and Rule Follow. Knowledge extracted from GP rules is injected into LLM prompting.
AI.result: GP-derived guidance generally improves unguided LLM performance, but representation matters: simplifying context (Feature Selection) or supplying explicit logic (Rule Reference, Rule Follow) is more effective than highlighting features (Feature Hint). Feature Selection offers best token efficiency, while Rule Follow achieves strongest performance at greater token cost. Guidance improves decision stability and changes feature focus in rationales.
AI.conclusion: GP-evolved scheduling rules can effectively guide LLMs in dynamic project scheduling, with different knowledge injection mechanisms offering trade-offs between performance, token efficiency, and decision stability. This reverse knowledge transfer (GP→LLM) shows promise compared to existing LLM→GP hybrids.

title: Memory Efficient Tabular Foundation Models
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures Accepted at FMSD @ ICML 2026
summary: Tabular Foundation Models, such as TabPFN, have received a large amount of recent attention due to their performance on in-context tabular machine learning tasks, which often exceeds classical baselines. However, practical deployment considerations of these models has received less attention. In this paper we investigate the memory requirements for these models. We demonstrate that employing model compression approaches can enable memory reductions of up to 7.6 with similar levels of performance, reducing deployment requirements by nearly 87%. Our work provides insight to practitioners seeking efficient deployment of these models in practical settings.

AI.tldr: Tabular Foundation Models like TabPFN can be compressed to reduce memory requirements by 7.6× while maintaining similar performance, enabling more efficient practical deployment.
AI.motivation: Tabular Foundation Models have shown strong performance on in-context tabular ML tasks but their practical deployment considerations, particularly memory requirements, have received insufficient attention. There's a need to address the deployment challenges of these models in real-world settings.
AI.method: The paper investigates memory requirements of Tabular Foundation Models and employs model compression approaches to reduce memory usage while maintaining performance.
AI.result: Model compression enables memory reductions of up to 7.6× (nearly 87% reduction) with similar levels of performance compared to uncompressed models.
AI.conclusion: The work provides valuable insights for practitioners seeking efficient deployment of Tabular Foundation Models in practical settings, demonstrating that significant memory savings are achievable without substantial performance degradation.

title: SpatialCLI: Learning to Reason With Spatial Tools, Then Without Them
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used in embodied agents to interpret visual inputs, reason about spatial relationships, and make task-level decisions based on that reasoning. However, a fundamental capability mismatch remains: general VLMs can reason about the overall task but often miss the visual details that determine success, while specialist vision models can capture those details but cannot translate them into task-level decisions. In this work, we propose SpatialCLI, a framework that teaches VLMs to reason with spatial tools and progressively internalize the specialist perceptual capabilities they provide. SpatialCLI proceeds in three stages: (1) Call exposes specialist vision models as spatial tools to augment the VLM's perception; (2) Learn uses Cold-Start SFT and agentic RL to improve tool use; and (3) Internalize verbalizes successful tool-use trajectories to internalize specialist perceptual capabilities. We further introduce SpatialCLI-Bench, a 516-example benchmark for compositional perception across localization, segmentation, depth, and pose. On MindCube, SpatialCLI raises Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct from 29.3% to 84.6% with tools, surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol with tools (72.1%), while retaining 73.8% without tools after internalization.

AI.tldr: SpatialCLI is a framework that teaches vision-language models (VLMs) to use spatial tools and internalize specialist perceptual capabilities, bridging the gap between general reasoning and detailed visual perception.
AI.motivation: There's a fundamental capability mismatch in embodied agents: general VLMs can reason about tasks but miss critical visual details, while specialist vision models capture details but can't make task-level decisions. This gap limits effective embodied intelligence.
AI.method: SpatialCLI uses a three-stage framework: (1) Call - exposes specialist vision models as spatial tools to augment VLM perception; (2) Learn - uses Cold-Start SFT and agentic RL to improve tool use; (3) Internalize - verbalizes successful tool-use trajectories to internalize specialist perceptual capabilities.
AI.result: On the MindCube benchmark, SpatialCLI raises Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct from 29.3% to 84.6% with tools, surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol with tools (72.1%). After internalization, it retains 73.8% performance without tools. They also introduced SpatialCLI-Bench, a 516-example benchmark for compositional perception across localization, segmentation, depth, and pose.
AI.conclusion: SpatialCLI successfully bridges the perception-reasoning gap in VLMs by teaching them to use spatial tools and internalize specialist capabilities, enabling both strong tool-assisted performance and retained capability after tool internalization.

title: Strategies for Milestone-driven Start-ups in Multi-activity Settings
summary: New venture start-ups need to ``survive'' through multiple stages of reaching milestone targets. We investigate the strategies for start-ups in a milestone-oriented setting. We examine a model of an entrepreneurial start-up firm, where its state is captured by a diffusion process. The entrepreneur can choose between multiple activities (or controls), which incur different cost and determine the drift and the variance of the process. Depending on whether the process reaches a fixed upper boundary or a lower one, the start-up firm succeeds or fails. Continuous-time stochastic models with multiple ($\ge 3$) controls are typically very challenging to deal with. In this work, we are able to completely solve for the optimal policy and provide an explicit characterization of its structure. In particular, the optimal policy only uses controls from a set characterized by a so-called efficient frontier curve that orders the controls by two intuitive measures: riskiness (drift-to-volatility ratio) and cost-effectiveness (drift-to-cost ratio). A unique feature of our model is that depending on the model parameters, the efficient frontier curves can be of different types, resulting in qualitatively different structures of the optimal policy. As far as we know, this is the first study that analyzes a stochastic control model which admits efficient frontier curves of different types. Our work provides start-up firms with intuitive measures to evaluate their activities and offers valuable insights on how the optimal strategies in a milestone-oriented setting change qualitatively contingent upon the specific scenario. We believe the results provide a foundational block in the study of entrepreneurial decision-making.

AI.tldr: Start-ups can optimize survival strategies by choosing activities based on riskiness (drift-to-volatility ratio) and cost-effectiveness (drift-to-cost ratio), with optimal policies forming different frontier curve types depending on scenarios.
AI.motivation: New ventures need to survive through multiple milestone stages, requiring optimal activity selection strategies. Existing continuous-time stochastic models with multiple controls are mathematically challenging to solve, especially in milestone-oriented settings for start-ups.
AI.method: Models start-up firm state as a diffusion process where entrepreneur chooses between multiple activities (controls) affecting drift and variance. Activities incur different costs. Firm succeeds if process reaches upper boundary or fails if it reaches lower boundary. Solves for optimal policy explicitly using efficient frontier curves.
AI.result: Completely solves for optimal policy with explicit characterization. Optimal policy uses controls characterized by efficient frontier curves ordered by riskiness (drift-to-volatility ratio) and cost-effectiveness (drift-to-cost ratio). Efficient frontier curves can be of different types based on model parameters, leading to qualitatively different optimal policy structures.
AI.conclusion: Provides start-ups with intuitive measures to evaluate activities and insights on how optimal milestone-oriented strategies change qualitatively by scenario. Represents foundational work in entrepreneurial decision-making and first study analyzing stochastic control models with different types of efficient frontier curves.

title: Albilich: Steerable Proof-State Orchestration for LLM-Based Mathematical Research with CAS Integration
summary:
Large language models can contribute useful ideas to mathematical research, yet long-horizon proof attempts remain difficult to coordinate, evaluate, and reproduce. We present Albilich, an open-source agentic harness for autoresearch in mathematics that combines long-horizon reasoning, computer algebra systems (CAS), literature retrieval, and persistent SQLite-based context management.
  We evaluate Albilich on the RealMath benchmark (Zhang et al. 2025) and on open problems in group theory from the Kourovka Notebook (Khukhro and Mazurov 2026). It solved 10/10 problems on RealMath with CAS and 9/10 with no CAS. On the Kourovka problems, Albilich produced a counterexample to Problem 21.142 and a proof of a strengthening of Problem20.2. Anablation on Problem 17.91 demonstrates 32.0% token reduction when CAS is enabled. An ablation on Problem 21.142 demonstrates higher verifier-rejection rate and failure to synthesize proof routes in the absence of the advisor agent. These results support Albilich as a human-steerable, CAS-boosted environment for scalable AI-assisted mathematical research.

AI.tldr: Albilich is an open-source AI agent system for mathematical research that combines LLMs with computer algebra, literature search, and context management to solve complex math problems.
AI.motivation: Large language models can contribute to mathematical research, but long-horizon proof attempts are difficult to coordinate, evaluate, and reproduce. There's a need for better tools to manage AI-assisted mathematical discovery.
AI.method: Albilich combines long-horizon reasoning with computer algebra systems (CAS), literature retrieval, and persistent SQLite-based context management in an open-source agentic harness for autoresearch.
AI.result: Solved 10/10 problems on RealMath benchmark with CAS and 9/10 without CAS. On Kourovka Notebook problems: produced counterexample to Problem 21.142 and proof of strengthening of Problem 20.2. Ablation studies showed 32.0% token reduction with CAS and higher failure rates without advisor agent.
AI.conclusion: Albilich is a human-steerable, CAS-boosted environment for scalable AI-assisted mathematical research that demonstrates significant improvements in solving complex mathematical problems.

title: A Montage-Agnostic Encoder for Calibration-Light Cross-User Gesture Recognition from Surface Electromyography
summary: Pattern-recognition control promises a myoelectric prosthesis that responds to many intended gestures rather than one or two, but the promise has stayed in the laboratory. A recogniser trained on one person rarely transfers to the next, and useful performance usually demands a fresh round of labelled calibration from the end user. A montage-agnostic encoder is introduced that reads each electrode with shared weights and locates it by its physical coordinate rather than its index, so one architecture ingests any channel count without montage-specific parameters. Trained across users, it exceeds a per-user Hudgins and linear-discriminant classifier by 0.234 macro-F1 on DB1 for every held-out subject and by 0.108 on DB2, and falls below it on the ten-subject DB5. Each of the encoder's three key components individually accounts for more than half of its 3-shot macro F1 in an otherwise budget-matched ablation study. A controlled subject-count sweep shows the margin is close to flat from nine training subjects to thirty-nine, so the training pool binds only as a stability floor below which cross-user training fails to converge; what tracks the direction of the comparison across the three databases is instead the strength of the per-user baseline, which signal fidelity sets. Comparing against an LDA baseline depends on budget spent training models and on how good that baseline is, and self-supervised pretraining had no benefits once a supervised model was adequately trained.

AI.tldr: A novel montage-agnostic encoder for myoelectric pattern recognition that uses physical electrode coordinates rather than indices, enabling cross-user generalization without user-specific calibration.
AI.motivation: Pattern-recognition myoelectric prostheses require extensive user-specific calibration, limiting practical adoption. Current systems trained on one person don't transfer well to others.
AI.method: Introduces a montage-agnostic encoder that processes electrodes with shared weights using physical coordinates rather than channel indices. Architecture handles any channel count without montage-specific parameters. Includes three key components validated through ablation studies.
AI.result: Outperforms per-user Hudgins and LDA classifiers by 0.234 macro-F1 on DB1 and 0.108 on DB2 for every held-out subject. Falls below baseline on DB5. Three components individually account for more than half of 3-shot macro F1. Cross-user training shows stable performance from 9 to 39 subjects.
AI.conclusion: Montage-agnostic architecture enables better cross-user generalization than user-specific methods. Performance depends on signal fidelity and baseline strength rather than training pool size beyond a stability threshold. Self-supervised pretraining offers no additional benefits once supervised training is adequate.

title: MECA: A Mechanism-Centered Agent for Constructing Well-Specified and Valuable Mathematical Conjectures
comment: 78 pages, 5 figures. Includes appendices and the full collection of 100 generated conjectures
summary: Automatically constructing well-specified and valuable mathematical conjectures remains a central challenge in AI-assisted mathematical discovery. Many existing open problems and conjectures are often too broad, underspecified, or difficult to connect to plausible proof or refutation strategies. We view a mathematical mechanism as a structure or reasoning principle that connects the assumptions of a candidate problem to its target conclusion, such as an inequality, invariant, decomposition, or reduction to an intermediate claim. We present MECA (MEchanism-centered Conjecture Agent), a multi-agent framework that constructs conjectures by jointly developing candidate statements and their supporting mechanisms. Explorer agents propose mechanisms, test how they apply, and revise the candidate conjecture accordingly, while critic agents assess their mathematical validity and research value. Their feedback guides changes to the assumptions, scope, and conclusion. Through this process, MECA transforms broad research directions into precise conjectures with substantive mathematical support while retaining a clearly identified unresolved core. We evaluate MECA in two complementary settings. First, we compare it with a generate-and-revise baseline on reconstructing preselected target-paper conclusions from target-conditioned but article-blind source materials. Second, we construct 100 semi-open problems from literature-derived seeds and existing open problems and evaluate them through independent proof and refutation attempts by automated provers. Our results indicate that mechanism-centered refinement produces well-specified and research-worthy conjectures that remain challenging for current automated provers.

AI.tldr: MECA is a multi-agent AI framework that constructs mathematically valuable conjectures by jointly developing statements with supporting mechanisms through exploration-critique interaction.
AI.motivation: Current mathematical conjecture generation in AI often produces problems that are too broad, underspecified, or disconnected from plausible proof strategies, limiting their research value and practical utility.
AI.method: Uses a multi-agent framework with Explorer agents proposing mathematical mechanisms and testing their application, while Critic agents assess validity and research value, guiding iterative refinement of assumptions, scope, and conclusions.
AI.result: Evaluation shows MECA produces well-specified, research-worthy conjectures that remain challenging for automated provers. It outperforms generate-and-revise baselines in reconstructing paper conclusions and generates 100 semi-open problems from literature.
AI.conclusion: Mechanism-centered refinement enables transformation of broad research directions into precise, mathematically supported conjectures while maintaining clearly identified unresolved cores, advancing AI-assisted mathematical discovery.

title: Recognition and Label-Free Adaptation Across Recording Sessions in Surface-EMG Gesture Decoding
summary: Recognition accuracy obtained during a recording session does not persist when a user puts on the electrodes again after the electrodes had previously been removed. The electrodes may have moved slightly, the skin may be drier or wetter, or the elbow may be positioned differently; these factors all contribute to day-to-day variability and therefore represent a major obstacle to implementing successful pattern-recognition based myoelectric control systems in daily practice. However, simply recalibrating a user's hand for 20 min at every doff/don event is a clearly unrealistic expectation. A montage-agnostic encoder built for cross-user, cross-montage transfer is trained here using data collected during a particular recording session, and then applied to data collected later in a different recording session without adjusting anything, on the ten intact subjects of NinaPro DB6. The performance of this approach is compared to that of a per-user LDA classification pipeline, and to that of two published approaches that only rely on source data collected from the same recording session. Carried unchanged across recording sessions, the encoder retains 0.688 macro-F1 against 0.540 for the per-user pipeline, and, on the per-window metric the published baselines use, sits above both published source-only results, a band of two points that locates the encoder rather than ranking it. Of five label-free test-time adaptations, only feature-statistic alignment improves every subject; batch-normalisation re-estimation, a standard method in the domain-adaptation literature, collapses this architecture entirely. Aligning the encoder's feature statistics to the new session recovers about what a single labelled calibration repetition would.

AI.tldr: A montage-agnostic encoder trained on one session maintains better performance across different recording sessions than per-user classifiers, and simple feature-statistic alignment can recover performance comparable to single labeled calibration repetition.
AI.motivation: Day-to-day variability in EMG electrode placement, skin conditions, and arm positioning causes pattern-recognition based myoelectric control systems to lose accuracy between sessions, making recalibration impractical for daily use.
AI.method: Train a montage-agnostic encoder using data from one recording session, then apply it unchanged to different sessions without recalibration. Compare with per-user LDA and published source-only approaches. Test five label-free adaptation methods including feature-statistic alignment.
AI.result: Encoder retains 0.688 macro-F1 across sessions vs. 0.540 for per-user LDA. Outperforms published baselines on per-window metric. Feature-statistic alignment improves all subjects, recovering performance similar to single labeled calibration repetition. Batch-normalization re-estimation fails.
AI.conclusion: Montage-agnostic encoders enable better cross-session EMG classification without recalibration, with simple feature-statistic alignment providing effective label-free adaptation, addressing a major practical barrier for myoelectric control systems.

title: New Synchronous Computation Dynamics for Hopfield Networks
summary: The dynamics of the original Hopfield network is asynchronous (sequential) (updates the state of only one neuron per time step). In this paper, we propose a new tool and a new dynamics to reduce the processing time by updating one or more neurons simultaneously per instant while ensuring process convergence and aiming for the maximum energy decrease at each step, thus guaranteeing the shortest total processing time. From the point of view of synchronous dynamics, calculating the next network state at which energy decreases the most from the current state while ensuring convergence is itself a combinatorial optimization problem. We develop and use a new tool to solve it. We call this new tool Discrete Differential Filter (DDF) and, based upon it, we develop a new synchronous dynamics which we call SD-DDF (Synchronous Dynamics based upon Discrete Differential Filter). In this paper, we review the original asynchronous dynamics for Hopfield networks and present a new tool and a new synchronous dynamics with its theoretical justification and four computational experiments to assess the speed up in processing time empirically.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SD-DDF, a new synchronous dynamics for Hopfield networks that updates multiple neurons simultaneously to reduce processing time while ensuring convergence and maximum energy decrease at each step.
AI.motivation: The original Hopfield network uses asynchronous (sequential) dynamics that updates only one neuron per time step, which can be slow. The authors aim to reduce processing time by allowing simultaneous updates of multiple neurons while maintaining convergence guarantees.
AI.method: The authors develop a new tool called Discrete Differential Filter (DDF) to solve the combinatorial optimization problem of finding the next network state that decreases energy the most while ensuring convergence. They then develop SD-DDF (Synchronous Dynamics based upon Discrete Differential Filter) as a new synchronous dynamics for Hopfield networks.
AI.result: The paper presents theoretical justification for the new synchronous dynamics and provides four computational experiments to empirically assess the speedup in processing time compared to the original asynchronous dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The SD-DDF approach enables faster processing for Hopfield networks through synchronous updates of multiple neurons while maintaining convergence properties, with empirical evidence showing significant speed improvements over traditional asynchronous dynamics.

title: Baikal: Structured Search for Deep Research over Data Lakes
summary: Deep research over data lakes requires an LLM agent to investigate evidence across thousands of heterogeneous tables and passages to synthesize a report. Existing methods perform iterative retrieval and generation, letting accumulated context determine what to investigate next, which can overexploit locally promising evidence and fail to cover distinct semantic regions under a fixed budget. To address this, we cast deep research over data lakes as a budgeted search problem and present Baikal - a framework that clusters heterogeneous evidence into semantic regions, then searches over them adaptively to balance exploration and exploitation. Within each selected region, Baikal generates and investigates region-grounded subquestions, using finding quality as rewards to update region-level value estimates and guide search under policies ranging from random and LLM-guided selection to Bayesian $ε$-greedy and UCB. We evaluate Baikal on 15 queries each over HybridQA and TAT-QA data lakes containing 10,993 and 2,757 tables, respectively, together with 227K Wikipedia passages and 13K financial report passages. We assess research quality with a new rubric covering groundedness, relevance, diversity, and utility, and use GPT-5-mini to score Baikal and strong baselines, including DeepSearcher and an OpenCode research agent with retrieval and clustering variants. Across both data lakes, Baikal performs strongly under several region-selection policies; its best configuration improves report scores over the strongest baselines by 28% on HybridQA and 36% on TAT-QA. Our analyses attribute these gains to organizing and exploring semantic evidence regions, which improves groundedness and diversity and yields more useful findings under the same subquestion budget. These results demonstrate the value of structured semantic exploration for systematic research and discovery over heterogeneous data lakes.

AI.tldr: Baikal is a framework that treats deep research over data lakes as a budgeted search problem, clustering heterogeneous evidence into semantic regions and adaptively searching across them to balance exploration and exploitation, improving report quality by 28-36% over strong baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for deep research over data lakes use iterative retrieval and generation where accumulated context determines what to investigate next, which can overexploit locally promising evidence and fail to cover distinct semantic regions under a fixed budget.
AI.method: Clusters heterogeneous evidence (tables and passages) into semantic regions, then searches adaptively across them using region-level value estimates updated based on finding quality. Generates region-grounded subquestions within selected regions and uses various policies for region selection (random, LLM-guided, Bayesian ε-greedy, UCB).
AI.result: Evaluated on 15 queries each over HybridQA and TAT-QA data lakes containing thousands of tables and passages. Best configuration improves report scores over strongest baselines by 28% on HybridQA and 36% on TAT-QA. Gains attributed to organizing and exploring semantic evidence regions, improving groundedness, diversity, and utility under same subquestion budget.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the value of structured semantic exploration for systematic research and discovery over heterogeneous data lakes, showing that balancing exploration and exploitation through semantic region organization significantly improves research quality.

title: MUGEN: A Unified Framework for Efficient Motion Understanding and Generation
summary: Grounding human motion in language, and language in motion, is a central step toward physical AI systems that can understand, generate, and communicate human behavior. Unified motion--language systems first coupled the two directions through a shared discrete motion codebook, but quantization limits generation quality. The strongest generators buy quality back at growing cost: stacked residual codebooks enlarge the representation; masked decoding stages, long autoregressive rollouts, and denoising chains of tens to hundreds of steps stretch inference; even the continuous-latent designs among them reach their latent only through an iterative diffusion head; and none of this decoding machinery serves understanding. We therefore propose MUGEN, a unified motion--language framework that pays neither cost: no codebook, one draw. A single adaptive-length autoencoder compresses any-length motion into a few continuous latent slots, the system's only motion representation: the language model generates them for text-to-motion and reads them back for motion understanding. Depth-routed hidden states let each slot read from the transformer depth it needs, and a calibrated head predicts a joint distribution over the full latent set, so a single draw carries the text-conditional, cross-slot variation a description permits. At a decoding cost of K language-model steps, one draw, and one decoder pass, MUGEN leads language-model baselines on FID on HumanML3D while raising retrieval precision above the real-motion reference under the standard evaluator, achieves the best CIDEr and BLEU@4 scores, and surpasses the discrete-token state of the art on every retrieval and alignment metric on SnapMoGen.

AI.tldr: MUGEN: A unified motion-language framework that generates and understands human motion using continuous latent slots instead of discrete tokens, achieving state-of-the-art performance with efficient single-draw inference.
AI.motivation: Existing unified motion-language systems face quality vs. efficiency trade-offs. Discrete codebooks limit generation quality, while state-of-the-art generators require complex multi-stage decoding, long rollouts, and costly inference that doesn't serve understanding tasks. There's a need for a unified framework that achieves both high-quality generation and understanding without excessive computational cost.
AI.method: Proposes MUGEN framework with: 1) Adaptive-length autoencoder that compresses any-length motion into few continuous latent slots; 2) Language model that generates slots for text-to-motion and reads them for motion understanding; 3) Depth-routed hidden states allowing each slot to read from appropriate transformer depth; 4) Calibrated head predicting joint distribution over latent set for single-draw sampling.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art results: leads language-model baselines on FID on HumanML3D; raises retrieval precision above real-motion reference under standard evaluator; achieves best CIDEr and BLEU@4 scores; surpasses discrete-token SOTA on every retrieval and alignment metric on SnapMoGen. All with efficient decoding cost of K language-model steps, one draw, and one decoder pass.
AI.conclusion: MUGEN demonstrates that a unified motion-language framework can achieve both high-quality generation and understanding without the computational inefficiencies of previous approaches, using continuous latent representations and efficient single-draw inference.

title: VeriSkill: A Self-Evolution Framework for Program Verification Skills
summary: Automating program verification with LLM agents requires generating specifications, annotations, auxiliary lemmas, and tool invocations, all of which depend on reusable skills. A natural remedy is skill self-evolution: distilling skills from trajectories and refining them through feedback. However, existing evolution methods struggle with program verification tasks because they cannot reliably identify skill-specific failures or extract actionable signals from opaque verifier feedback. In this paper, we propose VeriSkill, a self-evolution framework built for program verification. It attributes verification failures to skill deficiencies, distills diagnostic signatures into reusable lessons, and iteratively refines candidate skills, admitting only revisions that improve verification performance while preserving program semantics. Experiments show that VeriSkill consistently outperforms all baselines across multiple verification tools, agent frameworks, and LLM backends.

AI.tldr: VeriSkill is a self-evolution framework that improves LLM-based program verification by distilling reusable skills from failures and refining them through targeted feedback.
AI.motivation: Existing skill evolution methods struggle with program verification tasks because they cannot reliably identify skill-specific failures or extract actionable signals from opaque verifier feedback. Program verification requires generating specifications, annotations, lemmas, and tool invocations that depend on reusable skills.
AI.method: VeriSkill attributes verification failures to skill deficiencies, distills diagnostic signatures into reusable lessons, and iteratively refines candidate skills. It only admits revisions that improve verification performance while preserving program semantics.
AI.result: Experiments show that VeriSkill consistently outperforms all baselines across multiple verification tools, agent frameworks, and LLM backends.
AI.conclusion: The proposed skill self-evolution framework effectively addresses the unique challenges of program verification by providing targeted skill refinement based on failure analysis, leading to improved verification performance.

title: Prox: Training-Free FFN Activation Sparsity via Approximate Intermediate-Channel Salience in LLMs
summary: Feed-forward networks (FFNs) dominate memory traffic and computation in large language model (LLM) inference, making them a primary target for activation sparsification. However, existing training-free methods suffer substantial model-quality degradation at high sparsity due to limitations in their channel-selection strategies. We observe that the SwiGLU intermediate state provides a highly effective channel-selection signal, but obtaining it requires costly dense computation. To address this, we present \emph{Prox}, a two-stage training-free framework for sparse SwiGLU FFNs. Prox hinges on the key insight: sparse execution requires only the channel mask induced by the intermediate state, which can be constructed from the magnitude ranking of its entries rather than their exact values. Specifically, Stage 1 uses input sparsity and quantized proxy weights to construct a shared mask; Stage 2 computes the selected channels exactly, enabling sparse execution of all three projections. Across ten LLMs from six model families, Prox outperforms training-free baselines at all sparsity levels, achieves up to a $1.99\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup at 70\% FFN sparsity, and is compatible with quantization and sparse attention.

AI.tldr: Prox is a two-stage training-free framework that enables sparse execution of SwiGLU FFNs in LLMs using proxy weights and input sparsity to construct channel masks, achieving significant speedups without training.
AI.motivation: Feed-forward networks dominate memory traffic and computation in LLM inference, making them prime targets for sparsification. Existing training-free methods suffer from substantial quality degradation at high sparsity due to poor channel-selection strategies.
AI.method: Prox uses a two-stage approach: Stage 1 leverages input sparsity and quantized proxy weights to construct shared channel masks based on magnitude ranking of SwiGLU intermediate states; Stage 2 computes only the selected channels exactly, enabling sparse execution of all three projections without needing exact intermediate values.
AI.result: Prox outperforms training-free baselines across ten LLMs from six model families at all sparsity levels, achieving up to 1.99× end-to-end decoding speedup at 70% FFN sparsity while being compatible with quantization and sparse attention.
AI.conclusion: The Prox framework successfully enables high-sparsity FFN execution without training by exploiting the insight that only channel mask information (not exact intermediate values) is needed for sparse execution, making it a practical solution for accelerating LLM inference.

title: SpecCal: Ambiguity-Aware Candidate Calibration for Infrared Spectrum-Based Molecular Structure Reconstruction
summary: Inferring molecular structures from infrared (IR) spectra is a fundamental yet challenging problem. A key difficulty is that an IR spectrum provides limited structural information: different molecules may share similar functional groups and local vibrational patterns, leading to highly similar spectral responses. Thus, even when an observed spectrum has a unique underlying structure, reconstructing it from the spectrum remains ambiguous. Existing IR-to-molecule models usually generate a ranked set of candidate molecules, but this set is largely determined by the model's learned generation preference and may not fully capture the structures that best satisfy the observed spectral constraints. To address this limitation, we propose SpecCal, a training-free candidate calibration framework for IR-to-molecule prediction. SpecCal operates on the candidate outputs of existing base models and improves the prediction set by re-ranking current candidates while introducing additional structurally plausible alternatives guided by spectral consistency. The framework is plug-and-play and model-agnostic, requiring no parameter updates for integration with diverse base models. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that SpecCal consistently improves top-k reconstruction at both SMILES and scaffold levels across different base models. Further analyses demonstrate that calibrating candidate sets under spectral ambiguity provides a practical way to improve molecular reconstruction from IR spectra. The code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SpecCal-B18A.

AI.tldr: SpecCal is a training-free calibration framework that improves IR-to-molecule prediction by re-ranking candidate molecules and introducing structurally plausible alternatives guided by spectral consistency.
AI.motivation: Infrared spectra provide limited structural information, leading to ambiguity in molecular reconstruction. Existing models generate ranked candidate sets that may not fully capture structures best satisfying spectral constraints due to model generation preferences.
AI.method: SpecCal operates as a plug-and-play, model-agnostic framework that calibrates candidate outputs from base models. It re-ranks existing candidates while introducing additional structurally plausible alternatives guided by spectral consistency, requiring no parameter updates.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple benchmarks show consistent improvement in top-k reconstruction at both SMILES and scaffold levels across different base models. Calibrating candidate sets under spectral ambiguity improves molecular reconstruction from IR spectra.
AI.conclusion: SpecCal provides a practical training-free approach to improve molecular structure inference from IR spectra by addressing the inherent ambiguity in spectral interpretation through candidate calibration.

title: Compliance2LoRA: On-Demand Safety Alignment on Arbitrary Policy Subsets via Hypernetwork-Generated LoRA Adapters
summary: Post-training alignment in large reasoning models (LRMs) has significantly improved their adaptability to diverse safety compliance settings. However, as LRMs personalization for downstream users takes center stage, the demand for varying levels of policy compliance grows as different user-specific LRMs must adhere to distinct subsets of safety policies. Training a separate LRM for each policy subset introduces severe combinatorial overhead. While in context learning methods overcome this combinatorial overhead, they introduce additional computational challenges associated with long context generation. To address this challenge, we propose \ours, a unified adaptive hypernetwork-based framework for multi-policy compliance. In our framework, safety policies serve as customizable inputs to a LoRA adapter generator, which learns to produce policy compliant LoRA weights for downstream LRM. When added to the LRM these weights enable the generation of responses compliant with the specified policy subsets. In this work, we demonstrate that training such a hypernetwork enables on-demand policy adjustments on a single LRM without sacrificing task performance across reasoning models of different sized and different evaluation datasets. This highlights the effectiveness and practicality of adaptive hypernetwork based alignment in LRMs.

AI.tldr: HyperLoRA: A unified adaptive hypernetwork framework that enables single large reasoning models to comply with multiple safety policies on-demand through LoRA adapter generation, avoiding combinatorial overhead of training separate models.
AI.motivation: As large reasoning models become personalized for downstream users, there's growing demand for varying levels of policy compliance. Different user-specific models must adhere to distinct safety policy subsets, but training separate models for each policy combination creates severe combinatorial overhead, while in-context learning methods introduce computational challenges with long context generation.
AI.method: Proposes HyperLoRA, a unified adaptive hypernetwork framework where safety policies serve as customizable inputs to a LoRA adapter generator. This generator learns to produce policy-compliant LoRA weights that, when added to the downstream LRM, enable generation of responses compliant with specified policy subsets.
AI.result: The trained hypernetwork enables on-demand policy adjustments on a single LRM without sacrificing task performance across reasoning models of different sizes and evaluation datasets.
AI.conclusion: The approach highlights the effectiveness and practicality of adaptive hypernetwork-based alignment in LRMs for achieving multi-policy compliance efficiently and flexibly.

title: Annotating Topical Legal Insights from Case Proceedings
summary: In this paper, we mainly concentrate on finding concepts or topics from the legal case proceedings, since adopting a structured representation for legal documents, as opposed to a mere bag-of-words flat text representation, can significantly enhance processing capabilities. To achieve this objective, we put forward a set of diverse concepts for legal case proceedings. With this motivation, we propose LeDA, a system for Legal Data Annotation. The system offers the generic functionality of annotating and adjudicating entities or concepts within documents via a web-based interface. A novel feature of our system is that it allows to dynamic create new tags for annotation, which is a particularly useful provision for situations where there exists no pre-defined ontology for the entities (concepts) that need to be annotated - these being rather discovered by annotators as they continue examining more documents. The system that we demonstrate is currently in use to annotate a set of concepts from legal documents to construct semantic representations of documents as bags of concepts that can then be used for several downstream tasks, such as prior case retrieval, judgment prediction, and so on. Along with the system features in general, we also describe how LeDA was used by 3 assessors to annotate and adjudicate legal concept names from Indian Supreme Court case proceedings.

AI.tldr: LeDA is a legal data annotation system with dynamic tag creation for discovering concepts in legal documents without pre-defined ontologies, enabling semantic representations for downstream legal tasks.
AI.motivation: Current legal document representations as mere bag-of-words flat text limit processing capabilities. Structured representations with discovered concepts can significantly enhance legal document processing for tasks like prior case retrieval and judgment prediction.
AI.method: Proposed LeDA system: a web-based annotation system that allows dynamic creation of new tags for annotation. This supports discovering concepts/topics from legal case proceedings without requiring pre-defined ontologies. The system enables collaborative annotation and adjudication among multiple assessors.
AI.result: System is currently in use to annotate concepts from legal documents, constructing semantic representations as bags of concepts. Three assessors successfully used LeDA to annotate and adjudicate legal concept names from Indian Supreme Court case proceedings. The system supports practical annotation workflows for legal domain.
AI.conclusion: LeDA provides an effective solution for legal data annotation with dynamic tag creation capability, addressing the challenge of no pre-defined ontologies in legal domain. The system enables construction of semantic document representations that can enhance various downstream legal AI tasks.

title: Back from the Future: Key-Value Cache Management by Counter-Causal Surprise
summary: Key-value (KV) cache management through compression and eviction strategies has emerged as an important research direction in recent years. Computational demands of large language models (LLMs) and their multi-modal variants during output generation can be partially alleviated by caching previous key and value calculations needed by subsequent scaled dot-product attention operations. However, this leads to another problem: the size of the resulting KV cache grows linearly with context length and quickly consumes all available GPU memory when either the prompt or the generated output are long. KV cache management periodically prunes entries from the cache thereby reducing its memory footprint while attempting to retain sufficient information for accurate generation. A by-product is faster inference speed. We propose a simple yet effective KV eviction scheme motivated by the insight that past tokens which can be well-predicted from more recent tokens are redundant and their associated keys and values can be removed from the cache. To score entries for eviction we run the model on the tokens in their original order, reusing the key and value representations already stored in the KV cache, and applying a counter-causal attention mask so that each position attends only to its future context. This is in-distribution, tied directly to the actual cache contents, and requires no additional training. To further reduce cost, we additionally propose a fast single-layer approximation that restricts the counter-causal pass to the last transformer layer, achieving a significant speedup per refresh cycle at marginal accuracy cost. We evaluate our strategy on various open-source LLMs and benchmark datasets showing competitive or improved performance over other state-of-the-art methods. Reference code is available at https://github.com/metacognitionai/counter_causal.

AI.tldr: A novel KV cache eviction method that removes redundant tokens by scoring them based on how well they can be predicted from future context, using counter-causal attention without additional training.
AI.motivation: The KV cache in LLMs grows linearly with context length, consuming excessive GPU memory during long prompts or outputs. Existing compression/eviction strategies are needed but current methods may not optimally identify which tokens are truly redundant for maintaining generation quality.
AI.method: Proposes a KV eviction scheme that scores cache entries by running the model with counter-causal attention masks - each position attends only to future context to determine if past tokens can be predicted from more recent ones. Also introduces a fast single-layer approximation that restricts this process to the last transformer layer for efficiency.
AI.result: The method shows competitive or improved performance over state-of-the-art KV cache management techniques on various open-source LLMs and benchmark datasets, while requiring no additional training.
AI.conclusion: Tokens that can be accurately predicted from future context are redundant and can be safely evicted from KV cache, enabling effective memory reduction and faster inference without compromising generation quality.

title: MemeBench: What LVLMs Miss When Interpreting Culture-Dependent Memes
summary: Large vision-language models have improved at describing visual content, but accurate descriptions do not ensure interpretation when meaning depends on knowledge beyond the pixels. Memes expose this gap because they rely on cultural entities, background knowledge, and community conventions. Most meme benchmarks reduce interpretation to labels or holistic scores, obscuring where an explanation breaks down. We introduce MemeBench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,253 Chinese and English memes with human-written references and quality-controlled VIKR annotations, centered on anime, comics, games, and adjacent online subcultures. Its VIKR schema decomposes explanations into Visual clues, Identity links, Knowledge units, and Reasoning mechanisms. Across 26 LVLMs, every model covers visible content more reliably than the knowledge needed to interpret it, and even the strongest retains a 22.6% Visual-Knowledge gap. To test whether this diagnosis can guide improvement, we introduce KAR, an entity-guided retrieval baseline built on CultureBase. Across four controlled models, KAR raises VIKR Success by 3.6-7.4% and, compared with generic retrieval, repairs more answers and breaks fewer. Yet both retrieval conditions improve Identity and Knowledge while reducing Visual coverage in every comparison. MemeBench reveals whether an interpretation succeeds, what is missing, and whether targeted evidence fills the diagnosed gap.

AI.tldr: MemeBench is a diagnostic benchmark for evaluating large vision-language models' ability to interpret memes, focusing on cultural knowledge gaps rather than just visual description.
AI.motivation: Large vision-language models can describe visual content but struggle with interpretation when meaning depends on cultural knowledge beyond pixels. Memes expose this gap as they rely on cultural entities, background knowledge, and community conventions. Existing meme benchmarks reduce interpretation to labels or scores, obscuring where explanations break down.
AI.method: Created MemeBench with 1,253 Chinese and English memes from anime, comics, games, and online subcultures with human-written references and quality-controlled VIKR annotations. VIKR schema decomposes explanations into Visual clues, Identity links, Knowledge units, and Reasoning mechanisms. Also introduced KAR (entity-guided retrieval baseline built on CultureBase) to test if diagnosis can guide improvement.
AI.result: Across 26 LVLMs, all models covered visible content more reliably than needed knowledge, with strongest models retaining 22.6% Visual-Knowledge gap. KAR improved VIKR Success by 3.6-7.4% across four controlled models, repairing more answers and breaking fewer compared to generic retrieval. Both retrieval conditions improved Identity and Knowledge but reduced Visual coverage.
AI.conclusion: MemeBench reveals whether interpretation succeeds, what is missing, and whether targeted evidence fills diagnosed gaps. It provides diagnostic capabilities to understand where vision-language models fail in cultural interpretation, guiding targeted improvements beyond visual description.

title: Kalman Meets Curriculum: Efficient Dynamic Prompt Selection for Adaptive RL Finetuning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) finetuning significantly enhances the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet its effectiveness critically depends on selecting prompts of appropriate difficulty for the current policy. This is challenging because prompt difficulty evolves throughout training. Existing online methods therefore face a trade-off: evaluation-based approaches are accurate but expensive, while prediction-based approaches are efficient but typically assume stationary difficulty, making them ill-suited to RL's non-stationary training dynamics. To address these issues, we propose a Kalman-Guided Prompt Selection method (KGPS), which reformulates prompt selection as a dynamic state estimation problem rather than static difficulty prediction. KGPS models each prompt's latent success rate in logit space using a linear-Gaussian state-space model, with process noise coupled to the magnitude of policy updates so that uncertainty increases when the policy changes more substantially. A Kalman filter then maintains a calibrated Gaussian posterior over prompt difficulty, and prompts are selected by maximizing a posterior-expected training utility that favors intermediate-difficulty prompts while naturally revisiting uncertain ones. The resulting procedure is adaptive to policy drift and requires no additional rollouts beyond standard policy training. Extensive experiments across mathematics, planning, and geometry reasoning benchmarks, as well as multiple RL algorithms, show that KGPS consistently improves both final accuracy and rollout efficiency over strong baselines, establishing state-of-the-art performance among online prompt selection methods. For example, on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, KGPS uses 83% fewer rollouts than DS while even improving the average performance by 0.12 point across six math reasoning benchmarks.

AI.tldr: KGPS uses a Kalman filter to dynamically select appropriate difficulty prompts for RL fine-tuning of LLMs, improving efficiency and performance without extra rollouts.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt selection methods for RL fine-tuning of LLMs face a trade-off: evaluation-based approaches are accurate but expensive, while prediction-based approaches are efficient but assume stationary difficulty, which doesn't fit RL's non-stationary training dynamics where prompt difficulty evolves as the policy changes.
AI.method: KGPS reformulates prompt selection as a dynamic state estimation problem using a linear-Gaussian state-space model. It models each prompt's latent success rate in logit space with process noise coupled to policy update magnitude (uncertainty increases when policy changes more). A Kalman filter maintains calibrated Gaussian posterior over prompt difficulty, and prompts are selected by maximizing posterior-expected training utility that favors intermediate-difficulty prompts while naturally revisiting uncertain ones.
AI.result: KGPS consistently improves both final accuracy and rollout efficiency across mathematics, planning, and geometry reasoning benchmarks with multiple RL algorithms. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, it uses 83% fewer rollouts than DS while improving average performance by 0.12 points across six math reasoning benchmarks, establishing state-of-the-art performance among online prompt selection methods.
AI.conclusion: KGPS provides an effective solution to the prompt selection problem in RL fine-tuning by treating it as dynamic state estimation, enabling adaptive selection to policy drift without requiring additional rollouts beyond standard policy training, leading to more efficient and effective RL-based reasoning enhancement for LLMs.

title: STEREODISCO: Discovering Stereotypicality in LLMs
summary: LLMs encode, convey, and perpetuate stereotypes. Prior computational research focuses on a small set of semantic axes investigated in social psychology, and operates on word embeddings produced by language models, leaving open which other semantic axes carry stereotypical associations in LLMs and how LLMs internally represent such axes. We introduce STEREODISCO, a framework that adapts the semantic differential method (Osgood et al., 1957) to the systematic study of stereotypes in LLM internal representations. STEREODISCO constructs approx. 2,000 candidate semantic axes from WordNet antonym synsets, recovers each as a geometric axis in the LLM's activation space via probing, and identifies stereotypical axes via a statistical test over concept projections. As a case study, we apply STEREODISCO to social group stereotypes with LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT and MISTRAL-7B-INSTRUCT. We find that the two LLMs agree with each other on social group ratings more than with humans, suggesting that LLM-encoded stereotype content diverges from that documented in social psychology. We also discover stereotypical axes not investigated in prior work -- including humble vs. proud, narrow-minded vs. broad-minded, and cowardly vs. brave, which human annotators independently confirm.

AI.tldr: STEREODISCO is a framework that systematically studies stereotypes in LLMs by constructing semantic axes from WordNet, probing LLM internal representations, and identifying stereotypical associations through statistical testing.
AI.motivation: Current computational research on stereotypes in LLMs is limited to a small set of semantic axes from social psychology and focuses on word embeddings, leaving gaps in understanding which other semantic axes carry stereotypes and how LLMs internally represent them.
AI.method: STEREODISCO adapts the semantic differential method to LLMs by: 1) constructing ~2,000 candidate semantic axes from WordNet antonym synsets, 2) recovering each as a geometric axis in the LLM's activation space via probing, and 3) identifying stereotypical axes via statistical tests over concept projections.
AI.result: Applied to LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT and MISTRAL-7B-INSTRUCT: 1) The two LLMs agree with each other on social group ratings more than with humans, suggesting LLM-encoded stereotype content diverges from documented social psychology, 2) Discovered new stereotypical axes (humble vs. proud, narrow-minded vs. broad-minded, cowardly vs. brave) that human annotators independently confirmed.
AI.conclusion: STEREODISCO provides a systematic framework for studying stereotypes in LLMs beyond traditional semantic axes, revealing that LLMs encode stereotype content that diverges from human psychology and includes previously unstudied dimensions.

title: Real-Time Hard Peak Age-of-Information Safety with No-Regret Learning
comment: Accepted to 2026 IEEE Real-Time Systems Symposium (RTSS)
summary: Safety-critical IoT systems such as industrial closed-loop control, V2X coordination, and remote teleoperation require every sensor's peak Age of Information (peak AoI, also abbreviated PAoI) to stay below a hard per-slot deadline, not merely an average bound. Existing approaches meet this requirement only under restrictive assumptions: stochastic channels for Whittle-index AoI, simulator rollouts for deep reinforcement learning, or sublinear cumulative violation for long-term constrained online convex optimization. Under adversarial coefficients, OCO-PAoI-Hard guarantees zero per-slot violation of the modeled AoI state under one-step viability and O(sqrt(T)) regret against any static safe comparator; packet-level safety requires stronger service assumptions. Our key observation is that the fractional peak-AoI deadline collapses exactly to an affine half-space constraint on the resource-allocation vector, turning hard real-time scheduling into time-varying constrained online convex optimization over a polyhedral safe set. A strictly causal proposal-shield-update loop enforces feasibility through one Euclidean projection per slot, the gradient step preserves no-regret behavior, and the classical virtual queue is reduced to an a-posteriori certificate. We establish closed-form static and dynamic regret bounds, a matching Omega(sqrt(T)) minimax lower bound, a margin-safe variant against execution noise, and a deadline-induced competitive ratio. On a four-sensor adversarial fluid-model trap channel, OCO-PAoI-Hard attains zero modeled-state deadline violations across all ten seeds, while four representative baselines miss between 1.65 percent and 64.0 percent of slots, and the empirical normalized regret stays below the theoretical envelope across two orders of magnitude in T.

AI.tldr: The paper presents OCO-PAoI-Hard, an online convex optimization framework that guarantees zero per-slot violations of peak Age of Information deadlines for safety-critical IoT systems, even under adversarial conditions, achieving O(√T) regret.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for ensuring peak Age of Information (PAoI) deadlines in safety-critical IoT systems only work under restrictive assumptions like stochastic channels, simulator rollouts, or allow sublinear cumulative violations. There's a need for a method that guarantees zero per-slot deadline violations under adversarial conditions.
AI.method: Key insight: fractional peak-AoI deadlines collapse to affine half-space constraints on resource allocation. The approach uses a strictly causal proposal-shield-update loop with one Euclidean projection per slot to enforce feasibility, with gradient steps preserving no-regret behavior. It transforms hard real-time scheduling into time-varying constrained online convex optimization over polyhedral safe sets.
AI.result: OCO-PAoI-Hard guarantees zero per-slot violation of modeled AoI state under one-step viability and O(√T) regret against static safe comparators. It achieves zero modeled-state deadline violations in adversarial fluid-model trap channel tests, while baselines miss 1.65-64.0% of slots. Provides closed-form static/dynamic regret bounds, Ω(√T) minimax lower bound, margin-safe variant, and deadline-induced competitive ratio.
AI.conclusion: The proposed OCO-PAoI-Hard framework successfully addresses the challenge of hard real-time PAoI deadlines in adversarial environments, providing both safety guarantees (zero per-slot violations) and performance guarantees (no-regret behavior), outperforming existing approaches that fail to meet hard deadlines consistently.

title: Sign Language Question Answering: A New Task, Benchmark, and Baseline for Sign Language Understanding
summary: Recent advances in sign language (SL) understanding (SLU) have led to remarkable progress in tasks such as continuous SL recognition and SL translation. However, these tasks are designed with predefined objectives, requiring models to learn a fixed mapping from sign videos to glosses or spoken-language sentences. As a result, they provide only a limited assessment of whether a model truly understands the semantic content of SL videos. To address this limitation, \textbf{we first propose a new task, Sign Language Question Answering (SLQA)}, which evaluates SL understanding by requiring models to answer arbitrary natural language questions about SL videos. Unlike previous SLU tasks, SLQA provides a more flexible and comprehensive evaluation framework that assesses multiple reasoning capabilities beyond recognition and translation. To facilitate this task, \textbf{we further construct two SignQA benchmarks} based on PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily by automatically generating question-answer pairs from existing gloss and sentence annotations using carefully designed templates. The resulting datasets cover five complementary question categories, including position reasoning, structural reasoning, visual search, gloss recognition, and translation understanding. \textbf{Finally, we propose a simple yet effective baseline model} equipped with a Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling module and an in-domain knowledge transfer strategy, enabling effective knowledge transfer from existing SLU tasks while enhancing question-aware temporal feature modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our baseline consistently outperforms representative vision-language models across all question categories, establishing a strong benchmark for future research on SLQA. Datasets are available at:{https://huggingface.co/datasets/hulala/SignQA-2026}.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Sign Language Question Answering (SLQA) as a new comprehensive task to evaluate SL understanding beyond fixed recognition/translation, creates two SignQA benchmarks, and proposes an effective baseline model with novel modules.
AI.motivation: Existing SLU tasks like continuous SL recognition and translation require models to learn fixed mappings from sign videos to glosses or sentences, providing limited assessment of whether models truly understand semantic content. There's a need for more flexible and comprehensive evaluation of SL understanding.
AI.method: 1) Proposed SLQA task requiring models to answer arbitrary natural language questions about SL videos. 2) Constructed two SignQA benchmarks using PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily by automatically generating QA pairs from existing annotations via carefully designed templates covering five question categories. 3) Developed baseline model with Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling module and in-domain knowledge transfer strategy.
AI.result: The proposed baseline consistently outperforms representative vision-language models across all five question categories, establishing a strong benchmark for future SLQA research. Datasets are publicly available.
AI.conclusion: SLQA provides a more flexible and comprehensive evaluation framework for SL understanding beyond traditional recognition/translation tasks. The created benchmarks and baseline model enable effective assessment of multiple reasoning capabilities and facilitate future research in this direction.

title: First-order Constrained Trilevel Optimization Over Distributed Networks for Robust Coreset Selection
summary: With the rapid advancement of the Internet of Things (IoT), massive amounts of data are generated across distributed edge networks. Training models on full data incurs significant computational overhead and storage bottlenecks, rendering coreset selection a critical paradigm. Furthermore, given the privacy-sensitive nature of local data and the escalating demand for model robustness in real-world deployments, developing an effective distributed optimization framework for robust coreset selection is vital, yet remains largely unexplored. To this end, this work first characterizes the hierarchical dependencies among coreset selection, robust optimization, and distributed learning, and formulates the distributed robust coreset selection as a trilevel optimization problem with level-wise constraints. Furthermore, to effectively solve the trilevel problem in a distributed manner, the \underline{F}ederated \underline{F}irst-order \underline{C}onstrained \underline{T}rilevel \underline{O}ptimization (F$^2$CTO) is proposed, which synergistically integrates a hierarchical composite value-function reformulation and a distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, F$^2$CTO is the first method developed for distributed robust coreset selection, as well as the first distributed optimization approach for trilevel optimization problems with level-wise constraints. Additionally, we prove that the proposed method achieves a non-asymptotic convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-3/2})$ for finding an $ε$-stationary point. Extensive empirical evaluations on reliable continual learning demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed F$^2$CTO.

AI.tldr: F²CTO: First federated trilevel optimization method for robust coreset selection in IoT edge networks with O(ε^{-3/2}) convergence rate.
AI.motivation: IoT generates massive distributed data where full data training faces computational overhead and storage bottlenecks. Privacy concerns and need for robust models in real-world deployments create a gap in effective distributed optimization for robust coreset selection.
AI.method: Formulates distributed robust coreset selection as trilevel optimization with level-wise constraints. Proposes F²CTO (Federated First-order Constrained Trilevel Optimization) combining hierarchical composite value-function reformulation with distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm.
