AI.result: Proves non-asymptotic convergence rate of O(ε^{-3/2}) for finding ε-stationary point. Extensive empirical evaluations on reliable continual learning demonstrate effectiveness and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: F²CTO is the first method for distributed robust coreset selection and first distributed optimization approach for trilevel problems with level-wise constraints, addressing critical IoT edge network challenges.

title: MemTxn: A Transaction Boundary for Source-Supported Updates and Complete-State Recovery in Agent Memory
summary: Persistent memory lets long-running large language model agents reuse information across sessions and tasks. Yet errors in writable memory can persist and corrupt future behavior. Existing systems improve storage and retrieval, but they do not provide a transaction boundary for reliable updates and recovery. We therefore propose MemTxn, a governance layer outside the answer model. MemTxn verifies whether an update is supported by its source. It also selects the visible version when facts conflict and restores the application-visible state after a fault. The system uses Ordered PatchTest to validate writes, a Temporal Resolver to select versions, and a durable snapshot journal to recover state. On an item-disjoint audit, MemTxn accepts all 60 supported originals and rejects all 179 hard negatives. Under persistent multi-key faults on LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo states, it restores the complete declared active map without knowing the actual physical write set. On MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation, MemTxn achieves the highest average F1 across all twelve answer-model configurations. It outperforms Dense by 17.06--24.07 points in five representative settings.

AI.tldr: MemTxn is a transaction layer for persistent memory in LLM agents that provides reliable updates, conflict resolution, and fault recovery while maintaining data integrity.
AI.motivation: Persistent memory allows LLM agents to reuse information across sessions, but errors in writable memory can persist and corrupt future behavior. Existing systems lack transaction boundaries for reliable updates and recovery.
AI.method: MemTxn introduces a governance layer with three key components: Ordered PatchTest to validate writes by checking if updates are supported by their sources, Temporal Resolver to select visible versions when facts conflict, and a durable snapshot journal to recover state after faults.
AI.result: MemTxn achieved perfect performance on item-disjoint audit (accepting all 60 originals, rejecting all 179 hard negatives), restored complete active maps under persistent multi-key faults without knowing physical write sets, and outperformed Dense by 17.06-24.07 points across five representative settings on MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation.
AI.conclusion: MemTxn successfully addresses the reliability issues in persistent memory for LLM agents by providing transaction boundaries, validation, conflict resolution, and fault recovery, achieving state-of-the-art performance on memory management tasks.

title: Certifying when decision-time information justifies adaptive experimentation
summary: Adaptive laboratories choose measurements during experiments, yet most methods begin after adaptation is permitted. We introduce Opportunity-aware Policy Authorization for Laboratories (\OPAL{}), a framework that decides whether adaptation should be enabled at all. \OPAL{} uses a precommitted contract to require non-trivial adaptation, controlled target risk and positive executed value after cost. We establish an impossibility boundary: source outcomes and unlabelled target covariates cannot uniformly support non-trivial authorization under unrestricted conditional outcome shift, and derive a target-calibrated recovery. Applied to an unseen 11,265-compound Cell Painting partition, the frozen gate selected 595 compounds, captured 384 positive opportunities and achieved strictly positive executed value under least-favourable completion; its 5.18\% false-activation upper bound remained below a 7.5\% limit. Among six methods, only \OPAL{} combined non-zero activation with this risk control. Locked pharmacogenomic and finite-campaign studies distinguish policy misalignment from non-certifiability, establishing authorization as a distinct layer for safe adaptive science.

AI.tldr: OPAL is a framework that decides when to enable adaptive measurements in labs, using contracts to ensure non-trivial adaptation with controlled risk and positive value after costs.
AI.motivation: Most adaptive laboratory methods begin after adaptation is permitted, but there's a need to determine whether adaptation should be enabled at all. Adaptive labs face the challenge of deciding when to allow adaptive measurements while controlling risks.
AI.method: OPAL uses a precommitted contract that requires non-trivial adaptation, controlled target risk, and positive executed value after cost. It addresses impossibility boundaries in authorization under conditional outcome shift and derives target-calibrated recovery methods.
AI.result: In an unseen 11,265-compound Cell Painting partition, OPAL selected 595 compounds, captured 384 positive opportunities, achieved strictly positive executed value, and maintained a 5.18% false-activation upper bound below the 7.5% limit. Among six methods, only OPAL combined non-zero activation with this risk control.
AI.conclusion: Authorization represents a distinct layer for safe adaptive science, distinguishing policy misalignment from non-certifiability. OPAL establishes that intelligent authorization gates can enable adaptive measurements while maintaining rigorous safety guarantees.

title: Crossing the Margin Cliff: Toward Relearn-Robust LLM Unlearning via Margin Calibration
summary: Large language model unlearning is consistently fragile under relearn attacks. On TOFU, fine-tuning on twenty forget examples substantially recovers held-out forget-set ROUGE for every method we evaluate, and we trace this fragility to optimization geometry. The per-token answer margin of fourteen post-hoc methods spanning gradient, preference, and distillation families converges into a narrow band above the retain reference in 41 of 42 method--size cells, a regularity we call the margin cliff. We prove that this cliff follows whenever the retain coupling holds the diagnostic log-odds of forget content above a floor, a condition that token-saturating losses induce at stationarity and that we verify directly on 34 of 42 cells. Margin Calibration (\textsc{MC}) is a plug-in polish adding a non-saturating margin hinge anchored at the reference's per-token margin plus a KL probe on a disjoint instruction corpus, restoring forget-side pressure where the native loss saturates. Under a stated gradient-dominance condition, whose on-trajectory gradient signature we measure by instrumenting the polish, its stationary set lies on the cliff-crossing side, yielding an attack-budget upper bound on the relearn margin lift. Across TOFU (three Llama-3 sizes, three forget tiers), MUSE-News on Llama-2-7B-hf, and a Phi-3.5 panel, a single frozen configuration wins all 14 head-to-head forget aggregates and all populated relearn cells (panel-mean post-attack ROUGE-L $0.41$ to $0.18$) and lowers raw membership AUC on 13/14, with reduced retain-side utility as the main cost. A deployment variant matches these gains without a retain-trained reference.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a fundamental fragility in LLM unlearning methods under relearn attacks and proposes Margin Calibration (MC) as a plug-in solution to strengthen unlearning by adding targeted margin constraints.
AI.motivation: Current large language model unlearning methods are fragile and vulnerable to relearn attacks where fine-tuning on a small number of forget examples can substantially recover the forgotten content. The authors discovered that various unlearning methods converge to a narrow margin band above retain references, making them susceptible to relearn attacks.
AI.method: The authors propose Margin Calibration (MC), a plug-in polish method that adds a non-saturating margin hinge anchored at the reference's per-token margin plus a KL probe on a disjoint instruction corpus. This restores forget-side pressure where native losses saturate. They validate their approach across multiple datasets (TOFU, MUSE-News) and models (Llama-3, Llama-2-7B-hf, Phi-3.5).
AI.result: MC significantly improves unlearning robustness: across all 14 head-to-head forget aggregates and all populated relearn cells, a single frozen configuration reduces post-attack ROUGE-L from 0.41 to 0.18 on average. It also lowers raw membership AUC on 13/14 cases, though with some reduced retain-side utility as a trade-off.
AI.conclusion: The margin cliff phenomenon explains the fragility of current unlearning methods, and Margin Calibration provides a practical solution that significantly improves robustness against relearn attacks while maintaining reasonable trade-offs in utility.

title: Evaluation Protocols and Cross-Subject Generalization in EEG Emotion Recognition
comment: 41 pages, 6 figures, 11 tables including supplementary information. Submitted to Applied Intelligence
summary: Reported accuracy in electroencephalography (EEG) emotion recognition depends on the complete evaluation procedure, not only the classifier. We separate the target quantity, development procedure, and reporting rule, then use one archived dynamical graph convolutional neural network (DGCNN) pathway on SEED and SEED-IV as an illustrative case. In a protocol-matched subject-dependent check, the SEED result was within 1.47 percentage points of the public reference value; the 3.40-point SEED-IV difference remained unresolved. Across 30 matched SEED subject-session trajectories, checkpoint selection based on repeated test-set evaluation increased mean window accuracy from 0.7855 at epoch 80 to 0.8892. Under five-fold subject-disjoint evaluation, validation-selected checkpoints achieved training-participant trial accuracies of 0.9990 on SEED and 0.9920 on SEED-IV. Accuracy for entirely held-out participants was 0.5348 (95% conditional subject-level bias-corrected and accelerated [BCa] interval [0.4667, 0.5985]) on SEED. The SEED-IV estimate was 0.3954 ([0.3343, 0.4648]) and is reported only as secondary sensitivity evidence because its protocol-matched compatibility check remained unresolved. The observed train-to-held-out-subject gaps are inconsistent with simple optimization underfitting, but they do not isolate subject identity from implementation, preprocessing, representation, or distributional factors. Supporting analyses further showed that participant rankings depended on representation and time scale, while a development-selected tail-risk ensemble did not establish a positive gain in a separate final evaluation. Subject-dependent, subject-disjoint, and cross-session results should therefore be reported as answers to different questions.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals that EEG emotion recognition accuracy depends heavily on evaluation procedures, showing significant performance gaps between subject-dependent and subject-disjoint settings, with held-out subject accuracy being substantially lower than training participant accuracy.
AI.motivation: To investigate how reported accuracy in EEG emotion recognition depends on the complete evaluation procedure, not just the classifier, and to highlight the importance of separating different evaluation protocols (subject-dependent vs. subject-disjoint).
AI.method: Used DGCNN on SEED and SEED-IV datasets, conducted protocol-matched subject-dependent checks, analyzed checkpoint selection strategies, performed five-fold subject-disjoint evaluation, and compared different evaluation scenarios including participant rankings and tail-risk ensembles.
AI.result: Subject-dependent checkpoints achieved near-perfect accuracy on training participants (0.9990 on SEED, 0.9920 on SEED-IV), but accuracy dropped dramatically for held-out participants (0.5348 on SEED, 0.3954 on SEED-IV). Checkpoint selection improved mean window accuracy significantly in subject-dependent settings.
AI.conclusion: Different evaluation procedures answer different research questions - subject-dependent, subject-disjoint, and cross-session results should be reported separately, as the observed train-to-held-out-subject gaps are inconsistent with simple optimization underfitting but affected by various factors including subject identity, implementation, and representation.

title: Virtual Process Dossier: A Process-Aware Data Catalogue
summary: We propose the Virtual Process Dossier (VPD), a Knowledge Graph-based data catalogue that also captures workflow provenance. We developed VPD for multi-stage manufacturing use-cases where downstream AI-based optimization tasks require to distinct between datasets generated during individual workflow steps. VPD provides these datasets in a FAIR manner and makes both prospective and retrospective workflow provenance explicit. Our contributions are: (1) the VPD ontology that serves as the catalogue's semantic core; (2) the VPD provenance framework that integrates ontology instantiation into the production environment; and (3) the VPD user interface that provides human-centered interaction with the VPD Knowledge Graph. The ontology and code are available at https://github.com/kubeluk/VirtualProcessDossier .

AI.tldr: VPD is a Knowledge Graph-based data catalogue for manufacturing that captures workflow provenance to support downstream AI optimization by distinguishing datasets from different workflow steps.
AI.motivation: Multi-stage manufacturing use-cases require downstream AI-based optimization tasks to distinguish between datasets generated during individual workflow steps, necessitating a system that provides these datasets in a FAIR manner with explicit workflow provenance.
AI.method: Developed a Knowledge Graph-based data catalogue with: (1) VPD ontology as semantic core, (2) provenance framework integrating ontology instantiation into production environment, and (3) user interface for human-centered interaction with the Knowledge Graph.
AI.result: Created the VPD system that makes both prospective and retrospective workflow provenance explicit, providing datasets in a FAIR manner for manufacturing workflows, with ontology and code made publicly available.
AI.conclusion: VPD successfully addresses the need for workflow provenance in manufacturing by combining Knowledge Graph technology with provenance capture, enabling better AI-based optimization through clear dataset distinction across workflow steps.

title: Looped Transformers with Source-Centered State Evolution
summary: Looped Transformers create a useful train- and test-time compute axis by reusing the same Transformer block over recurrent depth, increasing effective depth at a fixed parameter count. However, that shared block must then govern an entire trajectory of varying hidden states over trained and extrapolated depths. Furthermore, in additive-injection looped Transformers, an input-conditioned signal is reintroduced at every recurrent step, so applying the shared transition at an input-conditioned reference can still move the hidden state. In this paper, we propose Source-Centered State Evolution (SCSE), which is designed to reconcile input conditioning with reference-preserving shared recurrence. Specifically, SCSE retains input dependence through its learned anchor and initial deviation, allows nonzero deviations to drive recurrent computation while mapping zero deviation to zero, and guarantees exact anchor invariance through its zero-deviation mask. The designated anchor is thereby a one-step fixed point by construction. The zero-deviation forcing bias is the next deviation produced from the anchor itself and vanishes in SCSE, while nonzero deviations remain active and support state-dependent recurrent computation. Our theory shows that the zero-deviation forcing bias is a design degree of freedom whose task effect can be harmful, neutral, or beneficial; SCSE resolves this choice in favor of exact anchor invariance by setting the bias to zero. Across WikiText-2, WikiText-103, direct web-corpus pretraining, held-out web-text transfer, and LAMBADA completion, SCSE improves the controlled recurrent quality frontier. Ablation studies identify the learned anchor and the anchor-coordinate deviation recurrence as the primary contributors to the gain, and a trained-model case study grounds the anchor-response diagnostic in observed recurrent motion.

AI.tldr: Proposes Source-Centered State Evolution (SCSE) for looped Transformers to reconcile input conditioning with reference-preserving shared recurrence, improving performance on language modeling tasks.
AI.motivation: Looped Transformers reuse the same Transformer block over recurrent depth to increase effective depth at fixed parameter count, but the shared block must govern varying hidden states over trained and extrapolated depths. Current additive-injection looped Transformers reintroduce input-conditioned signals at every step, causing the shared transition at input-conditioned references to still move the hidden state.
AI.method: Source-Centered State Evolution (SCSE) retains input dependence through learned anchor and initial deviation, allows nonzero deviations to drive recurrent computation while mapping zero deviation to zero, and guarantees exact anchor invariance through zero-deviation mask. The designated anchor is a one-step fixed point by construction, with zero-deviation forcing bias set to zero to ensure exact anchor invariance.
AI.result: SCSE improves the controlled recurrent quality frontier across WikiText-2, WikiText-103, direct web-corpus pretraining, held-out web-text transfer, and LAMBADA completion. Ablation studies identify learned anchor and anchor-coordinate deviation recurrence as primary contributors to gains.
AI.conclusion: SCSE resolves the design choice of zero-deviation forcing bias in favor of exact anchor invariance, improving looped Transformer performance through better reconciliation of input conditioning with reference-preserving shared recurrence.

title: Simplifying Neural Networks During Training
summary: Understanding and exploiting the training dynamics of overparameterized deep neural networks remains a central challenge in modern machine learning. Recent evidence on Neural Collapse (NC) shows that class representations and classifiers exhibit highly structured geometry, while the Tunnel Effect suggests that only a subset of layers is essential for feature extraction. We combine these two perspectives and propose an NC-inspired training framework for simplifying deep networks during training. Our method monitors representation dynamics through the Inverse Fisher Criterion, a stable and efficient proxy for the variability collapse behavior, to identify both the split point between feature extraction and classification and the training stage at which simplification becomes viable. We then replace the trailing layers with a lightweight classification head and continue training the reduced model. Experiments on image-classification benchmarks across MLP, VGG, and ResNet architectures show that the proposed method achieves substantial parameter reductions while maintaining accuracy comparable to that of the full model. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at: https://github.com/LorenzoSciandra/NNS.

AI.tldr: Neural Collapse-inspired training framework that monitors representation dynamics to identify optimal points for simplifying deep networks by replacing trailing layers with lightweight classification heads, achieving substantial parameter reductions while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to address the challenge of understanding and exploiting training dynamics of overparameterized deep neural networks by combining insights from Neural Collapse (structured geometry of class representations) and the Tunnel Effect (only a subset of layers is essential for feature extraction). The goal is to develop a method for simplifying deep networks during training.
AI.method: Proposes an NC-inspired training framework that monitors representation dynamics through the Inverse Fisher Criterion, a stable proxy for variability collapse behavior. This monitoring identifies both the split point between feature extraction and classification and the training stage when simplification becomes viable. The method then replaces trailing layers with a lightweight classification head and continues training the reduced model.
AI.result: Experiments on image-classification benchmarks across MLP, VGG, and ResNet architectures show that the proposed method achieves substantial parameter reductions while maintaining accuracy comparable to that of the full model.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully demonstrates that combining Neural Collapse and Tunnel Effect insights enables effective simplification of deep networks during training, achieving significant parameter savings without compromising accuracy across multiple architectures and benchmarks.

title: Understanding Submodular Information Measure Based Objectives for Representation Learning: A Variance and Separation Perspective
summary:
Submodular Information Measures (SIMs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for representation learning and multimodal learning. In particular, the SCORE framework~\cite{majee2024score} demonstrated that SIMs can serve as effective objectives for supervised contrastive learning. Despite their empirical success, however, the geometric and statistical properties induced by different submodular information measures remain poorly understood.
  In this work, we develop a unified theoretical framework connecting SIMs to classical concepts in representation learning and statistical pattern recognition. We show that Total Information (TI) objectives characterize intra-class structure: Graph Cut TI recovers within-class variance, LogDet TI recovers generalized variance and covariance volume, and Facility Location TI induces imbalance-aware separation that emphasizes rare and confusable classes. We further show that Mutual Information (MI) objectives capture complementary notions of inter-class structure: Graph Cut MI is closely related to centroid separation and Fisher-style discrimination, LogDet MI captures covariance-aware separation through Mahalanobis distance, and Facility Location MI measures nearest-mode representational overlap.
  We validate these theoretical characterizations using controlled synthetic experiments that independently vary variance, covariance, class imbalance, class separation, and multimodal overlap. Across all settings, the empirical behavior closely matches the proposed theory. Our results provide the first unified geometric and statistical understanding of submodular information measures and offer principled guidance for selecting and designing SIM-based objectives for representation learning.

AI.tldr: Submodular Information Measures (SIMs) serve as objectives for representation learning, but their geometric/statistical properties were poorly understood. This work provides a unified theoretical framework connecting SIMs to classical representation learning concepts, showing how Total Information captures intra-class structure and Mutual Information captures inter-class structure, with empirical validation.
AI.motivation: Despite the empirical success of Submodular Information Measures (SIMs) in representation learning (as shown in the SCORE framework), their geometric and statistical properties remain poorly understood. There's a need to develop theoretical understanding of how different SIMs induce specific geometric and statistical properties in learned representations.
AI.method: Developed a unified theoretical framework connecting SIMs to classical representation learning and statistical pattern recognition concepts. The approach includes theoretical characterizations showing how different Total Information (TI) objectives (Graph Cut TI, LogDet TI, Facility Location TI) capture different aspects of intra-class structure, and how Mutual Information (MI) objectives capture inter-class structure. Validated theoretical characterizations using controlled synthetic experiments varying variance, covariance, class imbalance, class separation, and multimodal overlap.
AI.result: Theoretical results show: 1) Total Information objectives characterize intra-class structure - Graph Cut TI recovers within-class variance, LogDet TI recovers generalized variance and covariance volume, Facility Location TI induces imbalance-aware separation. 2) Mutual Information objectives capture inter-class structure - Graph Cut MI relates to centroid separation and Fisher-style discrimination, LogDet MI captures covariance-aware separation via Mahalanobis distance, Facility Location MI measures nearest-mode representational overlap. Empirical validation across all synthetic settings closely matches theoretical predictions.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first unified geometric and statistical understanding of submodular information measures, offering principled guidance for selecting and designing SIM-based objectives for representation learning. The theoretical framework bridges SIMs to classical concepts in representation learning and statistical pattern recognition.

title: Back to All-Entity Ranking: Sampler-Dependent Evaluation in Continuous-Time Dynamic Graphs
summary:
Next-destination prediction in continuous-time dynamic graphs (CTDGs) commonly ranks an observed interaction against sampled negative destinations. The resulting score is conditional on both the negative distribution and the number of candidates chosen by the researcher. We show that a non-uniform negative distribution changes the Bayes-optimal ranking, while even a finite candidate set drawn uniformly can destabilize model rankings and measured module effects.
  Time-varying source-destination history membership and model operations that use this information directly transmit the sampler's influence to the evaluation score. We examine this mechanism using a factorial evaluation of repeated and new positives against seen and unseen negatives, a minimal scorer based solely on pair-history membership, and controlled representation interventions. Across six models on LastFM, MOOC, Reddit, and Wikipedia, at least one model pair changes relative order between the expected Uniform-20 metric and the full catalog on three of the four datasets. The measured effect of the same module also changes in magnitude and direction with the candidate-set size and training objective.
  These results establish that model-superiority and ablation conclusions from sampled-negative benchmarks are conditional on the stated candidate configuration. All-entity ranking evaluates every destination in a fixed catalog, eliminating negative-selection freedom and sampling variation while retaining the original CTDG scorer. We therefore recommend all-entity ranking as the primary evidence for architecture comparisons on CTDG benchmarks with an enumerable, fixed destination catalog.

AI.tldr: Sampled-negative evaluation in continuous-time dynamic graphs produces conditional rankings that depend on negative distribution and candidate set size, while all-entity ranking provides stable, unconditional comparisons.
AI.motivation: Current next-destination prediction methods in continuous-time dynamic graphs use sampled-negative evaluation, which produces rankings conditional on the negative distribution and number of candidates, potentially leading to unstable model comparisons and misleading ablation study conclusions.
AI.method: The authors conduct factorial evaluation of repeated and new positives against seen and unseen negatives, use minimal scorer based solely on pair-history membership, perform controlled representation interventions, and test six models across four datasets (LastFM, MOOC, Reddit, Wikipedia) comparing Uniform-20 metrics with full catalog rankings.
AI.result: Non-uniform negative distributions change Bayes-optimal rankings, finite candidate sets destabilize model rankings, and module effects change in magnitude/direction with candidate-set size and training objective. At least one model pair changes relative order between Uniform-20 and full catalog rankings on three of four datasets.
AI.conclusion: Model-superiority and ablation conclusions from sampled-negative benchmarks are conditional on candidate configuration. All-entity ranking (evaluating every destination) eliminates negative-selection freedom and sampling variation while retaining original CTDG scorer, making it the recommended primary evidence for architecture comparisons on CTDG benchmarks with enumerable, fixed destination catalogs.

title: FedOGL: Combating Catastrophic Forgetting in Federated Open-World Multimodal Graph Learning
summary: Federated graph learning enables collaborative training over decentralized graph data without sharing raw graph information. As such risks evolve, clients must learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams, retain historical categories, and reject samples outside the known class space. In this setting, clients must learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams while preserving historical categories and rejecting samples outside the current known class space. The core challenge is catastrophic forgetting, which in federated multimodal graphs is not merely a classifier-level failure: old knowledge can be erased through modality-semantic overwriting, topology-induced structural erosion, and federated memory fragmentation. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{FedOGL}, a semantic-structural memory preservation framework. On the client side, FedOGL preserves historical decision behavior through replay and task-start distillation, while protecting graph-propagation memory via projection onto a globally shared structure basis. On the server side, FedOGL maintains and transfers compact category prototypes to facilitate cross-client knowledge sharing without exposing raw graph data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, compared with the best-performing baselines, FedOGL reduces performance degradation caused by catastrophic forgetting by \textbf{42.67\%}, while maintaining or improving performance on downstream tasks.

AI.tldr: FedOGL: A federated graph learning framework for continual learning that addresses catastrophic forgetting in multimodal graph streams while preserving privacy.
AI.motivation: Federated graph learning needs to handle evolving risks where clients must learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams while preserving historical categories and rejecting unknown samples. The core challenge is catastrophic forgetting in federated multimodal graphs, which occurs through modality-semantic overwriting, topology-induced structural erosion, and federated memory fragmentation.
AI.method: FedOGL is a semantic-structural memory preservation framework with client-side preservation through replay and task-start distillation, and protection of graph-propagation memory via projection onto globally shared structure basis. Server-side maintains and transfers compact category prototypes for cross-client knowledge sharing without exposing raw graph data.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show FedOGL reduces performance degradation caused by catastrophic forgetting by 42.67% compared to best-performing baselines, while maintaining or improving performance on downstream tasks.
AI.conclusion: FedOGL effectively addresses catastrophic forgetting in federated multimodal graph learning through its semantic-structural memory preservation approach, enabling clients to learn emerging classes while preserving historical knowledge and maintaining privacy.

title: Orca: Neural Operators for Causal Reasoning in Continuous Time
summary: Structural causal models are the standard language for reasoning about interventions and counterfactuals, but they describe static variables, typically measured once, and usually forbid cyclic dependencies. Many systems we care about, such as patients, climates, and economies, instead evolve continuously in time, are observed at irregular time points, and contain feedback loops. We argue that neural operator learning provides a natural foundation for causal reasoning in this setting, and propose Orca, a framework in which each node of the causal graph is a function of time and each mechanism is a learned map between function spaces. We extend existing neural operator architectures to express causal mechanisms: a mechanism computes the function value of a node from its parent nodes by taking several parent functions as input, respects the arrow of time, and treats latent exogenous noise as a function that can be inferred and reused for counterfactuals. We formalize the model class and demonstrate counterfactual reasoning on synthetic continuous-time examples. Code is available at https://github.com/gerritgr/orca

AI.tldr: Orca is a framework that extends structural causal models to continuous-time systems with feedback loops by using neural operators to represent causal mechanisms as mappings between function spaces, enabling counterfactual reasoning on evolving systems.
AI.motivation: Traditional structural causal models are limited to static variables measured once and typically forbid cyclic dependencies, but many real-world systems (patients, climates, economies) evolve continuously in time, have irregular observation times, and contain feedback loops. There's a need for causal reasoning frameworks that can handle these dynamic, continuous-time systems.
AI.method: Orca proposes representing each node in a causal graph as a function of time, with each causal mechanism being a learned neural operator that maps between function spaces. The framework extends neural operator architectures to: 1) compute node functions from parent node functions, 2) respect the arrow of time, and 3) treat latent exogenous noise as an inferable function that can be reused for counterfactual reasoning.
AI.result: The authors formalize the Orca model class and demonstrate successful counterfactual reasoning on synthetic continuous-time examples, showing the framework's capability to handle dynamic systems with feedback loops.
AI.conclusion: Neural operator learning provides a natural foundation for causal reasoning in continuous-time systems with feedback, bridging the gap between traditional static causal models and the dynamic nature of many real-world systems. Orca enables counterfactual reasoning on evolving systems that were previously challenging for standard causal models.

title: Tight Sample Complexity for Low-Rank Adaptation: Matching Bounds and Rank Selection
summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard mechanism for fine-tuning large pretrained models, yet its statistical properties remain only partially understood. Existing generalization results provide upper bounds of the form O~(sqrt(rd/n)) or O~(rd/n), but a matching lower bound is missing, and the question of how to choose the LoRA rank r has no formal answer. Both gaps are closed here. A local Rademacher argument establishes an upper bound of O~(rd/n) on the excess risk of the empirical risk minimizer over rank-r LoRA, whenever the target adaptation has rank at most r. A matching minimax lower bound of Omega(rd/n) is then proved via a Fano-type packing of the rank-r subspace of R^{d x d}; the bound applies to any estimator whose output lies in the rank-r LoRA class. Combining the two yields a rank-selection dichotomy. For the constrained empirical risk minimizer, the optimal rank equals the intrinsic rank r*, and over-ranking strictly hurts. For adaptive estimators of the nuclear-norm-then-truncate type, over-ranking is harmless and the rate saturates at Theta~(r* d / n) regardless of r. Taken together, the three results characterize the statistical complexity of LoRA fine-tuning within the well-specified locally quadratic regime, and identify the empirically observed over-parameterization penalty as a property of unregularized empirical risk minimization rather than of the LoRA class itself. Predictions of the theory are verified on a synthetic trace-regression benchmark and on real LoRA fine-tuning across three (model, task) configurations covering DistilBERT and RoBERTa on SST-2 and MRPC. All configurations exhibit the predicted U-shape in validation loss, with two showing statistically significant loss inflation at large ranks (paired permutation p = 0.016).

AI.tldr: This paper provides the first complete statistical characterization of LoRA fine-tuning, establishing matching upper and lower bounds on generalization error, proving that over-ranking hurts unregularized ERM but not adaptive nuclear-norm estimators, and validating predictions with real experiments.
AI.motivation: LoRA has become standard for fine-tuning large pretrained models, but its statistical properties are poorly understood. Existing results only provide upper bounds without matching lower bounds, and there's no formal guidance on how to choose the LoRA rank r.
AI.method: 1) Used local Rademacher analysis to prove O~(rd/n) upper bound for empirical risk minimizer over rank-r LoRA; 2) Constructed minimax lower bound Ω(rd/n) via Fano-type packing of rank-r subspaces; 3) Analyzed rank-selection dichotomy for constrained ERM vs adaptive nuclear-norm-then-truncate estimators; 4) Validated theory on synthetic trace-regression benchmark and real LoRA fine-tuning experiments with DistilBERT and RoBERTa on SST-2 and MRPC tasks.
AI.result: 1) Established matching upper and lower bounds of Θ~(rd/n) on excess risk; 2) Proved dichotomy: for constrained ERM, optimal rank equals intrinsic rank r* and over-ranking hurts; for adaptive nuclear-norm estimators, over-ranking is harmless; 3) Empirical validation shows predicted U-shape in validation loss with statistically significant loss inflation at large ranks for two configurations (p = 0.016).
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first complete statistical characterization of LoRA fine-tuning, showing that the observed over-parameterization penalty is a property of unregularized ERM rather than the LoRA class itself. The theory guides practical rank selection and distinguishes between different estimation approaches.

title: Search as Computation Allocation
summary: Many algorithms spend an internal resource before returning a decision and are evaluated only by the quality of that terminal output. We formalize such procedures as terminal computation-allocation problems: costly computations produce observations, update beliefs about a latent environment, and matter only through terminal decision loss. Bellman equations characterize optimal allocation under fixed budgets, priced computation, and exact certification. We then relate value of computation (VOC) to information. Mutual information equals myopic VOC under log loss, whereas under simple regret VOC is a knowledge-gradient quantity; moreover, information gain can rank computations arbitrarily poorly, although it gives a one-sided upper bound on VOC. Bandit pulls, tree simulations, and node expansions illustrate the same model under different computation topologies. Finally, under an explicit frontier-resolution and heuristic-error model, maximizing approximate VOC recovers weighted A*, with A* and greedy best-first search as limiting cases. The theory identifies a shared decision problem without asserting that one acquisition rule is universally optimal.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes algorithms that consume internal resources before making final decisions as "terminal computation-allocation problems," analyzes the value of computation using Bellman equations, relates it to information theory, and shows how these principles recover classic search algorithms as special cases.
AI.motivation: Many algorithms consume computational resources before producing final decisions but are typically evaluated only by final output quality, not by how they allocate computation. The authors aim to formalize this resource allocation problem theoretically.
AI.method: Formalizes terminal computation-allocation problems using Bellman equations to characterize optimal computation allocation. Relates value of computation (VOC) to information measures like mutual information, and analyzes this framework under different computation topologies (bandit pulls, tree simulations, node expansions). Develops explicit frontier-resolution and heuristic-error models.
AI.result: Shows mutual information equals myopic VOC under log loss, while under simple regret VOC is a knowledge-gradient quantity. Information gain can rank computations poorly but provides one-sided upper bound on VOC. Under heuristic-error model, maximizing approximate VOC recovers weighted A*, with A* and greedy best-first search as limiting cases.
AI.conclusion: The theoretical framework identifies a shared decision problem structure across diverse algorithms without asserting universal optimality of any acquisition rule, providing principled analysis of computation allocation in terminal decision-making scenarios.

title: Event-Structured Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Differentiable Critical Clearing Boundaries
summary: Transient-stability assessment determines whether a power system can recover after a disturbance and is therefore essential to preventing generator trips and cascading outages. A key metric is the critical clearing time (CCT), which specifies the maximum time available to clear a fault before synchronism is lost. Reliable CCT estimation is challenging because complicated fault-clearing dynamics require repeated simulations over many fault severities and clearing times. We propose an event-structured physics-informed neural network (ES-PINN) that aligns its representation with the pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing swing dynamics and enforces exact state chaining across event interfaces. A smooth trajectory-induced stability margin defines a differentiable approximation of the CCT boundary, enabling accurate boundary extraction, local sensitivity analysis, and optional direct CCT prediction through a distilled readout. We further prove a local residual-to-trajectory-to-CCT error estimate, in which exact event chaining eliminates separate state-interface defect terms. Experiments on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems show that ES-PINN consistently improves held-out trajectory and stability-boundary accuracy over matched neural-surrogate baselines across mechanical and electrical contingencies with multiple clearing configurations. Additional full-network DAE validation, multi-fault experiments, and runtime analyses further demonstrate the effectiveness and computational efficiency of the proposed framework.

AI.tldr: ES-PINN: A physics-informed neural network that structures learning around power system fault dynamics to accurately estimate critical clearing times, improving over standard neural surrogates through exact event chaining and differentiable stability margins.
AI.motivation: Transient stability assessment is crucial for power system reliability but computationally expensive. Current methods require repeated simulations for different fault scenarios and clearing times, making CCT estimation challenging and time-consuming.
AI.method: Developed an event-structured PINN (ES-PINN) that aligns representation with pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing swing dynamics while enforcing exact state chaining across event interfaces. Introduced a smooth trajectory-induced stability margin for differentiable CCT boundary approximation.
AI.result: ES-PINN consistently improved held-out trajectory and stability-boundary accuracy over matched neural-surrogate baselines on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems across various contingencies. Demonstrated computational efficiency with additional DAE validation and multi-fault experiments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ES-PINN framework provides an effective and efficient approach for CCT estimation in power systems, enabling accurate boundary extraction, sensitivity analysis, and direct CCT prediction through structured alignment with physical event dynamics.

title: An Empirical Study of Coordination Mode as the First-Class Citizen in From-Scratch Multi-Agent Coding
summary:
Multi-agent vibe coding promises to accelerate software development, yet existing benchmarks rely on synthetic environments that ignore practical time and monetary costs, conflate reasoning with communication, and reward only superficial completion. We introduce multi-agent from-scratch evaluation benchmark, MSEval, evaluating multi-agent coding on real-world tasks. Grounded in 10 authentic, full-stack projects across 10 domains, MSEval scores performance using hierarchical requirements and deterministic rubrics.
  Its execution engine, LegoGent, tests 10 collaboration topologies where agents coordinate via periodic sync intervals and deploy through native CI/CD pipelines. Concurrently, the automated grader TAgent dynamically probes implementations to jointly measure functional success, latency, and prefix-cached token cost. Across 100 runs, MSEval reveals that organizational topology rivals model capability in shaping the speed--cost--quality trade-off. For identical tasks and models, varying the topology shifts scores by over 30 points and doubles wall-clock time. Structured pipelines converge fastest with the highest quality, whereas heavy managerial oversight degrades performance. Ultimately, MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible standard for measuring how multi-agent teams actually build software. The benchmark is released at https://github.com/robinren03/MSEval.

AI.tldr: MSEval is a new benchmark for evaluating multi-agent coding systems using real-world projects, assessing performance through functional testing, latency, and cost metrics across different collaboration topologies.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent coding benchmarks rely on synthetic environments that ignore practical costs, conflate reasoning with communication, and only reward superficial completion. There's a need for benchmarks that evaluate how multi-agent teams actually build software in real-world scenarios.
AI.method: MSEval evaluates multi-agent coding on 10 authentic, full-stack projects across 10 domains using hierarchical requirements and deterministic rubrics. The execution engine (LegoGent) tests 10 collaboration topologies with agents coordinating via periodic sync intervals and deploying through native CI/CD pipelines. An automated grader (TAgent) dynamically probes implementations to measure functional success, latency, and prefix-cached token cost.
AI.result: Across 100 runs, organizational topology was found to rival model capability in shaping the speed-cost-quality trade-off. For identical tasks and models, varying the topology shifted scores by over 30 points and doubled wall-clock time. Structured pipelines converged fastest with highest quality, while heavy managerial oversight degraded performance.
AI.conclusion: MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible standard for measuring how multi-agent teams actually build software, revealing that collaboration structure is as important as model capability in determining development outcomes.

title: NMINE: Normalized Mutual Information Neural Estimation
summary:
Mutual information is a general measure of statistical dependence that captures both linear and nonlinear relationships between random variables. For continuous and multidimensional variables For continuous multidimensional variables, mutual information must be estimated from samples. Because mutual information is unbounded, its values are not directly comparable across datasets, dimensions, or applications. Normalized mutual information addresses this limitation by converting mutual information into a normalized dependency score. Recent work has demonstrated the practical value of normalized mutual information in applications such as molecular dynamics {arXiv:2405.04980} and interpretable machine learning {arXiv:2409.16768}, but existing estimators remain sensitive to dimensionality and numerical stability {arXiv:2410.07642}.
  In this paper, we propose a fully neural normalized mutual information estimator for continuous variables. The proposed approach combines a MINE-based neural mutual information estimator {arXiv:1801.04062} with MI-NEE-inspired neural marginal entropy estimators {arXiv:1905.12957}. Mutual information is estimated using the Donsker--Varadhan representation, while marginal entropies are estimated by learning the divergence between each marginal distribution and a uniform reference distribution, from which entropy is recovered. The resulting estimator provides a neural alternative to k-nearest-neighbor-based normalized mutual information estimation {arXiv:2405.04980}.
  Experiments on Gaussian data from one to eight dimensions show that the proposed estimator improves accuracy over a KSG-based normalized mutual information baseline. These results indicate that neural estimation is a promising direction for normalized dependency measurement in continuous multidimensional settings.

AI.tldr: Neural normalized mutual information estimator combining MINE-based MI estimation with neural marginal entropy estimation for continuous multidimensional variables, showing improved accuracy over k-nearest-neighbor baselines.
AI.motivation: Mutual information is a general dependency measure but unbounded, making values incomparable across datasets. Normalized mutual information addresses this but existing estimators are sensitive to dimensionality and numerical stability, motivating development of a more robust neural approach.
AI.method: Combines MINE-based neural mutual information estimator (using Donsker-Varadhan representation) with MI-NEE-inspired neural marginal entropy estimators (learning divergence between marginals and uniform reference distribution). Provides neural alternative to k-nearest-neighbor-based normalized mutual information estimation.
AI.result: Experiments on Gaussian data from 1-8 dimensions show improved accuracy over KSG-based normalized mutual information baseline, indicating neural estimation is promising for normalized dependency measurement in continuous multidimensional settings.
AI.conclusion: Neural normalized mutual information estimation is a viable and accurate approach for continuous multidimensional variables, offering advantages over traditional k-nearest-neighbor methods in terms of accuracy and potential robustness to dimensionality challenges.

title: Not All Tokens Deserve Equal Credit: Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation for Long-CoT Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is central to improving long-CoT reasoning in large language models. Critic-free methods such as GRPO convert response-level rewards into advantages and uniformly broadcast them across tokens, overlooking their unequal contributions to the final outcome. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) instead provides dense distributional supervision by minimizing the forward KL divergence between an unprivileged policy and a privileged self-teacher, implicitly assuming that the resulting likelihood shifts encode reliable answer-aligned information. We test this premise by fixing each sampled trajectory and re-scoring it under two opposing outcome conditions, one asserting correctness and the other incorrectness. Most affected tokens shift in the same direction under both conditions, with few sign reversals and substantial overlap in the induced optimization signals. Large shifts also concentrate on highly substitutable surface-form tokens, whereas tokens carrying problem-specific reasoning content are less sensitive. These findings show that privileged shifts fail to provide reliable answer-aligned directions, while their magnitudes primarily reflect counterfactual sensitivity rather than token-level learning value. Based on these observations, we propose Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation (CSCR), a simple extension of GRPO that reduces credit for highly sensitive tokens and renormalizes token-level advantages to preserve both the original credit budget and verifier-determined direction. On long-CoT mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CSCR consistently outperforms GRPO baseline with the same number of policy updates. Targeted ablations further corroborate our diagnosis: privilege-induced directions are unreliable, moderate downweighting is most effective, and stronger modulation destabilizes optimization.

AI.tldr: A new method called Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation (CSCR) improves reinforcement learning for long-chain-of-thought reasoning by addressing issues with existing privilege-based methods, showing that token-level reward distribution based on counterfactual sensitivity outperforms uniform credit assignment or privilege-based approaches.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to improve reinforcement learning for verifiable rewards (RLVR) in long-chain-of-thought reasoning. Current methods have limitations: critic-free methods like GRPO uniformly broadcast rewards across tokens, ignoring unequal token contributions, while on-policy self-distillation assumes privileged shifts encode reliable answer-aligned information, which may not be true.
AI.method: The authors first test the assumption behind privilege-based methods by analyzing token-level behavior under opposing outcome conditions. They find that most tokens shift similarly under both conditions, with few sign reversals, and sensitive tokens are often substitutable surface forms rather than reasoning content. Based on this, they propose Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation (CSCR), which extends GRPO by reducing credit for highly sensitive tokens and renormalizing token-level advantages while preserving the original credit budget and verifier-determined direction.
AI.result: CSCR consistently outperforms the GRPO baseline on long-chain-of-thought mathematical reasoning benchmarks with the same number of policy updates. Ablation studies corroborate the diagnosis: privilege-induced directions are unreliable, moderate downweighting is most effective, and stronger modulation destabilizes optimization.
AI.conclusion: Privilege-based shifts in on-policy self-distillation fail to provide reliable answer-aligned directions, and their magnitudes primarily reflect counterfactual sensitivity rather than token-level learning value. The proposed CSCR method successfully addresses these issues by reallocating credits based on sensitivity analysis, demonstrating improved performance in long-reasoning tasks.

title: VESTIGE: A Knowledge-Guided Masking Strategy for Corruption-Aware Fine-Tuning of Genomic Transformers, Validated on Ancient DNA Reconstruction
summary: Standard masked-language-model fine-tuning applies a uniform masking probability across every token position, assuming reconstruction difficulty is position-agnostic. When the degradation process is characterised and concentrated at predictable positions, this assumption fails: at peak damage sites the model can underperform a frequency-matched random predictor. We introduce VESTIGE, a parameter-free, drop-in replacement for the standard MLM collator that aligns the masking distribution with an empirically measured per-position corruption profile. We apply it to ancient DNA (aDNA) reconstruction, where cytosine deamination produces a position-dependent C-to-T / G-to-A gradient quantified per-position by mapDamage2. Rescaling so the mean C/G masking rate equals 15% - identical to standard MLM - isolates spatial redistribution as the sole variable, with model, data, seed, and hyperparameters held fixed across both DNABERT-2 runs on a mammoth CDS corpus (two specimens, seven genes). Across six terminal-zone widths and 626 paired windows, VESTIGE leads standard MLM at every width (Delta = +4.18 to +10.35 pp, all p < 10^-8), cuts validation cross-entropy by 13% (3.274 vs. 3.757), and yields ESMFold reconstructions with TM-score > 0.95 across all six reconstructions (three genes) even under damage amplified 10-30x beyond authentic PMD rates. A 1D CNN biosecurity classifier returns AUC = 0.935 and clears 98.2% of reconstructed windows, the 1.76% remainder attributable to reference-genome features, not reconstruction artefacts. The principle is domain-agnostic: any measurable position- or context-specific corruption profile - FFPE, bisulfite, metagenomic, or nanopore - substitutes directly for the PMD array, making VESTIGE a knowledge-guided training routine for intelligent systems operating on degraded or noisy sequence inputs.

AI.tldr: VESTIGE is a parameter-free method that improves masked language model fine-tuning by aligning masking distributions with empirically measured per-position corruption profiles, demonstrated to significantly outperform standard MLM in ancient DNA reconstruction tasks while maintaining biosecurity.
AI.motivation: Standard MLM assumes uniform masking probability across positions, but this fails when degradation processes are position-dependent and concentrated at predictable sites (like in ancient DNA where cytosine deamination creates position-dependent C-to-T/G-to-A gradients). This can cause models to underperform random predictors at peak damage sites.
AI.method: VESTIGE replaces the standard MLM collator by aligning the masking distribution with empirically measured per-position corruption profiles (using mapDamage2 for ancient DNA). It rescales so the mean C/G masking rate equals 15% (identical to standard MLM), isolating spatial redistribution as the only variable while keeping model, data, and hyperparameters fixed.
AI.result: Applied to mammoth CDS corpus (two specimens, seven genes), VESTIGE outperforms standard MLM across all terminal-zone widths (+4.18 to +10.35 percentage points, all p < 10^-8), cuts validation cross-entropy by 13% (3.274 vs. 3.757), yields ESMFold reconstructions with TM-score > 0.95 across all six reconstructions even under amplified damage, and a biosecurity classifier shows AUC = 0.935 with 98.2% clearance rate.
AI.conclusion: VESTIGE is a knowledge-guided training routine that improves performance on degraded or noisy sequence data by incorporating position-specific corruption profiles. The approach is domain-agnostic and can be applied to various contexts with measurable corruption patterns (FFPE, bisulfite, metagenomic, nanopore).

title: Dynamic Spectral Filtering for Temporal Graph Learning: Learning Evolving Propagation Operators
summary: Temporal graph learning is commonly organized around the evolution of node states or the encoding of interaction histories. We study an underexplored, operator-centric question: should the graph propagation mechanism itself evolve over time? We introduce Dynamic Spectral Filtering (DSF), which represents propagation at snapshot t by a Chebyshev polynomial filter with vector-valued, time-dependent coefficients. DSF explicitly treats these compact multi-order coefficients as recurrent temporal states. A recurrent branch proposes updates, while multiplicative global and order-specific gates regulate their magnitude. The temporal state is independent of the number of nodes. On MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit temporal link-prediction benchmarks, converged DSF runs attain AP scores of 0.7851, 0.9088, and 0.9860, respectively, with 93K to 133K trainable parameters, 68 to 182 MB peak GPU memory, and 1.6 to 2.1 seconds of training per epoch. Against the closely related DEFT baseline, DSF is better on MOOC, within 0.001 AP on Reddit, and modestly lower on Wikipedia, while using 8.3 to 8.6 times fewer parameters, 25 to 33 times less GPU memory, and 5 to 19 times less time per epoch. Relative to all measured alternatives, it uses 3.3 to 38.6 times less GPU memory. These results support direct spectral-response evolution as a useful temporal inductive bias when computational efficiency is a first-class requirement.

AI.tldr: Dynamic Spectral Filtering (DSF) introduces time-evolving graph propagation via learned Chebyshev polynomial filters with compact recurrent coefficients, achieving strong temporal link prediction with high computational efficiency.
AI.motivation: Current temporal graph learning focuses on node state evolution or interaction history encoding, while the evolution of graph propagation mechanisms themselves remains underexplored. The authors ask whether propagation should evolve over time.
AI.method: DSF represents propagation at each snapshot using Chebyshev polynomial filters with vector-valued, time-dependent coefficients treated as recurrent temporal states. It uses a recurrent branch for updates with multiplicative global and order-specific gates to regulate magnitude. The temporal state is node-count independent and compact.
AI.result: On MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit benchmarks, DSF achieves AP scores of 0.7851, 0.9088, and 0.9860 with only 93K-133K parameters, 68-182MB peak GPU memory, and 1.6-2.1 seconds per epoch. Compared to DEFT baseline, it uses 8.3-8.6× fewer parameters, 25-33× less GPU memory, and 5-19× less time per epoch.
AI.conclusion: Direct spectral-response evolution serves as a useful temporal inductive bias when computational efficiency is a primary requirement, demonstrating that time-evolving graph propagation can be both effective and highly efficient.

title: Towards joint scaling laws with optimal batch size schedules
summary: Modern deep learning typically keeps the batch size static throughout training, thus overlooking the joint effect of learning rate and batch size on the training dynamics. In this paper, we study the deep learning dynamics through the lens of convex optimization and derive a joint characterization of loss in terms of both schedules, applicable to general optimizers and model architectures. This characterization yields a closed-form optimal batch size schedule for any prescribed learning rate schedule, and further leads to joint scaling laws that consistently outperform static batch size baselines, highlighting the significance of dynamic batch size schedule in large language model training.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes dynamic batch size scheduling during training, showing that joint optimization of batch size and learning rate schedules outperforms static batch size approaches in large language model training.
AI.motivation: Current deep learning practices keep batch size static throughout training, ignoring the joint interaction between learning rate and batch size on training dynamics. This overlooks potentially better optimization strategies.
AI.method: The authors analyze deep learning dynamics through convex optimization theory, deriving a joint characterization of loss in terms of both learning rate and batch size schedules. They develop a closed-form optimal batch size schedule for any given learning rate schedule.
AI.result: The derived joint scaling laws consistently outperform static batch size baselines. The dynamic batch size scheduling approach proves effective for large language model training.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic batch size scheduling is significant for large language model training and should be considered alongside learning rate scheduling, as the joint optimization of both schedules leads to better performance than static batch size approaches.

title: MMHBench: A Multi-Perspective Benchmark for Mental Health Understanding in Long-Form Videos
summary: Mental health understanding in long-form videos requires nuanced reasoning over observable behavior, interpersonal context, and latent psychological states. Existing benchmarks largely reduce this task to coarse-grained classification, providing limited insight into whether models truly understand psychological phenomena or rely on superficial correlations. To address this limitation, we introduce MMHBench, a comprehensive multimodal benchmark for multi-perspective mental health understanding, comprising 268 long-form videos and 2,184 carefully curated questions. MMHBench organizes the evaluation into two complementary settings: (1) third-person assessment, consisting of 605 questions that focus on the interpretation of observable behaviors and multimodal evidence, and (2) first-person perspective-taking, comprising 1,579 questions that require perspective-conditioned reasoning to identify the interpretation of the mental state supported by the available multimodal evidence. We propose a Multi-Agent Question Generation (MAQG) framework that simulates diverse social roles to synthesize questions from multiple perspectives. The generated questions are refined through multi-role feedback and iterative optimization, followed by expert-guided verification to ensure quality and validity. Extensive evaluation of 22 representative multimodal large language models (MLLMs), spanning both open-source and leading closed-source models, demonstrates that long-form video mental health understanding remains highly challenging.

AI.tldr: Introduces MMHBench, a comprehensive multimodal benchmark for mental health understanding in long-form videos with 2,184 curated questions across third-person assessment and first-person perspective-taking settings.
AI.motivation: Existing mental health understanding benchmarks reduce the task to coarse-grained classification, providing limited insight into whether models truly understand psychological phenomena or rely on superficial correlations.
AI.method: Proposes a Multi-Agent Question Generation (MAQG) framework that simulates diverse social roles to synthesize questions from multiple perspectives, followed by multi-role feedback, iterative optimization, and expert-guided verification.
AI.result: Extensive evaluation of 22 representative MLLMs demonstrates that long-form video mental health understanding remains highly challenging for both open-source and leading closed-source models.
AI.conclusion: Mental health understanding in long-form videos requires nuanced reasoning over behavior, context, and psychological states, and current models struggle with this task despite comprehensive benchmarking.

title: Improving the Robustness/Accuracy Tradeoff Against Adversarial Attacks Using Information Bottleneck Distillation Through Dual Teachers
summary: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in classical machine learning problems. However, they are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Countermeasures proposed in the literature, notably Information Bottleneck Distillation (IBD) introduced by Kuang et al., degrade the classification accuracy on clean inputs while improving the robustness to adversarial inputs. In this work, we extend the IBD framework by introducing an extra teacher model (clean teacher) trained with only clean inputs, into the distillation process from a robust teacher model trained by adversarial training. The features of both clean and robust teachers are transferred to the student through a cross-layer attention matrix. Experimental results on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets show that the proposed method improves classification accuracy on clean samples compared to the original IBD, while maintaining similar accuracy on adversarial samples. Furthermore, our methods are competitive with state-of-the-art approaches, including the recent dual-teacher distillation framework B-MTARD, particularly in terms of the harmonic mean between clean and robust accuracy. We also analyze the impact of different training settings that have different influences on the attention module.

AI.tldr: Extended Information Bottleneck Distillation with dual teachers (clean & robust) using cross-layer attention to improve clean accuracy while maintaining adversarial robustness.
AI.motivation: Existing adversarial defense methods like Information Bottleneck Distillation (IBD) degrade clean classification accuracy while improving robustness. There's a need for methods that can achieve both good clean accuracy and adversarial robustness simultaneously.
AI.method: Extends IBD by introducing dual teacher distillation: a clean teacher (trained on clean inputs) and a robust teacher (trained via adversarial training). Features from both teachers are transferred to the student using a cross-layer attention matrix mechanism.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, the method improves clean classification accuracy compared to original IBD while maintaining similar adversarial robustness. Competitive with state-of-the-art approaches like B-MTARD, particularly in harmonic mean between clean and robust accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Dual-teacher distillation with cross-layer attention effectively balances clean accuracy and adversarial robustness, addressing limitations of existing adversarial defense methods that typically sacrifice one for the other.

title: A Cross-Architecture Audit of Direction-Based Inference-Time Defences in Vision-Language Models
summary: Inference time defences against vision language model jailbreaks often subtract a calibrated direction from the residual stream at a chosen decoder layer. We compare five defence candidates across 15 model and layer cells from four architectural families under a magnitude controlled protocol that matches the intervention size for each prompt and pairs every direction with a random control of the same norm. The candidates are the mean image conditioning shift, a CMRM style refusal direction, a ShiftDC style attack specific residual, a prompt instruction to ignore the image, and a random control. No single candidate dominates on both refusal recovery and utility preservation. The image conditioning shift leads on LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral 12B and is the only candidate whose utility loss remains at the measurement noise floor in every family. The prompt instruction leads on Qwen2.5 VL, while the attack specific residual leads on Qwen2 VL 2B. The image conditioning direction is direction specific in 13 of 15 cells, but strongly architecture specific and nontransferable across the only dimension compatible pair, LLaVA 1.5 13B and Pixtral 12B. We also connect text only and multimodal refusal geometry. The CMRM direction has positive cosine alignment with the image conditioning shift in all 15 cells, with mean 0.35, range 0.17 to 0.65, 15 to 25 times the random vector null, and a sign test p value of about 3e-5. These results show that the two recipes recover partially overlapping geometry and that direction based defences should be calibrated separately for each language decoder family.

AI.tldr: Comparing 5 VLM jailbreak defenses across 15 model/layer combos, image conditioning shift leads in LLaVA 1.5/Pixtral, prompt instruction leads in Qwen2.5 VL, and attack-specific residual leads in Qwen2 VL 2B, with no single defense dominating both refusal recovery and utility preservation.
AI.motivation: Vision language models are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, and inference-time defenses that subtract calibrated directions from the residual stream are common, but there's a need to systematically evaluate and compare different defense approaches to understand their effectiveness and limitations across different model architectures.
AI.method: Used a magnitude-controlled protocol comparing 5 defense candidates across 15 model/layer cells from 4 architectural families: 1) mean image conditioning shift, 2) CMRM-style refusal direction, 3) ShiftDC-style attack-specific residual, 4) prompt instruction to ignore image, and 5) random control. Each intervention was paired with a random control of the same norm, and cosine alignments were measured between different refusal directions.
AI.result: No single defense dominates both refusal recovery and utility preservation. Image conditioning shift performed best on LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral 12B with minimal utility loss. Prompt instruction led on Qwen2.5 VL, while attack-specific residual led on Qwen2 VL 2B. The image conditioning direction was architecture-specific and nontransferable between LLaVA 1.5 13B and Pixtral 12B. CMRM direction showed positive cosine alignment with image conditioning shift (mean 0.35) across all cells, indicating partially overlapping refusal geometry.
AI.conclusion: Direction-based defenses for vision language model jailbreaks should be calibrated separately for each language decoder family since refusal geometry is architecture-specific and no single approach works universally well. The overlap between different refusal recipes suggests they capture related but not identical aspects of refusal behavior.

title: ROCS: Request-Oriented Compute Sharing for Efficient Large-Scale Recommendation
summary:
Modern recommendation models gain prediction quality by scaling feature-interaction and sequence modules, but production cost constraints cap how far systems can scale.
  In this work, we propose Request-Oriented Compute Sharing (ROCS), a modeling and inference paradigm that exploits a unique property of recommendation inference: each user request is evaluated against many candidates, while request-side features are shared across candidates. ROCS defers request-candidate interactions as late as possible, isolates candidate-dependent representations, and evaluates substantial portions of the model once per request rather than once per candidate, significantly improving inference efficiency while maintaining or improving prediction quality. To realize this paradigm, we develop Generalized Layer Masking (GLM) to enforce candidate isolation in feature-interaction architectures, and Deep Cross Attention (DCA) to extend request-oriented sharing to sequence architectures. To support efficient GPU deployment, we co-design In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) that significantly accelerates ROCS model execution.
  Experiments on public benchmarks show that ROCS consistently improves the quality-efficiency tradeoff across recommendation backbones. On production-scale workloads, ROCS achieves up to a 3x QPS improvement on retrieval models without quality degradation and a 0.5% relative LogLoss improvement with a 50% QPS gain on a short-form video ranking model. ROCS has been deployed across large-scale recommendation systems spanning ads and organic surfaces, retrieval and ranking stages, and more than two orders of magnitude in inference complexity, delivering significant online gains at reduced infrastructure cost.

AI.tldr: ROCS is an efficient recommendation inference paradigm that shares computations across candidates by deferring request-candidate interactions, achieving significant speedups without quality loss.
AI.motivation: Modern recommendation models improve quality by scaling, but production cost constraints limit how far systems can scale. There's a need for more efficient inference that maintains quality while reducing computational costs.
AI.method: ROCS exploits the property that each user request is evaluated against many candidates while request-side features are shared. It defers request-candidate interactions as late as possible, isolates candidate-dependent representations, and evaluates portions once per request rather than per candidate. Includes Generalized Layer Masking for feature-interaction architectures, Deep Cross Attention for sequence architectures, and In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization for GPU acceleration.
AI.result: ROCS improves quality-efficiency tradeoff across recommendation backbones: up to 3x QPS improvement on retrieval models without quality degradation, and 0.5% relative LogLoss improvement with 50% QPS gain on short-form video ranking model. Successfully deployed across large-scale systems spanning ads/organic surfaces, retrieval/ranking stages.
AI.conclusion: ROCS provides an effective modeling and inference paradigm for recommendation systems that significantly improves inference efficiency while maintaining or improving prediction quality, enabling better scaling within production cost constraints.

title: IFHierBench: Hierarchical Instruction Following for Large Language Models
summary: Instruction-following ability is critical for deploying large language models in real-world applications, where downstream components depend on the output satisfying specific constraints. Modern deployments increasingly handle the full task in a single LLM call, with one prompt specifying a layered output whose overall artifact, structural sections, and nested fields must each satisfy concrete constraints. Existing instruction-following benchmarks treat the constraint set as a flat list applied uniformly to the response, so they cannot scope a check to a particular section of the output. We introduce IFHierBench, a hierarchical instruction-following benchmark of 600 prompts stratified across four constraint-tree depths and 35 distinct constraints, each prompt paired with a deterministic checker that verifies satisfaction at every scope. Evaluating seven leading proprietary and open-weight models, we find that even the strongest model only marginally exceeds 50% prompt-level accuracy and that accuracy degrades sharply as constraint depth grows. Reliably following nested constraints remains a substantial gap for current LLMs, motivating future training methods that consider constraint adherence at finer granularity to achieve better instruction-following ability.

AI.tldr: IFHierBench is a new hierarchical instruction-following benchmark that evaluates LLMs on complex nested constraints, revealing major gaps in current models' ability to follow layered instructions.
AI.motivation: Current instruction-following benchmarks treat constraints as flat lists applied uniformly to responses, but real-world applications often require LLMs to handle layered outputs where different sections and nested fields must satisfy specific constraints. This mismatch means existing benchmarks can't properly evaluate LLMs on the hierarchical constraint-following needed for practical deployment.
AI.method: The authors introduce IFHierBench, a hierarchical instruction-following benchmark with 600 prompts stratified across four constraint-tree depths and 35 distinct constraints. Each prompt is paired with a deterministic checker that verifies constraint satisfaction at every scope (overall artifact, structural sections, and nested fields). They evaluate seven leading proprietary and open-weight models on this benchmark.
AI.result: Even the strongest model only marginally exceeds 50% prompt-level accuracy, and accuracy degrades sharply as constraint depth grows. This demonstrates that reliably following nested constraints remains a substantial gap for current LLMs, with models struggling significantly with deeper constraint hierarchies.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical instruction-following is a critical challenge for LLM deployment, and current models have significant limitations. The findings motivate the development of new training methods that consider constraint adherence at finer granularity to achieve better instruction-following ability in real-world applications.

title: DAS-PMVC: A Framework for Partial Multi-View Clustering via Dual Alignment and Structure Enhancement
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Accepted by ACM Multimedia 2026
summary: In recent years, multi-view clustering has attracted widespread research interest. However, due to limitations in data collection devices, data across different views often suffer from misalignment, leading to the partial view alignment problem (PVAP).
