To mitigate the impact of view asymmetry and irrelevant samples, this paper proposes a framework for partial multi-view clustering via dual alignment and structure enhancement (DAS-PMVC), which leverages view structure consistency and semantic relevance. Specifically, DAS-PMVC includes three parts: \textbf{anchor graph structure alignment}, where sample joint embedding representations with consistent latent space are derived from anchor point relationships for initial view alignment; \textbf{structure-enhanced feature learning}, where the model learns view structure information through pretraining and combines multi-view graph convolutional networks to further extract deep latent features from the aligned graph structure to improve the discriminative power of representations; and \textbf{a dual alignment strategy}, where initial alignment is performed through the anchor graph in the pretraining phase, and contrastive learning loss and the Hungarian algorithm are introduced in the training phase to further optimize the alignment of latent features. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that the DAS-PMVC framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in clustering performance, showcasing its effectiveness and superiority.

AI.tldr: A novel framework called DAS-PMVC addresses partial view alignment in multi-view clustering through dual alignment and structure enhancement, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: Multi-view clustering faces challenges due to misalignment across views caused by data collection limitations, leading to the partial view alignment problem (PVAP) where views have asymmetry and irrelevant samples.
AI.method: DAS-PMVC framework with three key components: 1) Anchor graph structure alignment for initial view alignment using joint embedding representations from anchor point relationships; 2) Structure-enhanced feature learning that combines pretraining and multi-view graph convolutional networks to extract deep latent features; 3) Dual alignment strategy using initial anchor graph alignment followed by contrastive learning and Hungarian algorithm optimization during training.
AI.result: Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that DAS-PMVC outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in clustering performance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DAS-PMVC framework effectively addresses partial view alignment problems in multi-view clustering through its dual alignment and structure enhancement approach, showing superior effectiveness compared to existing methods.

title: One Anchor for All: Unified Multilingual and Multimodal Safety Alignment for LVLMs
summary: As large vision-language models (LVLMs) are deployed globally, the combination of multilingual instructions and visual information makes malicious attacks more covert and sophisticated than ever before. However, existing methods isolate language and modality defenses, which, coupled with the scarcity of safety data and high fine-tuning costs, makes it difficult for models to defend against compound attacks. To address this severe challenge, we propose a neuron-level cross-dimensional safety alignment framework driven by modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons). First, we identify monolingual and unimodal safety neurons by comparing responses to harmful and benign samples, quantifying functional saliency through activation strength and downstream impact. Then, by intersecting these unimodal neurons within each language, we extract modality-shared safety neurons (MS-Neurons) responsive to both visual and textual risks, bridging the safety representation gap between modalities. Furthermore, using English as a semantic anchor, we intersect MS-Neurons across languages to identify modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons), serving as key defenses against compound attacks. Finally, we update only this minimal subset of shared neurons (~0.03% of parameters), transferring English-only safety supervision to multilingual and multimodal scenarios. Extensive experiments show that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks while preserving general utility.

AI.tldr: A neuron-level cross-dimensional safety alignment framework that identifies modality- and language-shared safety neurons to defend against compound multilingual multimodal attacks in LVLMs.
AI.motivation: As large vision-language models are deployed globally, malicious attacks combining multilingual instructions and visual information become more covert and sophisticated. Existing defense methods isolate language and modality defenses, lack sufficient safety data, and have high fine-tuning costs, making them ineffective against compound attacks.
AI.method: Proposes MLS-Neurons framework: (1) Identifies monolingual and unimodal safety neurons by comparing responses to harmful/benign samples using activation strength and downstream impact metrics. (2) Intersects unimodal neurons to extract modality-shared safety neurons (MS-Neurons) bridging visual-textual safety gap. (3) Uses English as semantic anchor to intersect MS-Neurons across languages, identifying modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons). (4) Updates only minimal subset (~0.03% parameters) of these shared neurons.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show the method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks while preserving general utility of the models.
AI.conclusion: The neuron-level cross-dimensional safety alignment framework effectively defends against compound multilingual multimodal attacks by identifying and updating a minimal set of modality- and language-shared safety neurons, enabling efficient transfer of English safety supervision to multilingual and multimodal scenarios.

title: Train Small, Deploy Large: Zero-Shot GNN Transfer Through Geometric Renormalization
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) can operate on large graphs but become infrastructure-sensitive at the scale of millions of nodes and typically require scalable training techniques for even larger graphs. This raises a central question: when can a model trained on a smaller, scaled-down replica of a graph be deployed on the full-resolution graph without retraining? We introduce a zero-shot transfer protocol in which a GNN is trained on a graph coarse-grained by geometric renormalization (GR), and the resulting weights are transferred directly to the original network. Across synthetic and real-world networks, training on GR scaled-down replicas preserves much of the original-scale predictive performance while significantly reducing training cost. We further find that learned representations and predictive trajectories remain aligned across scales. These findings suggest that structural similarity may be more important than network size in determining GNN transferability, opening a path toward scale-equivariant graph architectures.

AI.tldr: GNNs trained on smaller, geometrically coarse-grained graphs can transfer directly to full-resolution graphs without retraining, preserving performance while reducing training costs.
AI.motivation: GNNs become infrastructure-sensitive at million-node scale and require scalable training for larger graphs, raising the question of whether models trained on smaller graphs can deploy on full-resolution graphs without retraining.
AI.method: Introduce zero-shot transfer protocol where GNNs are trained on graphs coarse-grained by geometric renormalization (GR), then transfer weights directly to original networks.
AI.result: Training on GR scaled-down replicas preserves much original-scale predictive performance while significantly reducing training cost. Learned representations and predictive trajectories remain aligned across scales.
AI.conclusion: Structural similarity may be more important than network size in determining GNN transferability, opening a path toward scale-equivariant graph architectures.

title: Meta-Task: Turning Terminal Task Synthesis into a Terminal Task for Scalable Agent Training
summary: Training terminal agents at scale requires diverse, verifiable terminal tasks and high-quality interaction trajectories, yet acquiring such data remains a significant challenge. Existing synthesis methods face two key limitations: (1) weak reliability caused by the disconnect between task generation and real execution, and (2) limited diversity and scalability due to dependence on existing repositories. We propose Meta-Task, a framework that redefines terminal task synthesis as a Terminal-Bench-format task itself: an agent operates within a real container environment to iteratively generate, execute, and verify tasks, so that synthesized components are checked for internal consistency and executability within the generation loop itself. Building upon this, we decouple the target task requirements along multiple dimensions, introduce a multi-phase mechanism that dynamically designs novel task specifications before producing the actual tasks, and incorporate optional external material support to enhance diversity and realism. We additionally apply LLM-as-Judge filtering to ensure the quality of the final training data. Experiments on Terminal-Bench 2.0 show that fine-tuning on only 3,221 Meta-Task synthesized trajectories achieves 22.5% and 31.8% Avg Pass@1 for Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B respectively, outperforming concurrent approaches with significantly less training data.

AI.tldr: Meta-Task is a framework that synthesizes terminal tasks by having an agent operate in a real container to iteratively generate, execute, and verify tasks, ensuring reliability and diversity while requiring minimal training data.
AI.motivation: Current methods for acquiring terminal task training data have two key limitations: weak reliability due to disconnect between task generation and real execution, and limited diversity/scalability due to dependency on existing repositories.
AI.method: Proposes Meta-Task framework that redefines terminal task synthesis as a Terminal-Bench-format task itself. An agent operates in a real container environment to iteratively generate, execute, and verify tasks. Decouples target requirements across multiple dimensions, uses multi-phase mechanism to dynamically design novel specifications before producing tasks, and incorporates optional external material support. Applies LLM-as-Judge filtering for quality assurance.
AI.result: Fine-tuning on only 3,221 Meta-Task synthesized trajectories achieves 22.5% and 31.8% Avg Pass@1 for Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B respectively on Terminal-Bench 2.0, outperforming concurrent approaches with significantly less training data.
AI.conclusion: Meta-Task provides an effective framework for synthesizing diverse, reliable terminal tasks with minimal training data requirements, addressing key limitations of existing synthesis methods through real-container execution verification and multidimensional task design.

title: Beyond the Best Teacher: Expanding and Compressing the Reasoning Solution Manifold
summary: A single reinforcement-learning run can produce a strong reasoner yet an incomplete teacher: it often amplifies only a subset of the valid solution modes. We argue that reinforcement learning (RL)-trained policies should therefore be viewed as local probes of a multi-basin reasoning solution manifold, rather than as globally reliable supervisors. Based on this view, we propose an expand-then-compress framework that couples teacher construction with multi-teacher policy distillation. In the expansion stage, Residual Group Relative Policy Optimization (RGRPO) trains a sequence of teachers from a common initialization and redirects each later round toward examples not yet covered by the accumulated teacher union. In the compression stage, reliability-gated Teacher-Union On-policy Distillation (TU-OPD) lets the student learn from its own response prefixes. For each example, only reliable teachers contribute, and their sampled-token OPD losses are weighted by their per-example quality. We further introduce Consensus-Residual Decomposition, which preserves a winner teacher's excess token preferences over its reliable peers, preventing specialist behavior from being suppressed during teacher aggregation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following show that the resulting Qwen3-1.7B student consistently outperforms the strongest individual teacher across all three domains, yielding relative improvements of 2.0%, 8.3%, and 6.9%, respectively, while retaining single-model inference. These results establish a simple but powerful principle: stronger students can be obtained not by selecting a single better teacher, but by deliberately constructing and compressing a complementary teacher union.

AI.tldr: Stronger AI students emerge from compressing complementary teacher unions, not selecting single best teachers, via expand-then-compress framework with multi-teacher policy distillation.
AI.motivation: Single RL-trained policies are incomplete teachers that amplify only subsets of valid solution modes, acting as local probes of reasoning solution manifolds rather than globally reliable supervisors.
AI.method: Expand-then-compress framework: 1) Expansion stage uses Residual Group Relative Policy Optimization (RGRPO) to train sequence of complementary teachers; 2) Compression stage uses reliability-gated Teacher-Union On-policy Distillation (TU-OPD) with Consensus-Residual Decomposition to preserve specialist behaviors during aggregation.
AI.result: Qwen3-1.7B student consistently outperforms strongest individual teacher across mathematical reasoning (2.0% improvement), code generation (8.3%), and instruction following (6.9%), while retaining single-model inference efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Stronger students can be obtained not by selecting a single better teacher, but by deliberately constructing and compressing complementary teacher unions, establishing this as a powerful principle for policy improvement.

title: The Geometric Nature and a Free Proxy for Flow-Matching Uncertainty
summary: Flow matching (FM) has become a popular action head paradigm for modern embodied models. However, as a conditional generative model, it does not explicitly expose its inherent uncertainty, producing faulty action chunks even when it misinterprets the scene or encounters out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. Therefore, determining when an FM-generated action can be trusted is essential for safe deployment, yet existing uncertainty estimation methods on real-time control suffer from several issues: extra training budget, high computational overhead, and low generalization ability. In this work, we provide a geometric interpretation of FM uncertainty in the velocity field, showing that uncertainty manifests as deviation from an ideal affine-isotropic contraction field. Building on this observation, we introduce denoising acceleration ($\mathrm{accel}$), a highly-generalizable and cost-free uncertainty proxy that measures the bending of the denoising trajectory from a single forward pass, without additional model evaluations, training, or resampling. We theoretically and empirically demonstrate that $\mathrm{accel}$ is a faithful proxy for FM uncertainty and further test its utility in online failure detection. Results show that $\mathrm{accel}$ identifies failing rollouts well before termination, matching or even outperforming costly resampling- and training-based baselines across settings under realistic deployment budget. Code and demos available at: https://github.com/rrrrrrzy/fm-geometry.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces denoising acceleration (accel), a cost-free uncertainty estimation method for flow matching models in embodied AI systems that measures trajectory bending from a single forward pass, enabling reliable failure detection without additional training or computation.
AI.motivation: Flow matching models used in embodied AI lack explicit uncertainty quantification, leading to faulty actions when encountering out-of-distribution inputs or scene misinterpretations. Existing uncertainty estimation methods suffer from high computational costs, extra training requirements, and poor generalization.
AI.method: The authors provide a geometric interpretation of flow matching uncertainty as deviation from an ideal affine-isotropic contraction field. They introduce denoising acceleration (accel), which measures the bending of the denoising trajectory from a single forward pass without additional model evaluations, training, or resampling.
AI.result: Denoising acceleration proves to be a faithful proxy for flow matching uncertainty and enables effective online failure detection. It identifies failing rollouts well before termination, matching or outperforming costly resampling- and training-based baselines across various settings under realistic deployment budgets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed denoising acceleration method provides a highly generalizable, cost-free uncertainty estimation solution for flow matching models in embodied AI, addressing safety concerns for real-world deployment by enabling reliable failure detection without additional computational overhead.

title: RIPPLE: Generating Multi-Channel Phase, Not Recovering It
summary: Generative models synthesize magnitude spectra with high fidelity, while phase is delegated to a recovery module---Griffin--Lim, a vocoder, or a latent decoder---applied independently to each channel. For multi-channel waveforms this delegation is costly: the physical content of spatial audio and three-component seismograms lives in the phase relationships between channels, precisely what channel-independent recovery cannot produce. The cost is also invisible, since the magnitude-based metrics common to both fields barely move when inter-channel phase coherence collapses---so a pipeline can discard the physical information in its output while still scoring well. We argue that phase should be generated, not recovered, and present RIPPLE (Rectified Inter-channel Phase with Prior-based LEarning), which reinterprets Griffin--Lim as a phase **prior** rather than a final estimator: initialized from the source phase, this prior carries the inter-channel structure to be preserved, and a rectified flow refines it toward the target under an explicit inter-channel phase loss. Tested on first-order ambisonics environment transfer and seismic cross-station translation---two physically unrelated domains---RIPPLE outperforms recovery-based pipelines on the coherence metrics that downstream analyses consume. The seismic case is decisive: across architecturally distinct generators, per-channel recovery leaves S-wave polarization error near the $57.3^\circ$ random expectation, whereas learned phase reduces it to $33.8^\circ$.

AI.tldr: RIPPLE is a method that generates phase directly instead of recovering it separately per channel, preserving inter-channel coherence crucial for spatial audio and seismic data, significantly outperforming recovery-based approaches.
AI.motivation: Current generative models synthesize magnitude spectra well but delegate phase recovery to channel-independent modules, which destroys inter-channel phase relationships essential for spatial audio and multi-component seismograms. This problem is invisible because standard magnitude-based metrics don't detect coherence loss, allowing pipelines to discard physical information while still scoring well.
AI.method: RIPPLE reinterprets Griffin-Lim as a phase prior rather than final estimator, initializing from source phase to preserve inter-channel structure. A rectified flow then refines this prior toward the target under an explicit inter-channel phase loss, generating phase rather than recovering it channel-independently.
AI.result: RIPPLE outperforms recovery-based pipelines on coherence metrics for both ambisonics environment transfer and seismic cross-station translation. In the seismic case, per-channel recovery left S-wave polarization error near random expectation (57.3°), while learned phase reduced it to 33.8° across architecturally distinct generators.
AI.conclusion: Phase should be generated rather than recovered in multi-channel systems. RIPPLE successfully preserves inter-channel phase coherence by treating phase as a learnable component with explicit inter-channel structure constraints, demonstrating decisive improvements in physically meaningful metrics across diverse domains.

title: Shapes from Examples: Foundations of Shape Learning in Recursive SHACL
comment: full version of a paper accepted at ISWC26
summary: SHACL shapes enable data graph validation, making automatic shape learning essential for knowledge graph applications. We investigate the well-known fitting approach to this task: given sets P and N of positive and negative example nodes from an input graph, compute a shape expression C, possibly using shape names defined in a recursive shape catalogue, that validates at every node in P and none in N. We focus on the case where C is written in a core fragment of SHACL corresponding to the Description Logic ELI. For the catalogue, we consider the well-founded, stable, and supported semantics. We address fitting existence and most specific fitting computation, establish tight exponential-time upper bounds for both problems, and obtain polynomial bounds for relevant special cases.

AI.tldr: Automatic shape learning for SHACL data validation using fitting approach with positive/negative examples, focusing on ELI Description Logic fragment with three semantic catalogues.
AI.motivation: SHACL shapes enable data graph validation, making automatic shape learning essential for knowledge graph applications. There's a need for efficient methods to learn shape expressions from example data.
AI.method: Investigates the fitting approach: given sets P (positive) and N (negative) example nodes from an input graph, compute a shape expression C that validates at every node in P and none in N. Focuses on core SHACL fragment corresponding to Description Logic ELI, with three semantics for recursive shape catalogues: well-founded, stable, and supported.
AI.result: Addresses fitting existence and most specific fitting computation problems. Establishes tight exponential-time upper bounds for both problems. Obtains polynomial bounds for relevant special cases.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides theoretical foundations and complexity analysis for shape learning in SHACL validation, showing that while the general problems are exponential, polynomial solutions exist for important special cases, advancing practical shape learning for knowledge graphs.

title: LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO): A Sampling-Time Low-Rank Scaffold for Recovering Reinforcement-Learning Gradient on Zero-Reward Cliff Prompts
summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) for mathematical reasoning suffers from a structural blind spot: on "cliff" prompts-those on which every sampled rollout in a group fails-the group-normalized advantage is identically zero, so GRPO produces no gradient on precisely the prompts at the frontier of the model's capability. We introduce LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO), a sampling-time mechanism that recovers this lost gradient. Each RL step, LSPO detects cliff prompts, fits a small low-rank (LoRA) adapter by a brief supervised step on their ground-truth solutions, re-rolls the cliffs with the base-plus-adapter model, splices the now-successful completions back into the RL batch with an importance-sampling correction, and takes a GRPO step on the base alone; the adapter receives only the supervised gradient and is discarded at checkpoint, yielding a base-only model. On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, evaluated over n=5 paired seeds per arm at a matched 1000-step reporting horizon, LSPO's 5-seed mean matches or beats a DAPO baseline on all 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells (15 strict wins and one exact tie), with gains of up to +10.7 points on AIME24/pass@4, +6.7 points on AIME24 and AIME26 at pass@16, and +2.4 points on MATH500/pass@1; averaged over the 16 cells the improvement is +3.8 points.

AI.tldr: LSPO introduces a sampling-time mechanism to recover lost gradients in RLVR for mathematical reasoning, achieving significant performance improvements over baselines by addressing cliff prompts through temporary LoRA adapters.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) for mathematical reasoning has a structural blind spot on "cliff" prompts where every sampled rollout fails, resulting in zero gradient on precisely the frontier capability prompts where learning is most needed.
AI.method: LSPO detects cliff prompts each RL step, fits a small LoRA adapter via brief supervised learning on ground-truth solutions, re-rolls cliffs with base-plus-adapter model, splices successful completions back into RL batch with importance-sampling correction, then takes a GRPO step on the base model alone (adapter receives only supervised gradient and is discarded).
AI.result: On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, LSPO matches or beats DAPO baseline on all 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells (15 strict wins, 1 tie), with gains up to +10.7 points on AIME24/pass@4, +6.7 points on AIME24/AIME26 at pass@16, +2.4 points on MATH500/pass@1, averaging +3.8 points improvement across all 16 cells.
AI.conclusion: LSPO successfully addresses the structural gradient problem in RLVR for mathematical reasoning by recovering lost gradients on cliff prompts, demonstrating consistent and significant improvements over baseline methods while maintaining a base-only model architecture.

title: From Scoring to Acting: Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation for LLM Agents
summary: Recent work on LLM agents is shifting from external capability elicitation to capability internalization, enabling agents to retain useful skills without retrieval at inference time. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers a promising direction, but many existing methods typically supervise students by scoring actions along student-generated trajectories. Such supervision has two limitations: teacher preferences are not validated by environment outcomes, and action-level scores underuse information from student rollouts, teacher rollouts, and their behavioral relationship. We therefore advocate outcome-verified teacher supervision and comparative learning over teacher-student trajectories. Based on this view, we propose Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation (OVCSD). OVCSD organizes failed student rollouts into a prefix tree, adaptively invokes a skill-conditioned teacher from student-reached states, and retains only outcome-verified successful continuations. It then applies localized comparative learning at the first state-aligned divergence and distills the post-divergence teacher suffix to transfer completion behavior. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop across three model scales show that OVCSD consistently outperforms skill-free RL and existing self-distillation baselines, achieving up to 29.7 and 5.4 absolute success-rate gains over the strongest baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively, while adding less than 3% privileged interaction during training.

AI.tldr: OVCSD: A self-distillation method that improves LLM agent skill acquisition by using outcome-verified teacher supervision and comparative learning over teacher-student trajectories.
AI.motivation: Existing self-distillation methods have limitations: teacher preferences aren't validated by environment outcomes, and action-level scores underuse information from student rollouts, teacher rollouts, and their behavioral relationship.
AI.method: OVCSD organizes failed student rollouts into a prefix tree, adaptively invokes skill-conditioned teachers from student-reached states, retains only outcome-verified successful continuations, applies localized comparative learning at first state-aligned divergence, and distills post-divergence teacher suffix.
AI.result: OVCSD outperforms skill-free RL and existing self-distillation baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop across three model scales, achieving up to 29.7% and 5.4% absolute success-rate gains respectively, while adding less than 3% privileged interaction during training.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that outcome-verified teacher supervision combined with comparative learning over trajectories effectively improves LLM agent skill internalization, enabling better performance with minimal additional privileged interaction.

title: Revisiting Predictive Process Monitoring in the Age of Foundation Models: A Comparative Study of Sequence, Tabular, and LLM Approaches
summary: Predictive process monitoring (PPM) leverages event logs to forecast the future of running process instances, for instance, predicting the next activity, the remaining time until case completion, or the time to the next event. While PPM research in recent years has been dominated by deep sequence models trained from scratch, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models, foundation-model approaches---particularly large language models (LLMs)---are increasingly explored for PPM. At the same time, tabular foundation models with in-context learning capabilities offer a promising alternative but have not yet been systematically benchmarked for PPM. Thus, it remains unclear whether classical sequence-based models remain competitive in this evolving landscape. This paper compares the three modeling paradigms both conceptually and empirically through a controlled benchmark across multiple datasets and prediction tasks. The results show that sequence models consistently perform best for next activity prediction, whereas tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal tasks, with LLMs usually lagging behind despite higher cost.

AI.tldr: LLMs and tabular foundation models are emerging for predictive process monitoring, but traditional sequence models remain competitive, especially for next activity prediction, while tabular models work well for temporal tasks.
AI.motivation: While deep sequence models have dominated PPM research, foundation models (particularly LLMs) are gaining attention, and tabular foundation models with in-context learning offer promising alternatives. However, there's no systematic benchmarking comparing these approaches, leaving uncertainty about whether classical sequence models remain competitive.
AI.method: The paper conducts both conceptual and empirical comparison of three modeling paradigms through a controlled benchmark across multiple datasets and prediction tasks. The three paradigms are: classical sequence-based models (like LSTMs), large language models (LLMs), and tabular foundation models with in-context learning.
AI.result: Sequence models consistently perform best for next activity prediction tasks. Tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal prediction tasks (like remaining time and time to next event). LLMs usually lag behind despite their higher computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Traditional sequence models remain state-of-the-art for certain PPM tasks (next activity prediction), while tabular foundation models offer competitive performance for temporal tasks. LLMs, despite their popularity, don't outperform specialized approaches and come with higher costs, suggesting a task-specific approach to model selection in PPM.

title: MARS-RA: Rank Aggregation for Credit Assignment via Multimodal Comparisons in Embodied Multi-Agent Cooperation
summary: Credit assignment is a fundamental challenge in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly in embodied AI settings characterized by limited and delayed feedback as well as dynamically changing numbers of active agents. We propose MARS-RA, a framework that reformulates credit assignment as a rank aggregation problem using contribution-based pairwise comparisons among agents generated by large multimodal models. This shift from absolute to relative estimation ensures robustness against noise and dynamic agent participation, converting comparison results into contribution scores for potential-based reward shaping. We provide theoretical justification for the convergence and robustness of the proposed framework, and show that Shapley values can be used as an interpretive reference. Experimental results on challenging tasks of different types indicate that MARS-RA can guide agents toward effective cooperation.

AI.tldr: MARS-RA reformulates credit assignment in multi-agent RL as rank aggregation using pairwise comparisons from large multimodal models, enabling robust cooperation in noisy, dynamic environments.
AI.motivation: Credit assignment is challenging in cooperative multi-agent RL, especially in embodied AI with limited/delayed feedback and dynamically changing numbers of active agents.
AI.method: Reformulates credit assignment as rank aggregation using contribution-based pairwise comparisons generated by large multimodal models, converting comparisons to contribution scores for potential-based reward shaping.
AI.result: Theoretical justification for convergence and robustness is provided, and experimental results on challenging tasks show MARS-RA can guide agents toward effective cooperation.
AI.conclusion: MARS-RA offers a robust framework for credit assignment in cooperative multi-agent RL by shifting from absolute to relative estimation, handling noise and dynamic agent participation effectively.

title: Learning-Augmented and Randomized Algorithms for Line Aggregation with Delays
summary: This paper studies learning-augmented and randomized online aggregation with delays on a line metric. We consider advice given as online suggested service lengths, and evaluate the algorithms in terms of robustness and consistency. For each $λ\in (0,1]$, we first propose a deterministic learning-augmented \textsc{Balance} algorithm that is $(4/λ+1/λ^2)$-robust and $(4+λ)$-consistent. We also propose a randomized algorithm for the problem in the classical adversarial model, which is $(e+1)$-competitive against an oblivious adversary, improving over the deterministic $5$-competitive \textsc{Balance} benchmark~\cite{bienkowski2013chain}. Notably, this competitive ratio is even lower than the lower bound of $4$ for deterministic online algorithms. Moreover, we establish a lower bound of $e$ on the competitive ratio of randomized online algorithms, improving the previous lower bound of $e/(e-1)$. Besides, we combine the two ideas and obtain a randomized learning-augmented algorithm that is $(e/λ+1/λ^2)$-robust and $(e+λ)$-consistent. Finally, we conduct numerical experiments to complement our theoretical analysis and evaluate the empirical performance of our algorithms.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes learning-augmented and randomized algorithms for online aggregation with delays on a line metric, achieving improved competitive ratios over existing benchmarks through deterministic, randomized, and hybrid approaches.
AI.motivation: To improve upon existing deterministic online algorithms for aggregation with delays on a line metric, particularly addressing the gap between deterministic lower bounds (4) and current algorithms, while incorporating learning-augmented approaches for better practical performance.
AI.method: 1) A deterministic learning-augmented Balance algorithm with trade-off parameter λ; 2) A randomized algorithm for classical adversarial model; 3) A randomized learning-augmented algorithm combining both ideas; 4) Theoretical analysis establishing bounds; 5) Numerical experiments for empirical evaluation.
AI.result: 1) Deterministic algorithm achieves (4/λ+1/λ²)-robustness and (4+λ)-consistency; 2) Randomized algorithm achieves (e+1)-competitive ratio, beating deterministic lower bound of 4; 3) Improved lower bound of e for randomized algorithms; 4) Combined algorithm achieves (e/λ+1/λ²)-robustness and (e+λ)-consistency; 5) Empirical validation through experiments.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully develops improved algorithms for online aggregation with delays, demonstrating that learning augmentation and randomization can significantly improve competitive ratios beyond deterministic limits, with both theoretical guarantees and empirical validation.

title: Share the Judge, Learn the Deferral: Where Specialization Helps LLM Evaluation
summary: Agentic systems have widened the gap between producing candidate outputs and reviewing them. This paper asks a practical architectural question: should domain specialization be built into an evaluator's weights, or into the rule that decides when its judgment can be trusted? We study 99,952 public, rubric-conditioned examples. Supplying the correct rubric improves locked-test accuracy by 2.11 points over a response-only control; replacing it with an unrelated rubric costs 2.66 points. Dividing the same training corpus among eight criterion-family LoRA judges, however, loses 10.05 points and cuts audited coverage at a 5% risk target from 24.44% to 5.43%. Matching the bank's stored capacity with one rank-64 adapter does not reproduce this loss. Nor is the result explained by learning rate or optimizer steps. Initializing the family adapters from a shared, trained judge recovers test accuracy to 76.85%, 19.94 points above scratch training at the same learning rate (95% interval 18.88-21.02). The result changes when specialization governs deferral rather than judgment. On RewardBench 2, learned correctness heads route examples through a 0.6B-4B-8B cascade without changing any reward score. Across 20 locked repartitions, the cascade attains 89.40% accuracy, compared with 84.75% for 8B alone, at 0.415 normalized parameter compute. Every run passes an exact one-sided 95% risk audit; margin-based rules remain near 84.8% accuracy while using at least 0.94 compute. These results suggest a qualified design rule: share the learning of judgment until there is enough data to justify a split, and place domain-specific adaptation in an audited release boundary.

AI.tldr: Specializing evaluators via fine-grained LoRA judges harms performance; sharing judgment learning works better, while putting domain specialization in audited deferral rules enables efficient cascades.
AI.motivation: Agentic systems create a gap between generating outputs and reviewing them. The paper investigates architectural design: should domain specialization be built into evaluator weights or into rules deciding when to trust judgments?
AI.method: Studied 99,952 public rubric-conditioned examples. Compared rubric supply effects. Divided training corpus among eight criterion-family LoRA judges vs. shared adapters. Tested learned correctness heads routing examples through a 0.6B-4B-8B cascade on RewardBench 2 across 20 locked repartitions.
AI.result: Rubric supply improves accuracy (+2.11 points). Fine-grained LoRA judges lose 10.05 points, cutting coverage. Shared trained judge recovers accuracy (76.85% vs 56.91% scratch). Cascade with learned deferral achieves 89.40% accuracy vs 84.75% for 8B alone at 0.415 compute, all passing risk audits.
AI.conclusion: Share judgment learning until sufficient data justifies split; place domain-specific adaptation in audited release boundaries. Specialization in deferral rules, not weights, enables efficient cascades without sacrificing reliability.

title: Contrastive Concept Importance: Explaining Pairwise Class Decisions Through Automatically Extracted Concept Representations
summary:
Concept-based explanations are a prevalent way to explain the decisions of complex black-box methods through semantically meaningful, human-interpretable concepts. To attribute the contribution of such concepts to a model's decisions, feature attribution methods are used to quantify how strongly each concept contributes to a model output. These attributions are typically computed for a single output class and therefore answer a non-contrastive "why P?" question. In many situations, however, such as cases of misclassification, class confusion, and low-margin predictions, the more natural question to ask is "why P rather than Q?".
  We introduce contrastive concept importance (CCI), which attributes the logit margin between a target class and a contrast, or foil, class to concepts in an automatically extracted visual concept basis. The resulting scores are signed, indicating whether a concept supports the target over the foil or the foil over the target, and can be decomposed into target-logit and foil-logit effects. This makes it possible to distinguish globally important concepts from concepts that specifically influence a class-pair distinction, including whether their effect is shared, one-sided, or directly contrastive.
  We evaluate the method on ImageNet class pairs using CRAFT-style concept bases, insertion and deletion curves, logit-wise decomposition analysis, and semantic class hierarchy. The results show that contrastive concept importance reveals class-pair-specific model behavior that is not captured by ordinary concept importance alone, and that highly contrastive concepts can be evaluated against semantic superclass structure to assess whether they affect fine-grained distinctions rather than broad category evidence.

AI.tldr: CCIs extend concept-based explanations by computing signed concept importance scores that attribute logit margins between target and foil classes, enabling contrastive "why P rather than Q?" explanations rather than just "why P?" explanations.
AI.motivation: Traditional concept importance methods answer non-contrastive "why P?" questions by attributing concepts to a single output class. However, in cases of misclassification, class confusion, and low-margin predictions, the more natural question is contrastive: "why P rather than Q?"
AI.method: Introduces Contrastive Concept Importance (CCI) which attributes the logit margin between a target class and a foil class to concepts in automatically extracted visual concept bases. The resulting scores are signed (supporting target over foil or vice versa) and can be decomposed into target-logit and foil-logit effects.
AI.result: CCI reveals class-pair-specific model behavior not captured by ordinary concept importance alone. Highly contrastive concepts can be evaluated against semantic superclass structure to assess whether they affect fine-grained distinctions rather than broad category evidence.
AI.conclusion: CCI provides a framework for contrastive concept-based explanations that better addresses real-world scenarios like misclassification and class confusion by answering "why P rather than Q?" questions through signed concept importance attributions.

title: SKIMIX: Multi-Agent Harness-Time Scaling with Skill Mixture for Dynamic Harness Engineering
summary: AI agents increasingly rely on large skill libraries, but selecting, combining, and maintaining skills remains difficult. We propose SKIMIX, a multi-agent framework in which agents with different skill portfolios collaborate through iterative refinement. SKIMIX combines embedding-based skill retrieval, submodular anti-dilution routing, and adaptive skill evolution. Across six reasoning benchmarks, multi-agent collaboration substantially improves open-ended mathematical reasoning but offers limited or negative gains on multiple-choice tasks. Agent-count scaling is non-monotonic, and most improvements arise during the first refinement round. These results show that task characteristics determine whether skill-level ensembles help and provide practical guidance for scalable agent design.

AI.tldr: SKIMIX is a multi-agent framework that enables agents with different skills to collaborate through iterative refinement, improving open-ended mathematical reasoning but showing limited benefits for multiple-choice tasks.
AI.motivation: AI agents increasingly rely on large skill libraries, but face challenges in selecting, combining, and maintaining skills effectively.
AI.method: Proposes SKIMIX: a multi-agent framework combining embedding-based skill retrieval, submodular anti-dilution routing, and adaptive skill evolution for iterative collaboration.
AI.result: Multi-agent collaboration substantially improves open-ended mathematical reasoning across six benchmarks, but offers limited or negative gains on multiple-choice tasks. Agent-count scaling is non-monotonic, with most improvements arising during the first refinement round.
AI.conclusion: Task characteristics determine whether skill-level ensembles help, providing practical guidance for scalable agent design.

title: Class-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Counterfactual Explanation Generation
summary: Counterfactual explanations (CFEs) enhance the interpretability of black-box models by generating alternative instances with adjusted feature values that achieve a contrastive outcome. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising approach for CFE generation, enabling efficient exploration of counterfactual instances while ensuring control over key metrics like validity, sparsity, and proximity. Previous studies have formulated RL states exclusively using features derived from the predictors in the supervised dataset. This study explores the impact of including an instance's predicted class, alongside features derived from the predictors, in the RL state representation for generating CFEs. The hypothesis is that class-awareness enhances exploration efficiency and improves policy optimality. We compare the proposed class-aware RL method with the class-blind RL method, which is similar but excludes the instance's class information from the state representation. The comparison was conducted using seven datasets from diverse domains, varying in size. The results show that during training, class-aware RL offers benefits in terms of convergence speed, reward optimization, and episode length reduction. Moreover, it generates significantly more valid CFEs compared to class-blind RL. Finally, the instance's class-based feature consistently ranks among the most influential predictors in RL's action-selection, as shown by the SHAP and LIME values, underscoring the significance of class-awareness in RL for CFE generation. The impact is heightened clarity, faster learning, improved validity, and more effective counterfactual generation across diverse datasets.

AI.tldr: Class-aware RL for counterfactual explanations outperforms class-blind RL with faster convergence, better validity, and more efficient exploration by incorporating predicted class in state representation.
AI.motivation: Previous RL approaches for counterfactual explanation generation used only features from predictors in supervised datasets, ignoring the instance's predicted class information. The researchers hypothesize that including class awareness in RL state representation could enhance exploration efficiency and policy optimality for generating better counterfactual explanations.
AI.method: The study proposes a class-aware RL method that includes an instance's predicted class alongside features derived from predictors in the RL state representation. This is compared against a class-blind RL method that excludes class information from the state. Experiments were conducted using seven diverse datasets of varying sizes to evaluate the impact of class-awareness on CFE generation.
AI.result: Class-aware RL demonstrated superior performance: faster convergence during training, better reward optimization, reduced episode lengths, and significantly higher validity of generated counterfactuals. SHAP and LIME analyses confirmed that class-based features consistently ranked among the most influential predictors in RL's action selection process.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating predicted class information into RL state representation significantly improves counterfactual explanation generation, leading to heightened clarity, faster learning, improved validity, and more effective counterfactuals across diverse datasets. Class-awareness proves to be a valuable enhancement for RL-based CFE generation methods.

title: MMLDSum-LLM: Multimodal Long-Document Summarization with Visual-Alignment and Keyword-Aware
summary: Multimodal long documents are core carriers of professional knowledge, where critical evidence is sparsely distributed across paragraphs and modalities. This easily causes key information omission and cross-modal hallucinations in summarization by multimodal LLMs. These issues stem from attention drift in long-range dependency modeling and gaps in inter-modal alignment. To address this, we introduce MMLDSum-Bench, a high-quality benchmark for multimodal long-document summarization, covering multiple domains, context-length scales, and visual-textual modality distributions. We further propose MMLDSum-LLM, a reproducible two-stage training framework that combines supervised fine-tuning with visual-alignment weighted loss and keyword-aware weighted loss, followed by GRPO with a multi-objective reward (keyword coverage, image-text alignment, ROUGE, and length control). Extensive experiments on MMLDSum-Bench, comparing against leading closed-source and open-source multimodal models under a unified evaluation protocol - including LLM-as-a-judge scoring, atomic-claim precision/recall, image-text alignment (ITA), and ROUGE - demonstrate that our approach significantly improves key-information coverage and cross-modal consistency.

AI.tldr: Proposed MMLDSum-Bench benchmark and MMLDSum-LLM framework for multimodal long-document summarization to address attention drift and cross-modal alignment issues, achieving improved key-information coverage and consistency.
AI.motivation: Multimodal long documents as core professional knowledge carriers suffer from critical evidence being sparsely distributed across paragraphs and modalities, leading to key information omission and cross-modal hallucinations in summarization by multimodal LLMs, stemming from attention drift in long-range dependency modeling and gaps in inter-modal alignment.
AI.method: Introduced MMLDSum-Bench benchmark covering multiple domains, context-length scales, and visual-textual modality distributions, and proposed MMLDSum-LLM framework with two-stage training: 1) supervised fine-tuning with visual-alignment weighted loss and keyword-aware weighted loss, followed by 2) GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) with multi-objective reward (keyword coverage, image-text alignment, ROUGE, and length control).
AI.result: Extensive experiments on MMLDSum-Bench comparing against leading closed-source and open-source multimodal models under unified evaluation protocol (LLM-as-a-judge scoring, atomic-claim precision/recall, image-text alignment, ROUGE) demonstrated significant improvements in key-information coverage and cross-modal consistency.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach effectively addresses attention drift and cross-modal alignment problems in multimodal long-document summarization, providing a comprehensive solution through benchmark creation and a reproducible two-stage training framework that enhances key-information coverage and cross-modal consistency.

title: S-CEReBrO: Breaking the Memory Barrier in Continuous EEG Monitoring
comment: This is the pre-rebuttal version of a paper accepted at MICCAI 2026. The camera-ready version will be posted following the embargo
summary: Foundation models offer a promising paradigm for Electroencephalography (EEG) analysis, leveraging generalizable representations from vast unlabeled datasets. Yet, Transformer-based architectures face a critical bottleneck: global attention mechanisms couple the attention memory state to the signal duration, causing memory overflow during continuous monitoring. To address this, we introduce S-CEReBrO (Streaming CEReBrO), an evolution of the CEReBrO architecture designed for continuous monitoring. Our novel Windowed Alternating Attention mechanism factorizes attention computation into fixed-size spatiotemporal windows, guaranteeing constant KV cache memory as only the active window requires resident attention maps. Empirical scaling analysis confirms that windowed alternating attention can process signals 100X longer than full self-attention and 3X longer than low-rank linear attention. Compared to low-rank linear attention on long contexts, windowed alternating attention requires 55% of the memory while increasing inference throughput by 2.1X. Pre-trained on >25,000 hours of recordings from >12,000 subjects, S-CEReBrO achieves state-of-the-art performance on 7 of 11 downstream tasks, with up to 60% fewer parameters. This work represents a significant step toward the realization of efficient, generalizable, and continuous EEG monitoring. An accompanying code repository is available.

AI.tldr: S-CEReBrO introduces windowed alternating attention for continuous EEG monitoring, enabling 100x longer signal processing with 55% less memory than alternatives, achieving SOTA on 7/11 tasks with fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Transformer-based EEG models face memory bottlenecks from global attention mechanisms that scale with signal duration, making continuous monitoring impractical due to memory overflow.
AI.method: S-CEReBrO extends CEReBrO with Windowed Alternating Attention that factorizes attention into fixed-size spatiotemporal windows, maintaining constant KV cache memory by keeping only active window attention maps resident.
AI.result: The method processes signals 100x longer than full self-attention and 3x longer than low-rank linear attention, uses 55% less memory while providing 2.1x throughput, and achieves SOTA on 7 of 11 downstream tasks with up to 60% fewer parameters after pre-training on >25,000 hours from >12,000 subjects.
AI.conclusion: S-CEReBrO represents significant progress toward efficient, generalizable continuous EEG monitoring by solving the memory bottleneck of global attention in Transformer architectures.

title: MUL-T: Decoding Spatial Cellular Architecture in Multiplexed Tissue Images
summary: Understanding tissue organisation in multiplexed imaging requires modelling both cellular phenotypes and their spatial context. Existing approaches typically rely on handcrafted features, such as marker intensity statistics or cell-type proportions, which often fail to scale or generalise across cohorts with heterogeneous marker panels. We introduce MUL-T, a lightweight transformer framework that reframes tissue architecture as a masked contextual prediction task over discrete cell tokens. By learning contextualised [CLS] embeddings without task-specific supervision, the model captures higher-order cellular interactions while remaining computationally efficient. We evaluate MUL-T on several clinically relevant downstream tasks, including core-level tumour pattern classification, patient-level grading, PD-L1 positivity prediction, and cross-dataset treatment response prediction. Across tasks, MUL-T consistently outperforms classical feature-based baselines and achieves performance comparable to a foundation ViT model, despite substantially fewer parameters and lower training cost.

AI.tldr: MUL-T is a lightweight transformer framework that learns tissue architecture by modeling cellular interactions as masked contextual prediction over discrete cell tokens, outperforming classical feature-based methods on multiple clinical tasks with lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for understanding tissue organization in multiplexed imaging rely on handcrafted features that don't scale or generalize well across cohorts with heterogeneous marker panels, creating limitations for clinical applications.
AI.method: The authors introduce MUL-T, a lightweight transformer framework that reframes tissue architecture analysis as a masked contextual prediction task over discrete cell tokens. The model learns contextualized [CLS] embeddings without task-specific supervision to capture higher-order cellular interactions while maintaining computational efficiency.
AI.result: MUL-T consistently outperforms classical feature-based baselines across multiple clinically relevant downstream tasks including core-level tumour pattern classification, patient-level grading, PD-L1 positivity prediction, and cross-dataset treatment response prediction. It achieves performance comparable to a foundation Vision Transformer model despite having substantially fewer parameters and lower training cost.
AI.conclusion: MUL-T represents an effective and computationally efficient approach for modeling tissue architecture in multiplexed imaging that generalizes well across cohorts and clinical tasks while overcoming the limitations of handcrafted feature-based methods.

title: Exact Action Values Are Not Enough: Rollout-Verified Reinforcement Fine-Tuning of a Reasoning Model for Multi-Zone VAV Control
summary: Multi-zone variable-air-volume control must balance thermal comfort, indoor air quality, and electricity use across several continuous actuators. Model predictive control and reinforcement learning are widely studied, but deployment typically requires building-specific modeling or training, limiting scalability. We first test whether a frontier reasoning model (an LLM trained to use additional inference-time computation) can achieve competitive VAV control from text without building-specific training. With that capability established, we then test whether TD3-guided reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) can transfer control knowledge into a locally deployable open-weight model. Five controllers are evaluated over three summer days in a physics-based four-zone emulator. Relative to a Guideline 36-based baseline, TD3 reduced HVAC electricity by 4.5% while improving temperature and CO$_2$ compliance. Without building-specific training, GPT-5 achieved the largest reduction (6.2%) but reduced the ventilation margin. For RFT, deterministic rollouts restore a saved state, apply one candidate, and follow TD3 to score each action. Auditing a learned critic against these rollouts exposed a failure hidden by its near-perfect across-time correlation ($r=0.9998$): within-state ranking was unreliable; the critic selected the rollout-best candidate in only 5 of 10 states. Even with the rollout verifier, 200 RFT steps produced no sustained improvement in sampled-action return; the open-weight controller used more electricity than the baseline before and after training, and its five-minute predictions remained worse than persistence. GPT-5 predicted transitions far better. Exact rollout scores rank sampled actions but reveal neither next-state effects nor an improvement direction. The unchanged transition errors motivate transition-focused supervised fine-tuning before value-based RFT.

AI.tldr: The paper explores using LLMs for VAV control without building-specific training, showing GPT-5 achieved 6.2% HVAC electricity reduction but reduced ventilation. Reinforcement fine-tuning failed to transfer knowledge to open-weight models due to unreliable critic ranking.
AI.motivation: Traditional model predictive control and reinforcement learning for multi-zone VAV control require building-specific modeling or training, limiting scalability. The paper investigates whether frontier LLMs can achieve competitive control from text without building-specific training, and whether reinforcement fine-tuning can transfer this knowledge to deployable open-weight models.
AI.method: Five controllers evaluated over three summer days in a physics-based four-zone emulator: Guideline 36 baseline, TD3 (RL benchmark), GPT-5 (without building-specific training), and reinforcement fine-tuning attempts. Methods include deterministic rollouts to score actions, critic auditing against rollout verification, and comparison of transition prediction accuracy.
AI.result: TD3 reduced HVAC electricity by 4.5% while improving temperature/CO₂ compliance. GPT-5 achieved largest reduction (6.2%) but reduced ventilation margin. Reinforcement fine-tuning failed: critic's near-perfect across-time correlation hid unreliable within-state ranking (selected best candidate in only 5 of 10 states). 200 RFT steps produced no sustained improvement, open-weight controller used more electricity than baseline, and its predictions remained worse than persistence. GPT-5 predicted transitions far better than RFT models.
AI.conclusion: Frontier LLMs can achieve competitive VAV control without building-specific training, but reinforcement fine-tuning fails to transfer this knowledge to open-weight models due to unreliable critic ranking. The results suggest transition-focused supervised fine-tuning should precede value-based reinforcement fine-tuning for effective knowledge transfer.

title: DataClawEval: A Benchmark for Data Engineering Agents in Real Industrial Harness
summary: Large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly being deployed to automate complex workflows, promising to revolutionize data management and processing. However, existing benchmarks predominantly focus on simplified Text-to-SQL translation or data analysis, leaving the critical and complex domain of end-to-end data engineering largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce DataClawEval, the first comprehensive benchmark designed specifically to evaluate the end-to-end task completion capabilities of autonomous agents in real-world data engineering scenarios. Built upon production-grade code authored by professional enterprise data engineers, it comprises 100 rigorous, end-to-end tasks spanning five execution engines: PySpark, MySQL, HiveSQL, PrestoSQL/Trino, and FlinkSQL. Rather than non-deterministic LLM-as-a-judge scoring, each task is executed within a case-specific, isolated sandbox and graded by deterministic, rule-based scripts. Evaluating 16 frontier agents exposes critical limitations: The strongest model attains only 74.9 overall, and no single model dominates, as each excels on a different engine, revealing strict domain specialization rather than omnipotent proficiency. Thus, autonomous data engineering remains a formidable, unresolved challenge. We release our dataset, containerized environments, and deterministic evaluation scripts at https://github.com/Dicemy/DataClawEval/tree/master

AI.tldr: DataClawEval is the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating autonomous agents in end-to-end data engineering tasks across multiple execution engines, revealing significant limitations in current LLM-based systems.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks focus on simplified Text-to-SQL or data analysis, leaving the complex domain of end-to-end data engineering largely unexplored. There's a need to evaluate autonomous agents' capabilities in real-world data engineering scenarios.
AI.method: Created DataClawEval benchmark with 100 rigorous, end-to-end tasks based on production-grade code from professional enterprise data engineers. Tasks span five execution engines: PySpark, MySQL, HiveSQL, PrestoSQL/Trino, and FlinkSQL. Evaluation uses case-specific isolated sandboxes with deterministic, rule-based script grading instead of LLM-as-a-judge scoring.
AI.result: Evaluation of 16 frontier agents shows critical limitations: strongest model achieves only 74.9% overall accuracy, no single model dominates across all engines, and each model excels on different engines revealing strict domain specialization rather than omnipotent proficiency.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous data engineering remains a formidable, unresolved challenge. The benchmark exposes the need for more specialized models rather than expecting general proficiency across all data engineering domains.

title: ODEWorld: A Continuous Predictive Architecture via Physical-Time Flow
summary: In the physical world we inhabit, space and time are fundamentally continuous. However, existing machine learning paradigms for world modeling are largely confined to discrete-time prediction, thereby exhibiting significant inefficiency in capturing the dynamics of physical world. We introduce Physical-Time Flow (\textbf{PT-Flow}), a novel approach that learns a continuous latent velocity field operating in physical time. Crucially, the underlying dynamics of sequential data are parameterized by an ordinary differential equation (ODE) embedded in a well-structured representation space. Under this paradigm, the prediction of future can be recast as temporal integration via an ODE solver in the compressed latent space. Building upon PT-Flow, we construct \textbf{ODEWorld}, a continuous-time latent world model that is both efficient and versatile. By extracting time-variant features and enforcing ODE properties on both the dynamical representation space and the latent velocity field, ODEWorld effectively addresses the long-standing representation collapse issue in latent world model literature. This also enables high-quality image reconstruction even after long-horizon prediction. Moreover, its continuous nature allows for arbitrary temporal resolution and even backward prediction, which is impossible for most discrete-time models. Lastly, ODEWorld can provide rich planning-oriented information to facilitate downstream policy learning. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that ODEWorld successfully reconciles planning-conducive dynamics abstraction with visual realism, excelling in both video generation and robotic control. \href{https://dstate.github.io/odeworld_website/}{Project Website}.

AI.tldr: ODEWorld introduces a continuous-time latent world model that uses physical-time flow and ODEs to model physical world dynamics, enabling efficient prediction with arbitrary temporal resolution, backward prediction, and better planning for downstream tasks.
AI.motivation: Current machine learning world models are largely confined to discrete-time prediction, which is inefficient for capturing the continuous nature of physical world dynamics. There's a need for models that can handle continuous time more effectively.
AI.method: Proposes PT-Flow (Physical-Time Flow) - a continuous latent velocity field operating in physical time, parameterized by an ODE in a well-structured representation space. Builds ODEWorld as a continuous-time latent world model that extracts time-variant features and enforces ODE properties on both dynamical representation space and latent velocity field to prevent representation collapse.
AI.result: ODEWorld successfully reconciles planning-conducive dynamics abstraction with visual realism, excels in video generation and robotic control, enables arbitrary temporal resolution and backward prediction, prevents representation collapse, and maintains high-quality image reconstruction even after long-horizon prediction.
AI.conclusion: ODEWorld represents a significant advancement in world modeling by bridging the gap between continuous physical time and discrete machine learning paradigms, offering versatile applications in both video generation and robotic control while providing rich planning information for downstream tasks.

title: SKILL-KD: Contrastive Skill Distillation for LLM Agents
summary: Skill-based prompting has become a practical mechanism for improving large language model (LLM) agents, yet existing skill acquisition methods often treat skills as experience summaries, memory entries, or direct summaries of successful demonstrations. This creates a mismatch for weaker student agents: when a student fails because it lacks task knowledge or operational strategy, its failed trajectory may not contain enough evidence to infer the missing behavior, while the teacher trajectory may be too implicit to be internalized as reusable guidance. We propose SKILL-KD, a contrastive skill distillation framework that treats skills as an explicit distillation medium between agents of different capabilities. Given a student failure and the teacher trajectory on the same task, SKILL-KD distills their actionable discrepancy into a textual skill patch, evaluates the patch by re-running the student, and iteratively refines the patch when the student still fails. To prevent repeated local updates from causing skill drift, SKILL-KD further maintains trace-linked edit histories and performs Drift-Aware Skill Consolidation, deciding whether each patch should add a new rule, delete or modify an existing rule, or be skipped. Across five agent benchmarks and two student settings, SKILL-KD consistently improves frozen student agents over fixed-model adaptation baselines.

AI.tldr: SKILL-KD is a contrastive skill distillation framework that distills actionable discrepancies between failed student and successful teacher trajectories into textual skill patches, then iteratively refines them through drift-aware consolidation.
AI.motivation: Existing skill acquisition methods treat skills as experience summaries or direct demonstrations, which creates problems for weaker student agents. Failed student trajectories may not contain enough evidence to infer missing behaviors, while teacher trajectories may be too implicit for reusable guidance.
AI.method: SKILL-KD treats skills as explicit distillation medium between different capability agents. Given a student failure and teacher success on same task, it: 1) distills actionable discrepancy into textual skill patch, 2) evaluates patch by re-running student, 3) iteratively refines patch when student still fails, and 4) maintains trace-linked edit histories with Drift-Aware Skill Consolidation to prevent skill drift from repeated updates.
AI.result: Across five agent benchmarks and two student settings, SKILL-KD consistently improves frozen student agents over fixed-model adaptation baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed contrastive skill distillation framework effectively addresses the skill acquisition mismatch for weaker agents by making skill transfer more explicit and actionable through iterative patch refinement and drift-aware consolidation.

title: Harnessing the Potential of Optimizing Data Mixtures via Bayesian Domain Reweighting
summary: The performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) is fundamentally influenced by the distributional composition of multi-domain pre-training data. While manual heuristics were prevalent in early models, they increasingly fail to capture the intricate synergies between domains as data complexity grows. To overcome the issue, a dominant approach seeks to fit a proxy function mapping between domain weights and their corresponding validation losses, and then find the optimal domain weights to minimize validation losses. These methods rely on strong structural assumptions, such as rank invariance or scaling laws, which are often violated, resulting in non-negligible estimation bias. A promising approach is to directly optimize the weighting scheme from data. However, it suffers from unstable optimization trajectory and prohibitive computational overhead, limiting its potential to search better domain weights configurations. This paper presents a Bayesian domain weighting method to infer the weights from a Dirichlet distribution via introducing Gamma prior information learned from observations. Experimental results demonstrate that proposed method could achieve stable and efficient domain weights learning, and identifies optimal mixtures while consuming substantially less data than search-based function-fitting methods, revitalizing optimization-based domain weighting for large-scale applications.

AI.tldr: Proposes a Bayesian domain weighting method using Dirichlet distribution with Gamma priors to optimize LLM pre-training data mixtures more efficiently and stably than existing approaches.
AI.motivation: Current methods for optimizing domain weights in LLM pre-training data have limitations: manual heuristics fail to capture domain synergies; function-fitting methods rely on structural assumptions (rank invariance/scaling laws) that are often violated; direct optimization suffers from instability and high computational costs.
AI.method: Bayesian domain weighting approach that infers weights from a Dirichlet distribution using Gamma prior information learned from observations. This provides a probabilistic framework for domain mixture optimization that's more robust and efficient than search-based methods.
AI.result: Method achieves stable and efficient domain weights learning, identifies optimal mixtures while consuming substantially less data than search-based function-fitting methods, making optimization-based domain weighting feasible for large-scale applications.
AI.conclusion: The Bayesian approach revitalizes optimization-based domain weighting by overcoming the limitations of previous methods, offering a practical solution for optimizing LLM pre-training data mixtures at scale with better stability and efficiency.

title: IndustryForge-27B: A Domain-Enhanced Multimodal Foundation Model for Industrial CAD
summary: Automating industrial CAD design and manufacturing places distinctive demands on multimodal foundation models: the model must see engineering drawings and 3D geometry screenshots, write correct parametric-modelling scripts and Windows COM API code, and cover the full range from single parts to assemblies. General-purpose multimodal models fall short on these tasks, while single-task fine-tuning is too narrow to support the diverse calls that upper-layer agents issue. We build IndustryForge-27B on top of Qwen3.5-VL-27B by curating and integrating six industrial-CAD sub-corpora totalling $\sim$52k multimodal samples---CAD Visual QA (CAD-VQA), parametric CAD code (text2cadquery), assembly-level CAD code (text2cadquery-assembly), and three COM sub-corpora for Inventor / SolidWorks (com_2d / com_3d / com_assembly)---and training with a unified multi-task SFT recipe. Across four CAD-domain benchmarks IndustryForge-27B lifts the base model by $+33.65$~pp on average and outperforms the strong closed-source model GPT-5.4 on all four; across eleven general-capability benchmarks it retains, and slightly improves upon, the base model ($+1.56$~pp mean, no catastrophic forgetting). IndustryForge-27B will serve as the common substrate for downstream industrial-agent projects, providing a unified starting point for a full-stack industrial agent that spans from CAD design to industrial-software operation, from parts to assemblies, and from single-shot generation to closed-loop self-improvement.

AI.tldr: IndustryForge-27B is a specialized multimodal foundation model for industrial CAD design and manufacturing, built on Qwen3.5-VL-27B and trained on six curated industrial-CAD datasets to handle visual inputs, parametric code generation, and Windows COM API calls.
AI.motivation: General-purpose multimodal models fail to meet the specialized requirements of industrial CAD tasks, while single-task fine-tuning is too narrow for the diverse needs of upper-layer agents in industrial automation workflows.
AI.method: Built on Qwen3.5-VL-27B foundation model, curated six industrial-CAD sub-corpora (~52k multimodal samples) covering CAD visual QA, parametric CAD code, assembly-level CAD code, and three Windows COM API datasets for Inventor/SolidWorks, trained with unified multi-task SFT recipe.
AI.result: Outperformed base model by +33.65 percentage points on four CAD-domain benchmarks and beat closed-source GPT-5.4 on all four; maintained and slightly improved general capabilities (+1.56 pp mean) without catastrophic forgetting on eleven general benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: IndustryForge-27B serves as a common substrate for downstream industrial-agent projects, enabling unified industrial automation from CAD design to software operation, spanning parts to assemblies, and supporting both single-shot generation and closed-loop self-improvement.

title: TriShield: Zero-Utility-Loss Defense Against Privacy Backdoors in Federated Language Model Fine-Tuning via Orthogonal Gradient Projection and Optimizer State Entanglement
summary: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) enables collaborative training without exposing raw data. However, a recent attack, NeuroImprint [1] (arXiv:2606.20553), demonstrates that a malicious parameter server can corrupt a PEFT adapter into a privacy backdoor: by assigning a dedicated memorization neuron to each training sample and ensuring each neuron updates at most once, the server can analytically reconstruct 59\%--79\% of client training data with high semantic fidelity. Existing defenses---including local differential privacy (LDP) [8] and gradient clipping---either fail against this attack or impose unacceptable utility degradation. We present \textbf{TriShield}, a three-layer deterministic defense that completely prevents NeuroImprint-style reconstruction with \textbf{zero model utility loss} and \textbf{no additional communication rounds}. TriShield consists of: (1) a \textbf{Parameter Artifact Detector} that identifies memory-neuron signatures in distributed model parameters before local training begins; (2) a \textbf{Stateful Virtual Iteration} mechanism that forces Adam/AdamW's momentum state to irreversibly entangle gradients across virtual steps, invalidating NeuroImprint's closed-form inversion; and (3) a \textbf{Zero-Utility Orthogonal Projection} operator that projects all local gradient updates onto the main-task semantic subspace computed via SVD, physically eliminating any gradient components that carry private memorization. We prove theoretically that after Layers 2 and 3, the mutual information between the uploaded gradient and any individual training sample is zero. Experiments on GPT-2 (117M) and Llama-Guard-3-1B verify that TriShield reduces NeuroImprint reconstruction rate to \textbf{0\%} across all tested attack variants, while maintaining or improving training accuracy, with less than 5\% additional GPU computation overhead.

AI.tldr: TriShield is a three-layer defense that completely prevents NeuroImprint-style data reconstruction attacks in federated fine-tuning of LLMs with zero model utility loss and no additional communication rounds.
AI.motivation: The NeuroImprint attack can reconstruct 59-79% of client training data with high semantic fidelity in federated fine-tuning of LLMs by corrupting PEFT adapters into privacy backdoors. Existing defenses like LDP and gradient clipping either fail against this attack or cause unacceptable utility degradation.
AI.method: TriShield employs three deterministic layers: 1) Parameter Artifact Detector that identifies memory-neuron signatures before training, 2) Stateful Virtual Iteration that forces Adam/AdamW's momentum state to irreversibly entangle gradients across virtual steps, and 3) Zero-Utility Orthogonal Projection that projects local gradient updates onto the main-task semantic subspace using SVD.
AI.result: TriShield reduces NeuroImprint reconstruction rate to 0% across all tested attack variants while maintaining or improving training accuracy, with less than 5% additional GPU computation overhead. Theoretically proves zero mutual information between uploaded gradients and individual training samples.
AI.conclusion: TriShield provides a comprehensive defense against NeuroImprint-style reconstruction attacks in federated LLM fine-tuning without compromising model utility, offering a practical solution to the privacy-utility trade-off.

title: SemPIC: Learning Semantic Position-Independent KV Caches
summary: Long-context retrieval and agentic workloads repeatedly reuse the same documents under changing instructions, histories, and document orders.
