Prefix caching cannot exploit this reuse, while position-independent caching (PIC) remains unreliable because independently compiled KV states lack the future context in which they will be consumed. Our diagnostics show that a learned boundary-conditioned baseline sharply reduces attention deviation near reusable-block boundaries but leaves interior and task-level residuals, motivating adaptation of the document representation itself. We present \emph{SemPIC}, which trains a LoRA-enabled Writer to compile native per-layer document KVs through behavioral distillation while retaining the pretrained decoder as an unchanged Reader. Adaptation is confined to offline cache construction, preserving the standard KV interface and cache-hit decoding path. We further introduce KV Gradient Checkpointing, which reduces peak training memory without severing gradients through cached KVs. Across three models and four tasks, SemPIC raises mean micro-F1 over KV Packet from 0.53 to 0.60, approaching Full Recompute at 0.62.

AI.tldr: SemPIC introduces semantic position-independent caching through LoRA-enabled Writer adaptation for efficient document reuse in long-context retrieval and agentic workloads.
AI.motivation: Current caching methods (prefix caching and position-independent caching) are inefficient for document reuse in long-context scenarios. Position-independent caching remains unreliable because independently compiled KV states lack future context, motivating adaptation of document representations.
AI.method: SemPIC trains a LoRA-enabled Writer to compile native per-layer document KVs through behavioral distillation while keeping the pretrained decoder as an unchanged Reader. Adaptation occurs during offline cache construction, preserving standard KV interface. Also introduces KV Gradient Checkpointing to reduce training memory without severing gradients through cached KVs.
AI.result: Across three models and four tasks, SemPIC raises mean micro-F1 over KV Packet from 0.53 to 0.60, approaching Full Recompute performance at 0.62.
AI.conclusion: SemPIC demonstrates effective semantic position-independent caching that significantly improves performance over existing methods while maintaining standard interfaces and approaching full recompute accuracy.

title: AutoPref: Automatic Discovery of Task-Specific Preference Objectives for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
summary: Combinatorial optimization problems (COPs) underpin many real-world decisions, but their exponentially large search spaces make high-quality solutions costly to obtain. Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) learns fast construction policies, typically with reinforcement learning (RL), while preference-based NCO improves sample efficiency by learning from relative solution quality. However, existing preference objectives combine two distinct design choices in manually specified, one-size-fits-all formulations: what learning signal to extract from each solution pair and how to weight each pair relative to the sampled set. We present AutoPref, the first LLM-guided framework for automated preference-objective discovery in NCO. AutoPref factorizes the objective into a pairwise loss program, which defines the learning signal, and a set-aware weighting program, which determines each pair's relative contribution. Their composition forms a unified programmatic objective space containing existing preference objectives as special cases. To make its search tractable, we introduce a staged conditional search strategy with behavioral gates that filter inadmissible programs before short-horizon training and evaluation. Across TSP, CVRP, FFSP, and JSSP, AutoPref consistently outperforms strong hand-designed baselines across problem scales, demonstrating the benefits and scalability of automated objective discovery for NCO.

AI.tldr: AutoPref: An LLM-guided framework for automated discovery of preference objectives in neural combinatorial optimization, outperforming hand-designed baselines across multiple optimization problems.
AI.motivation: Existing preference-based neural combinatorial optimization methods use manually specified, one-size-fits-all formulations that combine two distinct design choices: what learning signal to extract from solution pairs and how to weight each pair relative to the sampled set. These hand-designed objectives may not be optimal for different problems.
AI.method: AutoPref factorizes the preference objective into a pairwise loss program (defining the learning signal) and a set-aware weighting program (determining each pair's relative contribution). It uses LLM guidance to search this programmatic objective space, with a staged conditional search strategy featuring behavioral gates that filter inadmissible programs before short-horizon training and evaluation.
AI.result: AutoPref consistently outperforms strong hand-designed baselines across multiple combinatorial optimization problems (TSP, CVRP, FFSP, JSSP) and across different problem scales, demonstrating the benefits and scalability of automated objective discovery.
AI.conclusion: Automated objective discovery through AutoPref's LLM-guided framework provides superior performance over manually designed preference objectives in neural combinatorial optimization, showing the potential for AI-guided optimization of AI learning objectives.

title: Echoverse: Deep, Evolving Environments for Training Computer-Use Agents at Scale
summary: Computer-use agents learn from what their actions change, so training one needs applications it can act on, break and reset. The applications that matter most are login-gated and stateful, so synthetic environments stand in for them. Recent pipelines generate such environments in bulk, which moves the bottleneck from how many exist to what is inside each one. The returns, we find, come from three properties: how much behavioural depth an environment carries, whether it targets the interaction an agent actually fails, and whether it improves alongside the model. We present Echoverse, which compiles specifications into stateful applications whose tasks are graded against the application's own database, and a co-evolution loop that reads every graded rollout twice: as repairs to the environment, its tasks and its verifier, and as training signal for the model. Trained on twelve such environments, a 9B model improves from $36.5\%$ to $67.1\%$ across fourteen evaluation splits, within fourteen points of the much larger frontier model that taught it. We examine each property in turn. On the same domains, shallow environments push live-site accuracy below the base model ($80.0 \to 75.0$) while deep ones raise it ($80.0 \to 85.0$ and $48.0 \to 65.0$); drilling one interface control across many renderings transfers to held-out widget families and to the open web; and repairing a single environment lifts the model trained on it from $16.2\%$ to $38.5\%$. The same worlds serve as reinforcement-learning environments, where a reward combining the grounded verifier with a dense per-step judge raises held-out score from $58.8\%$ to $68.0\%$. We release four environments as a benchmark, with their applications, seed data and grounded graders. Code: https://aka.ms/echoverse

AI.tldr: Echoverse is a system that creates stateful applications with graded tasks for training computer-use agents, using a co-evolution loop that improves both environments and models simultaneously, achieving significant performance gains.
AI.motivation: Training computer-use agents requires applications they can interact with, but real applications are login-gated and stateful, making synthetic environments necessary. Existing bulk environment generation pipelines have shifted the bottleneck from quantity to quality - specifically what's inside each environment.
AI.method: Echoverse compiles specifications into stateful applications with tasks graded against the application's own database. It uses a co-evolution loop that reads graded rollouts twice: as repairs to the environment, its tasks, and verifier, and as training signal for the model. This creates environments with three key properties: behavioral depth, targeted interaction on agent weaknesses, and continuous improvement alongside the model.
AI.result: A 9B model trained on twelve Echoverse environments improved from 36.5% to 67.1% across fourteen evaluation splits, coming within 14 points of the much larger frontier model that taught it. Deep environments improved live-site accuracy (80.0→85.0, 48.0→65.0) while shallow ones degraded it (80.0→75.0). Single environment repairs boosted model performance from 16.2% to 38.5%. As RL environments, combining grounded verifier with dense per-step judge raised held-out scores from 58.8% to 68.0%.
AI.conclusion: The effectiveness of training environments for computer-use agents depends on three key properties: behavioral depth, targeted interaction on agent failures, and co-evolutionary improvement with the model. Echoverse demonstrates that high-quality, evolving environments can substantially boost agent performance and bridge the gap with larger models, with applications released as benchmarks for further research.

title: What Makes Graph Unified? Principles and Generative Sliding-Window Transformer for Graph Foundation Models
summary: Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose graph learning, aiming to learn reusable knowledge that generalizes across diverse graph domains and downstream tasks, reducing the need for specific model development. Achieving this goal requires reconciling the substantial heterogeneity in node features, graph structures, and semantic information across domains. Among them, heterogeneous node features constitute a fundamental input-level barrier, as their dimensionality and semantics vary substantially across datasets. Existing studies typically project or map heterogeneous node features into a fixed-dimensional space, often implicitly equating dimensional uniformity with effective feature unification. Yet dimensional consistency alone does not ensure that the unified features preserve informative semantics and capture transferable patterns that can support cross-domain knowledge transfer. To bridge this conceptual gap, we distill four desiderata for cross-domain graph feature unification: formal uniformity, cross-domain transferability, information preservation, and backbone compatibility. Guided by these principles, we propose SliGFM, a graph foundation model built upon topology-aware sliding-window feature encoding and generative reconstruction. SliGFM orders feature dimensions by topological smoothness and scans the reordered features with a shared sliding-window feature encoder, transforming heterogeneous features into a common space of ordered fixed-dimensional feature tokens. This formulation enables a smoothness-aware transformer to capture transferable relational patterns among feature tokens within each node, while the generative reconstruction objective encourages preservation of the original feature information.

AI.tldr: SliGFM is a graph foundation model that uses topology-aware sliding-window feature encoding and generative reconstruction to unify heterogeneous node features across different graph domains while preserving semantic information and enabling cross-domain knowledge transfer.
AI.motivation: Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) aim to learn reusable knowledge across diverse graph domains, but face challenges with heterogeneous node features that vary in dimensionality and semantics across datasets. Current approaches focus on dimensional uniformity but don't ensure effective feature unification for cross-domain transfer.
AI.method: SliGFM uses topology-aware sliding-window feature encoding: it orders feature dimensions by topological smoothness, scans reordered features with a shared sliding-window encoder to transform heterogeneous features into ordered fixed-dimensional tokens. A smoothness-aware transformer captures relational patterns, and generative reconstruction encourages information preservation.
AI.result: The proposed approach addresses four desiderata for cross-domain graph feature unification: formal uniformity, cross-domain transferability, information preservation, and backbone compatibility. It transforms heterogeneous features into a common space while preserving original feature information and capturing transferable patterns.
AI.conclusion: SliGFM provides a principled approach to cross-domain graph feature unification that goes beyond dimensional consistency to ensure semantic preservation and transferability, enabling more effective general-purpose graph learning across diverse domains.

title: Group-Reflective Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is effective for training large language model agents. However, terminal rewards provide only coarse trajectory-level supervision, leaving successful behaviors, recurring mistakes, and incidental choices entangled in the same outcome signal. Existing agentic self-distillation methods enrich sparse supervision with natural-language skills, but skills retrieved externally or extracted from a single trajectory by stronger models may mismatch current experience, exceed the policy's capability, or remain path-specific. We propose Group-Reflective Self-Distillation (GRSD), which derives capability-aligned and outcome-discriminative guidance from the policy's own verified rollouts. For each prompt, the policy reflects on each verified trajectory in an on-policy group, and a stop-gradient snapshot contrasts the resulting reflections from successful and failed rollouts to construct group-level privileged guidance. Conditioned on this guidance, a self-teacher refines turn-level credit assignment by modulating outcome-based advantages while preserving the verifier-determined learning direction. Experiments across multiple agentic environments and model scales demonstrate that GRSD consistently outperforms competitive baselines and generalizes more effectively to unseen tasks.

AI.tldr: GRSD is a self-distillation method for RL agents that derives guidance from the agent's own verified rollouts by contrasting successful vs failed trajectories, improving credit assignment while preserving verifier-determined learning direction.
AI.motivation: Terminal rewards in RLVR provide only coarse trajectory-level supervision, mixing successful behaviors, recurring mistakes, and incidental choices in the same outcome signal. Existing self-distillation methods can mismatch experience, exceed policy capabilities, or remain path-specific.
AI.method: GRSD derives guidance from the policy's own verified rollouts. For each prompt, the policy reflects on each verified trajectory in an on-policy group, and a stop-gradient snapshot contrasts reflections from successful and failed rollouts to construct group-level privileged guidance. A self-teacher refines turn-level credit assignment by modulating outcome-based advantages while preserving verifier-determined direction.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple agentic environments and model scales show GRSD consistently outperforms competitive baselines and generalizes more effectively to unseen tasks.
AI.conclusion: GRSD effectively addresses limitations of sparse terminal rewards in RLVR by using the agent's own experience to derive capability-aligned, outcome-discriminative guidance, leading to better performance and generalization.

title: Beyond Binary Rewards: A Comparative Study of Reward Design for Reinforcement Unlearning
summary: Machine unlearning seeks to selectively remove specific knowledge from trained language models without full retraining, a growing necessity under privacy regulations such as GDPR and the EU AI Act. Recent work has reformulated unlearning as a Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) problem, where models are optimized against verifiable rewards computed directly from their outputs. However, existing methods rely on sparse binary rewards that provide minimal learning signal, indicating only whether forbidden content was avoided, and limiting convergence speed. In this paper, we study how reward design affects unlearning efficiency within the Reinforcement Unlearning (RUL) framework. We introduce a principled reward decomposition framework that decouples verifiability from sparsity, and propose two new reward functions: an exponential reward that provides graded penalties based on the count of forbidden-concept occurrences, and a PageRank inspired reward that weights penalties by semantic importance. We conduct experiments on the Real World Knowledge Unlearning (RWKU) benchmark, demonstrating that both rewards consistently outperform the binary setting, while reaching similar forgetting performance up to $3\times$ faster and preserving general model utility. Our results show that reward design is a key driver of unlearning efficiency offering a practical path toward scalable and efficient machine unlearning.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that well-designed reward functions in reinforcement learning-based machine unlearning can achieve similar forgetting performance up to 3× faster than binary rewards while preserving model utility.
AI.motivation: Machine unlearning is necessary for privacy compliance (GDPR, EU AI Act), but current RL-based methods use sparse binary rewards that provide minimal learning signal, limiting convergence speed and efficiency.
AI.method: The authors introduce a reward decomposition framework separating verifiability from sparsity, and propose two new reward functions: 1) exponential reward with graded penalties based on forbidden-concept counts, and 2) PageRank-inspired reward weighting penalties by semantic importance.
AI.result: Experiments on the Real World Knowledge Unlearning benchmark show both proposed rewards consistently outperform binary rewards, achieving similar forgetting performance up to 3× faster while preserving general model utility.
AI.conclusion: Reward design is a key driver of unlearning efficiency, offering a practical path toward scalable and efficient machine unlearning systems.

title: Distilling Answer Set Programming Theories from Large Language Models
summary: Writing Answer Set Programming (ASP) theories from scratch is a difficult and time-consuming task. We take a neurosymbolic approach to study whether a model can distill complete and correct theories, given a fixed agent harness with the solver in the loop. The protocol is dataset-agnostic: with a single prompt and an empty file as the starting point the model is given a 1-hour time limit to derive a complete theory. We chose VQA as the application domain, three benchmarks (CLEVR, GQA, CLEVRER), as these are publicly available and non-trivial. In order to study the model scale required for solving this task we nine different models: four frontier (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5, DeepSeek V4 Pro), two mid-tier (DeepSeek V4 Flash, gpt-oss-120b), and three open-weights (qwen3.6-27b, gpt-oss-20b, qwen3.5-9b). Three of four frontier models reach 100% on CLEVR and 92.8%-98.8% on GQA; on CLEVRER, Sonnet, Opus, DeepSeek V4 Pro score 92.7%-95.3%. GPT-5 reaches 98.7% on CLEVR but drops to 41.8% on GQA and to 86.7% on CLEVRER. Adding handwritten reference theories from other datasets moves the other three frontier models by at most +/-3.4 pp but reduces GPT-5's accuracy by 3-19 pp. We release the code, prompts, and theories distilled.

AI.tldr: Large language models can autonomously generate complete Answer Set Programming theories for visual question answering tasks within time constraints, with frontier models achieving near-perfect performance on CLEVR and GQA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Manually writing Answer Set Programming (ASP) theories is difficult and time-consuming, so researchers explore whether AI models can automatically distill complete and correct ASP theories through a neurosymbolic approach.
AI.method: Used a dataset-agnostic protocol with single prompt and empty file starting point, giving models 1-hour time limit to derive complete ASP theories for VQA tasks on three benchmarks (CLEVR, GQA, CLEVRER). Tested nine models across frontier, mid-tier, and open-weight categories.
AI.result: Three of four frontier models (Claude Sonnet, Claude Opus, DeepSeek V4 Pro) achieved 100% on CLEVR and 92.8%-98.8% on GQA; on CLEVRER they scored 92.7%-95.3%. GPT-5 got 98.7% on CLEVR but dropped to 41.8% on GQA and 86.7% on CLEVRER. Adding reference theories hurt GPT-5's performance by 3-19 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Frontier language models can effectively distill complete ASP theories autonomously for non-trivial VQA tasks, though performance varies across models and tasks, with GPT-5 showing unexpected sensitivity to additional reference theories.

title: TAPO: Transition-Aware Policy Optimization for LLM Agents
summary: Recently, Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a crucial paradigm for the post-training of Large Language Model (LLM) agents. However, existing methods predominantly rely on sparse task rewards for policy optimization, failing to fully exploit another class of inherently dense supervisory signals naturally present during online interaction: environmental feedback following action execution. Recent theoretical studies suggest that generalization in multi-step, goal-oriented tasks hinges on predictive knowledge of environmental consequences. Inspired by this, we propose TAPO: Transition-Aware Policy Optimization for LLM Agents, a unified training framework that alternates between policy optimization and transition supervision. Beyond standard RL updates, TAPO repurposes rollout data to apply action-conditioned next-observation prediction supervision on a shared backbone model. This approach enhances the model's sensitivity to environmental transition dynamics and action consequences while concurrently optimizing the policy. It serves as a computationally lightweight, plug-and-play enhancement module for existing agent RL algorithms, requiring no additional expert data, extra sampling costs, or inference-time overhead. We conduct systematic experiments on WebShop and ALFWorld, integrating foundation models of various scales with different policy optimization algorithms. Empirical results demonstrate that TAPO consistently improves task performance over pure policy optimization baselines.

AI.tldr: TAPO: Transition-Aware Policy Optimization enhances LLM agent training by combining standard RL policy optimization with environmental transition supervision through action-conditioned next-observation prediction, improving task performance without additional costs.
AI.motivation: Existing RL methods for LLM agents rely primarily on sparse task rewards and fail to exploit the dense supervisory signals naturally available during online interaction: environmental feedback after action execution. Theoretical studies suggest that generalization in multi-step, goal-oriented tasks depends on predictive knowledge of environmental consequences.
AI.method: TAPO is a unified training framework that alternates between policy optimization and transition supervision. Beyond standard RL updates, it repurposes rollout data to apply action-conditioned next-observation prediction supervision on a shared backbone model. This enhances the model's sensitivity to environmental transition dynamics and action consequences while concurrently optimizing the policy.
AI.result: Systematic experiments on WebShop and ALFWorld with foundation models of various scales and different policy optimization algorithms show that TAPO consistently improves task performance over pure policy optimization baselines.
AI.conclusion: TAPO serves as a computationally lightweight, plug-and-play enhancement module for existing agent RL algorithms that requires no additional expert data, extra sampling costs, or inference-time overhead, making it an effective approach for improving LLM agent training by leveraging environmental transition information.

title: Diversifying Personalized Research Ideation against AI-Induced Homogenization
summary: AI-assisted research ideation has emerged as a promising paradigm for accelerating scientific discovery, with systems now capable of generating research directions conditioned on papers, topics, or lightweight researcher contexts. Yet current systems largely optimize individual suggestions in isolation. This leaves two blind spots. First, coarse researcher representations may elicit mainstream directions that appear broadly feasible, but lack sufficient researcher-specific grounding. Second, independent recommendations can concentrate a community's portfolio around recurring high-probability themes. To address these blind spots, we propose DivAlign, a four-stage pipeline for alignment-preserving de-homogenization. DivAlign extracts fine-grained researcher profiles, generates profile-conditioned candidate directions, scores them along three alignment dimensions (Executability, Comprehensibility, and Growth Potential), and surfaces researcher-local directions while reducing redundancy across the community portfolio. On a benchmark we construct from 95 AI researchers across five subfields, DivAlign reduces community-level redundancy while preserving researcher-direction fit. Compared with coarse single-shot ideation, it lowers average pairwise similarity from 0.331 to 0.294 and nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.704 to 0.608. Compared with the independent top-choice variant, DivAlign reduces nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.663 to 0.608 while retaining 99.9% of the researcher-direction fit score. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Ruixxxx/DivAlign.

AI.tldr: DivAlign is a four-stage pipeline for AI-assisted research ideation that reduces community portfolio redundancy while preserving researcher-direction fit by generating personalized research suggestions through fine-grained researcher profiling and multi-dimensional scoring.
AI.motivation: Current AI-assisted research ideation systems optimize individual suggestions in isolation, leading to two problems: 1) coarse researcher representations produce mainstream directions lacking researcher-specific grounding, and 2) independent recommendations concentrate community portfolios around recurring high-probability themes, creating redundancy.
AI.method: DivAlign uses a four-stage pipeline: 1) extracts fine-grained researcher profiles, 2) generates profile-conditioned candidate research directions, 3) scores them along three alignment dimensions (Executability, Comprehensibility, and Growth Potential), and 4) surfaces researcher-local directions while reducing redundancy across the community portfolio.
AI.result: On a benchmark of 95 AI researchers across five subfields, DivAlign reduces community-level redundancy while preserving researcher-direction fit. Compared to coarse single-shot ideation, it lowers average pairwise similarity from 0.331 to 0.294 and nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.704 to 0.608. Compared to independent top-choice variant, it reduces nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.663 to 0.608 while retaining 99.9% of researcher-direction fit score.
AI.conclusion: DivAlign effectively addresses the blind spots in current AI-assisted research ideation by providing personalized, diverse research directions that reduce community portfolio redundancy while maintaining alignment with individual researcher profiles and interests.

title: Generalization Bounds on Optimal Control for Transformer Training and Wasserstein Distributional Robustness
summary: We derive finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers trained with dynamic programming recursions. Building on the doubly lifted, measure-valued formulation of Transformer dynamics, we view data sets as probability laws on pairs of empirical input-output measures, allowing us to interpret the training problem as a finite-horizon Markovian control problem. We then analyze a quantized model, derived by quantizing the state, action, and measure-state spaces, and derive explicit finite-sample generalization bounds using concentration inequalities for empirical laws on finite metric spaces together with a Lipschitz stability estimate for the value function. These bounds are transferred to the base model at the cost of an explicit approximation error. Finally, we show that the same machinery yields a distributionally robust control formulation of the training problem, connecting Transformer generalization to Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization.

AI.tldr: Finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers trained with dynamic programming, connecting to Markovian control and distributionally robust optimization.
AI.motivation: To provide rigorous finite-sample generalization guarantees for Transformers trained using dynamic programming recursions, which has been lacking in the literature.
AI.method: 1. Formulate Transformer dynamics using doubly lifted, measure-valued formulation; 2. View datasets as probability laws on empirical input-output measures; 3. Interpret training as finite-horizon Markovian control; 4. Analyze quantized model with state, action, and measure-state space quantization; 5. Derive bounds using concentration inequalities for empirical laws on finite metric spaces and Lipschitz stability estimates; 6. Transfer bounds to base model with explicit approximation error; 7. Connect to distributionally robust control using Wasserstein distances.
AI.result: Derived explicit finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers, showing the training problem can be framed as distributionally robust control with Wasserstein metrics, establishing connections between Transformer generalization and distributionally robust optimization.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a novel control-theoretic framework for analyzing Transformer generalization, with explicit finite-sample bounds and connections to distributionally robust optimization, offering a principled approach to understanding Transformer training dynamics.

title: PerturbMap: Cross-Context Transfer of Single-Cell Perturbation Responses
summary: Single-cell perturbation atlases rarely measure every intervention in every cellular context: a query perturbation is often observed in one or more source contexts but missing in the recipient context where its effect is needed. Ignoring those measured responses discards query-specific experimental evidence, whereas copying or weakly calibrating them across contexts risks transferring the wrong signal. We propose PerturbMap, which predicts a missing recipient-context effect by combining a recipient-local low-rank base with accepted proposals that transport the same perturbation's measured source responses through source-to-recipient ridge experts fit on paired training perturbations, with proposal weights determined by route reliability estimated on validation anchors. On the Perturb-CITE-seq melanoma cohort, PerturbMap improves full-effect MSE by 4.1\% over a recipient-local low-rank base and achieves lower MSE than FedAvg, zero-response, raw-copy, calibrated-copy, and identity-shuffled affine controls. It remains within $2.82\times10^{-6}$ MSE of our centralized token-matched pooled reference, which uses a stronger training interface. A condition-mean specificity diagnostic shows the same direction: same-recipient top-10 counterpart retrieval by cosine increases from 74.5\% for the low-rank base to 80.5\% for PerturbMap.

AI.tldr: PerturbMap predicts missing perturbation effects across cellular contexts by combining recipient-local low-rank bases with transported source responses using ridge experts, outperforming baseline methods in accuracy and specificity.
AI.motivation: Single-cell perturbation studies often have missing data where a perturbation is measured in some cellular contexts but not others. Current approaches either discard useful experimental evidence or risk transferring incorrect signals when copying or weakly calibrating responses across contexts.
AI.method: PerturbMap predicts missing recipient-context effects by: 1) using a recipient-local low-rank base, 2) transporting measured source responses through source-to-recipient ridge experts trained on paired perturbations, and 3) weighting proposals based on route reliability estimated on validation anchors.
AI.result: On Perturb-CITE-seq melanoma cohort, PerturbMap improves full-effect MSE by 4.1% over recipient-local low-rank base and outperforms FedAvg, zero-response, raw-copy, calibrated-copy, and identity-shuffled affine controls. It approaches centralized pooled reference performance and improves same-recipient retrieval accuracy from 74.5% to 80.5%.
AI.conclusion: PerturbMap provides an effective framework for predicting missing perturbation effects across cellular contexts by intelligently combining local information with transported experimental evidence, significantly outperforming existing baselines while maintaining specificity.

title: It's All Just Vectorization: einx, a Universal Notation for Tensor Operations
summary:
Tensor operations represent a cornerstone of modern scientific computing. However, the Numpy-like notation adopted by predominant tensor frameworks is often difficult to read and write and prone to so-called shape errors, i.a., due to following inconsistent rules across a large, complex collection of operations. Alternatives like einsum and einops have gained popularity, but are inherently restricted to few operations and lack the generality required for a universal model of tensor programming.
  To derive a better paradigm, we revisit vectorization as a function for transforming tensor operations, and use it to both lift lower-order operations to higher-order operations, and conceptually decompose higher-order operations to lower-order operations and their vectorization.
  Building on the universal nature of vectorization, we introduce einx, a universal notation for tensor operations. It uses declarative, pointful expressions that are defined by analogy with loop notation and represent the vectorization of tensor operations. The notation reduces the large APIs of existing frameworks to a small set of elementary operations, applies consistent rules across all operations, and enables a clean, readable and writable representation in code. We provide an implementation of einx that is embedded in Python and integrates seamlessly with existing tensor frameworks: https://github.com/fferflo/einx

AI.tldr: The paper introduces einx, a universal tensor operation notation based on vectorization, addressing limitations of existing approaches like Numpy, einsum, and einops.
AI.motivation: Existing tensor operation notations (Numpy-like, einsum, einops) suffer from readability issues, shape errors, inconsistent rules, or lack generality for universal tensor programming.
AI.method: The authors revisit vectorization as a transformation function for tensor operations, using it to lift lower-order operations to higher-order operations and decompose higher-order operations to lower-order ones. They introduce einx, a declarative, pointful notation defined by analogy with loop notation that represents vectorization of tensor operations.
AI.result: Einx reduces large tensor framework APIs to a small set of elementary operations, applies consistent rules across all operations, and enables clean, readable, writable code representation. An implementation is provided that integrates with existing Python tensor frameworks.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents einx as a universal notation for tensor operations that addresses limitations of current approaches through vectorization-based declarative expressions.

title: An Instrument to Evaluate Governance Proposals: AI Policy Analysis at Scale
summary:
This paper introduces a policy analysis framework for systematic, transparent assessment of AI governance proposals in an evolving and contested regulatory landscape. AI policy debates often collapse into binary positions that obscure underlying tradeoffs and normative assumptions. The framework structures policy analysis around multiple policy attributes, allowing users to surface priorities and tensions without prescribing outcomes. We use a mixed-methods approach that integrates qualitative insights from subject matter experts with computational text analysis to inform the design of policy attribute rubrics. This quantifies the relative emphasis of different policy objectives and presents them through comparative visualizations that support interpretability and cross-policy comparison. The paper also examines the use of commercial LLMs for rubric-based policy analysis, benchmarking their outputs against a domain-trained rubric-calibrated model with explicitly defined analytical assumptions. Rather than assessing policy effectiveness or desirability, the framework focuses on relevance and alignment across attributes. By making analytical assumptions explicit, including attribute selection, rubric construction, and weighting schemes, the framework enables users to evaluate whether its embedded priorities align with the users' own normative commitments. The approach is jurisdiction-agnostic and intended to support policymakers, analysts, and researchers navigating complex AI governance environments.
  Contributions: (1) multidimensional policy assessment through empirically grounded rubrics that surface tradeoffs rather than resolving them; (2) a transparent hybrid methodology combining feedback from subject-matter experts with computational validation; and (3) use of domain-trained rubric-calibrated models as a benchmark for comparing different general-purpose large language models.

AI.tldr: A framework for systematic AI governance policy analysis using transparent rubrics, computational methods, and comparative visualizations to surface tradeoffs without prescribing outcomes.
AI.motivation: AI policy debates often collapse into binary positions that obscure underlying tradeoffs and normative assumptions, making systematic assessment difficult in an evolving regulatory landscape.
AI.method: Mixed-methods approach integrating qualitative insights from subject matter experts with computational text analysis to design policy attribute rubrics, plus benchmarking commercial LLMs against domain-trained rubric-calibrated models.
AI.result: Develops jurisdiction-agnostic framework that quantifies policy objective emphasis through comparative visualizations, enabling users to surface priorities and tensions while making analytical assumptions explicit for alignment evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides systematic, transparent assessment of AI governance proposals without judging effectiveness, instead focusing on relevance and alignment across attributes to support policymakers navigating complex regulatory environments.

title: Building a User Foundation Model for the Open Web
summary: User foundation models have demonstrated strong results in e-commerce and social recommendation, but most industrial deployments assume environments where user identity is stable and persistent. Open-web real-time bidding (RTB) operates on a structurally different data distribution: user identity is fragmented and non-persistent across browsing sessions, and the availability of browsing history depends on user privacy choices. Consequently, a significant portion of traffic carries no historical data, and available records often consist of relatively short, disjointed sessions. As a result, historical signals in this domain are typically represented as aggregated counters and recency buckets, leaving the sequential structure unexploited. To address this limitation, we present a user foundation model that applies self-supervised learning on user browsing histories and show that the learned representation improves multiple downstream production tasks, demonstrating the viability of this approach on the open web. We pre-train a Transformer encoder with masked language modeling and a sequence-level contrastive objective, then fine-tune it on the click prediction task. We optimize the encoder's pre-training pipeline with an LLM-in-the-loop search over a curated catalog of reviewable, code-level edits (lifters), instantiating the LLM-as-optimizer paradigm in an industrial setting. The same encoder representation yields +1.197% RIG on the production bid win-rate model and +1.354% RIG on the production CTR ranker; a 7-day live A/B test confirms +2.13% CTR, -1.13% eCPC (80% CI excluding zero on both metrics).

AI.tldr: A user foundation model for open-web RTB that uses self-supervised learning on fragmented user browsing histories to improve ad performance metrics despite identity fragmentation and privacy constraints.
AI.motivation: Traditional user foundation models assume stable user identity, but open-web real-time bidding faces identity fragmentation, non-persistent sessions, and privacy limitations that leave historical sequential structure unexploited.
AI.method: Pre-trained Transformer encoder with masked language modeling and sequence-level contrastive objective on user browsing histories, fine-tuned on click prediction, optimized via LLM-in-the-loop search over code-level edits (lifters).
AI.result: +1.197% RIG on production bid win-rate, +1.354% RIG on production CTR ranker; 7-day A/B test shows +2.13% CTR, -1.13% eCPC (both statistically significant).
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised user foundation models can effectively leverage fragmented browsing histories in open-web RTB, demonstrating viability through production task improvements and LLM-driven optimization.

title: SciDataSailor: Deep Scientific Data Exploring
summary: Scientific datasets are commonly organized as hierarchical repositories containing heterogeneous and interdependent files, making their inspection, integration, and analysis labor-intensive and reliant on domain expertise. Although large language model (LLM) agents have advanced substantially in planning, reasoning, and tool use, existing research has largely overlooked their ability to interact with real scientific data assets through executable environments. We introduce Deep Scientific Data Exploration, an agentic task paradigm in which agents navigate repositories, interpret heterogeneous files and schemas, execute analyses, integrate cross-file evidence, and produce conclusions grounded in executed observations. To operationalize this paradigm, we present SciDataSailor, a framework for synthesizing tool-interactive trajectories by balancing broad exploration with targeted exploitation. SciDataSailor instantiates trajectory synthesis as Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with four task-specific mechanisms: difficulty-stratified exploration seeds, dual-feedback first-play urgency, hierarchical strategy-to-tool action generation, and entropy-guided branching. Using this framework, we construct SciDataSailor-SFT-2K for supervised fine-tuning and SciDataSailor-Bench for evaluation, with the latter comprising 627 meta-information summarization tasks and 586 scientific question-answering tasks across 27 datasets spanning the life, earth, and physical sciences.

AI.tldr: SciDataSailor: A framework using LLM agents to autonomously explore and analyze hierarchical scientific datasets through Monte Carlo Tree Search with task-specific mechanisms for trajectory synthesis.
AI.motivation: Scientific datasets are complex hierarchical repositories with heterogeneous, interdependent files that are difficult to inspect, integrate, and analyze, requiring significant domain expertise. Existing LLM agent research has overlooked their ability to interact with real scientific data through executable environments.
AI.method: Proposes Deep Scientific Data Exploration as an agentic task paradigm where agents navigate repositories, interpret files/schemas, execute analyses, and integrate cross-file evidence. Introduces SciDataSailor framework for synthesizing tool-interactive trajectories using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with four key mechanisms: difficulty-stratified exploration seeds, dual-feedback first-play urgency, hierarchical strategy-to-tool action generation, and entropy-guided branching.
AI.result: Created two resources: SciDataSailor-SFT-2K for supervised fine-tuning and SciDataSailor-Bench for evaluation, comprising 627 meta-information summarization tasks and 586 scientific QA tasks across 27 datasets spanning life, earth, and physical sciences.
AI.conclusion: The SciDataSailor framework enables autonomous exploration and analysis of complex scientific datasets through intelligent agent interactions, addressing the gap in LLM research for handling real scientific data environments and providing tools for future research in scientific data exploration.

title: Flux-OPD: On-Policy Distillation with Evolving Contexts
summary: Large language model training in open-ended domains lacks verifiable rewards, making task preferences difficult to formalize as effective supervision. Contexts can convey such preferences, yet provide little additional supervision once distilled into the student, motivating contexts that evolve with student performance. However, directly using evolving contexts as in-training supervision results in an unstable distillation target and conflicting distributions, requiring mechanisms to stabilize target and downweight conflicts. In this paper, we analyze the effect of contexts through a decomposition of the reverse KL objective, revealing two findings: the student is distilled toward the geometric mean of context-conditioned teachers, and the objective contains a conflict term that measures conflicts among these teachers. Based on this decomposition, we propose Flux-OPD, an OPD paradigm that uses evolving contexts as in-training supervision to capture task preferences in open-ended domains. Flux-OPD treats the differences between context-conditioned and context-free teachers as contextual difference signals, injects them as contextual corrections into the context-free teacher anchor, and weights their correction strength using the conflict term as an indicator. Experiments on open-ended tasks show that Flux-OPD outperforms existing OPD paradigms, highlighting the potential to combine teacher supervision with evolving contexts.

AI.tldr: Flux-OPD is a new OPD paradigm that uses evolving contexts as in-training supervision for LLM distillation in open-ended domains, stabilizing the distillation by weighting contextual corrections based on conflict measures.
AI.motivation: Large language model training in open-ended domains lacks verifiable rewards, making task preferences difficult to formalize as effective supervision. While contexts can convey preferences, they provide little additional supervision once distilled, motivating the need for evolving contexts that adapt to student performance.
AI.method: Flux-OPD treats differences between context-conditioned and context-free teachers as contextual difference signals, injects them as contextual corrections into the context-free teacher anchor, and weights their correction strength using a conflict term as an indicator derived from reverse KL decomposition analysis.
AI.result: Experiments on open-ended tasks show that Flux-OPD outperforms existing OPD paradigms, demonstrating effectiveness in combining teacher supervision with evolving contexts.
AI.conclusion: Flux-OPD successfully addresses the challenge of using evolving contexts as in-training supervision for LLM distillation in open-ended domains, highlighting the potential to effectively combine teacher supervision with evolving contexts.

title: MIND: Lightweight and Effective Memory Injection Defense for LLM Agents via Intent-Aware Information Bottleneck
summary: Memory-augmented LLM-based agents are vulnerable to memory injection attacks: Agents may retrieve poisoned memory from attackers, which diverts their behavior from initial user intent and finally causes task failure. However, existing defense mechanisms either incur high computational cost or suffer from information redundancy in multi-turn contexts. To address these challenges, we propose Memory Intent-Aware Neural Denoising(MIND), a lightweight defense framework for memory injection attack. Our preliminary analysis reveals that benign and poisoned trajectories exhibit distinguishable relationships between the initial user intent and subsequent behavior. Building on this observation, MIND employs an intent-aware Information Bottleneck(IB) to extract compact intent--behavior representations from the initial intent and turn-level behavior. The IB preserves intent-relevant cross-turn attack signals while filtering task-irrelevant and repetitive information, and a lightweight detector identifies malicious memories from the resulting representations. As such, MIND mitigates information redundancy in multi-turn contexts while avoiding the overhead of repeated LLM auditing. Extensive experiments show that MIND reduces attack success rates while preserving task accuracy and inference efficiency. Notably, on ReAct-StrategyQA, MIND reduces mean ASR-r and ASR-a by 55.4% and 55.3%, respectively, while matching the undefended agent in average accuracy and latency.

AI.tldr: MIND is a lightweight defense framework against memory injection attacks on memory-augmented LLM agents that uses intent-aware Information Bottleneck to filter poisoned memories while preserving task performance and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Memory-augmented LLM-based agents are vulnerable to memory injection attacks where poisoned memory diverts agent behavior from user intent, but existing defenses have high computational costs or suffer from information redundancy in multi-turn contexts.
AI.method: Proposes Memory Intent-Aware Neural Denoising (MIND) framework: 1) Initial analysis shows distinguishable relationships between user intent and behavior in benign vs. poisoned trajectories, 2) Uses intent-aware Information Bottleneck to extract compact intent-behavior representations, 3) Lightweight detector identifies malicious memories from these filtered representations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show MIND reduces attack success rates while preserving task accuracy and inference efficiency. On ReAct-StrategyQA, reduces mean ASR-r and ASR-a by 55.4% and 55.3% respectively while matching undefended agent's average accuracy and latency.
AI.conclusion: MIND provides an effective, lightweight defense against memory injection attacks by filtering out poisoned memories using intent-aware representations, addressing both security concerns and computational efficiency for practical deployment of memory-augmented LLM agents.

title: Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization via Privileged Self-Distillation
summary: Recent advances in post-training Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) or On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD). While OPSD provides dense, logit-level supervision, it inherently suffers from exposure bias due to the privileged information of the self-teacher. In multi-turn agentic settings, this leads to reasoning route convergence and the loss of clear optimization directions. To tackle these challenges, we introduce Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization (CRPO), which reformulates agentic OPSD from a contrastive learning perspective. By leveraging predictive entropy to distinguish between positive positions (reflective exploration) and negative positions (exposure bias), CRPO conducts group-wise contrast to preserve reliable, fine-grained optimization signals. Extensive evaluations across 13 challenging reasoning and deep-search benchmarks demonstrate that CRPO consistently outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines, significantly enhancing training stability and generalization in long-horizon interactions.

AI.tldr: CRPO reformulates agentic On-Policy Self-Distillation as contrastive learning to address exposure bias and reasoning route convergence in multi-turn agent settings.
AI.motivation: On-Policy Self-Distillation suffers from exposure bias due to privileged teacher information, leading to reasoning route convergence and loss of clear optimization directions in multi-turn agentic settings.
AI.method: Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization reformulates agentic OPSD from a contrastive learning perspective, using predictive entropy to distinguish positive positions (reflective exploration) from negative positions (exposure bias) and conducting group-wise contrast to preserve fine-grained optimization signals.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations across 13 challenging reasoning and deep-search benchmarks demonstrate CRPO consistently outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines, with significant improvements in training stability and generalization in long-horizon interactions.
AI.conclusion: CRPO effectively addresses the limitations of existing OPSD approaches by introducing a contrastive learning framework that maintains optimization signals and improves performance in complex multi-turn agentic reasoning tasks.

title: Beyond Rephrasing: Book-Level Organization Improves Synthetic Textbook Data for Mid-Training
summary: Synthetic textbook data has improved language model pre-training, but prior work largely treats the benefit as a property of generated content or local rewriting style. We study a different factor: whether related content is organized into coherent book-level documents. We contribute both a scalable synthesis pipeline and controlled evidence that this organization matters. The pipeline retrieves source material from a pre-training corpus, clusters it into topical units, plans hierarchical tables of contents, and assembles source-grounded sections into complete books (our Full setting), yielding 686K textbooks (32B tokens) across 15,000+ disciplines. Replacing natural books in a mid-training mix with this corpus improves downstream performance by +1.09 on average. Controlled comparisons then disentangle the relevant design factors. A content-matched Split condition holds generated text and tokens fixed but treats each section as an independent document; Full's +1.02 mean gain isolates document packaging. A length-matched RandomConcat control that joins sections from different books remains below Full, ruling out document length alone. A retrieval-pool-matched Rephrase condition independently rewrites individual retrieved documents under the same audience-by-style scheme, without clustering, TOC planning, or book assembly; Full's +1.17 gain demonstrates the value of structured synthesis. On Llama3-8B, Full likewise outperforms both RandomConcat and Natural Books, supporting book-level organization as a useful axis for synthetic pre-training data design.

AI.tldr: Synthetic textbooks organized as coherent book-level documents outperform independent content chunks, with +1.09 average improvement in downstream performance, demonstrating the importance of document-level organization in synthetic pre-training data design.
AI.motivation: Prior work on synthetic textbook data has focused on generated content or local rewriting style, but hasn't systematically examined whether organizing related content into coherent book-level documents provides additional benefits for language model pre-training.
AI.method: Developed a scalable synthesis pipeline that: 1) retrieves source material from pre-training corpus, 2) clusters into topical units, 3) plans hierarchical tables of contents, 4) assembles source-grounded sections into complete books. Created controlled comparisons: Full (complete books), Split (same content as independent sections), RandomConcat (mixed sections from different books), and Rephrase (independently rewritten documents).
AI.result: Full synthetic books outperformed natural books by +1.09 on average. Controlled experiments showed: Full vs Split (document packaging alone) gives +1.02 gain; Full beats RandomConcat (ruling out length effects); Full vs Rephrase shows +1.17 gain from structured synthesis. On Llama3-8B, Full also outperforms both RandomConcat and Natural Books.
AI.conclusion: Book-level organization of synthetic pre-training data matters significantly. The structured synthesis approach with clustering, TOC planning, and coherent assembly provides meaningful improvements over treating content as independent documents or simple rewriting, establishing document packaging as a useful axis for synthetic data design.

title: Enhancing Irregular Time Series Forecasting with Continuous-Time Modeling Framework
summary: Irregular multivariate time series are widely encountered in applications such as healthcare monitoring, human activity recognition, and environmental sensing. Their core challenges stem from asynchronous observations, non-uniform sampling intervals, and the fact that temporal patterns themselves carry critical dynamic information. Existing approaches either rely on discretization-based preprocessing (e.g., interpolation, imputation, or aggregation), which disrupts the underlying continuous-time semantics, or adopt continuous-time modeling via ODE-based frameworks, which typically require specialized architectures and incur substantial computational overhead due to numerical solvers. To address these limitations, we propose WrapFlow, a continuous-time modeling framework for irregular time series forecasting. On the input side, WrapFlow introduces Continuous-Time Tokenization, which directly encodes raw observation events and explicitly models long unobserved intervals via gap-aware tokens. The resulting continuous-time tokens are then processed by a standard Transformer backbone to capture long-range temporal dependencies. On the output side, we develop a simulation-free training paradigm for Residual Flow Matching, which learns conditional residual vector fields around base predictions while avoiding numerical-solver simulation and backpropagation during training. This design enables high-quality continuous forecasting using only a small number of fixed rollout steps at inference. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that WrapFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: WrapFlow is a continuous-time modeling framework for irregular time series forecasting that uses continuous-time tokenization with gap-aware tokens and simulation-free flow matching training, achieving state-of-the-art performance without numerical solvers.
AI.motivation: Irregular multivariate time series with asynchronous observations and non-uniform sampling intervals are common in healthcare, activity recognition, and sensing applications. Existing methods either disrupt continuous-time semantics through discretization or require computationally expensive ODE-based numerical solvers.
AI.method: 1) Continuous-Time Tokenization: Encodes raw observation events with gap-aware tokens to handle long unobserved intervals. 2) Standard Transformer backbone for capturing long-range dependencies. 3) Simulation-free training of Residual Flow Matching to learn conditional residual vector fields without numerical solver simulation during training.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. The framework enables high-quality continuous forecasting using only a small number of fixed rollout steps at inference.
AI.conclusion: WrapFlow effectively addresses limitations of existing irregular time series forecasting methods by combining continuous-time tokenization with simulation-free flow matching, providing an efficient and accurate framework that preserves continuous-time semantics while avoiding computational overhead of numerical solvers.

title: BlueprintRepair: Typed Local Edits for Failed Lean Proof Blueprints
summary: LLM-based Lean proving systems increasingly organize a proof as a blueprint: a dependency graph of formal statements. We introduce BlueprintRepair, a repair interface that lets a model change this graph through ten schema-checked local operations. An operation names the node it edits, so the target theorem cannot be changed. Lean checks every applied change, and an accepted repair must declare every blueprint lemma its proof uses. We also construct BlueprintTrace, a benchmark of 142 controlled failures with complete accepted and rejected repair trajectories. We compare typed edits, exact source patches, and complete module rewrites under matched source, feedback, model, and budget, one episode per state and interface. With DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the three interfaces solve almost the same number of the benchmark's localized failures. Typed repair is the cheapest per solved state (patching is 1.30x as expensive, rewriting 2.06x), and within 10,000 completion tokens per task it reaches almost all of its final coverage, while both free-form interfaces are well behind. A second model, Qwen3.6-Flash, solves fewer states but keeps typed repair cheapest, puts it ahead on the proof-authoring states, and repeats the localized pattern.

AI.tldr: BlueprintRepair introduces a repair interface for LLM-based Lean proving systems that allows controlled editing of proof blueprints through schema-checked local operations, with typed edits proving most efficient compared to free-form patching or rewriting.
AI.motivation: LLM-based Lean proving systems organize proofs as blueprints (dependency graphs of formal statements), but need better repair mechanisms that maintain the target theorem while allowing controlled changes to the proof structure.
AI.method: BlueprintRepair provides ten schema-checked local operations for editing proof blueprints, ensuring target theorems remain unchanged. Created BlueprintTrace benchmark with 142 controlled failures and repair trajectories. Compared typed edits, exact source patches, and complete module rewrites under matched conditions using DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3.6-Flash models.
AI.result: Typed repairs were cheapest per solved state (patching was 1.30x as expensive, rewriting 2.06x). Typed repair reached almost full coverage within 10,000 tokens while free-form interfaces lagged behind. Both models showed similar efficiency patterns with typed repairs being most cost-effective.
AI.conclusion: Typed blueprint repair is a more efficient approach for proof repair in LLM-based Lean proving systems compared to free-form editing methods, offering better cost efficiency and faster coverage while maintaining control over proof structure.

title: Learning features from Newton's algorithm: a way to accelerate nonlinear parametrized PDE solvers
summary: It is well known that Newton's method converges faster when the initial guess is closer to a root of a system of nonlinear equations. In this paper, a two-stage Newton initial guess strategy is proposed by learning features from a parameter-space sampling and a database of precomputed solutions. The method uses discrete Newton trajectories to construct two complementary reduced spaces: a solution feature space, built from converged states, and a corrective search direction feature space, built from intermediate Newton increments. For an unseen parameter, a regression model is used to predict a surrogate solution approximation. Then, in a second step, a residual-minimizing correction is computed using a dedicated GMRES-based approach. The resulting state is then used as an initial guess for the high-fidelity Newton method, which completes convergence. The corrective step is computationally inexpensive since it only requires residual evaluations and the solution of a small least-squares problem. The methodology is weakly intrusive once the high-fidelity residual fields and a script-based programming interface are available. This strategy reduces the number of Newton iterations and decreases the overall CPU time. Numerical experiments on representative PDE problems show quantifiable speedups compared with standalone surrogate initialization. Significant speedups are observed. This generic approach can be applied to a broad class of large-scale nonlinear problems.

AI.tldr: A two-stage Newton initial guess strategy that learns from parameter-space sampling and precomputed solutions to predict better initial guesses, reducing Newton iterations and CPU time for nonlinear PDE problems.
AI.motivation: Newton's method converges faster with better initial guesses closer to roots, but finding good initial guesses for large-scale nonlinear systems is challenging, especially for unseen parameters in parameterized problems.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: 1) Learn from discrete Newton trajectories to build reduced spaces (solution feature space from converged states and corrective search direction feature space from intermediate Newton increments). For unseen parameters, use regression to predict surrogate solution. 2) Apply residual-minimizing correction using GMRES-based approach. Use resulting state as initial guess for high-fidelity Newton method.
AI.result: Reduces number of Newton iterations and overall CPU time. Numerical experiments on representative PDE problems show quantifiable speedups compared to standalone surrogate initialization. The corrective step is computationally inexpensive (only residual evaluations and small least-squares problems).
AI.conclusion: The generic approach can be applied to a broad class of large-scale nonlinear problems. The methodology is weakly intrusive and only requires high-fidelity residual fields and script-based programming interface.

title: ConMem: Contribution-Aware Memory for Long-Horizon Manufacturing Inspection Logs
summary: Long-horizon steel-equipment inspection requires reasoning over heterogeneous records accumulated across repeated inspection cycles. Existing retrieval-augmented generation systems treat historical logs as a static corpus and retain records without estimating their diagnostic value, failing to report early risk. To this end, we propose ConMem, a contribution-aware memory framework for LLM-assisted equipment inspection, supporting a human-in-the-loop early-risk screening system. Specifically, our ConMem first segments inspection logs into functional evidence units, then estimates each memory unit's contribution to downstream diagnosis through a Shapley-style estimation, and finally retains high-value evidence under a constrained memory budget. In experiments, we evaluate ConMem on real-world dataset and ConMem achieves 76.0% QA accuracy, exceeding the strongest directly comparable baseline. Relative to the naive 8K-context LLM baselines, it reduces the average number of input tokens by 88.2% and response time by 86.6%. Ablation studies also show that the functional-role-aware segmentation and contribution-based valuation are helping prioritize weak degradation signals for targeted field inspection. Practical deployments further confirm that ConMem retains the weak early signal across three inspection cycles, providing an early-stage seal-wear alert targeted for on-site inspectors.

AI.tldr: ConMem is a contribution-aware memory framework for LLM-assisted equipment inspection that intelligently selects and retains high-value historical evidence from inspection logs to enable early risk detection.
AI.motivation: Current retrieval-augmented generation systems for steel equipment inspection treat historical logs as static corpora without assessing diagnostic value, leading to failure in detecting early risk signals.
AI.method: ConMem segments inspection logs into functional evidence units, estimates each unit's contribution to diagnosis using Shapley-style estimation, and selectively retains high-value evidence under memory constraints.
AI.result: ConMem achieves 76.0% QA accuracy on real-world data, surpassing baselines while reducing input tokens by 88.2% and response time by 86.6% compared to naive 8K-context LLMs.
AI.conclusion: The framework effectively prioritizes weak degradation signals for targeted inspection and has been practically deployed to retain early warning signals across multiple inspection cycles, providing actionable alerts for field inspectors.

title: ClawTrack: Towards Trace-Level Evaluation and Improvement of Real-World Autonomous Agents
summary:
As LLM-based agents are deployed in complex, multi-step workflows, a critical evaluation gap has emerged: most existing benchmarks judge only final outcomes, unable to distinguish reliable reasoning from lucky success or attribute failures to specific process deficiencies, hindering attribution in long-horizon tasks.
  In this work, we present ClawTrack, a dual-assessment benchmark that simultaneously measures what an agent achieves (Task Score) and how it achieves it (Process Score). ClawTrack comprises 320 tasks across 8 domains with 25+ deterministic mock services. A Process Grader scores each reasoning turn along four dimensions (goal alignment, efficiency, information utilization, and result verification), anchored by 12,541 task-specific rubric items. Evaluating 21 models over 16,000+ trials, we find that: (1) process scores effectively attribute success and failure to specific reasoning dimensions, filtering lucky passes invisible to outcome-only evaluation; (2) the four dimensions are complementary, with result verification as the systematic bottleneck; (3) the framework is robust to evaluator choice across different judge LLMs; and (4) process-based trajectory filtering yields consistent post-training improvements across model scales.

AI.tldr: ClawTrack is a dual-assessment benchmark for LLM agents that evaluates both what they achieve (Task Score) and how they achieve it (Process Score) across 320 multi-step tasks with detailed process grading.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks only judge final outcomes, making it impossible to distinguish reliable reasoning from lucky success or attribute failures to specific process deficiencies in complex, multi-step workflows of LLM-based agents.
AI.method: ClawTrack includes 320 tasks across 8 domains with 25+ deterministic mock services, using a Process Grader that scores each reasoning turn along four dimensions (goal alignment, efficiency, information utilization, result verification) anchored by 12,541 task-specific rubric items.
AI.result: Evaluation of 21 models over 16,000+ trials showed: 1) process scores effectively attribute success/failure to specific reasoning dimensions, 2) the four dimensions are complementary with result verification as the systematic bottleneck, 3) framework is robust to different judge LLMs, and 4) process-based trajectory filtering yields consistent post-training improvements.
AI.conclusion: ClawTrack provides a comprehensive evaluation framework that addresses the critical gap in assessing LLM agents' reasoning processes, enabling better attribution of performance to specific reasoning capabilities and supporting more targeted improvements.

title: AgenticASR: Refining Speech Recognition in Real-World Scenarios via an Agentic Approach
summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) has achieved substantial gains in transcription accuracy, yet verbatim transcription does not necessarily produce readily usable text. It retains fillers, repetitions, false starts, and self-corrections that increase reading effort, obscure the speaker's final intent, and propagate unresolved or abandoned content to downstream tasks. Existing spoken-to-written methods process completed audio or transcripts but cannot revise emitted text when later speech changes how preceding content should be interpreted. We therefore formulate Agentic Speech Recognition (AgenticSR), an audio-to-clean-text task that removes disfluencies, resolves self-corrections, and normalizes written form while preserving the speaker's final intent. AgenticASR implements this task through an ASR--Refiner architecture that repeatedly transforms a bounded active context and replaces its corresponding output span as audio arrives. This enables continual emission and revision over streams of arbitrary duration. We also introduce AASR-Bench, a bilingual benchmark with fine-grained atomic rubrics. Across multiple ASR front ends, AgenticASR attains the highest AASR-Bench scores among evaluated systems. A human--AI agreement study shows that rubric-based judgments align with independent expert assessments. Ablations characterize Refiner capacity, context length, and the quality--latency trade-off between online and offline inference. Together, these results establish AgenticASR as a practical framework for intent-preserving clean transcription during ongoing speech. Code, AASR-Bench, and a demo will be released at https://github.com/AnXMuy/AgenticASR.

AI.tldr: AgenticASR is a framework for real-time speech recognition that continuously revises transcriptions as new speech arrives, removing disfluencies and preserving final speaker intent.
AI.motivation: Traditional ASR produces verbatim transcripts with fillers, repetitions, and self-corrections that obscure speaker intent and propagate errors to downstream tasks. Existing methods can't revise emitted text when later speech changes interpretation of preceding content.
AI.method: AgenticASR uses an ASR-Refiner architecture that repeatedly transforms a bounded active context and replaces corresponding output spans as audio arrives. This enables continual emission and revision over streams of arbitrary duration.
AI.result: AgenticASR achieves the highest scores on AASR-Bench (a new bilingual benchmark) across multiple ASR front ends. Human-AI agreement studies show rubric-based judgments align with expert assessments. The system demonstrates practical quality-latency trade-offs for online inference.
AI.conclusion: AgenticASR establishes a practical framework for intent-preserving clean transcription during ongoing speech, addressing limitations of verbatim transcription and enabling real-time revision of emitted text.

title: GVR-Coder: A Visual-Feedback Framework for Structured SVG Generation in Complex Document and Meeting Scenarios
summary: In demanding professional environments and meeting review scenarios, lengthy text often imposes a high cognitive load. To facilitate efficient information communication, transforming verbose text into logically clear diagrams is essential. Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) provide an effective representation for this purpose due to their editability and resolution independence. However, current research on Text-to-SVG generation remains hindered by three major challenges: (1) the scarcity of datasets for complex, logic-rich diagrams; (2) the absence of explicit layout priors, which leads to chaotic spatial arrangements; and (3) the lack of fine-grained visual feedback to validate rendered outputs and correct aesthetic defects. To address these challenges, at the data level, we introduce DocMeetSVG-100K, a large-scale SVG dataset tailored for document authoring and meeting review scenarios. At the model level, we propose GVR-Coder, a novel framework designed to generate high-quality logical diagrams from lengthy professional texts. Specifically, we adopt a curriculum-driven rejection sampling fine-tuning to progressively enhance the model's capability in modeling complex structures, while explicitly incorporating layout constraint knowledge during training. In addition, we introduce reinforcement learning from dual rendering feedback, a mechanism that provides implicit feedback through reward signals to jointly optimize structural complexity and visual aesthetics. Furthermore, we design a generate-verify-repair agent loop, which improves generation quality through explicit, fine-grained feedback and targeted refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GVR-Coder outperforms competitive baselines and reliably produces logically coherent and visually appealing diagrams. Code and data are available at https://github.com/CurryaNa/GVR-Coder.

AI.tldr: GVR-Coder is a novel framework that generates high-quality logical diagrams from lengthy professional texts by combining curriculum learning, layout constraints, reinforcement learning from dual rendering feedback, and a generate-verify-repair agent loop, supported by a new 100K SVG dataset.
AI.motivation: In professional and meeting review scenarios, lengthy text imposes high cognitive load. Transforming verbose text into logically clear diagrams is essential for efficient communication. However, Text-to-SVG generation faces three major challenges: scarcity of datasets for complex diagrams, absence of explicit layout priors leading to chaotic arrangements, and lack of fine-grained visual feedback for validation and correction.
AI.method: The approach includes: 1) DocMeetSVG-100K dataset for document authoring and meeting review scenarios; 2) GVR-Coder framework with curriculum-driven rejection sampling fine-tuning to enhance complex structure modeling; 3) Explicit layout constraint incorporation during training; 4) Reinforcement learning from dual rendering feedback to optimize structural complexity and visual aesthetics; 5) Generate-verify-repair agent loop for explicit feedback and targeted refinement.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that GVR-Coder outperforms competitive baselines and reliably produces logically coherent and visually appealing diagrams. The code and dataset are publicly available.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach successfully addresses the key challenges in Text-to-SVG generation through a comprehensive solution combining dataset creation, progressive learning techniques, layout constraints, and feedback mechanisms, enabling efficient transformation of professional text into high-quality logical diagrams.

title: Old Tricks, New Models: How Simple Image Transformations Break Modern AI-based Content Moderation
summary: While automated content-moderation systems have become essential for screening harmful content at scale, conventional task-specific classifiers often provide limited policy cov- erage and contextual understanding. Recently, commercial multimodal moderation APIs built on large foundation models have been introduced with the promise of providing broader and more capable safety filters. In this work, we analyze whether this shift also yields more robust image moderation. We conduct a large-scale black-box evaluation on three established commercial image-moderation services and compare their robustness. By evaluating seven simple, model-agnostic image transformations across multiple providers, datasets, harm categories, perceptual-similarity constraints, and transformation intensities, we find that: (1) all three commercial services can be bypassed using inexpensive image transformations that require no gradients, surrogate models, or knowledge of the target system; (2) even fixed transformations such as color inversion and grayscale conversion induce unsafe-to-safe decision changes while preserving content that remains recognizable to humans; (3) their robustness varies substantially across datasets and harm categories, with multimodal content and self-harm exhibiting pronounced vulnerabilities. This yields the conclusion that replacing conventional moderation classifiers with foundation-model-based APIs does not, by itself, provide a reliable security boundary. Such systems must be evaluated under realistic transformations and deployed as one component of a layered moderation pipeline rather than as standalone safety filters.
