AI.tldr: Commercial multimodal moderation APIs based on foundation models are vulnerable to simple image transformations, compromising their reliability as standalone safety filters.
AI.motivation: To evaluate whether the shift from conventional task-specific moderation classifiers to commercial multimodal APIs built on large foundation models actually yields more robust image moderation systems.
AI.method: Conducted large-scale black-box evaluation of three commercial image-moderation services using seven simple, model-agnostic image transformations across multiple providers, datasets, harm categories, perceptual-similarity constraints, and transformation intensities.
AI.result: 1) All three commercial services can be bypassed using inexpensive image transformations requiring no gradients, surrogate models, or system knowledge; 2) Fixed transformations like color inversion and grayscale conversion induce unsafe-to-safe decision changes while preserving human-recognizable content; 3) Robustness varies substantially across datasets and harm categories, with multimodal content and self-harm showing pronounced vulnerabilities.
AI.conclusion: Replacing conventional moderation classifiers with foundation-model-based APIs does not provide a reliable security boundary by itself. Such systems must be evaluated under realistic transformations and deployed as one component of a layered moderation pipeline rather than as standalone safety filters.

title: Chem World: A Large-Scale Benchmark and Physics-Informed Framework for Trustworthy Chemical Property Prediction
summary: Chemical property prediction plays a critical role in accelerating scientific discovery in chemistry, materials science, and drug development. However, existing benchmarks often suffer from limited task diversity, fragmented datasets, and inconsistent evaluation protocols, making it challenging to systematically assess the reliability and generalization of AI models. In this work, we introduce Chem World, a comprehensive benchmark for chemical property prediction that integrates 17 diverse chemical datasets with over 800,000 molecular samples, covering various properties including density, electrical conductivity, solubility, and other molecular characteristics. Chem World provides a unified platform for evaluating AI models across multiple property prediction tasks. Furthermore, we propose Mixture-PINN, a physics-informed neural network based prediction framework that incorporates chemical prior knowledge into data-driven learning, improving the accuracy, robustness, and reliability of chemical property prediction. Extensive experiments on Chem World demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach compared with existing methods. By combining large-scale standardized evaluation with physics-informed learning, Chem World establishes a foundation for developing trustworthy AI systems for computational chemistry and advancing AI-driven scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: Chem World is a comprehensive chemical property prediction benchmark with 17 diverse datasets (800K+ samples) plus Mixture-PINN, a physics-informed neural network that incorporates chemical prior knowledge to improve prediction accuracy and reliability.
AI.motivation: Existing chemical property prediction benchmarks have limitations: limited task diversity, fragmented datasets, and inconsistent evaluation protocols, making it difficult to systematically assess AI model reliability and generalization in computational chemistry.
AI.method: 1) Introduced Chem World benchmark with 17 chemical datasets covering 800,000+ molecular samples and diverse properties. 2) Proposed Mixture-PINN, a physics-informed neural network framework that incorporates chemical prior knowledge into data-driven learning to improve prediction performance.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on Chem World demonstrate that the proposed Mixture-PINN approach outperforms existing methods, showing improved accuracy, robustness, and reliability for chemical property prediction tasks.
AI.conclusion: Chem World provides a standardized, large-scale evaluation platform that, combined with physics-informed learning approaches like Mixture-PINN, establishes a foundation for developing trustworthy AI systems for computational chemistry and advancing AI-driven scientific discovery.

title: Qwen-UI-Agent Technical Report: Toward Next-Generation Real-World Centric Foundation GUI Agents
summary:
GUI agents have the potential to become a general purpose executor over existing digital devices. To advance them toward real-world use, we envision agents that operate reliably on real devices, execute workflows across platforms, combine GUI interaction with CLI execution, complete long-horizon tasks, proactively initiate useful services, and autonomously improve their capabilities with minimal human effort. Guided by this vision, we present Qwen-UI-Agent, a real-world centric foundation GUI agent spanning mobile, computer-use, web, and DeepSearch environments. Qwen-UI-Agent combines diverse sandbox environments with a large-scale real-device mobile runtime. Its unified action space interleaves GUI operations with CLI execution and generates batched actions in a single model turn. An AutoResearch-style data flywheel uses agents to construct tasks and environments, diagnose failures, and plan subsequent iterations. Online RL supports training on trajectories exceeding 100 turns, with over 10,000 concurrent environments accelerating rollout. A lightweight harness layer supports proactive service initiation and stateful workflows across mobile and computer.
  Across a broad suite of evaluations, Qwen-UI-Agent sets state-of-the-art performance on mobile-use benchmarks while delivering competitive performance on computer- and browser-use tasks against frontier models, including Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.6 Sol. On mobile use, it achieves 82.1% on MobileWorld, 92.2% on MobileWorld-Real, and 97.5% on AndroidDaily. On computer use, it achieves 79.5% on OSWorld-Verified and a 40.0% partial-progress score on OSWorld-v2. On browser use and GUI grounding, it achieves 73.6% on WebArena and 81.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro, respectively.

AI.tldr: Qwen-UI-Agent is a real-world GUI agent framework that operates across mobile, computer, web, and DeepSearch environments with unified GUI/CLI actions, online RL training, and autonomous capability improvement.
AI.motivation: To advance GUI agents toward real-world use by creating agents that can reliably operate on real devices, execute workflows across platforms, combine GUI with CLI execution, complete long-horizon tasks, initiate services proactively, and autonomously improve capabilities with minimal human effort.
AI.method: Combines diverse sandbox environments with large-scale real-device mobile runtime; uses unified action space interleaving GUI operations with CLI execution; employs AutoResearch-style data flywheel for task construction, failure diagnosis, and iterative planning; implements online RL with training on 100+ turn trajectories using 10,000+ concurrent environments; includes lightweight harness layer for proactive service initiation and stateful workflows.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on mobile-use benchmarks: 82.1% on MobileWorld, 92.2% on MobileWorld-Real, 97.5% on AndroidDaily. Competitive performance on computer-use: 79.5% on OSWorld-Verified, 40.0% partial-progress on OSWorld-v2. Browser use and GUI grounding: 73.6% on WebArena, 81.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro.
AI.conclusion: Qwen-UI-Agent presents a comprehensive real-world GUI agent framework that demonstrates strong performance across multiple platforms, outperforming frontier models like Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.6 Sol on mobile tasks while being competitive on computer and browser tasks.

title: From Expert Reduction to Behavioral Divergence: Tracing Numerical State through Sparse MoE Inference
summary: Mathematically equivalent expert-reduction orders can produce observably different sparse-MoE executions. We isolate this effect in native DeepSeek-V4-Flash by freezing local MoE state and varying only aggregation semantics. Four schemes separate operand representation from accumulator precision. At one layer-5 fork, 720 A-mode orders yield 10 continuation basins; 720 B-mode orders form 360 exact structural classes and 11 basins. Under one Chinese prompt, the B classes split into 202 layoffs, 113 hiring, and 45 other continuations. Maximum-L-infinity B-branch selection separates 12, 24, and 36 of 50 prompts by 8, 16, and 32 tokens. Across 192 persistent trajectories per scheme, P32, A, and B change every native-reference route trajectory, while C preserves routes, token sequences, and texts. A separate 192-trajectory C check matches native MoE, post-mHC, next-router, and LM states bitwise. For one controlled B branch, exact post-mHC endpoint reconstruction reproduces the measured downstream trajectory. At the next decode boundary, exact FP64 reconstruction of the branch's full persistent state yields agreement for 301 downstream post-mHC states, 301 persistent-state checkpoints, 301 routes, predictions, and text over seven steps, given the same naturally generated next input. These controls identify post-mHC as an intra-token boundary and full persistent state as a cross-token continuation boundary. Identical tokens need not imply identical autoregressive state: divergence can survive a token boundary and become visible later. These results make expert operand conversion, accumulator precision, and reduction order part of a numerical compatibility contract for sparse-MoE runtimes and hardware backends. They establish controlled causal possibility, not deployment incidence; C's order invariance is limited to evaluated six-term states and schedules.

AI.tldr: Different expert reduction orders in sparse MoE architectures can cause observable execution differences even when mathematically equivalent, revealing numerical compatibility requirements for MoE runtimes.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to investigate why mathematically equivalent expert-reduction orders can produce different sparse-MoE execution behaviors in systems like DeepSeek-V4-Flash, particularly focusing on how numerical precision and aggregation semantics affect model behavior.
AI.method: The researchers isolated the effect by freezing local MoE state and varying only aggregation semantics. They used four schemes that separate operand representation from accumulator precision. They analyzed different reduction orders (720 A-mode and 720 B-mode orders), examined their structural classes and continuation basins, and conducted controlled experiments with 192 persistent trajectories per scheme.
AI.result: Different reduction schemes produced different behaviors: P32, A, and B schemes changed every native-reference route trajectory, while C preserved routes, token sequences, and texts. B-mode orders formed 360 exact structural classes and 11 basins, with different prompts separating by 8-32 tokens. The study demonstrated that identical tokens don't necessarily imply identical autoregressive state, and divergence can survive token boundaries.
AI.conclusion: Expert operand conversion, accumulator precision, and reduction order are part of a numerical compatibility contract for sparse-MoE runtimes and hardware backends. The results establish causal possibilities but not deployment incidence, with C's order invariance limited to evaluated six-term states and schedules.

title: CDAE: Enhancing Perturbation Robustness in Pretrained Language Models with Contrastive Denoising
comment: Submitted to 16th International Conference on Computer and Knowledge Engineering (ICCKE 2026)
summary: Pre-trained language models have significantly improved sentence representation learning, yet their embedding remain sensitive to semantic preserving textual perturbations such as synonym substitution, masking and word dropout. This work proposes a lightweight Contrastive Denoising Autoencoder (CDAE) that refines pre-trained BERT embedding by jointly optimizing contrastive and reconstruction objective to learn perturbation-invariant representation. We evaluate the proposed framework using multiple perturbation strategies with varying strengths and compare it against the original BERT embeddings and SimCSE. Experimental results show that CDAE consistently preserves higher embedding similarity under perturbations, with the improvements becoming more pronounced as framework effectively enhances representation stability while preserving semantic information, highlighting perturbation-invariant learning as a promising direction for improving sentence embeddings. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ComputationIASBS/CDAE

AI.tldr: CDAE is a lightweight Contrastive Denoising Autoencoder that refines BERT embeddings to be more robust against semantic-preserving text perturbations like synonym substitution, masking, and word dropout.
AI.motivation: Pre-trained language models like BERT have significantly improved sentence representation learning, but their embeddings remain sensitive to semantic-preserving textual perturbations such as synonym substitution, masking, and word dropout. This sensitivity limits their robustness in real-world applications where text variations occur.
AI.method: The paper proposes a lightweight Contrastive Denoising Autoencoder (CDAE) that refines pre-trained BERT embeddings by jointly optimizing contrastive and reconstruction objectives. This approach learns perturbation-invariant representations by training the model to handle various text perturbations while preserving semantic meaning.
AI.result: Experimental results show that CDAE consistently preserves higher embedding similarity under perturbations compared to original BERT embeddings and SimCSE. The improvements become more pronounced as perturbation strength increases, demonstrating that CDAE effectively enhances representation stability while preserving semantic information.
AI.conclusion: The CDAE framework effectively enhances representation stability against text perturbations while maintaining semantic fidelity. This highlights perturbation-invariant learning as a promising direction for improving sentence embeddings, with the source code being publicly available for further research and application.

title: Information Bottleneck Learning for Faithful Time Series Forecasting Explanations
summary: As forecasts increasingly drive decisions in fields such as energy, transportation, and healthcare, understanding the historical data behind these predictions has become as crucial as the predictions themselves. Although existing interpretable-by-design forecasters reveal their internal structures, they offer no guarantee that these structures faithfully reflect the underlying evidence driving the predictions. In contrast, while faithfulness-oriented methods explicitly verify model behavior, they are almost exclusively designed for post-hoc classification tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose IB-Forecast, an inherently interpretable multivariate time-series forecasting framework. It decomposes forecasting into a learned periodic component and a residual component computed with explainable masks over input tokens. With a budget-constrained information bottleneck, end-to-end optimization enables users to directly control explanation sparsity. With a rigorous faithfulness evaluation protocol, extensive experiments demonstrate that IB-Forecast matches the forecasting error of leading black-box models while providing faithful explanations at no additional inference cost. Furthermore, under a matched sparsity budget, these native explanations consistently surpass gradient-based, occlusion-based, and optimization-based baselines across all evaluated datasets. Ultimately, whereas the native explanations of existing interpretable forecasters exhibit poor faithfulness, IB-Forecast guarantees high explanation fidelity, requiring only 14-20% of the observations to deliver low-error predictions.

AI.tldr: IB-Forecast is an interpretable multivariate time-series forecasting framework that guarantees faithful explanations through information bottleneck optimization, matching black-box accuracy while providing native explanations with controlled sparsity.
AI.motivation: Existing interpretable forecasters reveal internal structures but offer no guarantee of faithfulness to underlying evidence, while faithfulness-oriented methods are designed only for post-hoc classification tasks, creating a gap for trustworthy forecasting explanations.
AI.method: Decomposes forecasting into learned periodic component and residual component with explainable masks over input tokens. Uses budget-constrained information bottleneck for end-to-end optimization, allowing direct control over explanation sparsity.
AI.result: Matches forecasting error of leading black-box models while providing faithful explanations at no additional inference cost. Native explanations surpass gradient-based, occlusion-based, and optimization-based baselines across all datasets under matched sparsity budgets.
AI.conclusion: IB-Forecast guarantees high explanation fidelity requiring only 14-20% of observations for low-error predictions, addressing the faithfulness gap in interpretable forecasting where existing methods exhibit poor faithfulness despite being interpretable.

title: AI and Authenticity in Islamic Research: A Critical Evaluation of Generative AI Reliability, Hallucination, and Source Fidelity in Quranic, Hadith, and Fiqh Knowledge
summary:
Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used by Muslims for religious guidance, Qur'anic interpretation, Hadith explanation, jurisprudential rulings, and Islamic education. Despite its growing adoption, there is limited empirical evidence on whether current AI systems provide authentic, verifiable, and trustworthy Islamic knowledge suitable for high-trust religious contexts. This study evaluates six leading generative AI systems using fifty realistic open-ended Islamic questions covering Qur'anic interpretation, Hadith, Fiqh, ethics, pastoral advice, and Madhhab-sensitive topics. Responses were collected under real-world conditions from participants in Australia and the United Kingdom and analysed using a mixed-method framework examining domain accuracy, citation verification, hallucinations, jurisprudential consistency, uncertainty handling, source provenance, and geographical variation.
  The study addresses four research questions: (1) How accurate and authentic are AI-generated responses across major Islamic knowledge domains? (2) To what extent do AI systems produce hallucinations, incomplete citations, or unverifiable religious references? (3) How consistently do models handle jurisprudential disagreement, Madhhab diversity, and uncertainty? (4) Are current AI systems sufficiently reliable for religious guidance, Islamic education, and scholarly research?
  Overall, current generative AI systems are valuable as assistive tools for introductory Islamic learning but should not be treated as authoritative sources for religious rulings or Islamic research without verification against authenticated primary sources and qualified scholarly expertise. This study provides one of the first comprehensive empirical evaluations of AI reliability within Islamic knowledge, offering practical guidance for researchers, educators, AI developers, and the wider Muslim community.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates six leading generative AI systems on their ability to provide accurate, authentic Islamic knowledge across various domains, finding them suitable as introductory learning tools but not as authoritative sources for religious rulings without verification.
AI.motivation: Generative AI is increasingly used by Muslims for religious guidance, Qur'anic interpretation, Hadith explanation, jurisprudential rulings, and Islamic education, but there's limited empirical evidence on whether current AI systems provide authentic, verifiable, and trustworthy Islamic knowledge suitable for high-trust religious contexts.
AI.method: The study evaluates six leading generative AI systems using fifty realistic open-ended Islamic questions covering Qur'anic interpretation, Hadith, Fiqh, ethics, pastoral advice, and Madhhab-sensitive topics. Responses were collected under real-world conditions from participants in Australia and the United Kingdom and analyzed using a mixed-method framework examining domain accuracy, citation verification, hallucinations, jurisprudential consistency, uncertainty handling, source provenance, and geographical variation.
AI.result: The study found that current generative AI systems are valuable as assistive tools for introductory Islamic learning but should not be treated as authoritative sources for religious rulings or Islamic research without verification against authenticated primary sources and qualified scholarly expertise.
AI.conclusion: This study provides one of the first comprehensive empirical evaluations of AI reliability within Islamic knowledge, offering practical guidance for researchers, educators, AI developers, and the wider Muslim community on the appropriate use of AI for religious purposes.

title: LM-GRASP: Instance-Specific Language Models for Combinatorial Construction via Online Imitation Learning
summary:
Machine learning for combinatorial optimization typically relies on neural constructors trained via reinforcement learning on large offline datasets for a fixed problem class-incurring high pretraining costs and generalizing poorly outside the training distribution. We propose an alternative: a metaheuristic framework that reformulates the randomized constructive phase of GRASP as an online imitation learning task, trained from scratch on each problem instance. A local search procedure acts as an expert oracle, while a decoder-only Transformer serves as the constructive policy. Unlike classical GRASP, which relies on static, myopic heuristic rules based on localized scalar costs, our approach is fully data-driven: the construction policy emerges from high-quality solutions discovered during the search itself, with no problem-specific feature engineering required.
  We instantiate this as LM-GRASP, a hybrid metaheuristic following an iterative learn-infer-improve cycle, training the policy online via behavioral cloning on a dynamic archive of elite trajectories-no external data or offline pretraining needed. The pipeline interfaces with the domain solely through the objective evaluator used by local search.
  Evaluated on the Taillard PFSP benchmark (ta51-ta60), the most discriminating block due to half its optima being unknown, LM-GRASP outperforms GPU-GRASP by 28.4 makespan units on average-comparable to the gain from GPU acceleration over sequential execution (27.2 units), though with overlapping standard deviations. This suggests instance-specific, online-trained language models are a promising, practical alternative to hand-engineered constructors, especially for landscapes resistant to classical greedy construction.

AI.tldr: LM-GRASP: A hybrid metaheuristic that uses online imitation learning with Transformers to train constructive policies from scratch for each combinatorial optimization instance, eliminating need for pretraining and outperforming traditional GRASP methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional machine learning for combinatorial optimization requires expensive pretraining on large offline datasets and generalizes poorly outside training distribution. Hand-engineered heuristic rules in classical GRASP are static and myopic, limiting performance on complex problems.
AI.method: Reformulates GRASP's randomized constructive phase as online imitation learning task. Uses local search as expert oracle and decoder-only Transformer as constructive policy. Follows learn-infer-improve cycle training via behavioral cloning on dynamic archive of elite trajectories, with no external data or offline pretraining.
AI.result: On Taillard PFSP benchmark (ta51-ta60), LM-GRASP outperforms GPU-GRASP by 28.4 makespan units on average, comparable to GPU acceleration gains over sequential execution (27.2 units), though with overlapping standard deviations.
AI.conclusion: Instance-specific, online-trained language models are a promising alternative to hand-engineered constructors, especially for optimization landscapes resistant to classical greedy construction, offering practical advantages without feature engineering or pretraining costs.

title: Operationally Guided Placement-Aware Learning for Industrial Online 3D Bin Packing
summary: The online three-dimensional bin packing problem (3D-BPP) is a longstanding challenge in logistics and industrial palletizing. Recent learning-based methods use a learned policy to select among feasible candidate placements. Performance depends on the candidate generator and representation, especially in industrial settings where packings must be space-efficient, stable, compact, and balanced. However, prior work has mainly optimized the policy, while candidate generation and representation remain largely geometry-driven. We address this gap with OPAL, an operationally guided placement-aware learning framework for industrial online 3D-BPP which combines an Operationally Guided Empty-Maximal-Space generator (OG-EMS), an operational representation for each candidate placement, and a masked ranking policy trained with proximal policy optimization. OG-EMS evaluates multiple anchors within each free-space region and prioritizes low, well-supported, compact, and spatially diverse placements. An xLSTM-based Placement Encoder models dependencies among geometric and operational candidate attributes, while a lightweight recurrent core combines the resulting embeddings with the current item and pallet state to rank feasible actions. On the BED-BPP benchmark, OPAL achieves a mean space utilization of 0.49, with improvements of 15.1% from operationally guided candidate generation and 6.3% from learned ranking, while maintaining robust inference-time performance.

AI.tldr: OPAL is a learning framework for industrial online 3D bin packing that integrates operationally-guided candidate generation with learned ranking, achieving 49% space utilization and outperforming prior methods by combining OG-EMS candidate generation with xLSTM-based placement encoding.
AI.motivation: Existing learning-based 3D-BPP methods focus mainly on policy optimization while candidate generation and representation remain geometry-driven, limiting performance in industrial settings where packings require space efficiency, stability, compactness, and balance.
AI.method: OPAL combines an Operationally Guided Empty-Maximal-Space generator (OG-EMS) that evaluates multiple anchors within free-space regions, an xLSTM-based Placement Encoder modeling geometric and operational dependencies, and a lightweight recurrent core with masked ranking policy trained via proximal policy optimization.
AI.result: On BED-BPP benchmark, OPAL achieves 0.49 mean space utilization with 15.1% improvement from operationally guided candidate generation and 6.3% from learned ranking, while maintaining robust inference-time performance.
AI.conclusion: Integrating operational guidance into candidate generation and representation alongside learned ranking significantly improves online 3D-BPP performance, demonstrating the importance of holistic approach addressing both candidate generation and policy optimization for industrial applications.

authors: Jacobus G. M. van der Linden
title: Search Strategies for Optimal Classification and Regression Trees
summary: Optimal decision trees (ODTs) are compact, interpretable machine learning models that globally optimize a given objective, but their scalability remains challenging. While recent work has proposed a variety of search strategies to improve scalability, the precise contribution of each strategy remains unclear. To address this gap, we introduce a general algorithmic framework for ODTs that instantiates previously used search strategies and enables the definition of new ones. This provides a common lens through which to understand and compare different strategies, which we use to empirically investigate the effect of 18 search strategies. Compared to the state of the art, the best strategy in our evaluation achieves significantly better anytime performance for classification, and improves runtime by more than an order of magnitude for regression.

AI.tldr: A general algorithmic framework for optimal decision trees that unifies and enables comparison of 18 search strategies, revealing superior performance over state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Optimal decision trees offer interpretable machine learning models with global optimization, but face scalability challenges. Existing research uses various search strategies without clear understanding of each strategy's individual contribution to performance.
AI.method: The authors introduce a general algorithmic framework for optimal decision trees that can instantiate previously used search strategies and enable definition of new ones. This provides a common lens for understanding and comparing different approaches, which they use to empirically investigate 18 search strategies.
AI.result: Compared to state-of-the-art methods, the best strategy identified in their evaluation achieves significantly better anytime performance for classification tasks, and improves runtime by more than an order of magnitude for regression tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully unifies different search strategies for optimal decision trees, enabling systematic comparison and identification of superior approaches that substantially improve both performance and efficiency over existing methods.

title: LLM-Guided Evolutionary Search for Constraint Model Reformulation to Improve Solver Efficiency
summary: Combinatorial problems appear in numerous industrial applications. A common approach is to formulate these problems as declarative constraint models that can subsequently be compiled to and solved by a range of back-end solvers. Recent work shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can produce correct models from natural language, but even a correct model can be expensive to solve because performance remains sensitive to modelling choices. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs can automate performance-oriented model reformulation. Inspired by Automatic Heuristic Design (AHD), we use an evolutionary framework in which an LLM proposes candidate reformulations that are verified and benchmarked against the user-defined baseline model. We compare AHD-adapted search strategies that control which prior attempts, instructions, and measured feedback enter each prompt. Existing retention strategies prioritize recency or performance, but do not explicitly diversify the context. To cover this gap, we introduce Profile-Diverse Retention (PDR), which applies Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) to instance-level runtime vectors to retain behaviourally diverse attempts. We systematically evaluate the strategies on eight CSPLib problems using validation-based final model selection. The results show that: (i) iterative reformulation can produce substantial held-out speedups; (ii) strategies that keep the retained context diverse outperform those that retain only recent or the fastest attempts; and (iii) validation-based selection improves the held-out speedup of every strategy.

AI.tldr: LLMs can automate performance optimization of constraint models through evolutionary reformulation with diversity-based context retention strategies.
AI.motivation: While LLMs can produce correct constraint models from natural language, solving performance remains sensitive to modeling choices, creating a need to automate performance-oriented model reformulation.
AI.method: Evolutionary framework where LLM proposes candidate reformulations verified/benchmarked against baseline; compares search strategies controlling prompt context; introduces Profile-Diverse Retention (PDR) using Maximal Marginal Relevance on runtime vectors.
AI.result: Iterative reformulation produces substantial held-out speedups; diversity-based retention strategies outperform recency/performance-only strategies; validation-based selection improves held-out speedup for all strategies.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can effectively automate performance optimization of constraint models, with diversity-aware retention strategies and validation-based selection delivering better held-out performance improvements.

title: Multi-channel Uplift Policy Learning
summary: E-commerce platforms must allocate fixed marketing budgets across multiple channels to maximize business utility. However, standard predict-then-optimize (PTO) paradigms fail in this compositional space due to observational confounding and severe extrapolation. We formulate this challenge as a simplex-constrained uplift decision problem and propose ReAlloc, a fast-slow causal framework. Specifically, an agile Orthogonal Teacher extracts unbiased local gradients from short-term logs, while an Explanation-Guided Student distills them into a structured marginal field over long-term horizons. This design enables support-aware, conservative decisions that capture cross-channel substitutions. Extensive simulations and large-scale online A/B tests on Taobao platform demonstrate that ReAlloc achieves simultaneous lifts in both pay order and income.

AI.tldr: ReAlloc is a causal framework for marketing budget allocation that addresses observational confounding and extrapolation issues in compositional spaces through an Orthogonal Teacher-Explanation Guided Student architecture.
AI.motivation: E-commerce platforms need to allocate fixed marketing budgets across channels to maximize utility, but standard predict-then-optimize paradigms fail due to observational confounding and severe extrapolation in this compositional space.
AI.method: Formulates the problem as a simplex-constrained uplift decision problem and proposes ReAlloc, a fast-slow causal framework with an agile Orthogonal Teacher extracting unbiased local gradients from short-term logs, and an Explanation-Guided Student distilling them into structured marginal fields over long-term horizons.
AI.result: Extensive simulations and large-scale online A/B tests on Taobao platform demonstrate that ReAlloc achieves simultaneous lifts in both pay order and income metrics.
AI.conclusion: ReAlloc enables support-aware, conservative decisions that capture cross-channel substitutions, effectively addressing the limitations of standard predict-then-optimize approaches for marketing budget allocation in e-commerce platforms.

title: MemHarness: Memory Is Reconstructed, Not Replayed
summary: Retrieving past experiences has become a common strategy to enhance large language model agents. However, most existing memory-augmented agents treat retrieved experiences as static records to be replayed verbatim, injecting them into the context regardless of whether they align with the agent's current situation. This ``replay'' paradigm ignores the gap between the abstract, general nature of stored experience and the concrete, ever-changing states encountered at decision time, frequently causing negative transfer. In contrast, humans rarely recall past experiences verbatim; instead, they reorganize and adapt retrieved memories to fit the present context. Inspired by this, we propose MemHarness, a framework that equips LLM agents to actively harness and reconstruct past experiences based on the present context. At each decision step, a unified policy model critiques and reconstructs the retrieved experience conditioned on the current state, producing context-grounded guidance before acting. This reconstructive ability emerges naturally through end-to-end training with GRPO. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show that MemHarness substantially outperforms pure RL and static memory-augmented baselines, demonstrating strong robustness in out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. Furthermore, our analyses reveal that this reconstruction objective not only prevents negative transfer but also serves as latent guidance during training, fundamentally improving the agent's intrinsic reasoning capabilities.

AI.tldr: MemHarness enables LLM agents to actively reconstruct and adapt retrieved past experiences to fit current context, preventing negative transfer and improving reasoning capabilities.
AI.motivation: Current memory-augmented agents treat retrieved experiences as static records for verbatim replay, ignoring the gap between abstract stored experience and concrete current states, causing negative transfer. Humans adapt memories to fit context, inspiring a reconstructive approach.
AI.method: MemHarness framework where a unified policy model critiques and reconstructs retrieved experience conditioned on current state at each decision step, producing context-grounded guidance before acting. Trained end-to-end with GRPO.
AI.result: Substantially outperforms pure RL and static memory-augmented baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop, demonstrating strong robustness in OOD scenarios. Reconstruction prevents negative transfer and serves as latent guidance improving intrinsic reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Active reconstruction of past experiences to fit current context is superior to static replay, fundamentally enhancing LLM agents' reasoning capabilities and robustness through emergent reconstructive abilities.

title: Persistent Gaussian Perturbations Prevent Oversmoothing in Recurrent Graph Neural Networks
summary: Oversmoothing is a fundamental limitation of deep graph neural networks (GNNs), where repeated message passing causes node representations to become increasingly similar, eventually collapsing toward a low-dimensional subspace. This phenomenon limits the effective depth of message-passing architectures and motivates the search for mechanisms that preserve representation diversity. In this paper, we study a recurrent graph neural network in which independent Gaussian noise is injected after every propagation step and analyze the resulting architecture as a stochastic dynamical system. Under a standard global contraction assumption on the deterministic update, we prove that the hidden representations form a geometrically ergodic Markov chain admitting a unique invariant probability measure. Our main theoretical result establishes an explicit positive lower bound on the expected stationary Dirichlet energy, proportional to both the noise variance and the spectral gap of the underlying graph. Consequently, the stationary representations cannot collapse onto the constant manifold, providing a rigorous guarantee that asymptotic oversmoothing is prevented in the sense of non-vanishing Dirichlet energy. Our analysis reveals persistent stochastic perturbations as a fundamentally different mechanism for combating oversmoothing, complementing existing deterministic approaches based on residual connections, normalization, and graph rewiring. Finally, numerical experiments on both linear and nonlinear recurrent graph neural networks closely match the theoretical predictions, illustrating the emergence of a stationary distribution and the predicted dependence of the limiting Dirichlet energy on the noise intensity.

AI.tldr: Recurrent GNNs with Gaussian noise injection prevent oversmoothing by maintaining representation diversity through stochastic perturbations, with theoretical guarantees on non-vanishing Dirichlet energy.
AI.motivation: Oversmoothing in deep GNNs causes node representations to become increasingly similar, limiting effective network depth. Existing deterministic approaches (residual connections, normalization, graph rewiring) need complementary mechanisms to preserve representation diversity.
AI.method: Propose a recurrent graph neural network with independent Gaussian noise injection after every propagation step. Analyze it as a stochastic dynamical system under global contraction assumptions on deterministic updates. Prove the hidden representations form a geometrically ergodic Markov chain with unique invariant probability measure.
AI.result: Established explicit positive lower bound on expected stationary Dirichlet energy proportional to noise variance and spectral gap of the underlying graph. This ensures stationary representations cannot collapse onto constant manifold, providing rigorous guarantee against asymptotic oversmoothing. Numerical experiments on linear and nonlinear recurrent GNNs confirm theoretical predictions.
AI.conclusion: Stochastic perturbations offer fundamentally different mechanism to combat oversmoothing compared to deterministic approaches. The approach ensures persistent representation diversity through noise injection, with theoretical guarantees on maintaining non-vanishing Dirichlet energy in the stationary distribution.

title: Tycho: Active Abstraction with Programmatic World Models for ARC-AGI-3
comment: 52 pages, 18 figures, 17 tables. Open-source implementation: https://github.com/NIMI-research/Tycho
summary:
ARC-AGI-3 turns abstraction into an interactive problem of skill acquisition. A player must infer an unfamiliar game's rules, hidden state, and goal while maintaining action efficiency because every move counts. We formalize these environments as parameterized rendered deterministic Moore machines and introduce Tycho, a coding-agent system that constructs and uses game-specific models during interaction. Tycho separates actionable observations from intermediate animation, level-completion, and game-over frames. From this structured history, an agent can model, test, plan with, repair, or bypass a free-form executable hypothesis.
  In one matched public-set run per policy, we compare four orchestration policies on all 25 public games using Claude Opus 4.8 under matched inference budgets. Actor-requested delegation to a model builder obtains the highest observed mean Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE), 88.49. With this selected policy, GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 both reach 100.00 RHAE and complete all 183 levels. Their game-balanced first-run human-replay midranks are 98.5 and 100.0. Opus 5 uses 61% fewer scored actions than the aggregate official human baselines.
  Automatic repair after verification failures produces models that reproduce observed transitions much more accurately, yet reaches only 83.07 RHAE. Transition match indicates whether a simulator reproduces observed dynamics, not whether it has identified the objective or improves the next action. Strong play also requires deciding when to construct, repair, use, or bypass a model. We call this joint problem active abstraction: generating a testable model from costly interaction and deciding when acquiring or using it is worth its cost.

AI.tldr: Tycho is a coding-agent system that tackles active abstraction in ARC-AGI-3 environments by constructing and using game-specific models during interaction, achieving human-level or better performance on all 25 public games with optimal orchestration policies.
AI.motivation: ARC-AGI-3 presents a challenging interactive problem where players must infer game rules, hidden state, and goals while maintaining action efficiency. This requires solving the "active abstraction" problem: creating testable models from costly interactions and deciding when model acquisition or use is worthwhile.
AI.method: The authors formalize environments as parameterized rendered deterministic Moore machines and introduce Tycho, a coding-agent system that constructs game-specific models during interaction. Tycho separates actionable observations from intermediate frames and uses structured history to model, test, plan with, repair, or bypass executable hypotheses. They compare four orchestration policies on 25 public games using advanced AI models under matched inference budgets.
AI.result: Actor-requested delegation to a model builder achieved highest mean Relative Human Action Efficiency (88.49 RHAE). GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 both reached 100.00 RHAE and completed all 183 levels. Opus 5 used 61% fewer actions than human baselines. Automatic repair after verification failures produced more accurate models but only achieved 83.07 RHAE, showing that transition accuracy doesn't guarantee good gameplay.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that successful gameplay in ARC-AGI-3 requires more than just accurate transition models - it requires deciding when to construct, repair, use, or bypass models. This "active abstraction" problem is crucial for intelligent agents operating in unfamiliar environments where every action counts.

title: TopoFormer: Topology Meets Attention for Graph Learning
summary: We introduce Topoformer, a lightweight and scalable framework for graph representation learning that encodes topological structure into attention-friendly sequences. At the core of our method is Topo-Scan, a novel module that decomposes a graph into a short, ordered sequence of topological tokens by slicing over node or edge filtrations. These sequences capture multi-scale structural patterns, from local motifs to global organization, and are processed by a Transformer to produce expressive graph-level embeddings. Unlike traditional persistent homology pipelines, Topo-Scan is parallelizable, avoids costly diagram computations, and integrates seamlessly with standard deep learning architectures. We provide theoretical guarantees on the stability of our topological encodings and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across graph classification and molecular property prediction benchmarks. Our results show that Topoformer matches or exceeds strong GNN and topology-based baselines while offering predictable and efficient compute. This work opens a new path for parallelizable and unifying approaches to graph representation learning that integrate topological inductive biases into attention frameworks.

AI.tldr: Topoformer is a lightweight Transformer-based framework that encodes graph topological structure into attention-friendly sequences using a novel Topo-Scan module, achieving SOTA performance on graph tasks with parallelizable efficiency.
AI.motivation: Traditional persistent homology pipelines for topological graph analysis are computationally expensive, non-parallelizable, and don't integrate well with standard deep learning architectures. There's a need for scalable methods that capture multi-scale topological patterns while being compatible with modern neural networks.
AI.method: The core innovation is Topo-Scan, which decomposes graphs into ordered sequences of topological tokens by slicing over node or edge filtrations. These sequences capture structural patterns from local to global scales, and are processed by a Transformer to produce graph-level embeddings. Unlike persistent homology, it avoids costly diagram computations and is fully parallelizable.
AI.result: Topoformer achieves state-of-the-art performance on graph classification and molecular property prediction benchmarks, matching or exceeding strong GNN and topology-based baselines. It provides theoretical guarantees on topological encoding stability and offers predictable, efficient computation.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a new path for parallelizable graph representation learning that integrates topological inductive biases into attention frameworks, creating a unifying approach that bridges topological analysis with modern deep learning.

title: One Human, $N$ Agents: Audit-Budget Allocation for LLM Agent Fleets under Miscalibrated, Correlated Confidence
summary: A single human must audit $N$ LLM agents under a budget of $B \ll N$ audits per round, guided by self-reported confidence that may be adversarially miscalibrated and by correlated errors. We model this as budgeted noisy inspection over a two-level Gaussian copula and locate the miscalibration threshold $δ^*$ past which confidence-ranked auditing is \emph{worse} than random. Two a-priori expectations reverse: $δ^*$ \emph{rises} as the budget shrinks, and cross-family correlation is not low---shared difficulty dominates lineage. Five open-weight LLMs show operationally useless (near-constant) confidence, point estimates at or beyond the flip though CIs straddle it; a proprietary model is informative and lands below it. We give a quantitative criterion for \emph{vacuous} oversight, and replaying policies on recorded traces confirms the ordering.

AI.tldr: Auditing many LLM agents with limited budget is problematic when their self-reported confidence is miscalibrated; beyond a threshold, confidence-ranked auditing becomes worse than random, and many open-weight LLMs show useless constant confidence.
AI.motivation: A single human auditor needs to monitor N LLM agents but has a limited budget B << N audits per round. The challenge is that LLMs provide self-reported confidence that can be adversarially miscalibrated and their errors are correlated, making effective oversight difficult.
AI.method: Model the problem as budgeted noisy inspection over a two-level Gaussian copula to analyze confidence miscalibration effects. Study five open-weight LLMs and one proprietary model to measure confidence calibration. Replay policies on recorded traces to validate findings.
AI.result: Identified a miscalibration threshold δ* beyond which confidence-ranked auditing becomes worse than random. Surprisingly, δ* rises as budget shrinks, and cross-family correlation isn't low due to shared difficulty dominating lineage. Open-weight LLMs show operationally useless near-constant confidence, while the proprietary model is informative and below the threshold.
AI.conclusion: Developed a quantitative criterion for vacuous oversight. Confidence calibration issues in many LLMs undermine budgeted auditing, making confidence-based selection counterproductive beyond a certain miscalibration level. Proprietary models perform better but still raise concerns about effective human oversight of multiple LLM agents.

title: HARGO: Heterogeneity-Aware Reward-Guided Optimization for RL Post-Training of LLMs on HPC Tasks
summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can equip large language models (LLMs) with domain knowledge for high-performance computing (HPC) tasks such as data race detection and benchmark question answering. However, knowledge alone does not guarantee task-appropriate behavior: the same SFT model that correctly classifies 88.65\% of C/C++ data race samples produces verbose, imprecise answers to factual queries, with 65.9\% of MLPerf responses exceeding 40 characters. Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training addresses this gap by optimizing for task-specific rewards rather than token-level imitation. Yet HPC tasks exhibit extreme heterogeneity, with binary classification, factual QA, and semantic generation differing by 58x in answer length, spanning three distinct reward distributions, and showing widely varying SFT accuracy. This makes uniform-weight RL methods such as GRPO suboptimal. We propose HARGO, Heterogeneity-Aware Reward-Guided Optimization, which introduces per-response importance weighting via confidence-modulated advantage: computing a discrimination signal from group-level reward contrast and a confidence signal from reference model log-probabilities, then modulating the advantage before computing per-response weights, without requiring task-type labels. Across four HPC tasks and nine methods, HARGO achieves the best performance on all three primary metrics: WinRate 54.62\%, Data Race F1 91.30\%, and PLP Similarity 0.8558. Ablation confirms complementary contributions from both signals. HARGO establishes the best overall alignment quality among compared methods for heterogeneous HPC tasks.

AI.tldr: HARGO (Heterogeneity-Aware Reward-Guided Optimization) improves RL post-training for heterogeneous HPC tasks by using confidence-modulated advantage weighting to handle varying task types without needing task labels.
AI.motivation: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) alone is insufficient for HPC tasks because it produces inconsistent behavior - models may have good classification accuracy but generate verbose/imprecise answers. Standard RL methods (like GRPO) fail on heterogeneous HPC tasks where different tasks (binary classification, factual QA, semantic generation) vary dramatically in answer length, reward distributions, and SFT accuracy.
AI.method: HARGO introduces per-response importance weighting using two signals: 1) discrimination signal from group-level reward contrast (comparing responses to identify useful ones), and 2) confidence signal from reference model log-probabilities. These are combined to modulate advantage before computing per-response weights, all without requiring explicit task-type labels.
AI.result: Across four HPC tasks and nine methods, HARGO achieves best performance on all three primary metrics: WinRate 54.62%, Data Race F1 91.30%, and PLP Similarity 0.8558. Ablation studies confirm that both discrimination and confidence signals contribute to the improvement.
AI.conclusion: HARGO establishes the best overall alignment quality for heterogeneous HPC tasks by effectively handling task heterogeneity through confidence-modulated advantage weighting, outperforming uniform-weight RL methods and showing complementary contributions from both signal components.

title: PathView-Bench: Can Multimodal Large Language Models Achieve Fine-grained Multiscale Understanding of Pathology Images?
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to analyze pathology images. However, dominant multimodal benchmarks in pathology mainly score final diagnostic answers, captions, or reports. These evaluations provide limited insight into whether a model understands the multiscale visual content needed for pathology reasoning and decision-making. We introduce PathVU, a vision-anchored benchmark for fine-grained and multiscale visual understanding in computational pathology. Built from 23 public pathology imaging datasets with human-supervised labels and spatial annotations, PathVU evaluates MLLM understanding in two fields of view: Region FOV for high-resolution local regions and Slide FOV for macro whole-slide views. By converting raw annotations into deterministic task targets, PathVU enables programmatic scoring of region localization, visual recognition, quantity estimation, spatial reasoning, and insufficient-context judgment. The benchmark contains 14 VQA-style tasks, 61,673 images, and 308,070 samples across 28 organs and 7,253,526 annotations. Evaluating 18 representative general-purpose, medical-domain, and pathology-oriented MLLMs, we observe substantial limitations even in advanced models on fine-grained visual tasks across multiscale pathology images. PathVU provides a reproducible basis for developing and evaluating pathology MLLMs with explicit multiscale visual understanding.

AI.tldr: PathVU is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multimodal LLMs' fine-grained and multiscale visual understanding in pathology, focusing on tasks like region localization, visual recognition, and spatial reasoning across different scales.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal benchmarks in pathology mainly score diagnostic answers, captions, or reports, providing limited insight into whether models truly understand the multiscale visual content necessary for pathology reasoning and decision-making.
AI.method: Built PathVU from 23 public pathology imaging datasets with human-supervised labels and spatial annotations. The benchmark evaluates MLLM understanding across two fields of view: Region FOV for high-resolution local regions and Slide FOV for macro whole-slide views. Converts raw annotations into deterministic task targets for programmatic scoring.
AI.result: The benchmark contains 14 VQA-style tasks, 61,673 images, and 308,070 samples across 28 organs with 7,253,526 annotations. Evaluation of 18 representative MLLMs revealed substantial limitations even in advanced models on fine-grained visual tasks across multiscale pathology images.
AI.conclusion: PathVU provides a reproducible basis for developing and evaluating pathology MLLMs with explicit multiscale visual understanding, addressing gaps in current pathology evaluation methods.

title: Semi-Supervised Learning for Molecular Graphs via Ensemble Consensus
summary: Machine learning is transforming molecular sciences by accelerating property prediction, simulation, and the discovery of new molecules and materials. Acquiring labeled data in these domains is often costly and time-consuming, whereas large collections of unlabeled molecular data are readily available. Standard semi-supervised learning methods often rely on label-preserving augmentations, which are challenging to design in the molecular domain, where minor changes can drastically alter properties. In this work, we show that semi-supervised methods that rely on an ensemble consensus can boost predictive accuracy across a diverse range of molecular datasets, task types, and graph neural network architectures. We find that training with an ensemble consensus objective increases robustness in models and exhibits an effect similar to knowledge distillation; an individual member of an ensemble trained this way outperforms a full ensemble trained in a traditional supervised fashion in almost all cases. In addition, this type of semi-supervised training reduces calibration error.

AI.tldr: Semi-supervised learning using ensemble consensus improves molecular property prediction accuracy, robustness, and calibration without needing label-preserving augmentations.
AI.motivation: Labeled molecular data is expensive and scarce while unlabeled data is abundant. Traditional semi-supervised methods rely on label-preserving augmentations that are difficult to design for molecular data where small changes can dramatically alter properties.
AI.method: Using ensemble consensus approach instead of label-preserving augmentations for semi-supervised learning. Models are trained with an ensemble consensus objective across diverse molecular datasets, task types, and graph neural network architectures.
AI.result: Ensemble consensus training boosts predictive accuracy, increases model robustness, exhibits knowledge distillation-like effects, reduces calibration error, and allows individual ensemble members to outperform traditional supervised full ensembles in most cases.
AI.conclusion: Semi-supervised methods based on ensemble consensus provide an effective alternative to augmentation-dependent approaches for molecular machine learning, addressing data scarcity challenges while improving performance metrics across multiple dimensions.

title: Paying for Honesty Without Knowing the Truth: Reputation-Penalty Design for LLM Marketplace Agents
summary: LLM agents increasingly act as autonomous merchants that write their own product listings, and under competitive pressure, they fabricate attributes to win sales. Even under instructions to be honest, they fabricate attributes in a majority of listings across models. A platform's obvious remedy---verifying each claim against the truth---is unavailable, because it observes only a noisy, biased complaint signal, never the ground truth. We design CARP, a reputation-penalty mechanism with a deadband that forgives complaint noise and a state-dependent severity that counters reputation-driven detection erosion. CARP requires no product-level ground truth and is robust to strategic gaming. CARP protects consumers by suppressing the sales volume of low-rated liars while sparing honest sellers. Paired with SPARC, it closes most of the consumer-welfare gap relative to a perfect-information oracle, without ever accessing the truth. It also achieves the best welfare of the policies we compare. We further show that this felt penalty becomes behaviorally binding through SPARC, a byte-clean code-gated reflection mechanism: LLM merchants fabricate when lying is free but restrain themselves when fabrication costs them sales, a self-interested response rather than compliance. We trace this distinction to penalty-gated self-correction reasoning, and observe the binding across models, with supporting confidence intervals.

AI.tldr: CARP is a reputation-penalty mechanism that suppresses lying LLM merchants without needing ground truth verification, using complaint signals and paired with SPARC for behavioral binding.
AI.motivation: LLM agents acting as autonomous merchants increasingly fabricate product attributes to win sales, even when instructed to be honest. Platforms face the challenge of detecting lies without access to ground truth, observing only noisy, biased complaint signals.
AI.method: The paper designs CARP (complaint-adjusted reputation penalty), a mechanism with a deadband that forgives complaint noise and state-dependent severity to counter reputation-driven detection erosion. It's paired with SPARC, a byte-clean code-gated reflection mechanism that makes penalties behaviorally binding.
AI.result: CARP suppresses sales volume of low-rated liars while sparing honest sellers, closing most of the consumer-welfare gap relative to a perfect-information oracle without accessing ground truth. SPARC makes penalties behaviorally binding - LLM merchants fabricate when lying is free but restrain themselves when fabrication costs sales.
AI.conclusion: CARP with SPARC effectively addresses LLM merchant dishonesty without ground truth verification, achieving good consumer welfare through self-interested penalty responses rather than compliance, and works across different LLM models with statistical confidence.

title: Beyond Geometric Complementarity: Coherent Overlap in Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Routing
summary: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models route each token to multiple experts, suggesting a geometric account of their benefit: co-selected experts should contribute distinct representation directions. Existing evidence often conflates route coherence, candidate quality, and candidate-by-context interaction. We distinguish these quantities using an Expert Subspace Separation Index (ESSI), matched-route residuals, and a prefix-controlled $2\times2$ factorial; frozen-route interventions and a controlled Top-$k$ study assess functional value. Three paired contrasts organize the findings. First, across six MoE architectures, expert subspaces overlap substantially, yet actual routes explain token representations better than matched alternatives. Second, across the 39 factorial cells in OLMoE, Mixtral, and DeepSeek, the selected candidate explains more of the residual representation than the strongest unselected rival in every cell, yet the actual prefix narrows this advantage throughout: all interactions are negative, and every 95% confidence interval lies below zero. Third, this geometric narrowing does not imply functional redundancy: adding later experts improves next-token prediction in 24 of 39 frozen-route comparisons, while the other 15 estimates are inconclusive; a controlled training study also favors Top-2 over Top-1 in all three seeds. We call this joint pattern coherent overlap: routing selects token-relevant experts from a shared geometric neighborhood, while useful multi-expert computation persists without disjoint linear coverage. Separating these quantities clarifies why geometric similarity alone cannot determine redundancy or pruning value.

AI.tldr: Sparse MoE models show that while expert subspaces overlap substantially, routing selects relevant experts from shared neighborhoods, and multi-expert computation remains useful despite geometric similarity.
AI.motivation: To understand the geometric basis of MoE benefits by distinguishing route coherence, candidate quality, and candidate-by-context interactions that are often conflated in existing evidence.
AI.method: Developed Expert Subspace Separation Index (ESSI), matched-route residuals, and prefix-controlled factorial design; used frozen-route interventions and controlled Top-k studies across six MoE architectures.
AI.result: 1) Expert subspaces overlap substantially but actual routes explain token representations better than alternatives. 2) Selected experts explain more residual representation than rivals, though prefix narrows advantage. 3) Despite geometric narrowing, multi-expert computation improves predictions in most comparisons.
AI.conclusion: The pattern of "coherent overlap" shows routing selects relevant experts from shared geometric neighborhoods while maintaining useful multi-expert computation, clarifying why geometric similarity alone doesn't determine redundancy or pruning value.

title: Correcting What You Cannot See: Credit Assignment for Perception Distillation in Multimodal Reasoners
summary: On-policy distillation provides dense supervision for multimodal reasoners, but its trajectory-level reward cannot determine whether a failed answer arose from perception or subsequent reasoning. Perception Success Rate (PSR), estimated from multiple reasonings sharing one perception, remains ambiguous because low success conflates perceptual insufficiency with reasoning difficulty. We introduce \textbf{Perception-Correction Distillation (PCD)}, a label-free method that identifies correctable perception failures using downstream failure and teacher--student disagreement as complementary witnesses. Their product, , forms a soft AND gate that strengthens distillation only when both witnesses are present. We motivate this rule through Bayesian evidence combination and show that multiplication is the unique normalized bilinear gate that vanishes when either witness is absent. PCD uses separated perception--reasoning rollouts and mean-preserving weights, leaving the reasoning objective unchanged. Across eight benchmarks, PCD improves the 8B 2B macro average from 44.50 with OPD to 47.28 and the 32B 8B result from 56.94 to 61.22. In matched 2B ablations, removing PCD and separated rollout reduces held-out average by 2.22 and 0.88 points, respectively. Effective multimodal distillation therefore depends not only on what the teacher predicts, but also on identifying when perception is the appropriate target of correction.

AI.tldr: PCD is a label-free distillation method that identifies correctable perception failures in multimodal reasoners by using downstream failure and teacher-student disagreement as complementary witnesses, improving performance over standard on-policy distillation.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation for multimodal reasoners has limitations: trajectory-level rewards can't distinguish perception failures from reasoning failures, and Perception Success Rate (PSR) estimation remains ambiguous as low success conflates perceptual insufficiency with reasoning difficulty.
AI.method: Proposes Perception-Correction Distillation (PCD) that uses downstream failure and teacher-student disagreement as complementary witnesses. Their product forms a soft AND gate that strengthens distillation only when both witnesses are present. Uses separated perception-reasoning rollouts and mean-preserving weights while leaving reasoning objective unchanged.
AI.result: Across eight benchmarks, PCD improves 8B→2B macro average from 44.50 to 47.28 and 32B→8B from 56.94 to 61.22. Ablations show removing PCD reduces held-out average by 2.22 points and removing separated rollout reduces by 0.88 points.
AI.conclusion: Effective multimodal distillation depends not only on what the teacher predicts, but also on identifying when perception is the appropriate target of correction. PCD provides a principled approach to address perception failures in distillation.

title: Measuring Distortion in the Empty Regions of Dimensionality Reduction Scatterplots with the Gap Index
summary: Quality metrics play a crucial role in the proper use of dimensionality reduction projections for visual analysis of high-dimensional data. They quantify the degree of distortion of a projection compared to the high-dimensional data and provide a reliable indication of how confident users can be in the structures they see in the resulting layouts. However, most popular metrics focus on capturing direct relationships between points (e.g., distances or neighborhoods) while neglecting distortions in empty areas of the layout, even though these often compose visually relevant features of a 2D layout. In this paper, we introduce the Gap Index (GI), a quality metric for 2D projections that captures visual distortion by measuring spatial distortion in empty areas of a projection. It does so by decomposing the space into empty triangles, which are then compared to their high-dimensional counterparts to compute the deformation. This per-triangle deformation can be aggregated into a single scalar value or overlaid on a projection to visualize regional distortion patterns. Results show that, contrary to popular quality metrics, the GI is sensitive to small structural deformations that have high visual impact. It is also fast to compute and interpretable.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Gap Index (GI), a new quality metric for 2D dimensionality reduction projections that measures visual distortion in empty areas, addressing limitations of existing metrics that focus only on point relationships.
AI.motivation: Current quality metrics for dimensionality reduction projections focus on distortions between data points (distances/neighborhoods) but neglect distortions in empty layout areas, which are visually important features of 2D layouts.
AI.method: The Gap Index decomposes the 2D space into empty triangles, compares them to their high-dimensional counterparts, and computes deformation. This per-triangle deformation can be aggregated into a single scalar value or visualized as regional distortion patterns.
AI.result: The GI metric is sensitive to small structural deformations with high visual impact, unlike popular quality metrics. It is also fast to compute and interpretable.
AI.conclusion: Gap Index provides a valuable new quality metric that captures visual distortion in empty areas of 2D projections, addressing a gap in current evaluation methods and offering better sensitivity to visually relevant structural deformations.

title: How Benchmarks Mis-Score Computer-Use Agents
summary: Computer-use agents (CUA) are being deployed to browse the web and operate desktop software, yet their benchmark scores are still commonly produced by brittle scripted oracles. A score is the output of a pipeline in which tasks can be stale, trajectories can omit decisive visual evidence, evaluators can reject valid alternatives, and aggregate reports can hide the cause of failure. We organize these problems into a reliability framework spanning task construction, trajectory observation, scoring, and reporting. We then audit 150 public failure-scored trajectories from five web, enterprise-workflow, and desktop-control benchmarks, find that 15.3\% of FAIL verdicts are wrong: 10.7\% are evaluator false negatives and 4.7\% are broken tasks. For genuine failures, a three-tier diagnostic taxonomy shows that verification/feedback and planning failures dominate execution/grounding errors, while a single scalar success rate can not explain. We connect these findings to newer long-horizon CUA benchmarks and derive stage-specific design rules for CUA evaluation.

AI.tldr: Current computer-use agent benchmarks are unreliable due to brittle evaluation methods, with 15.3% of failure verdicts being wrong, and single success rate metrics fail to explain genuine failure patterns.
AI.motivation: Computer-use agents (CUAs) are increasingly deployed for web browsing and desktop software operation, but their benchmark evaluations are unreliable. The current practice uses brittle scripted oracles for scoring, leading to problems throughout the evaluation pipeline: stale tasks, incomplete trajectory evidence, evaluators rejecting valid alternatives, and aggregated reports hiding failure causes.
AI.method: The authors developed a reliability framework covering task construction, trajectory observation, scoring, and reporting. They then conducted an audit of 150 public failure-scored trajectories from five web, enterprise-workflow, and desktop-control benchmarks. For genuine failures, they created a three-tier diagnostic taxonomy to analyze error patterns.
AI.result: The audit revealed that 15.3% of FAIL verdicts were incorrect: 10.7% were evaluator false negatives and 4.7% were due to broken tasks. For genuine failures, the analysis showed that verification/feedback and planning failures dominate execution/grounding errors. The study also found that a single scalar success rate cannot adequately explain failure patterns.
AI.conclusion: Current CUA evaluation methods are unreliable and need improvement. The findings highlight the need for more robust evaluation frameworks and better diagnostic approaches. The authors connect these insights to newer long-horizon CUA benchmarks and derive stage-specific design rules for more reliable CUA evaluation.

title: Encryption-Compatible Clustered Federated Learning via Distributed Expectation-Maximization over Metadata
summary: Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) addresses data heterogeneity in federated settings by grouping clients with similar data distributions to enable effective training. Existing methods face a trade-off between privacy preservation, communication cost, and computational efficiency. We formalize this as the CFL trilemma, according to which improving two of these dimensions comes at the expense of the third. A prominent paradigm relies on metadata (i.e., low-dimensional representations of client datasets shared with the server) to enable communication- and computation-efficient clustering. However, such approaches are not compatible with standard FL privacy-preserving mechanisms. To address this limitation, we propose FLAMECHE, which reformulates metadata-based CFL as a distributed Expectation-Maximization (EM) procedure, restricting server updates to additive operations while preserving efficiency. This design enables compatibility with practical secure FL schemes. We conducted extensive experiments on multiple datasets under various heterogeneous scenarios. Results show that FLAMECHE improves the effectiveness of client models. It enables encryption-compatible metadata-based clustering, enhancing its positioning within the CFL trilemma.

AI.tldr: FLAMECHE is a new CFL method that enables encryption-compatible metadata-based clustering through distributed EM, addressing the privacy-communication-computation trilemma.
AI.motivation: Existing Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) methods face a trade-off between privacy preservation, communication cost, and computational efficiency - the "CFL trilemma." Metadata-based approaches enable efficient clustering but are incompatible with standard FL privacy mechanisms.
AI.method: Reformulates metadata-based CFL as a distributed Expectation-Maximization (EM) procedure that restricts server updates to additive operations while preserving efficiency, enabling compatibility with practical secure FL schemes.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple datasets under various heterogeneous scenarios show FLAMECHE improves effectiveness of client models and enables encryption-compatible metadata-based clustering.
AI.conclusion: FLAMECHE successfully addresses the CFL trilemma by making metadata-based clustering compatible with privacy-preserving mechanisms, enhancing its positioning within the privacy-communication-computation trade-off.

title: HyperClaim: Fine-Grained Cross-Modal Hypergraph Reasoning for Video Misinformation Detection
summary: Video misinformation detection is often approached through global multimodal fusion or free-form multimodal reasoning. Both paradigms can under-represent localized authenticity cues that arise from coupled interactions among query phrases, contextual text, and short temporal spans of frames. Because such interactions are inherently higher-order, pairwise graph formulations are insufficient to capture multi-way cross-modal dependencies, whereas hypergraphs offer a suitable representation for these relations. We propose HyperClaim, a discriminative temporal hypergraph framework for sample-level authenticity classification. Using the title or benchmark-provided paired text as a claim-like query, HyperClaim constructs a sparse heterogeneous hypergraph over query tokens, evidence tokens, and sampled frames; applies confidence-aware filtering and source budgeting to form compact text-frame and short-range temporal evidence units; performs adaptive soft-incidence reasoning with residual text-video calibration; and aggregates textual, visual, and hyperedge states through a discrepancy-aware readout. Without relying on generated rationales or external tool calls, HyperClaim preserves fine-grained cross-modal and temporal structure that global fusion tends to flatten. Under the FactGuard temporal protocol, it achieves 83.7%, 82.0%, and 87.3% accuracy on FakeSV, FakeTT, and FakeVV, respectively, outperforming strong discriminative and reasoning-centric baselines. Learned incidence and attention weights further reveal token- and frame-level structure.

AI.tldr: HyperClaim: A temporal hypergraph framework for video misinformation detection that captures higher-order cross-modal interactions between query phrases, contextual text, and temporal video frames through sparse heterogeneous hypergraphs.
AI.motivation: Current video misinformation detection approaches (global multimodal fusion or free-form multimodal reasoning) often under-represent localized authenticity cues that arise from coupled interactions among query phrases, contextual text, and short temporal spans of frames. These interactions are inherently higher-order, requiring representations beyond pairwise graphs.
AI.method: HyperClaim constructs a sparse heterogeneous hypergraph over query tokens, evidence tokens, and sampled frames; applies confidence-aware filtering and source budgeting to form compact text-frame and short-range temporal evidence units; performs adaptive soft-incidence reasoning with residual text-video calibration; and aggregates textual, visual, and hyperedge states through a discrepancy-aware readout.
AI.result: Achieves 83.7%, 82.0%, and 87.3% accuracy on FakeSV, FakeTT, and FakeVV datasets respectively under the FactGuard temporal protocol, outperforming strong discriminative and reasoning-centric baselines. Learned incidence and attention weights reveal token- and frame-level structure.
AI.conclusion: HyperClaim provides an effective discriminative temporal hypergraph framework that preserves fine-grained cross-modal and temporal structure without relying on generated rationales or external tool calls, offering improved video misinformation detection by capturing higher-order localized authenticity cues.

title: LEDGERMIND: Provenance-Constrained Multimodal Agentic Reasoning with a Structured Evidence Ledger
summary: Multimodal agents for visual question answering increasingly operate as multi-step trajectories that interleave perception, retrieval, and reasoning, yet evaluation still largely reduces to final-answer accuracy. This aggregate signal cannot tell whether a correct answer was reached through grounded evidence, language priors, or accidental error cancellation.
